cards.title: The evolution of accounting is traditionally divided into three chronological…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition:
The evolution of accounting is traditionally divided into three chronological phases that reflect increasing sophistication in recording, verifying, and communicating financial information. Phase 1 – Primitive / Ancient Accounting (pre-15th century).
Early civilisations — Harappan, Mesopotamian, Egyptian, and Indian (Kautilya's Arthashastra, 4th century BCE) — used physical tokens, clay tablets, palm-leaf manuscripts, and single-entry registers. The purpose was stewardship: rulers and temple administrators needed to track grain, livestock, and tax revenue. Records were narrative, lacked a systematic dual-aspect principle, and were often kept by a single scribe. The test of a good record was simply "does the stock on hand match the register?" — there was no second column, no counter-check, and therefore no way to detect an arithmetic slip, a forgotten entry, or deliberate fraud. Phase 2 – Double-Entry Book-keeping (15th-19th century).
Luca Pacioli's Summa de Arithmetica (1494) codified the Venetian merchants' practice of recording each transaction in two accounts — debit and credit — ensuring the accounting equation (Assets = Liabilities + Capital) always balances. This innovation introduced the ledger, trial balance, and the concept of a complete accounting cycle: journalising, posting, balancing, and extracting a trial balance at period end. Verification became structural: because every entry appears twice, an imbalance in the trial balance signals an error somewhere in the books. In India, the British colonial administration adopted double-entry for railway, banking, and trading companies (e.g., the Bank of Bengal, 1806). Phase 3 – Modern / Computerised Accounting (20th century-present).
Mechanical calculators, then mainframes, and now cloud-based ERP (Tally, SAP, Zoho Books) automate the cycle. Regulatory frameworks — Companies Act 2013, SEBI LODR, GST Act 2017, and Ind-AS (converged with IFRS) — mandate uniform recognition, measurement, and disclosure. The focus shifts from mere recording to decision-useful information for diverse users: shareholders, creditors, tax authorities, and management. Software now embeds the accounting rules themselves: a voucher that violates the debit-credit pairing cannot even be saved, and tax fields (CGST/SGST/IGST) are computed at the point of entry. Together, the three phases show a trajectory from stewardship → accountability → decision-support, each building on the previous one's conceptual foundation.
steps: Accounting evolved through five distinct stages of increasing capability. 1.
The Granary Keeper (c. 3000 BCE): Stewardship is the primary objective of Phase 1.

cards.title: An event in accounting is any occurrence…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: An event in accounting is any occurrence, incident or happening that has a bearing on the financial position of an entity. It may be internal (e.g., depreciation charge, issue of shares) or external (e.g., sale of goods, purchase of machinery, fire loss). An event becomes a transaction only when it is measurable in monetary terms, involves a dual aspect (give‑and‑take), and is supported by a voucher. Events that cannot be quantified — such as the appointment of a director or a change in government policy — are noted in the minutes but do not enter the books. The distinction is crucial because the accounting cycle begins with identifying events, filtering them into transactions, recording them via vouchers, and finally summarising in financial statements. Thus, an event is the broadest trigger; a transaction is a qualified subset that satisfies the measurability and duality criteria.
steps: Every transaction is an event, but not every event is a transaction.
This distinction is the primary filter used to keep financial statements reliable and relevant.
Measurability: The event must be expressible in monetary units (Rupees).
Dual Aspect: The event must involve a give-and-take, affecting at least two accounts.
Evidence: The event must be supported by a voucher (e.g., cash memo, invoice, or report).
Relevance: Only events that change the financial position are recorded, excluding strategic or administrative happenings.

cards.title: A transaction in accounting is any event that involves a transfer of value…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: A transaction in accounting is any event that involves a transfer of value between two parties and can be measured reliably in monetary terms. It must satisfy three criteria: (1) it is a business activity, not a personal one; (2) it results in a change in the financial position — assets, liabilities, capital, revenue or expense — of the entity; and (3) it is evidenced by a source document (voucher) such as a cash memo, invoice, or bank pay‑in slip. Transactions are classified as cash (immediate settlement) or credit (settlement later), and as external (with outsiders) or internal (e.g., depreciation, inter‑department transfers). Every transaction obeys the dual‑aspect concept: it affects at least two accounts, keeping the accounting equation (Assets = Liabilities + Capital) in balance. The recording of a transaction is the first step of the accounting cycle and feeds directly into the preparation of vouchers (next node) and journal entries.

Step 1 – Recognise the event.

A customer walks in, picks a saree priced at ₹2,500, and pays by UPI. The moment the payment is confirmed, a business event has occurred.
Step 2 – Check the criteria.
Is it a business activity?
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “any event that involves money”) reveals the misconception that mere cash movement alone qualifies, ignoring the need for a business context and dual‑aspect impact.

cards.title: A voucher is a documentary evidence that authorises and records a financial…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: A voucher is a documentary evidence that authorises and records a financial transaction in the accounting system. It serves as the primary source document from which entries are made in the journal and subsequently posted to ledgers. Vouchers are classified by nature of transaction: cash vouchers (receipt and payment), bank vouchers (cheque deposit, electronic transfer), journal vouchers (non‑cash adjustments such as depreciation, provisions), and supporting vouchers (invoices, bills, challans, delivery notes). Each voucher contains essential elements — voucher number, date, parties involved, description of transaction, amount in figures and words, authorised signatures, and reference to supporting documents. Under the Companies Act, 2013 and GST law, businesses must retain vouchers for a minimum of eight years for audit and tax compliance. Vouchers link the event (economic occurrence) to the transaction (recordable exchange) and provide the audit trail that distinguishes accounting from mere bookkeeping. They also enable internal control: segregation of duties (preparer, authoriser, recorder) reduces fraud risk. In computerised accounting (e.g., Tally, SAP), vouchers are entered as voucher types (Receipt, Payment, Contra, Journal, Sales, Purchase) and the system auto‑generates the double‑entry effect.
steps: A voucher is the bridge that converts a business event into a recorded transaction, and every entry in the books must originate from a valid voucher.
Here is why: without a voucher there is no evidence, no authorisation, and no audit trail, making the accounts unreliable for owners, tax authorities, and lenders.
First, vouchers are classified by the cash flow they represent — cash receipt, cash payment, bank receipt, bank payment, contra (cash‑bank transfer), and journal (non‑cash adjustments).

Second, each voucher carries a unique serial number, date, parties, narration, amount in words and figures, and signatures of the preparer, authoriser, and receiver, satisfying the Companies Act, 2013 requirement for…
Third, supporting documents such as purchase invoices, sales bills, expense receipts, and bank challans are attached to the voucher, creating a complete trail from source to ledger.

Fourth, in a manual system the accountant writes the voucher, gets it approved, then posts the double entry; in Tally the user selects the voucher type (e.g., F5 for Payment) and the software automatically debits and…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “to calculate profit”) reveals the misconception that vouchers are a computational tool rather than a source document.

cards.title: In accounting, capital (also called owner’s equity) is the residual interest of…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: In accounting, capital (also called owner’s equity) is the residual interest of the owner in the assets of an enterprise after deducting all its liabilities. It represents the amount the proprietor has invested in the business plus any accumulated profits retained in the business, less any drawings made by the owner. Capital is a claim on the assets of the firm and appears on the liabilities side of the balance sheet under the heading “Owner’s Equity.” It changes with every transaction that affects the owner’s stake: additional capital introduced increases it; profits increase it; losses and drawings decrease it. The accounting equation Assets = Liabilities + Capital makes this relationship explicit. Capital is distinct from revenue (income earned from operations) and from liabilities (obligations to outsiders). In a sole proprietorship it is a single capital account; in a partnership each partner has a separate capital account; in a company it is represented by share capital and reserves. Understanding capital is essential for preparing the balance sheet and for analysing the financial position of the entity.
steps: Let’s walk through capital step by step, linking it to what you already know about vouchers and transactions. 1.
Start with the owner’s pocket.
When Ramesh decides to open a stationery shop in Delhi, he puts ₹1,00,000 cash into the business.
The cash receipt (a voucher) records this inflow.
In accounting terms, the business now has an asset (cash ₹1,00,000) and a claim by Ramesh of the same amount — that claim is capital. 2.
The accounting equation.

cards.title: An intangible asset is an identifiable non‑monetary asset without physical…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: An intangible asset is an identifiable non‑monetary asset without physical substance, held for use in the production or supply of goods or services, for rental to others, or for administrative purposes. Under the CISCE ISC Accounting syllabus (and consistent with Ind‑AS 38), an intangible asset must satisfy three criteria: (1) identifiability — it is separable (can be sold, transferred, licensed) or arises from contractual/legal rights; (2) control — the enterprise can obtain future economic benefits and restrict others’ access; (3) future economic benefits — it is expected to generate revenue or cost savings over more than one accounting period. Typical examples in Indian business include: - Goodwill (purchased, not internally generated) — the excess of purchase price over fair value of net identifiable assets in a business combination. - Patents, trademarks, copyrights, designs — legal rights granted by the Controller General of Patents, Designs & Trade Marks (CGPDTM). - Computer software (acquired or developed for internal use) — licences from vendors such as Tally, SAP, or custom‑built ERP modules. - Franchise agreements, licences, import quotas — contractual rights to operate under a brand (e.g., a McDonald’s franchise in Delhi). Intangible assets are initially measured at cost (purchase price plus directly attributable expenditure). After initial recognition, the entity chooses either the cost model (cost less accumulated amortisation and impairment) or the revaluation model (fair value less subsequent amortisation/impairment) — the latter only if an active market exists, which is rare for most intangibles. Amortisation is the systematic allocation of the depreciable amount over the asset’s useful life. The useful life is finite for most intangibles (e.g., a patent 20 years, software licence 5 years) and indefinite for goodwill and certain brands; indefinite‑life intangibles are not amortised but tested annually for impairment. Relationships with sibling concepts: - Tangible assets (node) have physical substance; intangible assets do not. - Fixed assets (node) include both tangible and intangible items held for long‑term use. - Current assets (node) are expected to be realised within 12 months; intangibles are usually non‑current unless they are held for sale. - Fictitious assets (node) such as preliminary expenses are not true assets; intangible assets are genuine resources.
steps: Intangible assets are valuable rights without physical form that a business controls to earn future income.
Here is why: 1.
Identifiability separates true intangibles from mere ideas.
A recipe written down and licensed is identifiable; a chef’s skill is not. 2.
Control means the firm can prevent others from using the asset.
A patent granted by the Indian Patent Office gives exclusive rights for 20 years. 3.

cards.title: Tangible assets are physical resources owned by an enterprise that have a…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Tangible assets are physical resources owned by an enterprise that have a material substance, can be perceived by the senses (seen, touched, or measured), and are used in the production or supply of goods and services, for rental to others, or for administrative purposes. They constitute a subclass of the broader asset category in the accounting equation (Assets = Liabilities + Capital). Tangible assets are further divided into fixed (non‑current) assets – long‑term items such as land, building, plant, machinery, furniture, and vehicles – and current assets – short‑term items expected to be converted into cash or consumed within one operating cycle, such as inventory (stock of raw materials, work‑in‑progress, finished goods), cash, and bank balances. Unlike intangible assets (covered in node), which lack physical substance (e.g., goodwill, patents, trademarks), tangible assets have a observable, measurable existence. Their valuation in the books is generally at historical cost less accumulated depreciation for fixed assets, and at cost or net realizable value for current assets. Understanding tangible assets is essential because they form the bulk of an enterprise’s investment, influence liquidity and solvency ratios, and directly affect profit through depreciation expense and cost of goods sold.
steps: Tangible assets are the physical, touchable resources a business owns — the building, the machines, the stock, the cash — and recognising them correctly is the first step toward accurate financial reporting.
Why does this matter?
Every resource that helps a business earn revenue must be recorded so stakeholders can assess the firm's financial health, and the recording rule depends on the asset's physical nature.
Recall that assets split into tangible and intangible groups; tangible assets are the "touchable" part of that definition.

Visit a small Indian textile mill in Surat: the factory building, the looms, the bales of cotton yarn, the finished cloth rolls, and the cash in the till all have physical presence — you can see, touch, weigh, or…
Recording follows three rules.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “An asset is tangible if it generates revenue”) reveals the misconception that tangibility is linked to earning capacity rather than physical form; many intangible assets (like patents) also generate revenue but lack physical substance.

cards.title: Fixed assets are tangible resources owned by an enterprise with a useful life…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Fixed assets are tangible resources owned by an enterprise with a useful life extending beyond one accounting period, held for use in production, supply of goods or services, or for administrative purposes, and not intended for sale in the ordinary course of business. They form a sub‑category of tangible assets (covered in node) and include land, buildings, plant and machinery, furniture, vehicles, and equipment. Key characteristics: (1) long‑term utility — typically more than one year; (2) physical substance — they can be seen and touched; (3) capitalisation — acquisition cost plus directly attributable costs (freight, installation, trial runs) are recorded as asset value; (4) depreciation — systematic allocation of cost over useful life, except land which is not depreciated; (5) presentation — shown in the balance sheet under “Property, Plant and Equipment” at net book value (cost less accumulated depreciation). Fixed assets differ from current assets (node) which are expected to be realised or consumed within the operating cycle. They also differ from intangible assets (node) which lack physical substance. The accounting equation (Assets = Liabilities + Capital) reflects fixed assets on the asset side, financed either by owner’s capital or borrowed funds. Proper classification ensures accurate financial reporting, tax compliance (e.g., depreciation under Income Tax Act, 1961), and aids users in assessing earning capacity and solvency.
steps: Fixed assets are tangible, long-term productive resources held for business operations rather than resale, whose total acquisition cost is capitalized and systematically depreciated over time.
First, fixed assets are a specific subset of tangible assets defined strictly by their long-term use across multiple accounting periods rather than immediate conversion into sales.
Second, capitalizing an asset requires accumulating every necessary expense—such as purchase price, non-creditable GST, freight, and installation wages—into its initial recorded cost.

Third, compliance with accounting standards (AS 10 / Ind AS 16) mandates charging annual depreciation to reflect the loss of usefulness over time, with land remaining the sole exception due to appreciation.
Fourth, these resources appear on the balance sheet under "Property, Plant and Equipment" per Schedule III, balanced directly against owner capital and liabilities.

cards.title: Current assets are resources owned by an enterprise that are expected to be…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Current assets are resources owned by an enterprise that are expected to be realised, sold, or consumed within the normal operating cycle (usually twelve months) or within one year from the reporting date, whichever is longer. They include cash and cash equivalents, bank balances, trade receivables (debtors), inventories (stock of raw materials, work‑in‑progress, finished goods), short‑term investments, prepaid expenses, and other assets held for short‑term conversion. In the balance sheet they appear under “Current Assets” and are crucial for assessing liquidity and working‑capital management. They differ from fixed assets (long‑term use) and from liquid assets (a subset that can be instantly converted to cash without loss of value). The classification follows the Accounting Standard (AS) 1 – Disclosure of Accounting Policies and the Companies Act, 2013 schedule III format.
steps: Current assets are defined by their short-term nature, specifically their expected conversion into cash within the operating cycle or one year.
This classification is essential for understanding a firm's liquidity and operational health.
Cash & Bank: These are the most liquid assets, representing immediate purchasing power.
Trade Receivables (Debtors): These represent credit sales that will be collected within the normal credit period, typically well under a year.
Inventory (Stock): Raw materials, work-in-progress, and finished goods are held for sale or production, making them inherently current.
Short‑term Investments: These are temporary placements of surplus cash, such as treasury bills, intended to be liquidated within a year.

cards.title: Liquid assets are a subset of current assets that are either cash itself or can…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Liquid assets are a subset of current assets that are either cash itself or can be converted into cash within a very short period (usually 90 days) with negligible risk of value loss. They include cash in hand, cash at bank, cheques received but not yet deposited, short‑term deposits maturing within three months, and highly marketable securities such as treasury bills or listed equity shares that can be sold on the stock exchange at prevailing prices. In the balance sheet they appear at the top of the current‑asset section, often grouped as “Cash and Cash Equivalents”. The distinction from other current assets (e.g., inventory, trade receivables) lies in immediacy of realisation and certainty of amount. Liquidity ratios such as the Current Ratio and Quick (Acid‑Test) Ratio use liquid assets to assess a firm’s ability to meet short‑term obligations. Under the Companies Act, 2013 and Ind‑AS 1, liquid assets must be disclosed separately to give users a clear view of short‑term solvency.
steps: Liquid assets are the most readily available resources a business can use to settle its immediate liabilities.
Here is why: first, liquidity is a spectrum; cash sits at the extreme end because it needs no conversion.
Second, bank balances and short‑term deposits are one step away — they are claimable on demand or at a known maturity date.
Third, marketable securities such as treasury bills or actively traded shares can be sold on a recognised exchange within days, and their quoted price gives a reliable estimate of realisable value.
Fourth, the accounting standards (Ind‑AS 1) require these items to be presented separately as “Cash and Cash Equivalents” so that users can quickly gauge short‑term solvency.
Fifth, the Quick Ratio (Liquid Assets ÷ Current Liabilities) strips out inventory and prepaid expenses, focusing purely on this liquid pool.

cards.title: A wasting asset is a tangible fixed asset that consists of a natural resource…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: A wasting asset is a tangible fixed asset that consists of a natural resource — minerals, oil, gas, timber, stone — which is physically extracted or harvested and therefore diminishes in quantity and value over time. Unlike ordinary fixed assets (plant, machinery, buildings) that wear out through use, wasting assets are depleted; the accounting process is called depletion rather than depreciation. The asset is initially recognised at historical cost (purchase price, exploration, development, and any directly attributable costs). Subsequently, the carrying amount is reduced by the cumulative depletion charge, which is calculated on a units‑of‑production basis: Depletion per unit = (Cost - Residual value)/(Estimated total recoverable units) The periodic depletion expense = depletion per unit × units extracted during the period. This expense is debited to the Profit & Loss Account (or Cost of Goods Sold for manufacturing entities) and credited to an Accumulated Depletion account, a contra‑asset shown under the wasting asset on the Balance Sheet. Wasting assets are presented under Fixed Assets – Tangible in the Balance Sheet, separate from other fixed assets such as land (non‑depletable) and intangible assets. They differ from current assets (stock, debtors) because they are not intended for sale in the ordinary course of business, and from liquid assets because they cannot be quickly converted to cash without extraction. They also differ from fictitious assets (e.g., preliminary expenses) which have no physical existence. The concept links to the accounting equation (Assets = Capital + Liabilities) because depletion reduces the asset side and, through the expense, reduces profit and therefore capital.
steps: Wasting assets are natural‑resource fixed assets whose cost is allocated over the units extracted, not over time.
Here is why: a mine or oil well loses value only when the resource is physically removed; the passage of calendar time alone does not reduce its economic benefit.
Therefore, the matching principle requires that the expense be matched to the quantity sold or used, leading to the units‑of‑production depletion method.
Consider a company, Vindhya Minerals Ltd., that acquires a limestone quarry for ₹12 crore.
Geological surveys estimate 60 lakh tonnes of extractable limestone.
The quarry has no residual value after exhaustion.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “wasting assets are intangible”) reveals the misconception that “wasting” refers to loss of value over time rather than physical exhaustion of a natural resource.

cards.title: Fictitious assets are deferred revenue expenditures that have no physical…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Fictitious assets are deferred revenue expenditures that have no physical existence, no realizable market value, and cannot be sold or converted into cash. They arise when a business incurs expenses that benefit multiple accounting periods — such as preliminary expenses (incorporation fees, legal charges), discount on issue of shares or debentures, underwriting commission, and the debit balance of the Profit & Loss Account. Unlike intangible assets (e.g., patents, goodwill) which may have realizable value, fictitious assets are purely notional; they are shown on the asset side of the Balance Sheet under the heading “Miscellaneous Expenditure (to the extent not written off)” and are systematically written off (amortized) over the periods they benefit. The write‑off is debited to the Profit & Loss Account (or Statement of Profit and Loss) each year, reducing the fictitious asset balance until it becomes zero. Their treatment follows the matching principle: expense is recognized in the same periods as the related revenue. They are distinct from wasting assets (natural resources) and liquid assets (cash equivalents) covered in earlier nodes.
steps: Fictitious assets are not real assets; they are deferred revenue expenditures that appear on the asset side only until fully written off. Here is why: 1.
No realizable value — they cannot be sold, pledged, or converted to cash; they merely represent future expense allocation. 2.
Arise from specific transactions — incorporation costs, share issue discount, underwriting fees, and accumulated losses are the classic Indian examples. 3.
Matching principle drives write‑off — each year a portion is charged to Profit & Loss, reducing the fictitious asset balance. 4.
Balance Sheet disclosure — shown under “Miscellaneous Expenditure (to the extent not written off)” on the asset side, separate from intangible assets. 5.

Distinct from intangible assets — intangibles like patents may have market value; fictitious assets never do. Consider a new Indian private limited company, GreenTech Pvt. Ltd., incorporated on 1 April 2024.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., selecting A) reveals the misconception that any intangible‑looking item is fictitious — confusing intangible assets (which may have market value) with fictitious assets (which never do).

cards.title: A liability is a present obligation of an entity arising from past events…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: A liability is a present obligation of an entity arising from past events, the settlement of which is expected to result in an outflow of resources embodying economic benefits. Under the CISCE ISC syllabus, liabilities are classified as non‑current (long‑term) — payable after 12 months (e.g., long‑term bank loans, debentures) — and current (short‑term) — payable within 12 months (e.g., trade payables, short‑term borrowings, outstanding expenses, provisions). They are recorded at the amount expected to be paid (historical cost) and appear on the liabilities side of the Balance Sheet. Liabilities interact with capital (owner’s claim) and assets (resources) through the accounting equation: Assets = Capital + Liabilities. An increase in liabilities (e.g., taking a loan) raises assets (cash) without affecting capital; repayment reduces both liabilities and assets. This node links to the earlier fictitious assets node because fictitious assets are written off against profits, indirectly affecting the liability side via retained earnings, and it precedes the debtors node where receivables are contrasted with payables.
steps: A liability is a financial obligation to an external party that must be settled through the transfer of assets or services. - Liabilities represent the "outsider's claim" on a firm's assets, distinct from the owner's…
They are categorized by time: current (due within 12 months) and non-current (due after 12 months).
Every liability transaction must maintain the balance of the accounting equation (Assets = Capital + Liabilities).
The classification is critical for liquidity analysis, as it dictates how a firm manages its short-term cash flow.
In the case of “Raghav Textiles,” a Delhi-based shop, buying cloth on credit for ₹2,00,000 creates a trade payable, which is a current liability because it is due within 90 days.
Taking a 5-year bank loan of ₹10,00,000 for machinery creates a non-current liability because the repayment period exceeds one year.

cards.title: A debtor (also called a trade receivable) is a person or entity that owes money…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: A debtor (also called a trade receivable) is a person or entity that owes money to the business for goods sold or services rendered on credit. In the accounting equation, debtors appear on the asset side under current assets because they are expected to be realised within the operating cycle (usually 12 months). The relationship with other basic terms is direct: a credit transaction creates a debtor; the supporting voucher (sales invoice) evidences the claim; the amount increases capital indirectly through revenue and profit when the sale is recognised. When the debtor pays, cash (or bank) increases and the debtor balance decreases. If the debtor fails to pay, the amount may be written off as a bad debt (an expense) reducing profit. Debtors are distinct from creditors (liabilities) and from stock (inventory). They are also separate from bills receivable, which are formal written promises (promissory notes) rather than open account balances. Proper monitoring of debtors through an aged receivables schedule helps manage liquidity and assess credit risk.
steps: A debtor is a current asset representing money owed to the business by customers who bought on credit.
Here is why: when a sale occurs on credit, the business delivers goods but does not receive cash immediately.
The customer’s obligation to pay is an economic resource controlled by the business, satisfying the definition of an asset.
Because the amount is expected to be collected within the normal operating cycle, it is classified as a current asset.
Consider a Delhi‑based wholesale cloth merchant, M/s Sharma Textiles.
On 1 April 2025 they sell ₹2,00,000 worth of fabric to Retailer Gupta on 30‑day credit.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “debtor is a liability because the business owes the customer”) reveals the misconception that any party involved in a transaction is a liability, confusing the direction of the obligation.

cards.title: A creditor is any individual, firm…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: A creditor is any individual, firm, or institution to whom a business owes money for goods supplied, services rendered, or loans taken on credit. In the accounting equation, creditors appear on the liabilities side as trade payables (for purchases of inventory or services) or other payables (for expenses, loans, etc.). They are the counter‑party to debtors (who owe the business). When a purchase is made on credit, the business debits the relevant asset or expense account and credits the creditor’s personal account, increasing the liability. Subsequent payments debit the creditor’s account, reducing the liability. Creditors are classified as current liabilities if payable within the operating cycle (usually 12 months) and as non‑current if the credit period extends beyond that. Proper tracking of each creditor’s balance ensures timely payment, maintains supplier goodwill, and supports accurate financial statements. The concept links directly to liabilities (node 013), debtors (node 014), and later to stock (node 016) because credit purchases increase inventory.
steps: A creditor is a specific type of liability representing a person or firm to whom the business owes money due to credit transactions.
This concept is essential for managing business obligations and maintaining supply chain relationships.
Creditors represent an obligation to pay, distinguishing them from debtors who owe the business money.
Credit purchases increase liabilities, while payments to creditors decrease them.
Classification depends on the credit period, with most trade payables falling under current liabilities.
Proper recording ensures accurate financial reporting and maintains supplier goodwill.

cards.title: In accounting, stock (or inventory) refers to tangible goods held by an…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: In accounting, stock (or inventory) refers to tangible goods held by an enterprise for sale in the ordinary course of business, in the process of production for such sale, or in the form of materials or supplies to be consumed in the production of goods or rendering of services. It is a current asset because it is expected to be converted into cash or consumed within one operating cycle (typically 12 months). Stock comprises three main categories: raw materials (basic inputs like cotton for a textile mill), work‑in‑progress (partially completed goods such as half‑stitched garments), and finished goods (ready‑to‑sell items like packaged tea). The valuation of stock follows the lower‑of‑cost‑or‑net‑realisable‑value principle (AS‑2/Ind AS‑2), ensuring that the carrying amount does not exceed the amount recoverable from its sale. Stock interacts directly with the accounting equation: an increase in stock raises assets (debit stock account) and, when purchased on credit, raises liabilities (credit creditors). When stock is sold, it moves out of the asset side (credit stock) and generates revenue (credit sales) while the cost of goods sold (debit cost of goods sold) reduces profit. Accurate stock records are essential for determining gross profit, assessing liquidity, and complying with GST reporting requirements in India.
steps: Stock is the bridge between purchasing and selling — it turns cash into goods and goods back into cash, and its value determines whether a business shows a true profit.
Here is why: first, stock represents resources that have been acquired but not yet turned into revenue; until sold, they sit on the balance sheet as a current asset.

Second, the classification into raw material, work‑in‑progress, and finished goods mirrors the production cycle of any Indian manufacturer — a sugar mill in Uttar Pradesh holds sugarcane (raw), syrup (WIP), and bagged…
Third, the accounting equation stays balanced because every purchase of stock either reduces cash (debit stock, credit cash) or creates a payable (debit stock, credit creditors).
Fourth, when a sale occurs, the stock leaves the asset side (credit stock) and the cost of that stock is matched against revenue (debit cost of goods sold), giving a realistic gross profit.

Fifth, the valuation rule — lower of cost or net realisable value — protects users from overstated assets; for instance, if a fashion retailer’s winter jackets cost ₹1,200 each but can now be sold only at ₹900 after…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “stock includes only finished goods ready for sale”) reveals the misconception that stock excludes inputs and partially completed items, ignoring the full production pipeline.

cards.title: Profit is the excess of total revenue over total expenses incurred during an…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Profit is the excess of total revenue over total expenses incurred during an accounting period. In the accounting equation (Assets = Liabilities + Capital), profit increases capital because retained earnings belong to the owner. It is classified as gross profit (sales less cost of goods sold), operating profit (gross profit less operating expenses), and net profit (operating profit less non‑operating expenses and taxes). Profit is a flow concept measured over a period, unlike assets or liabilities which are stock concepts at a point in time. It links directly to revenue (income from ordinary activities) and expense (costs incurred to earn revenue). A profit raises the owner’s equity, while a loss reduces it. The matching principle requires that expenses be recognised in the same period as the revenues they help generate, ensuring profit reflects true performance. Profit also serves as a basis for managerial decisions, dividend distribution, and tax computation under the Income Tax Act, 1961.

Step 1: Identify the period.
Accounting measures performance over a defined period, say 1 April 2025 to 31 March 2026.
Step 2: Record revenue.
The shop sells fabrics worth ₹12,00,000 during the year.
This is revenue (node – debtors may arise if sold on credit).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "profit equals cash received because cash is what matters") reveals the misconception that cash basis and accrual basis are the same, ignoring the matching principle that aligns expenses with the revenues they generate.

cards.title: In accounting, loss is the excess of expenses over revenues for a given period…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: In accounting, loss is the excess of expenses over revenues for a given period or from a specific transaction that does not arise in the ordinary course of business. It decreases the owner’s equity (capital) and is recorded on the debit side of the Profit and Loss Account. A loss differs from an expense because an expense is incurred to generate revenue (e.g., rent, wages), whereas a loss yields no revenue‑generating benefit (e.g., loss on sale of a fixed asset, fire damage, theft). It also differs from profit (node), which is the excess of revenue over expenses. In the accounting equation Assets = Liabilities + Capital, a loss reduces Capital, thereby disturbing the equality unless assets or liabilities adjust accordingly. Losses are classified as operating losses (from core activities) and non‑operating losses (from peripheral events). They are disclosed separately in the Statement of Profit and Loss to show their impact on profitability.
steps: Let’s connect loss to what you already know.
In the previous node we saw that profit increases capital because revenues exceed expenses.
A loss is the mirror image: expenses exceed revenues, so capital falls.
Think of a Delhi‑based trader, M/s Sharma Traders, who buys a second‑hand delivery van for ₹3,00,000.
After two years the van’s book value (cost less depreciation) is ₹1,80,000.
The trader sells it for ₹1,50,000.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “loss and expense are the same because both are debited”) reveals the misconception that debit nature equals identical classification — confusing the purpose (revenue generation vs. no benefit) with the recording side.

cards.title: Classification of accounts organises every financial transaction into distinct…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Classification of accounts organises every financial transaction into distinct categories so that recording, summarising, and reporting become systematic. The traditional (British) approach divides accounts into three groups: Personal Accounts (relating to persons, firms, institutions — e.g., Debtors, Creditors, Bank), Real Accounts (tangible and intangible assets — e.g., Machinery, Goodwill, Cash), and Nominal Accounts (expenses, losses, incomes, gains — e.g., Salaries, Rent, Sales). The modern (American) approach aligns with the accounting equation (Assets = Liabilities + Equity) and classifies accounts into five elements: Assets (resources owned), Liabilities (obligations owed), Equity (owner’s claim), Revenue (inflows from operations), and Expenses (outflows for operations). Both systems cover the same universe of accounts; the traditional method emphasises the nature of the counterparty, while the modern method emphasises the element of the financial statement. Understanding both enables a student to interpret Indian GAAP (which follows the modern classification) and legacy textbooks that still use traditional terminology. The classification directly feeds into the double‑entry system (next node) because the debit‑credit rules differ for each category.
steps: Let’s start with a familiar scene: a small kirana store in Mumbai.
The owner, Mrs. Patel, records every rupee that moves.
When she sells rice to Mr. Shah on credit, she notes “Mr.
Shah” — a person.
When she pays electricity bill, she notes “Electricity Expense” — a cost.
When she buys a new weighing scale, she notes “Weighing Scale” — a thing.

cards.title: The double‑entry system is the foundational accounting principle that every…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: The double‑entry system is the foundational accounting principle that every financial transaction affects at least two accounts in opposite directions, maintaining the accounting equation Assets = Liabilities + Capital. For each transaction, the total debits equal total credits. Debits increase assets and expenses, decrease liabilities, capital and revenue; credits do the reverse. This dual recording provides an internal check — if debits ≠ credits, an error exists. The system relies on the classification of accounts (traditional: personal, real, nominal; modern: assets, liabilities, equity, income, expense) to decide which account is debited and which credited. It underpins journalising, ledger posting, trial balance preparation and ultimately the financial statements. In Indian practice, GST‑related transactions (CGST, SGST, IGST) also follow double‑entry, ensuring input‑tax credits and output‑tax liabilities are recorded symmetrically.

Start with the Accounting Equation Assets = Liabilities + Capital.
When Sharma invests ₹5,00,000 cash, Cash (Asset) rises by ₹5,00,000 and Capital (Equity) rises by ₹5,00,000.
Both sides increase equally — the equation stays balanced. 2.
Identify the Two Accounts Every transaction touches at least two accounts. - Purchase goods on credit from Gupta Wholesale ₹1,20,000: Purchases (Expense) increases → debit.
Gupta Wholesale (Liability – Creditor) increases → credit. 3.

cards.title: The rules of journalizing are the systematic guidelines that translate a…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: The rules of journalizing are the systematic guidelines that translate a business transaction into a double‑entry journal entry. They derive from the account classification (traditional: Personal, Real, Nominal; modern: Assets, Liabilities, Capital, Revenue, Expenses) and the double‑entry principle that every debit has an equal credit. For each transaction the accountant: (1) identifies the two (or more) accounts affected, (2) determines the nature of each account per the chosen classification, (3) applies the debit/credit rule — debit the receiver, credit the giver for personal accounts; debit what comes in, credit what goes out for real accounts; debit expenses/losses, credit incomes/gains for nominal accounts — and (4) records the entry in the journal with date, narration, and amounts. These rules ensure uniformity, auditability, and the foundation for posting to ledgers, preparing trial balances, and later financial statements. They also govern compound entries (multiple debits/credits) and opening entries, linking directly to the next nodes on simple/compound entries and opening entries.
steps: The rules of journalizing provide the grammar for the language of accounting, ensuring that every transaction is recorded with a balanced debit and credit.
Spot the accounts: Identify the two or more accounts involved in a transaction.
For example, in “Sold goods for cash ₹5,000,” the accounts are Cash and Sales.
Classify each account: Determine the nature of the accounts.
Using the traditional approach, Cash is a Real account and Sales is a Nominal account.
Using the modern approach, Cash is an Asset and Sales is Revenue.

cards.title: A simple journal entry records a transaction that affects exactly two accounts…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: A simple journal entry records a transaction that affects exactly two accounts — one is debited and the other credited with an equal amount. It follows the double‑entry rule: every debit has a matching credit. A compound journal entry records a single transaction that involves three or more accounts. It may contain multiple debits, multiple credits, or a mix of both, but the sum of all debit amounts must equal the sum of all credit amounts. Compound entries are used when a transaction simultaneously impacts several heads, such as a purchase that includes trade discount, cash discount, and GST components, or a payment that settles rent, electricity, and salary together. The classification of accounts (traditional: personal, real, nominal; modern: assets, liabilities, equity, income, expenses) and the rules of journalising (debit the receiver, credit the giver; debit what comes in, credit what goes out; debit expenses/losses, credit incomes/gains) are applied to each account in the entry. Proper narration is written below the entry to explain the transaction. Simple entries are the building blocks; compound entries reduce the number of journal lines and keep the journal concise while preserving the accounting equation.
steps: The one thing to remember: A simple entry touches two accounts; a compound entry touches three or more, but in both cases total debits must equal total credits.
Here is why: the double‑entry system (node) demands that every transaction keeps the accounting equation in balance.
When only two accounts change, a single debit‑credit pair suffices — that is a simple entry.

When a single business event changes several accounts — for example, a customer pays ₹5,000 cash and ₹2,000 by cheque for a ₹7,000 sale — we could write two simple entries, but a compound entry records it in one line…
This saves space and shows the transaction’s unity.
Consider a purchase of goods worth ₹10,000 from M/s Verma Traders on credit, receiving a trade discount of 10 % and paying ₹500 as carriage inwards.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “compound entry because cheque involves bank and cash”) reveals the misconception that the payment instrument creates an extra account — confusing the medium of payment with a separate account.

cards.title: An opening entry is the initial journal entry passed at the commencement of a…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: An opening entry is the initial journal entry passed at the commencement of a new accounting period or when a new set of books is started. It brings forward the balances of all real, personal and nominal accounts from the previous period (or from the statement of affairs of a newly formed entity) into the current ledger. Under the double‑entry system, every asset account is debited, every liability account is credited, and the difference is credited to the Capital (or Owner’s Equity) account. The entry follows the modern classification: assets (current and non‑current), liabilities (current and non‑current), and equity. It ensures that the accounting equation Assets = Liabilities + Capital holds true from day one. The opening entry is posted to the ledger accounts, which then carry opening balances for subsequent transactions. It is distinct from a closing entry, which transfers nominal account balances to the Trading and Profit & Loss Account at period‑end. The opening entry also sets the stage for GST‑related ledgers (Input CGST, Output SGST, etc.) that will be introduced later in the chapter.
steps: The opening entry is the single journal entry that records every asset, liability and capital balance on the first day of a new accounting period, ensuring the accounting equation balances from the start.
Here is why: when a business begins a new set of books — whether at incorporation, at the start of a financial year, or after a change of ownership — the ledger is empty.
Without an opening entry, the first transaction would have no prior balances to interact with, and the trial balance would never agree.
The opening entry solves this by pulling the closing balances of the previous period (or the statement of affairs of a new firm) into the current ledger in one compound entry.
Consider a sole‑proprietorship “Mehta Traders” that starts its books on 1 April 2025.
Its statement of affairs shows: Cash ₹45,000;
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “To record the first sale of the business”) reveals the misconception that opening entry records a transaction rather than establishing opening balances.

cards.title: Input CGST (Central Goods and Services Tax) is the tax paid on purchases of…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Input CGST (Central Goods and Services Tax) is the tax paid on purchases of goods or services within the same state. It is debited to Input CGST Account (an asset) because it represents a claim against the government. Output CGST is the tax collected on intra‑state sales; it is credited to Output CGST Account (a liability) because the business holds it on behalf of the government. Both accounts are maintained separately from SGST and IGST. At the end of each tax period, the business sets off Input CGST against Output CGST: if Output CGST > Input CGST, the net amount is paid to the government; if Input CGST > Output CGST, the excess is carried forward as a credit. The journal entries follow the modern classification: purchases attract a debit to Purchases and a debit to Input CGST; sales attract a credit to Sales and a credit to Output CGST. These entries feed into the ledger, trial balance, and ultimately the GST return (GSTR‑1/GSTR‑3B). The concept links directly to the double‑entry system (node 002) and the rules of journalizing (node 003), and it precedes the study of SGST (node 007), IGST (node 008) and the set‑off mechanism (node 009).

Step 1 – Identify the transaction type.
When Sharma buys goods from a Delhi supplier, the invoice shows CGST @ 9% and SGST @ 9%.
Because the supply is intra‑state, CGST goes to the central government.

Step 2 – Apply the modern classification. - Purchases Account (Expense) – Debit - Input CGST Account (Asset) – Debit - Input SGST Account (Asset) – Debit (covered later) - Supplier / Bank Account – Credit Step 3 –…
Purchases A/c Dr. 10,000

cards.title: SGST (State Goods and Services Tax) is one of the three components of India’s…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: SGST (State Goods and Services Tax) is one of the three components of India’s dual GST structure, the others being CGST (Central GST) and IGST (Integrated GST). SGST is levied by a state government on intra‑state supplies of goods and services. When a transaction occurs wholly within a single state (e.g., a dealer in Karnataka selling to a buyer in Karnataka), the supplier charges SGST and CGST at equal rates prescribed by the GST Council. The SGST collected is deposited with the respective state’s treasury. Input SGST paid on purchases can be set off against output SGST on sales, and any excess can be carried forward or refunded as per the GST Act. SGST rates are notified under the respective State GST Acts (e.g., Maharashtra GST Act, 2017) and mirror the central rates to maintain uniformity. The concept links directly to the journal entries for “Output SGST” (credit) on sales and “Input SGST” (debit) on purchases, and to the ledger accounts “SGST Payable” and “SGST Receivable”. It also connects to the set‑off mechanism where SGST credit can first offset SGST liability, then IGST liability, but never CGST liability.
steps: SGST is the state‑level component of GST charged on every intra‑state supply of goods or services.

Here is why: the Constitution (101st Amendment) empowers both Centre and States to levy GST concurrently, so a sale within Maharashtra attracts both CGST (central) and SGST (state) at identical rates.
Consider a Mumbai‑based trader selling goods worth ₹50,000 to a buyer in Pune at 18% GST (9% CGST + 9% SGST).
The invoice shows ₹4,500 CGST and ₹4,500 SGST.
The trader debits the buyer’s account ₹59,000, credits Sales ₹50,000, credits Output CGST ₹4,500, and credits Output SGST ₹4,500.

When the same trader purchases raw material from a Nagpur supplier for ₹30,000 plus 18% GST, the purchase entry debits Purchases ₹30,000, debits Input CGST ₹2,700, debits Input SGST ₹2,700, and credits Supplier ₹35,400.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Central Government collects SGST”) reveals the misconception that all GST components go to the Centre, confusing SGST with CGST.

cards.title: IGST (Integrated Goods and Services Tax) is the component of GST levied on the…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: IGST (Integrated Goods and Services Tax) is the component of GST levied on the supply of goods or services in the course of inter‑state trade or commerce, as defined under Section 5 of the IGST Act, 2017. It replaces the earlier Central Sales Tax (CST) and ensures seamless credit flow across states. When a registered dealer in State A sells to a registered dealer in State B, the supplier charges IGST at the applicable rate (e.g., 18 %) on the transaction value. The supplier deposits the IGST with the Central Government. The recipient (buyer) claims the IGST paid as Input Tax Credit (ITC) against his own output IGST, CGST, or SGST liability, following the set‑off hierarchy prescribed in Section 49 of the CGST Act. IGST also applies to imports (treated as inter‑state supplies) and to supplies to/from Special Economic Zones (SEZs). The revenue collected as IGST is apportioned between the Centre and the destination state as per the GST Compensation Cess Act and the recommendations of the GST Council. In accounting, IGST is recorded in separate ledger accounts: “IGST Input” (debit for purchases) and “IGST Output” (credit for sales). The net IGST payable or refundable is determined after setting off eligible ITC, which is the focus of the next node (setting off).
steps: IGST is the single tax that applies whenever a supply crosses a state border, ensuring that the destination state ultimately receives its share of tax revenue.

Here is why: the Constitution (Article 269A) empowers Parliament to levy IGST on inter‑state trade, and the IGST Act operationalises this by making the supplier collect IGST from the buyer and remit it to the Centre.
Consider a Mumbai‑based wholesaler (Maharashtra) selling 100 units of notebooks @ ₹200 each to a retailer in Bengaluru (Karnataka).
The taxable value is ₹20,000.
At 12 % IGST, the tax is ₹2,400.
The wholesaler debits “Accounts Receivable – Bengaluru Retailer” ₹22,400, credits “Sales” ₹20,000 and credits “IGST Output” ₹2,400.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “CGST and SGST both apply”) reveals the misconception that inter‑state transactions are taxed like intra‑state ones, ignoring the constitutional provision for a single integrated tax.

cards.title: Setting off under GST is the statutory mechanism that allows a registered…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Setting off under GST is the statutory mechanism that allows a registered person to adjust the input tax credit (ITC) accumulated on inward supplies against the output tax liability arising on outward supplies. The CGST Act, 2017 prescribes a strict utilisation sequence: 1. IGST credit is first applied to discharge IGST liability, then CGST liability, and finally SGST/UTGST liability. 2. CGST credit can be used only for CGST liability and, after that, for IGST liability. 3. SGST/UTGST credit can be used only for SGST/UTGST liability and, thereafter, for IGST liability. Cross‑utilisation between CGST and SGST is prohibited. The set‑off is performed at the time of filing the monthly/quarterly return (GSTR‑3B) and determines the net cash payable. Proper set‑off ensures compliance, avoids interest on delayed payment, and optimises cash flow. This node focuses solely on the hierarchy and mechanics of set‑off; the actual journal entries for CGST, SGST, IGST are covered in sibling nodes‑008.
steps: Let’s walk through the set‑off process as a Class 11 student would encounter it in a typical Indian trading firm, “Sharma Electronics”, which buys and sells both within Maharashtra (intra‑state) and to Gujarat…
Step 1 – Identify the credits.
At month‑end Sharma Electronics has the following ITC balances in its electronic credit ledger: IGST ₹12,000, CGST ₹8,000, SGST ₹6,000.
These arose from purchase invoices where GST was paid.
Step 2 – Identify the liabilities.
The same month’s sales generate output tax: IGST ₹15,000 (inter‑state sales), CGST ₹5,000, SGST ₹5,000 (intra‑state sales).

cards.title: Ledger posting is the systematic transfer of debit and credit amounts from the…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Ledger posting is the systematic transfer of debit and credit amounts from the journal (or subsidiary books) to the respective ledger accounts. Each journal entry contains at least one debit and one credit; posting records the debit amount on the left (debit) side of the debited account and the credit amount on the right (credit) side of the credited account. The ledger account follows the T‑format (or three‑column format) showing Date, Particulars, Journal Folio (J.F.), and Amount. Posting maintains the double‑entry principle — every transaction affects two accounts equally — and creates a permanent, classified record that enables later balancing, trial balance preparation, and financial statement drafting. The process also includes writing the ledger folio number in the journal (J.F. column) and the journal folio number in the ledger (J.F. column) to provide a cross‑reference trail. Posting is performed chronologically, usually daily or weekly, and must respect the rules of debit and credit derived from the account classification (traditional: Personal, Real, Nominal; modern: Assets, Liabilities, Capital, Revenue, Expenses). Errors in posting — such as posting to the wrong side, wrong amount, or omitting an entry — distort the ledger and consequently the trial balance.

cards.title: Balancing is the process of determining the closing balance of a ledger account…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Balancing is the process of determining the closing balance of a ledger account at the end of an accounting period. After all journal entries have been posted (see node), each account contains a series of debit and credit entries. The accountant totals the debit column and the credit column separately. If total debits exceed total credits, the difference is a debit balance (common for assets and expenses); if total credits exceed total debits, the difference is a credit balance (common for liabilities, capital and revenues). The balancing figure is entered on the smaller‑side column as “Balance c/d” (carried down) and then brought down on the opposite side as “Balance b/d” (brought down) to start the next period. This ensures the double‑entry principle — total debits equal total credits — holds for every individual account, which later guarantees a correct trial balance.
steps: Balancing an account ensures that the net position of an asset, liability, or expense is accurately captured by equalizing the debit and credit columns.
This process provides the foundation for financial reporting and error detection.

Balancing forces the total of both sides of an account to match, maintaining the integrity of the double-entry system.
It identifies the net value (debit or credit balance) of an account, which is essential for preparing the trial balance.
It provides a clear, standardized record of the opening position for the subsequent accounting period.

cards.title: Adjusting entries are journal entries made at the end of an accounting period…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Adjusting entries are journal entries made at the end of an accounting period to update account balances before financial statements are prepared. They ensure that revenues and expenses are recognised in the period they relate to, following the accrual concept. Common adjustments include accrued incomes (income earned but not received), accrued expenses (expenses incurred but not paid), prepaid expenses (payments made in advance), unearned incomes (money received in advance), depreciation on fixed assets, and provisions for doubtful debts. Each adjustment follows the double‑entry rule: one account is debited and another credited, keeping the accounting equation balanced. Closing entries are made after adjusting entries to transfer the balances of temporary (nominal) accounts — revenues, expenses, gains, losses — to the Trading and Profit & Loss Account, and finally to the Capital Account (or Retained Earnings in a company). This resets nominal accounts to zero for the next period. The sequence is: (1) close revenue accounts by debiting them and crediting Trading/P&L; (2) close expense accounts by crediting them and debiting Trading/P&L; (3) transfer the net profit or loss to Capital. Adjusting and closing entries together convert the trial balance into an adjusted trial balance and then into the final accounts, ensuring compliance with the matching principle and the periodicity concept under the CISCE ISC syllabus.
steps: Adjusting and closing entries are the bridge between a raw trial balance and the final accounts that show a true and fair view of a business’s performance.
Here is why: without them, revenues and expenses would be recorded only when cash moves, violating the accrual concept that underpins the ISC Accounting curriculum.

On 28 March it receives a ₹12,000 advance for a service to be rendered in April.
The cash is recorded, but the revenue belongs to next year — an unearned income adjustment debits Sales (or Revenue) and credits Unearned Income.
Similarly, the firm owes ₹5,000 for March electricity not yet billed; an accrued expense entry debits Electricity Expense and credits Outstanding Expenses.

cards.title: A simple cash book is a sub‑division of the journal used exclusively for…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: A simple cash book is a sub‑division of the journal used exclusively for recording cash receipts and cash payments. It has a single amount column on each side: the debit (receipts) side records every inflow of cash such as cash sales, capital introduced, loans received, and sale of assets for cash; the credit (payments) side records every outflow such as cash purchases, expenses paid, drawings, and repayment of liabilities. Because every entry is posted directly from source documents (cash memos, receipts, vouchers) the simple cash book serves as a book of original entry (journal) and, by virtue of its ledger‑style format, also functions as the cash account in the ledger — no separate posting to a cash ledger account is required. The book is balanced periodically (daily, weekly, or monthly) by totalling both sides; the difference (debit total − credit total) gives the closing cash balance, which must agree with the physical cash count. The simple cash book follows the double‑entry rule: every cash transaction affects the cash book and a corresponding ledger account (e.g., Sales, Purchases, Expenses). It is the foundation for more complex cash books (double‑column, triple‑column) and for the petty cash book.
steps: The simple cash book is a specialized journal that streamlines accounting by replacing the general journal for all cash-only transactions. - It reduces the workload of the general journal by isolating cash movements.
It serves as a dual-purpose tool, acting as both the book of original entry and the ledger account for cash.
It ensures accuracy by requiring a periodic match between the calculated balance and physical cash.
It provides a clear, chronological audit trail through the use of voucher references.

cards.title: The triple‑column cash book is a subsidiary book that combines the functions of…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: The triple‑column cash book is a subsidiary book that combines the functions of a cash account, a bank account and a discount account in a single ledger‑format register. It contains three amount columns on each side: Cash, Bank and Discount Allowed on the debit (receipt) side; Cash, Bank and Discount Received on the credit (payment) side. All cash receipts and payments, cheque deposits and withdrawals, and trade discounts allowed to customers or received from suppliers are recorded chronologically. The book serves both as a journal (original entry) and as a ledger (posting reference), eliminating the need for separate cash and bank ledger accounts. Balancing is done column‑wise: each column’s closing balance equals opening balance plus total debits minus total credits. The cash and bank columns reflect actual liquidity, while the discount columns capture the financial impact of early‑payment incentives. This format is mandatory for businesses that maintain a bank current account and regularly grant or avail trade discounts, as prescribed in the ISC Accounting syllabus.
steps: The triple‑column cash book provides a unified view of liquidity and financial incentives by consolidating cash, bank, and discount records into a single register.
This structure eliminates the need for redundant ledger accounts, ensures chronological accuracy, simplifies the balancing process, and provides an immediate snapshot of business health.
Efficiency: By recording all three categories in one place, the accountant performs a single posting cycle to the ledger, significantly reducing the risk of clerical errors.
Clarity: The column-wise format allows for instant verification of cash and bank balances, which are essential for daily operational decisions.
Integration: The inclusion of discount columns ensures that early-payment incentives are tracked alongside the actual cash flow, maintaining a complete record of financial transactions.
Standardization: The use of the "C" notation for contra entries ensures that internal transfers between cash and bank are clearly identified and not double-counted in the ledger.

cards.title: A contra entry is a transaction recorded in a triple‑column cash book that…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: A contra entry is a transaction recorded in a triple‑column cash book that simultaneously affects the cash column and the bank column. It arises only when cash is deposited into the bank (debit bank, credit cash) or cash is withdrawn from the bank (debit cash, credit bank). Because the dual effect stays inside the cash book, the entry is flagged with the letter ‘C’ in the Ledger Folio (L.F.) column on both sides, signalling that the amount must not be posted again to the cash or bank ledger accounts. Contra entries do not involve any third party, discount, or revenue/expense — they are pure internal transfers of funds. They are distinct from regular receipts (e.g., cash sales) or payments (e.g., cash purchases) which affect only one column and require ledger posting. The concept builds on the triple‑column cash book structure (cash, bank, discount columns) and the double‑entry rule that every transaction has two aspects; here both aspects reside in the same book. Mastery of contra entries ensures the cash book remains a complete primary record and prevents double‑counting when the ledger is later prepared.

cards.title: The analytical petty cash book is a specialised subsidiary book used to record…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: The analytical petty cash book is a specialised subsidiary book used to record minor, repetitive cash payments (petty expenses) under distinct analytical columns such as Postage, Stationery, Conveyance, Refreshments, and Miscellaneous. Unlike a simple petty cash book that has only a single “Amount” column, the analytical version provides analysis columns for each expense head, enabling immediate classification and control. Each entry records the date, particulars, voucher number, and the amount in the relevant analysis column; a Total column captures the gross payment. The book is maintained by the petty cashier under the imprest system (covered in the next node) where a fixed float is reimbursed periodically. Posting from the analytical petty cash book is done by debiting each expense head with its column total and crediting the Petty Cash Account with the overall total. This structure links directly to the ledger (posting, balancing) and supports the preparation of the trial balance. It also connects to earlier concepts: the cash book (simple, triple column) and contra entries (reimbursement entries). The analytical petty cash book therefore serves as a bridge between day‑to‑day cash handling and formal ledger accounting, ensuring that small expenditures are not lost in aggregation.

cards.title: The imprest system is a petty-cash control technique where a fixed amount
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: The imprest system is a petty-cash control technique where a fixed amount (the imprest amount) is handed to the petty-cashier at the start of a period. During the period the cashier makes small payments (postage, conveyance, refreshments) and records each in an analytical petty-cash book with separate columns for each expense head. At the end of the period the cashier submits vouchers; the total of all payments is reimbursed from the main cash book, restoring the petty-cash float to the original imprest amount. Key relationships: - Imprest amount = Opening petty-cash balance = Closing petty-cash balance after reimbursement. - Reimbursement = Σ (all petty expenses incurred in the period). - The analytical columns allow direct posting to respective ledger accounts (e.g., Postage, Conveyance) without routing through the journal proper. - The system limits the cashier’s custody to a known maximum, simplifies internal audit, and eliminates the need for frequent balancing of the petty-cash ledger. It builds on the analytical petty-cash book (node) and precedes the study of sales/purchase day books (node).

cards.title: Sales Day Book (Sales Journal) and Purchases Day Book (Purchases Journal) are…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Sales Day Book (Sales Journal) and Purchases Day Book (Purchases Journal) are subsidiary books used to record only credit sales and credit purchases respectively. Each entry captures date, party name, invoice number, and amount (including GST components). They are books of original entry — transactions are first recorded here, then periodically (usually monthly) the column totals are posted to the Sales Account, Purchases Account, and the respective Debtors/Creditors ledger accounts. The day books eliminate repetitive journalising of similar transactions, reduce errors, and provide a ready list of trade receivables and payables. They relate to the Journal Proper (for non‑routine entries) and the Ledger (where posting occurs). Under the modern classification, Sales and Purchases are Revenue and Expense accounts; under the traditional approach they are Nominal accounts. GST columns (CGST, SGST, IGST) are shown separately to facilitate input‑tax credit claims.

cards.title: A Bank Reconciliation Statement (BRS) is a periodic schedule that reconciles…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: A Bank Reconciliation Statement (BRS) is a periodic schedule that reconciles the bank balance shown in an entity’s cash book with the balance shown in the bank’s pass book (or bank statement). The need arises because timing differences — such as unpresented cheques, uncredited deposits, bank charges, interest credited, and direct collections or payments by the bank — cause the two balances to diverge. The chapter covers four core sub‑topics: (1) Meaning and need — why reconciliation is essential for accurate financial reporting and internal control; (2) Preparation from cash book balance/overdraft or pass book balance — starting with one balance and adjusting for timing differences to arrive at the other; (3) Preparation from extracts of cash book and pass book — when only selected entries are provided, the student must identify missing items and construct the reconciliation; (4) Amended cash book method — adjusting the cash book for errors and omissions before preparing the BRS, ensuring the corrected cash book balance matches the pass book balance. Together these topics build the skill to produce a reliable cash position, a prerequisite for preparing final accounts and for audit compliance under the Companies Act, 2013 and RBI guidelines for banking transactions.

cards.title: A Bank Reconciliation Statement (BRS) is a periodic statement prepared by a…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: A Bank Reconciliation Statement (BRS) is a periodic statement prepared by a business to reconcile the balance shown in its Cash Book (bank column) with the balance shown in the Pass Book (bank statement) issued by the bank. The need arises because the two records are maintained independently: the business records transactions when it becomes aware of them, while the bank records them when they are processed. Differences occur due to timing gaps (cheques issued but not presented, cheques deposited but not credited), bank-initiated entries (interest credited, charges debited, direct debits/credits), and errors in either record. The BRS identifies each cause, adjusts the respective balance, and proves that the corrected balances are identical. It serves three core purposes: (1) detection of errors or fraud in either book, (2) assurance that the cash book reflects the true bank position for accurate financial statements, and (3) a control tool for management to monitor bank transactions. The statement can be prepared starting from either the Cash Book balance (debit/credit) or the Pass Book balance, and the method chosen determines whether items are added or subtracted. Understanding the meaning and need of BRS is foundational before learning the specific preparation techniques covered in subsequent nodes.

Second, the bank acts independently by crediting interest, debiting service charges, honouring standing instructions like EMIs, or receiving direct NEFT/RTGS deposits.
Third, recording errors creep in from wrong amounts or misposted accounts.
Fourth, ignoring these differences leaves a misleading Cash Book balance that distorts final accounts and cash flow planning.

cards.title: A Bank Reconciliation Statement (BRS) prepared from the cash book balance
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: A Bank Reconciliation Statement (BRS) prepared from the cash book balance (or overdraft) or the pass book balance is a systematic schedule that explains the differences between the two records on a given date. The cash book (maintained by the trader) records all receipts and payments as they occur, while the pass book (bank’s ledger) reflects the same transactions only when the bank processes them. Timing differences — such as cheques issued but not yet presented, cheques deposited but not yet credited, bank charges, interest credited, direct deposits by customers, and dishonoured cheques — cause the balances to diverge. The reconciliation starts with one balance (cash book or pass book), then adjusts for each reconciling item: items that increase the bank balance (e.g., cheques deposited but not cleared, interest credited) are added; items that decrease it (e.g., cheques issued but not presented, bank charges, dishonoured cheques) are subtracted. The final adjusted figure must equal the other book’s balance. This process verifies the accuracy of both records, detects errors or fraud, and ensures the cash book is updated for items known only through the pass book (later done in the amended cash book method). The statement can be prepared in two formats: “Starting with Cash Book Balance” or “Starting with Pass Book Balance”, both yielding the same reconciled amount.

cards.title: Preparation from extract of cash book and pass book is the process of…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Preparation from extract of cash book and pass book is the process of reconciling the bank balance shown in the entity’s cash book (bank column) with the balance shown in the bank’s pass book (or bank statement) when only selected pages or extracts of both records are available. The method involves: (1) obtaining the opening balances from both extracts; (2) comparing each transaction — deposits, withdrawals, bank charges, interest, direct debits, standing instructions, dishonoured cheques — appearing in either extract; (3) ticking off items that appear in both records (these are already correctly recorded); (4) listing unticked items as reconciling items under two heads — “Add” (items credited by bank but not entered in cash book, e.g., interest credited, direct deposits) and “Less” (items debited by bank but not entered in cash book, e.g., bank charges, dishonoured cheques) when starting from cash book balance, or the reverse when starting from pass book balance; (5) arriving at the adjusted balance which must be identical whether derived from cash book or pass book. This technique is essential when the full ledger is not maintained or when only periodic statements are received, and it forms the basis for the amended cash book method taught later.

cards.title: The amended cash book method is a systematic approach to preparing a Bank…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: The amended cash book method is a systematic approach to preparing a Bank Reconciliation Statement (BRS) where the cash book is first updated for all errors, omissions, and direct bank transactions (interest, charges, direct deposits, dishonoured cheques) that have been recorded by the bank but not yet entered in the cash book. After these adjustments, the amended cash book balance becomes the starting point for the BRS. Only timing differences — cheques issued but not presented, cheques deposited but not credited, and any other items causing a lag between the two records — are then shown in the reconciliation statement. This method ensures the cash book reflects the true bank balance as per the entity’s books, and the BRS merely explains the residual gap due to uncleared items. It links directly to the earlier concepts of “preparation from cash book balance/overdraft” and “preparation from extracts” by providing a cleaner, more accurate base balance before reconciliation.
