cards.title: The “books of drawer” refer to the accounting records maintained by the party…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: The “books of drawer” refer to the accounting records maintained by the party who draws (issues) a bill of exchange. As the drawer, you initially record the bill as a Bill Receivable (asset) when it is accepted by the drawee. Subsequent events — discounting the bill with a bank, dishonour on due date, payment of noting charges by the drawer, renewal of the bill with fresh terms, retirement before due date, or partial/full loss due to drawee’s insolvency — each require specific journal entries in the drawer’s books. The drawer’s ledger tracks the Bill Receivable account, Bank account, Discount account, Drawee’s personal account, Noting Charges account, and Bad Debts account. The relationship between these sub‑concepts is sequential: a bill originates → may be discounted → may be dishonoured → noting charges incurred → may be renewed or retired → finally settled or written off. Mastery of this node means being able to pass correct journal entries and prepare ledger accounts for every possible lifecycle event of a bill from the drawer’s perspective, using the terms defined in sibling nodes (discounting, dishonour, noting charges, renewal, retirement, insolvency).
steps: Let’s walk through a typical bill lifecycle from the drawer’s desk. 1.
Drawing & Acceptance – You sell goods worth ₹50,000 to Raj Traders (drawee) and draw a 3‑month bill.
On acceptance, debit Bill Receivable A/c ₹50,000 and credit Raj Traders A/c ₹50,000. 2.
Discounting – You need cash, so you discount the bill at 12% p.a. with your bank 30 days before due date.
Debit Bank A/c ₹49,507, debit Discount A/c ₹493, credit Bill Receivable A/c ₹50,000. 3.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “no discount because the bill is not yet due”) reveals the misconception that discounting does not create an expense — confusing discounting with mere early collection.
remember: A student records the discounting of a ₹60,000 bill at 10% p.a. for 45 days as: Debit Bank….
When a discounted bill is dishonoured, the drawer debits the drawee’s account with the bill amount….
A bill of ₹30,000 is renewed for a further 3 months at 12% p.a. interest. The student calculates interest as ₹30,000 × 12% × 3 = ₹10,800. Evaluate this calculation.

cards.title: A drawee is the person on whom a bill of exchange is drawn and who is requested…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: A drawee is the person on whom a bill of exchange is drawn and who is requested to pay the amount stated therein. Under the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, the drawee becomes an acceptor only after signing the bill, thereby acknowledging the obligation to pay the payee (or any subsequent holder) on the due date. The drawee’s primary liability arises upon acceptance; before acceptance the drawee has no legal duty to pay. The drawee may be a trader, a company, or any legal entity capable of contracting. In the books of the drawee, acceptance creates a Bills Payable liability (a current liability) and the subsequent payment, dishonour, or retirement of the bill is recorded through appropriate journal entries. The drawee’s role is distinct from the drawer (who issues the bill), the payee (who receives payment), and the endorser (who transfers the bill). The drawee’s acceptance also triggers the calculation of days of grace and the due date, which are covered in separate nodes.
steps: Let’s walk through the life of a bill from the drawee’s perspective.
Suppose M/s Sharma Traders (drawer) sells goods worth ₹50,000 to M/s Gupta Enterprises (drawee) on credit.
To formalise the credit, Sharma draws a bill of exchange on Gupta for ₹50,000 payable 3 months after date.
The bill is sent to Gupta for acceptance.
When Gupta signs the bill (writes “Accepted” with date and signature), Gupta becomes the acceptor — the drawee who has now accepted the obligation.

This acceptance is the crucial moment: Gupta’s liability crystallises and a Bills Payable account is credited in Gupta’s books, while Purchases or Sharma Traders account is debited (depending on whether the bill was for…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the drawee is liable from the date of drawing”) reveals the misconception that drawing the bill creates an obligation for the drawee — confusing the drawer’s instruction with the drawee’s…
remember: What is the legal status of a drawee before he accepts a bill of exchange.
Explain why the drawee’s acceptance converts a bill of exchange into a negotiable instrument enforceable against the drawee.
Evaluate the statement: “The drawee can avoid liability by simply not presenting the bill for payment on the due date.”.

cards.title: An endorsee is the person in whose favour a bill of exchange…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: An endorsee is the person in whose favour a bill of exchange, promissory note or cheque is transferred by endorsement. Under the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (Sections 15‑19), endorsement is the signing of the instrument on its back or on an attached slip with the intention of transferring the right to receive payment. The endorsee acquires all the rights of a holder in due course provided the endorsement is regular, the instrument is not overdue, and the endorsee takes it in good faith and for value. The endorsee can further negotiate the instrument by another endorsement, present it for payment on the due date, and, if dishonoured, sue the drawer, the drawee and any prior endorsers. In the books of the endorsee, the instrument is recorded as a Bill Receivable (asset) at its face value; any discounting or endorsement charges are recognised as finance cost. The endorsee’s ledger reflects the receipt of the bill, subsequent endorsement (if any), discounting with a bank, and final realisation or dishonour with noting charges.
steps: The endorsee is the new holder who steps into the shoes of the payee once a bill is endorsed, gaining the right to demand payment from the drawee and to further negotiate the instrument.
Here is why: a bill of exchange is a negotiable instrument; its ownership transfers by endorsement, not by mere delivery.
The endorsee’s rights are protected under the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, provided the endorsement is regular and the endorsee takes the bill in good faith, for value, and before maturity.
Consider a typical trade cycle: M/s Sharma & Co. (drawer) draws a 90‑day bill on M/s Verma Ltd. (drawee) payable to M/s Gupta Traders (payee).
Gupta Traders endorses the bill to M/s Khan Enterprises (endorsee) to settle a purchase.
Khan Enterprises records the bill as a Bill Receivable (debit) and credits Gupta Traders (creditor).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “blank endorsement restricts further negotiation”) reveals the misconception that a blank endorsement limits transferability, confusing it with a restrictive endorsement.
remember: What is the legal effect of a blank endorsement on a bill of exchange.
Explain why an endorsee who receives a bill after its due date cannot become a holder in due course.
Evaluate the statement: “A restrictive endorsement ‘Pay to A only’ makes A a holder in due course for all subsequent transferees.”.

cards.title: The going concern concept is a fundamental GAAP assumption that an entity will…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: The going concern concept is a fundamental GAAP assumption that an entity will continue its operations for the foreseeable future, typically at least twelve months from the reporting date, without the intention or necessity of liquidation. Under this assumption, assets are recorded at historical cost and depreciated over their useful lives, liabilities are measured at settlement amounts, and revenue and expenses are recognised on an accrual basis. If the going concern assumption were not appropriate, assets would be re‑measured at net realisable value, liabilities at immediate settlement amounts, and the financial statements would require a “break‑up” basis of preparation. The concept interlinks with accrual (revenues/expenses matched to periods), historical cost (cost basis persists), and materiality (only significant doubts about continuity are disclosed). Management must assess going concern each reporting period; if substantial doubt exists, IAS 1 / Ind‑AS 1 requires explicit disclosure of the uncertainties and the basis of preparation.
steps: The going concern assumption means a business is presumed to operate indefinitely unless evidence shows otherwise.
Here is why: it allows accountants to use historical cost for assets, spread costs over useful lives through depreciation, and match revenues with expenses in the same period.
First, the assumption underpins the accrual basis — revenue is recognised when earned, not when cash is received, because the entity will be around to collect.

Second, it justifies depreciation; a machine bought for ₹5 lakh is not written off immediately but allocated over its 10‑year life, reflecting ongoing use. Third, it affects liability measurement; a loan due in five…
Consider a textile firm in Surat that has a temporary cash crunch but secured a new export order.
The auditor evaluates the order, cash‑flow forecasts, and management plans; finding no substantial doubt, the firm continues on a going concern basis.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the business will never make a loss”) reveals the misconception that going concern equals profitability rather than continuity of operations.
remember: State the going concern assumption in one sentence.
Explain why depreciation is justified only under the going concern assumption.
A company has incurred losses for three consecutive years but has a confirmed line of credit from a bank for the next two….

cards.title: The entity concept (also called the business entity principle) states that a…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: The entity concept (also called the business entity principle) states that a business enterprise is an accounting unit distinct from its owners, managers, and other entities. All financial transactions are recorded from the viewpoint of the business itself. Consequently, the assets, liabilities, revenues, and expenses of the business are separated from the personal assets, liabilities, income, and expenses of the proprietor(s) or shareholders. This principle applies to every form of organisation — sole proprietorship, partnership, Hindu Undivided Family (HUF), private limited company, public limited company, or LLP — and is the foundation for preparing a true and fair view of the entity’s financial position. It interacts with the going concern concept because the entity is assumed to continue indefinitely, and with the money measurement concept because only transactions expressible in monetary terms are recorded for the entity. The entity concept also underpins the dual aspect principle by ensuring that every transaction affects the entity’s own accounting equation (Assets = Liabilities + Capital) and not the owner’s personal equation.
steps: The entity concept ensures that a business’s financial performance is measured accurately by isolating it from the owner’s personal financial affairs.
This separation is essential for maintaining objective records, ensuring legal compliance, and providing reliable data for stakeholders.
The business is treated as a distinct accounting unit, regardless of its legal structure.
Personal transactions of the owner are excluded from business books to prevent the distortion of profit and asset values.

Capital is viewed as a liability the business owes to the owner, reflecting the separation between the two. Auditors use this principle as a primary filter to verify that only business-related expenses are recorded.
In a sole proprietorship like Mr. Sharma’s kirana store, an investment of ₹50,000 creates a business asset (cash) and a corresponding liability (capital).
remember: State the entity concept in one sentence and give a one-line reason why it is necessary for financial reporting.
Mr. Verma, a sole proprietor, pays his home electricity bill of ₹3,200 from the business cash box. Identify the correct accounting treatment and justify it using the entity….
A partnership firm “Rohan & Co.” purchases a delivery van for….

cards.title: The money measurement concept (also called monetary unit assumption) states…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: The money measurement concept (also called monetary unit assumption) states that only transactions and events that can be expressed in terms of money are recorded in the books of accounts. It requires a stable monetary unit — in India, the Indian Rupee (₹) — as the common denominator for measuring diverse economic resources and obligations. This concept underpins the entity concept by providing a uniform scale for the separate entity’s assets, liabilities, income, and expenses. It also links to the historical cost concept because the monetary amount recorded is the acquisition cost at the transaction date. The concept assumes the purchasing power of money remains relatively stable over the accounting period; however, it does not adjust for inflation, a limitation addressed later by accounting standards (e.g., Ind AS 29 for hyperinflation). Non‑monetary items such as employee skills, brand reputation, or market conditions are excluded unless they can be reliably quantified in monetary terms (e.g., purchased goodwill). The concept ensures objectivity, verifiability, and comparability across periods and entities, forming a foundation for the dual aspect concept where every transaction affects at least two accounts measured in the same monetary unit.
steps: The money measurement concept insists that accounting records only those facts that can be expressed in a common monetary unit, the Indian Rupee.
Here is why: without a single measuring rod, we cannot add a building, a fleet of trucks, and a patent together to show total assets.
First, the concept provides objectivity — a ₹10,000 cash sale is verifiable by a GST invoice, whereas “customer satisfaction” is subjective.
Second, it enables comparability — a textile mill in Surat and a software firm in Bengaluru both report revenue in ₹, allowing investors to compare performance.
Third, it supports the dual aspect — every debit has a matching credit measured in the same rupee, keeping the accounting equation balanced.
Fourth, it links to historical cost — the rupee amount recorded is the actual cash or cash equivalent paid at acquisition, not a current market estimate.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “all four are recorded because they affect the business”) reveals the misconception that any business event, regardless of measurability, must be accounted for — confusing economic relevance with accounting recognition criteria.
remember: Which of the following items would be recorded in the books of accounts under the money measurement….
A firm receives a donation of 100 square metres of land from a local….
Critically evaluate the statement: “The money measurement concept makes financial statements immune to the effects of inflation.”.

cards.title: The accounting period concept (also called periodicity concept) states that the…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: The accounting period concept (also called periodicity concept) states that the continuous life of an enterprise must be divided into regular, equal intervals — typically twelve months — so that financial performance and financial position can be measured, recorded, and reported at consistent points in time. In India the statutory financial year runs from 1 April to 31 March under the Income‑Tax Act, 1961, and the Companies Act, 2013, making this the default accounting period for most entities. The concept links directly to the accrual basis (node 009) and the matching concept (node 007): revenues and expenses are recognised in the period to which they relate, not when cash moves. It also underpins the disclosure concept (node 005) because users need comparable, periodic information. Without a defined period, profit could not be ascertained, trends could not be analysed, and legal filing deadlines could not be met. The period may be a calendar year (Jan‑Dec) for some partnerships or LLPs, but any change requires disclosure and justification under Accounting Standard 1 (Disclosure of Accounting Policies). The concept applies to all entities — sole proprietorships, partnerships, companies, and not‑for‑profits — and is a fundamental assumption in both Indian GAAP and IFRS.
steps: The accounting period concept requires that the life of a business be divided into regular, equal intervals so that financial performance and position can be measured and reported at consistent points in time.
Here is why: first, without a fixed period there would be no common basis to compare this year’s profit with last year’s, making trend analysis impossible for investors and lenders.
Second, Indian law (Companies Act, 2013;
Income‑Tax Act, 1961) mandates annual filing of financial statements and tax returns for the financial year 1 April–31 March, so the period is a legal necessity.

Third, the accrual concept (node 009) and matching concept (node 007) only work when revenues and expenses are assigned to a specific period; otherwise, a sale in March could be matched with an expense in May…
Consider a startup incorporated on 15 September 2023.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “January to December”) reveals the misconception that the calendar year is universally used, ignoring the statutory financial year that governs corporate reporting and tax compliance in India.
remember: What is the standard length of an accounting period for most Indian companies and which months does it cover.
Why must a business adopt a fixed accounting period instead of preparing statements whenever the owner wishes.
A firm prepares interim financial statements every six months but files its annual tax return for the April‑March….

cards.title: The disclosure concept requires that financial statements provide all material…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: The disclosure concept requires that financial statements provide all material information necessary for users to make informed economic decisions. Under the Companies Act 2013, Ind AS 1 (Presentation of Financial Statements) and SEBI (LODR) Regulations, an entity must disclose: (a) accounting policies adopted; (b) changes in those policies with reasons and financial impact; (c) contingent liabilities and commitments; (d) related‑party transactions; (e) events after the reporting period that affect the financial position; and (f) any other information required by specific standards. Disclosure is not limited to the face of the statements; notes to accounts, supplementary schedules, and management commentary also serve this purpose. The concept links closely with materiality (only material items need disclosure) and consistency (changes must be explained). It ensures transparency, reduces information asymmetry, and supports the reliability of the financial reports prepared for each accounting period.
steps: The disclosure concept is the “show your cards” rule: every material fact that could influence a user’s decision must appear in the financial statements or their notes.

Here is why: first, users such as shareholders, lenders, and regulators rely on complete information to assess risk and return; hiding a pending lawsuit or a major related‑party deal would mislead them.

Second, the law mandates specific disclosures — Schedule III of the Companies Act 2013 prescribes the format of the balance sheet and profit‑and‑loss statement, while Ind AS 1 requires a statement of accounting policies…
Third, materiality filters the volume: only items that could change a decision need disclosure, preventing clutter.
Fourth, consistency demands that any change in accounting policy be disclosed with its quantitative effect, so comparability across periods is preserved.

Fifth, events after the reporting period (e.g., a fire destroying inventory) must be disclosed if they indicate conditions that existed at the period end. Consider a Mumbai‑based textile firm that changes its inventory…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “to minimise tax liability”) reveals the misconception that disclosure serves the preparer’s interest rather than the user’s need for transparency.
remember: What is the primary objective of the disclosure concept in accounting.
Why must a contingent liability be disclosed even though it is not recognised as a liability on the balance sheet.
Evaluate the impact on stakeholders if a company fails to disclose a change in its revenue recognition policy from point‑in‑time to over‑time.

cards.title: Revenue recognition is the GAAP principle that determines the specific…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Revenue recognition is the GAAP principle that determines the specific conditions under which income becomes realized as revenue. Under Ind AS 115 (aligned with IFRS 15), revenue is recognized when control of promised goods or services transfers to the customer, at an amount that reflects the consideration the entity expects to be entitled to. The standard prescribes a five‑step model: (1) identify the contract, (2) identify performance obligations, (3) determine the transaction price, (4) allocate the price to each obligation, and (5) recognize revenue when (or as) each obligation is satisfied. This principle interacts directly with the accrual basis (node 009) — revenue is recorded in the period the economic activity occurs, not when cash flows. It also underpins the matching principle (node 007) because expenses incurred to generate that revenue must be reported in the same period. Disclosure requirements (node 005) mandate that entities describe their revenue recognition policies, significant judgments, and the disaggregation of revenue streams. In the Indian context, the Companies Act 2013 and SEBI (LODR) Regulations require compliance with Ind AS 115 for listed companies, while GST law expects the time of supply to align with the transfer of control, reinforcing the same timing concept.
steps: Revenue is recognized when control of goods or services transfers to the customer, not merely when cash is received.
Here is why: (1) The principle ensures that profit reflects the economic activity of the period, aligning with the accounting period concept.
(2) It operationalises the accrual basis — transactions are recorded when they occur, not when cash moves.

(3) Ind AS 115’s five‑step model provides a structured framework: identify the contract, separate performance obligations, set the transaction price, allocate that price, and recognize revenue as obligations are…
(4) Reliable measurement and probable inflow are prerequisites; if either is missing, recognition is deferred.
(5) The timing directly affects reported profit, tax liability under GST, and compliance with SEBI disclosure norms.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Revenue is recognized when cash is received”) reveals the misconception that cash receipt equals earning — confusing cash‑basis with accrual‑basis accounting.
remember: State the core principle of revenue recognition under Ind AS 115.
A company delivers goods on 31 March but receives payment on 15 April. Under accrual basis, in which period should revenue be recognized? Justify.
Critique the practice of recognizing revenue at the time of invoicing rather than at delivery for a manufacturing firm.

cards.title: The matching principle (also called the expense recognition principle) requires…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: The matching principle (also called the expense recognition principle) requires that expenses be recognised in the same accounting period as the revenues they help to generate. It is a cornerstone of accrual accounting and works hand‑in‑hand with the revenue recognition concept (node): revenue is recorded when earned, and the costs incurred to earn that revenue — whether paid, payable, or prepaid — are recorded in that same period. This ensures that the profit or loss for a period reflects the true economic performance, not merely cash flows. The principle applies to direct costs (cost of goods sold), indirect costs (depreciation, amortisation, accrued wages), and prepaid expenses (rent, insurance) which are allocated systematically over the periods benefitted. It also underpins the accrual concept (node) and the accounting period concept (node) by forcing periodic allocation of costs.
steps: Let’s walk through the matching principle as if you are the accountant of “Mohan Textiles Pvt. Ltd.”, a small fabric manufacturer in Surat. 1.
Revenue first – In March the firm sells ₹5,00,000 worth of cotton fabric on credit.
Under revenue recognition (node) you record ₹5,00,000 as sales revenue in March, even though cash arrives in April. 2.

Identify costs that earned that revenue – To produce the fabric you used raw cotton purchased in February (₹2,00,000), paid wages for March (₹80,000), and the factory’s depreciation for March (₹30,000).
All three costs directly helped generate the March sales. 3.
Match them in the same period – You record the raw‑material cost as Cost of Goods Sold in March, the wages as Wages Expense in March, and depreciation as Depreciation Expense in March.
remember: State the matching principle in one sentence and name the two other GAAP concepts it directly relies on.
A firm pays ₹60,000 on 1 April 2025 for a one‑year fire‑insurance policy covering 1 April 2025 – 31 March….
Critically evaluate: “If a company follows the matching principle, its net profit will always equal the cash generated from operations.”.

cards.title: The historical cost principle is a fundamental GAAP concept requiring that…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: The historical cost principle is a fundamental GAAP concept requiring that assets, liabilities and equity transactions be recorded at their original acquisition cost — the cash or cash‑equivalent amount paid at the time of the transaction. It provides an objective, verifiable basis for measurement because the purchase invoice, contract or bank receipt serves as documentary evidence. Under this principle, subsequent changes in market value, inflation or technological obsolescence are ignored until a transaction (such as sale, impairment or revaluation under a permitted model) occurs. Historical cost links closely with the matching concept because depreciation allocates the original cost over the asset’s useful life, and with prudence because it avoids recognising unrealised gains. It also supports the entity concept by keeping the business’s records separate from owners’ personal valuations. While Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS) allow fair‑value measurement for certain financial instruments and investment property, the default for property, plant and equipment (PPE) and inventories remains historical cost unless a revaluation model is adopted. The principle ensures comparability across periods and entities, as all firms use the same entry‑point — the actual price paid — rather than subjective current‑value estimates.
steps: Historical cost provides a reliable, verifiable foundation for financial reporting by recording assets at their actual acquisition price rather than fluctuating market estimates.

This principle ensures that financial statements remain objective, prevents the recognition of unrealised gains, facilitates consistent depreciation, and allows for meaningful comparisons between different businesses.
The historical cost principle is essential for three primary reasons:
Objectivity: It relies on documented evidence like invoices and bank receipts, removing management bias.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “assets are recorded at current market value supported by a valuation report”) reveals the misconception that accounting uses fair value by default, confusing historical cost with revaluation models.
remember: State the historical cost principle in one sentence and name the source document that typically supports the recorded amount.
A firm purchases a delivery van for ₹6,00,000, paying ₹5,50,000 by bank transfer and ₹50,000 by….
Evaluate the statement: “Historical cost makes financial statements irrelevant during high inflation because the carrying amounts become outdated.” Provide two arguments for and….

cards.title: The accrual concept requires that revenues be recognised when they are earned…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: The accrual concept requires that revenues be recognised when they are earned (i.e., goods delivered or services rendered) and expenses be recognised when they are incurred (i.e., benefit received), irrespective of the timing of cash receipts or payments. It is a cornerstone of GAAP and underpins the matching principle and the accounting period concept. Accrual creates two key adjusting entries at period‑end: accrued revenues (assets) for earnings not yet billed, and accrued expenses (liabilities) for obligations not yet paid. It also generates deferred revenues (liabilities) and prepaid expenses (assets) when cash moves before the economic event. By aligning financial statements with the economic reality of a period, accrual enables comparability across periods and entities, satisfying the disclosure and consistency requirements. The concept applies to all entities — sole proprietorships, partnerships, companies — and is mandatory under the Companies Act, 2013 and Ind‑AS for Indian reporting.
steps: The core takeaway for students is that the accrual principle dictates that financial records must track economic events when they happen, isolating performance from cash flow timing. - A neighbourhood kirana store…
Cash basis recording would incorrectly push this sale into April and distort March performance metrics.
The four adjusting entry families handle situations where cash and economic events do not align in the same period.
Regulatory requirements under the Companies Act, 2013 Schedule III mandate accrual reporting to ensure a true and fair view of accounts.
A neighbourhood kirana store sells ₹2,000 of groceries on 30 March, and the customer pays on 10 April.
The sale must appear in March's profit because that is when the exchange took place, contrasting sharply with the cash basis alternative.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Accrual means recording when invoice is raised”) reveals the misconception that accrual equals invoicing rather than earning; invoicing may occur before or after earning.
remember: A student says, “Accrual accounting means we record every transaction only when cash is received or paid.” Identify the error and state the correct principle.
A firm receives ₹50,000 on 28 March for a service to be rendered evenly over….
Evaluate: “Accrual accounting always shows higher profit than cash accounting.”.

cards.title: The dual aspect concept (also called the double‑entry principle) states that…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: The dual aspect concept (also called the double‑entry principle) states that every financial transaction affects at least two accounts in opposite directions, keeping the accounting equation Assets = Liabilities + Capital in balance. It arises from the entity concept (business separate from owner) and the money‑measurement concept (only monetary events are recorded). When a transaction occurs, one account is debited (increase in asset/expense or decrease in liability/income) and another is credited (decrease in asset/expense or increase in liability/income). This ensures that the total debits always equal total credits, providing an internal check on arithmetic accuracy. The concept underpins the entire double‑entry system used in Indian GAAP and IFRS, and it links directly to the accrual concept because transactions are recognised when they occur, not when cash flows.
steps: Let’s walk through the dual aspect step by step, using a familiar Indian shop – “Ravi’s Kirana Store”. 1.
Start with the accounting equation – Before any transaction, Ravi’s business has Assets = Liabilities + Capital.
If he invests ₹5,00,000 cash, the equation becomes: Cash (Asset) ₹5,00,000 = Capital ₹5,00,000.
Both sides rose by the same amount – the seesaw stays level. 2.

Identify the two aspects of every event – When Ravi buys goods worth ₹1,00,000 on credit from M/s Gupta Wholesale, two things happen: - Asset (Inventory) increases by ₹1,00,000. - Liability (Creditors) increases by…
The equation now reads: Cash ₹5,00,000 + Inventory ₹1,00,000 = Creditors ₹1,00,000 + Capital ₹5,00,000.
remember: State the dual aspect concept and write the accounting equation it produces.
Explain why every transaction must affect at least two accounts under the dual aspect concept.
A student records a cash purchase of goods by debiting Purchases and crediting Cash only. Evaluate whether this satisfies the dual aspect concept.

cards.title: Materiality is a fundamental accounting concept that sets a threshold for the…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Materiality is a fundamental accounting concept that sets a threshold for the significance of financial information. An item is material if its omission, misstatement, or non‑disclosure could reasonably influence the economic decisions of users of the financial statements — such as investors, creditors, or regulators. The concept is relative: a ₹10,000 expense may be material for a small proprietorship (turnover ₹5 lakh) but immaterial for a listed company (turnover ₹500 crore). Materiality interacts with other GAAP concepts: it qualifies the disclosure requirement (only material facts need full note disclosure), it guides the matching principle (immaterial costs may be expensed immediately rather than capitalised), and it supports prudence (avoid overstating assets by ignoring trivial revaluations). Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS) and the Companies Act, 2013 require materiality assessments for recognition, measurement, presentation, and disclosure. Auditors use quantitative benchmarks (e.g., 0.5 %–1 % of profit before tax) and qualitative factors (nature of item, statutory requirements, user expectations) to judge materiality. The concept ensures financial statements remain relevant and not cluttered with insignificant detail.
steps: Materiality is the filter that decides whether financial information is significant enough to affect users’ decisions.
Here is why: 1.
Decision‑usefulness – Financial statements exist to help investors, lenders, and regulators make choices.
If every ₹1 transaction were shown, the statements would be unreadable; materiality keeps them concise. 2.
Relative threshold – No universal rupee amount defines materiality; it depends on the entity’s size, nature, and the item’s context.
A ₹50,000 repair is material for a kirana store (annual profit ₹2 lakh) but not for a listed manufacturer (profit ₹200 crore). 3.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “materiality means any amount above ₹10,000”) reveals the misconception that materiality is a fixed monetary threshold rather than a relative, qualitative‑quantitative judgement.
remember: State the definition of materiality as per the accounting concept.
A small partnership firm has profit before tax of ₹5….
Evaluate whether a ₹500 cash discount received by a listed company (profit before tax ₹200 crore) must be disclosed separately.

cards.title: The consistency concept requires that once an entity adopts an accounting…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: The consistency concept requires that once an entity adopts an accounting policy or method — such as depreciation method, inventory valuation (FIFO, weighted average), or revenue recognition basis — it must continue to apply that same policy in all subsequent accounting periods unless a change is justified by a new accounting standard, a change in law, or a significant change in the nature of operations. Consistency enables inter‑period comparability, a cornerstone of reliable financial reporting under GAAP. It works together with the accrual concept (recognising transactions when they occur) and the matching concept (matching expenses to revenues) because a shift in policy would distort the matching of costs and revenues across periods. If a change is unavoidable, the entity must disclose the nature, reason, and financial impact of the change in the notes to accounts, as required by the disclosure concept. Consistency does not forbid improvement; it only demands transparency when improvement occurs.
steps: Consistency means applying the same accounting policies period after period so that users can compare financial performance and position over time.
Here is why: first, comparability is the primary qualitative characteristic of useful financial information; without consistent methods, trends in revenue, expenses, and profit become meaningless.
Second, consistency supports the matching concept because a stable depreciation or inventory method ensures that costs are matched to revenues in a uniform way each year.
Third, it protects against earnings management — managers cannot switch methods to inflate profit in a particular year.

Fourth, when a change is genuinely required (e.g., a new Ind AS mandates a different lease accounting model), the entity must disclose the nature, reason, and quantitative effect of the change, satisfying the disclosure…
Consider a small manufacturing firm, “Shree Textiles”, which has used the straight‑line method for machinery depreciation for five years.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Consistency means never changing any accounting method”) reveals the misconception that consistency prohibits all changes, ignoring the permitted change with disclosure.
remember: State the consistency concept in one sentence.
Why does consistency enhance the reliability of financial statements.
A company changes its inventory valuation from FIFO to weighted average in Year 3 without any new accounting standard. Evaluate whether this complies with the consistency concept.

cards.title: Capital versus revenue classification distinguishes transactions by the period…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Capital versus revenue classification distinguishes transactions by the period over which benefits are expected. Capital expenditure (CapEx) is incurred to acquire, improve, or extend the life of a fixed asset (e.g., purchase of machinery, building, vehicle). The benefit spans multiple accounting periods, so the cost is capitalised and depreciated. Revenue expenditure (RevEx) is incurred for day‑to‑day operations (e.g., rent, wages, electricity, repairs) and is fully charged to the Profit & Loss Account of the current period. Capital income/receipts arise from non‑recurring sources such as sale of fixed assets, issue of shares, or long‑term loans; they increase liabilities or reduce assets but do not form part of trading profit. Revenue income/receipts are the regular earnings from the core business — sales of goods, fees, commission, interest received — and are credited to the Profit & Loss Account. Correct classification ensures the matching principle: expenses are matched with the revenues they help generate. Misclassification distorts profit, asset values, and tax liability. The distinction also guides the preparation of the Trading Account, Profit & Loss Account, and Balance Sheet, where capital items appear in the Balance Sheet and revenue items flow through the income statement.
steps: Let’s walk through the logic step by step, using a familiar Indian setting — a neighbourhood “Sharma Electronics” shop. 1.
Identify the transaction — e.g., Sharma buys a new delivery van for ₹6,00,000. 2.
Ask: “How long will this help the business earn?” The van will be used for deliveries for 5‑7 years.
Benefit > 1 year → capital expenditure. 3.
Record — Debit “Vehicle Account” (asset) and credit Bank/Creditor.
The van appears on the Balance Sheet; its cost is spread via depreciation (later node).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “it’s capital because it improves appearance”) reveals the misconception that any outlay that makes an asset look better is capital. Students confuse aesthetic improvement with capacity‑enhancing…

cards.title: Provisions are amounts charged against profit to meet a known liability or loss…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Provisions are amounts charged against profit to meet a known liability or loss whose exact amount or timing is uncertain (e.g., provision for doubtful debts, provision for depreciation, provision for taxation, provision for warranty). They are expenses in the Profit & Loss Account and reduce net profit. Reserves are appropriations of profit set aside to strengthen the financial position or for specific future purposes (e.g., general reserve, specific reserve, capital reserve, revenue reserve, secret reserve). Reserves appear under Reserves & Surplus on the liabilities side of the Balance Sheet and do not reduce profit. The key distinction: provisions are charges (debited to P&L), reserves are appropriations (debited to Profit & Loss Appropriation Account). Both are created from profits, but provisions are mandatory when a liability is probable, while reserves are discretionary. Provisions are specific to a liability; reserves can be general or earmarked. Accounting Standards (AS‑29) govern provisions; reserves follow the Companies Act, 2013 and ICAI guidelines.
steps: Takeaway: Provisions are mandatory charges for probable liabilities; reserves are voluntary appropriations of profit for future strength.
Here is why: 1.
Nature of obligation — A provision arises when a present obligation exists from a past event (e.g., credit sales create doubtful‑debt risk).
A reserve arises from management’s decision to retain earnings. 2.
Effect on profit — Provisions are debited to the Profit & Loss Account, reducing net profit.
Reserves are debited to the Profit & Loss Appropriation Account after net profit is ascertained, leaving profit unchanged. 3.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “It is a reserve because it appears on the liabilities side”) reveals the misconception that any item shown on the liabilities side is a reserve — confusing presentation with nature; depreciation provision reduces the asset’s carrying…
remember: State whether “Provision for depreciation” is a provision or a reserve and give one reason.
A firm creates a “General Reserve” of ₹50,000 from current year’s profit. Explain why this is an appropriation and not a charge.
Evaluate the statement: “Secret reserves are created by overstating liabilities or understating assets.”.

cards.title: The Trading Account is the first part of the final accounts of a sole trader…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: The Trading Account is the first part of the final accounts of a sole trader, prepared to ascertain the gross profit or gross loss for an accounting period. It records only revenue‑generating activities directly related to the core trading operation: opening stock, net purchases (purchases minus purchase returns), direct expenses (carriage inward, wages on loading, import duty, GST paid on purchases not claimable as input credit), and closing stock. The credit side shows net sales (sales minus sales returns) and any other direct incomes such as commission received on purchases. The balancing figure — gross profit if credit side exceeds debit side, otherwise gross loss — is transferred to the Profit and Loss Account. The Trading Account follows the matching principle: only costs incurred to bring goods to a saleable condition are matched against the revenue from those goods. It is prepared in horizontal (T‑form) format as prescribed by the ISC syllabus, with items marshalled in order of permanence (stock, purchases, expenses) on the debit side and order of liquidity (sales, closing stock) on the credit side. Adjustments such as closing stock valuation, outstanding/prepaid direct expenses, accrued direct income, depreciation on trading assets, abnormal loss of stock, free samples given from goods, and drawings of goods are incorporated before finalising the account. The resultant gross profit/loss becomes the opening figure for the Profit and Loss Account (node).
steps: The Trading Account is the gateway to final accounts — it isolates the pure trading result by matching only direct costs of goods sold against direct revenue from goods sold.
Here is why: every other expense (rent, salary, advertising) belongs to the Profit and Loss Account, not the Trading Account.
Consider a Delhi‑based wholesale cloth merchant, M/s Sharma Textiles.
At 1‑Apr‑2025 opening stock of fabric is ₹2,50,000.
During the year net purchases (after purchase returns) are ₹12,00,000; carriage inward ₹30,000; import duty ₹20,000; wages for loading ₹15,000.
Sales (less sales returns) are ₹18,00,000.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., choosing Closing Stock) reveals the misconception that all stock‑related items are debits — confusing the treatment of opening stock (debit) with closing stock (credit).
remember: Which of the following items appears on the debit side of a Trading Account? A) Sales Returns B) Carriage Inward C) Commission Received D) Closing Stock.
A firm’s opening stock is ₹1,20,000, net purchases ₹8,00,000, direct expenses ₹50,000, and closing stock….
Evaluate the statement: “Free samples distributed to customers should be debited to the Trading Account as a direct expense.”.

cards.title: The Profit & Loss Account (horizontal format) for a sole trader is a two‑column…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: The Profit & Loss Account (horizontal format) for a sole trader is a two‑column statement where all revenue‑nature items (sales, commission received, interest earned) appear on the credit side and all expense‑nature items (purchases, wages, rent, depreciation, bad debts) appear on the debit side. The Trading Account (prepared first) determines Gross Profit = Net Sales – Cost of Goods Sold. This gross profit is transferred to the credit of the Profit & Loss Account. After adding other incomes and deducting operating expenses, Net Profit (or Net Loss) emerges and is transferred to the Capital Account. The Balance Sheet (horizontal format) is a two‑column statement dated at the close of the accounting period. The left column (Liabilities & Capital) lists Capital (opening capital + net profit – drawings), Long‑term Liabilities (bank loan), Current Liabilities (creditors, outstanding expenses). The right column (Assets) lists Fixed Assets (land, building, furniture – at cost less depreciation), Current Assets (closing stock, debtors, cash, bank, prepaid expenses). Marshalling follows the order of permanence (fixed assets first, then current assets) on the asset side and order of liquidity (long‑term liabilities first, then current liabilities) on the liability side. The fundamental accounting equation Total Assets = Total Liabilities + Capital must hold. This node covers only the presentation of these two statements in horizontal layout; all adjustment entries (closing stock, outstanding/prepaid, depreciation, etc.) are treated in sibling nodes 005‑018.
steps: Final accounts are prepared by systematically categorizing Trial Balance items into Trading, Profit & Loss, and Balance Sheet buckets.
Gross Profit is the primary takeaway: It is the starting point for the Profit & Loss Account, representing the surplus of sales over the cost of goods sold.
Marshalling provides clarity: Organizing assets by permanence and liabilities by liquidity ensures that the Balance Sheet reflects the business's solvency and stability.
The accounting equation is the anchor: Total assets must always equal the sum of liabilities and capital, confirming the accuracy of the final accounts.
Net profit flows to equity: The final profit or loss from the P&L account must be adjusted against the owner's capital to reflect the true equity at year-end.
Step 1 – Trading Account (horizontal).
remember: In a horizontal‑format Profit & Loss Account, where is Gross Profit recorded.
Why must the Balance Sheet in horizontal format be marshalled in order of permanence (assets) and liquidity (liabilities).

cards.title: Closing stock represents the value of unsold goods held by a sole trader at the…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Closing stock represents the value of unsold goods held by a sole trader at the end of an accounting period. Under the accrual concept, only the cost of goods actually sold (Cost of Goods Sold) is matched against revenue; the remainder stays as an asset. The adjustment requires a journal entry: Closing Stock A/c Dr. → Trading A/c Cr. This entry brings the stock into the Trading Account, reducing the debit side (cost of goods sold) and increasing gross profit. Simultaneously, the same amount appears on the assets side of the horizontal Balance Sheet under Current Assets → Stock-in-Trade. The valuation follows the lower of cost or net realisable value (AS‑2/Ind‑AS 2). Closing stock also links to the Adjusted Purchases concept (node) where Adjusted Purchases = Purchases + Opening Stock – Closing Stock, and to Cost of Goods Sold (node). It does not involve revenue recognition, depreciation, or provisions — those are covered in sibling nodes.
steps: Closing stock is the single adjustment that simultaneously reduces cost of goods sold in the Trading Account and creates a current asset in the Balance Sheet.
Here is why: the matching principle demands that only the cost of goods sold be charged to the period’s revenue.
Goods still on hand have not generated revenue, so their cost must be removed from the Trading Account debit side.

The journal entry Closing Stock A/c Dr. → Trading A/c Cr. achieves this — the credit to Trading Account lowers the total debits (opening stock + purchases + direct expenses), thereby increasing gross profit.
The debit to Closing Stock Account creates an asset that appears on the Balance Sheet under Current Assets.
Consider a Delhi‑based sole trader, M/s Sharma Traders, with Opening Stock ₹ 1,20,000, Purchases ₹ 8,50,000, Direct Expenses ₹ 30,000, and a physical count revealing Closing Stock ₹ 1,80,000.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Trading A/c Dr. → Closing Stock A/c Cr.”) reveals the misconception that closing stock is an expense to be debited to Trading Account, confusing it with opening stock which is debited.
remember: What is the correct journal entry to record closing stock of ₹ 1,50,000 at the end of the accounting period.
Why is closing stock credited to the Trading Account rather than debited.
A firm values its closing stock at cost ₹ 2,00,000, but the net realisable value is ₹ 1,70,000. Evaluate the correct treatment and its impact on financial statements.

cards.title: Outstanding expenses (also called accrued expenses) are costs incurred during…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Outstanding expenses (also called accrued expenses) are costs incurred during an accounting period but not yet paid by the end of that period. They are recognised as liabilities (Outstanding Expenses Account) and added to the respective expense in the Profit & Loss Account. Prepaid expenses are payments made in advance for benefits that will be received in future periods; the unexpired portion is shown as an asset (Prepaid Expenses Account) and deducted from the expense in the Profit & Loss Account. Both adjustments follow the matching principle — expenses must be matched with the revenues of the same period. In the horizontal format of final accounts, outstanding expenses appear on the liabilities side of the Balance Sheet under “Current Liabilities”, while prepaid expenses appear on the assets side under “Current Assets”. The journal entries are: - For outstanding expense: Debit Expense Account, Credit Outstanding Expense Account. - For prepaid expense: Debit Prepaid Expense Account, Credit Expense Account (or Cash/Bank). These entries ensure that the Trading and Profit & Loss Account reflects only the expense relating to the current year, and the Balance Sheet shows the correct financial position.
steps: Let’s walk through the two adjustments step by step, using a typical Indian sole‑trader, “Ramesh Traders”, who closes his books on 31 March. 1.
Outstanding Expenses Suppose the electricity bill for March ₹4,500 is received on 10 April.

The expense belongs to March, so we must record it in the current year. - Journal Entry (31 March): Electricity Expenses A/c … Dr. 4,500 To Outstanding Electricity Expenses A/c … 4,500 - Effect on Profit & Loss…
Prepaid Expenses Ramesh pays the annual insurance premium of ₹12,000 on 1 October.

Only six months (Oct‑Mar) belong to the current year; the remaining six months (Apr‑Sep) are prepaid. - Journal Entry (31 March): Prepaid Insurance A/c … Dr. 6,000 To Insurance Expenses A/c … 6,000 - Effect on Profit &…
Why the matching principle matters Without these adjustments, March’s profit would be overstated (missing electricity) and understated (full insurance charged).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “it’s an asset because it will be paid later”) reveals the misconception that any future cash outflow creates an asset, confusing the direction of the…

cards.title: Accrued income (also called outstanding income) is revenue that has been earned…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition:
Accrued income (also called outstanding income) is revenue that has been earned during the accounting period but not yet received in cash by the end of that period. Under the accrual basis of accounting — mandatory for ISC Class 11 — income is recognised when the right to receive it arises, not when cash is collected. The adjustment ensures the Profit & Loss Account reflects the true earnings of the period and the Balance Sheet shows a current asset (Accrued Income) representing the amount receivable. Relationship with other adjustments: - Outstanding expenses (node) are the mirror image — expenses incurred but not paid. - Prepaid expenses are payments made in advance for future periods. - Unearned income (income received in advance) is a liability, the opposite of accrued income. Journal entry at year‑end: ```
Accrued Income A/c Dr. To Respective Income A/c ``` In the Trading / Profit & Loss Account the income is added to the relevant revenue head. In the Balance Sheet (horizontal format) it appears under Current Assets as “Accrued Income” or “Outstanding Income”. The adjustment is reversed in the next period when cash is received: ```
Cash/Bank A/c Dr. To Accrued Income A/c ```
steps: Accrued income must be recorded in the period it is earned, not when cash arrives, to satisfy the accrual principle and present a true profit.
Here is why: the matching concept requires revenues and related expenses to be recognised in the same period.
If a sole trader earns ₹10,000 commission in March but receives it in April, omitting it from March’s Profit & Loss understates profit and hides a receivable asset.
Consider a Delhi‑based freelance graphic designer, Priya.
On 28 March 2025 she completes a logo design for a client who agrees to pay ₹15,000 on 10 April 2025.
At 31 March 2025 (year‑end) the ₹15,000 is accrued income.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Debit Cash, Credit Income”) reveals the misconception that revenue is recorded only when cash is received — confusing cash basis with accrual basis.
remember: Define accrued income and state the adjusting journal entry required at year‑end.
A firm’s trial balance shows “Rent Received….
Evaluate: “Accrued income and unearned income are the same because both relate to future cash flows.”.

cards.title: Depreciation is the systematic allocation of the depreciable amount of a…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Depreciation is the systematic allocation of the depreciable amount of a tangible fixed asset over its estimated useful life. The depreciable amount equals the cost of the asset (including all expenditures necessary to bring it to working condition) minus its estimated residual (scrap) value. Under CISCE ISC Accounting, two principal methods are taught: the Straight‑Line Method (SLM) and the Diminishing Balance Method (DBM). SLM charges an equal amount each year: (Cost – Residual Value) ÷ Useful Life. DBM applies a fixed percentage to the reducing book value each year, so the charge declines over time. Depreciation is a non‑cash expense debited to the Profit & Loss Account and credited to the Accumulated Depreciation (a contra‑asset) shown on the Balance Sheet. It matches the cost of using the asset with the revenue it helps generate (matching principle) and ensures the asset is not overstated. The choice of method affects reported profit, tax liability, and financial ratios, so consistency and disclosure are required by Accounting Standard (AS) 10 (Property, Plant and Equipment) as adopted in the ISC syllabus.
steps: Let’s walk through depreciation as if you are the accountant for “Sharma Traders”, a sole‑proprietorship in Jaipur.
The firm buys a second‑hand delivery truck on 1 April 2023 for ₹8,00,000, spends ₹50,000 on registration and painting, and estimates a useful life of 5 years with a scrap value of ₹50,000.
Step 1 – Determine depreciable cost.
Cost = Purchase price + Direct costs = ₹8,00,000 + ₹50,000 = ₹8,50,000.
Depreciable amount = Cost – Residual value = ₹8,50,000 – ₹50,000 = ₹8,00,000.
Step 2 – Choose a method.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Depreciation reduces cash balance”) reveals the misconception that every expense on the P&L must involve a cash payment, confusing accrual accounting with cash accounting.
remember: A student writes: “Depreciation is a cash expense because the firm pays money to replace the asset.” Identify the error and state the correct classification.
Sharma Traders purchased machinery for ₹12,00,000 on 1 July….
Compare the impact on reported profit for Year 1 if a firm switches from SLM (10 % on cost) to DBM (15 % on reducing balance) for an asset costing ₹5,00,000 with no residual….

cards.title: Bad debts refer to trade receivables that are deemed irrecoverable and are…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Bad debts refer to trade receivables that are deemed irrecoverable and are written off from the books of accounts. When a debtor fails to honour the credit terms — due to insolvency, disappearance, or dispute — the seller recognises the loss by debiting Bad Debts Expense (or Bad Debts Written Off) and crediting the Debtor’s Account. This adjustment reduces both the profit in the Profit & Loss Account and the trade receivables shown in the Balance Sheet. Bad debts are distinct from provision for doubtful debts, which is an estimate of future losses; bad debts are actual, confirmed losses. The entry is: Bad Debts A/c Dr. → Debtor’s A/c Cr. The amount written off is transferred to the Profit & Loss Account as an expense under “Selling and Distribution Expenses” or “Administrative Expenses” depending on the firm’s policy. In the horizontal format of final accounts, bad debts appear on the debit side of the Profit & Loss Account and the debtor’s balance is reduced to zero in the Balance Sheet.
steps: Bad debts are confirmed losses on credit sales that must be written off immediately to reflect true profit and realistic receivables.

Here is why: the matching principle demands that expenses relating to revenue of the period be recognised in the same period; when a debtor is proven unable to pay, the related revenue was already recorded, so the loss…
In December, Rohan is declared insolvent and only 20 % is recoverable.
The firm writes off ₹80,000 as bad debts.
The journal entry: Bad Debts A/c Dr. 80,000 → Rohan A/c Cr. 80,000.
In the Profit & Loss Account, ₹80,000 appears on the debit side under “Bad Debts”.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., debiting Amit and crediting Bad Debts) reveals the misconception that the debtor’s account is increased when a loss occurs — confusing the direction of asset reduction.
remember: What is the correct journal entry to write off ₹15,000 as bad debts from debtor “Amit”.
Explain why bad debts are debited to the Profit & Loss Account and not to the Trading Account.
A firm writes off ₹20,000 as bad debts but had previously created a provision for doubtful debts of….

cards.title: Provision for doubtful debts is an accounting estimate created to anticipate…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Provision for doubtful debts is an accounting estimate created to anticipate that a portion of the sundry debtors (trade receivables) may become irrecoverable in the future. It is a contra‑asset shown on the asset side of the Balance Sheet by deducting it from Sundry Debtors, and the corresponding expense (or loss) is debited to the Profit and Loss Account under “Provision for Doubtful Debts”. The provision is calculated on the net debtors after writing off actual bad debts, using a percentage rate decided by management based on past experience, industry norms, or credit policy. Unlike a reserve, it is a charge against profit, not an appropriation of profit. The provision is adjusted each year: the opening provision is reversed, the new required provision is computed, and the difference (increase or decrease) is routed through the Profit and Loss Account. This ensures the matching principle — expenses of the period are matched with revenues of the same period — and presents a true and fair view of the realisable value of receivables. The concept links directly to bad debts (actual write‑offs) and to provisions and reserves (classification of provisions as charge against profit). It also interacts with adjusted purchases and cost of goods sold only indirectly through the overall profit determination.
steps: Provision for doubtful debts is an estimated charge against profit that reduces the book value of debtors to their expected realisable value.
Here is why: the matching principle requires that the cost of potential non‑collection be recognised in the same period as the related sales revenue.
Consider a Delhi‑based wholesale trader, M/s Gupta & Sons, with Sundry Debtors of ₹5,00,000 on 31 March 2025.
During the year, actual bad debts of ₹20,000 were written off. The firm’s policy is to maintain a provision at 5 % of net debtors.
Required provision = 5 % × ₹4,80,000 = ₹24,000.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “to set aside cash for future bad debts”) reveals the misconception that a provision involves cash segregation; provisions are non‑cash accounting estimates.
remember: What is the primary purpose of creating a provision for doubtful debts in the final accounts of a sole trader.
A firm has Sundry Debtors ₹8,00,000, Bad Debts written off ₹30,000, and maintains a provision at 4 %. Calculate the required provision for doubtful debts.
Evaluate the statement: “Provision for doubtful debts is a reserve created out of profits to strengthen the financial position.”.

cards.title: Manager’s commission is a contractual remuneration paid to a manager…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Manager’s commission is a contractual remuneration paid to a manager, usually expressed as a fixed percentage of the net profit of a sole‑trader business. It is an adjustment that must be incorporated while preparing the final accounts (Trading Account, Profit & Loss Account, and Balance Sheet) because it affects both the profit figure and the liabilities. Two bases are common: (1) Commission on profit before charging commission – the commission is simply the agreed percentage multiplied by the net profit ascertained before deducting the commission itself. (2) Commission on profit after charging commission – here the commission forms part of the expenses that reduce the profit; therefore the commission amount appears on both sides of the equation. Algebraically, if P is profit before commission and r% is the rate, commission C = r% × P for the first basis, and C = (r% × P) / (100 + r%) for the second. The commission is debited to the Profit & Loss Account (as an expense) and credited to a “Manager’s Commission Payable” account (a current liability) until actually paid. This adjustment follows other profit‑determining adjustments such as closing stock, outstanding/prepaid expenses, accrued income, depreciation, bad debts, and provision for doubtful debts, ensuring that the final profit reflects all contractual obligations.
steps: The manager’s commission is a contractual performance bonus that must be calculated based on the specific wording of the employment agreement.
The calculation method depends entirely on whether the contract specifies the commission is on profit "before" or "after" charging the commission itself.

The basis of calculation is determined by the contract: "on net profit" typically implies the before-commission basis, while "on net profit after charging such commission" explicitly requires the after-commission…
The before-commission basis is a straightforward percentage calculation: Commission = Rate% × Profit before commission.
The after-commission basis is self-referential, requiring the commission to be treated as a deduction from the profit base: Commission = (Rate% × Profit before commission) / (100 + Rate%).
The accounting treatment is consistent regardless of the basis: debit the Profit & Loss Account as an expense and credit the Manager’s Commission Payable account as a current liability.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “commission is always on profit after commission”) reveals the misconception that the commission must always be self‑referential, ignoring the contractual language that determines the base.
remember: A student states that manager’s commission is always calculated on the net profit after all adjustments including the commission….
The net profit before manager’s commission of a sole trader is….
A firm’s profit before manager’s commission is….

cards.title: Free samples are goods distributed without charge to promote sales.
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Free samples are goods distributed without charge to promote sales. Under the matching principle, the cost of such goods must be recognised as an expense in the period they are given away. The accounting treatment involves two steps: (1) Reverse the cost from Purchases/Trading Account — debit an expense head (usually “Advertising Expenses” or “Free Samples Account”) and credit Purchases (or Trading Account) with the cost of samples; (2) Show the expense in the Profit & Loss Account on the debit side. Consequently, Closing Stock is reduced by the quantity given as samples, because those units are no longer available for sale. This adjustment links to Closing Stock, Adjusted Purchases, Cost of Goods Sold and the Trading & P&L Account (,). It also relates to Capital vs Revenue Expenditure because the outlay is revenue in nature, and to Provisions and Reserves only if a provision for promotional expenses is created. The adjustment ensures that the financial statements reflect the true cost of generating revenue.
steps: Free samples are a promotional cost that must be moved out of purchases and charged to the Profit & Loss Account, while simultaneously reducing closing stock.
Here is why: 1.
Matching principle – Expenses belong to the period they help generate revenue.
Free samples given this year help this year’s sales, so their cost is an expense of this year. 2.
Stock integrity – Goods given away are no longer in the godown; if we leave them in Closing Stock we overstate assets and profit. 3.
Expense classification – The cost is a selling/distribution expense, usually shown as “Advertising Expenses” or a separate “Free Samples” line in the P&L. 4.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., Debit Sales ₹3,000; Credit Purchases ₹3,000) reveals the misconception that free samples generate revenue — confusing a marketing cost with a sale.
remember: What is the correct journal entry when goods costing ₹3,000 are distributed as free samples.
Why does the distribution of free samples reduce Closing Stock in the Balance Sheet.
Evaluate the statement: “Free samples should be credited to Sales Account because they increase customer goodwill.”.

cards.title: Drawings refer to any withdrawal of cash, goods…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Drawings refer to any withdrawal of cash, goods, or other assets by the proprietor of a sole‑trader business for personal or non‑business purposes. In accounting, drawings are not treated as an expense; they do not appear in the Trading or Profit & Loss Account. Instead, they are deducted from the owner’s capital in the Balance Sheet. The relationship is: Closing Capital = Opening Capital + Additional Capital + Net Profit – Drawings If goods are withdrawn, they are valued at cost (or market value if lower) and credited to the Purchases/Trading Account while debiting the Drawings Account. Cash drawings are debited to Drawings and credited to Cash/Bank. At year‑end, the Drawings Account is closed by transferring its balance to the Capital Account. This ensures the capital figure reflects the owner’s true stake after personal withdrawals.
steps: Let’s walk through drawings step by step, using a familiar Indian setting.
Stage 1 – Recognise a drawing.
Ravi owns “Ravi Electronics” in Mumbai.
On 15 March he takes ₹20,000 from the business bank account to pay his daughter’s school fees.
This is a cash drawing — personal use, not a business expense.
Stage 2 – Record the journal entry.

cards.title: Abnormal loss refers to a loss of inventory or assets that arises from…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition:
Abnormal loss refers to a loss of inventory or assets that arises from unexpected, non‑recurring events such as fire, theft, flood, accident, or natural calamity. Unlike normal loss (which is inherent to the business process, e.g., evaporation of liquids), abnormal loss is not part of the cost of goods sold. In final accounts it is treated as follows: 1. Trading Account – The full cost of the lost goods is credited (removed) from purchases/opening stock so that gross profit is not distorted. 2. Profit & Loss Account – The net loss after any insurance recovery is debited as an expense ( “Loss by Fire”, “Loss by Theft”, etc.). 3. Balance Sheet – Any insurance claim receivable is shown as a current asset; any claim received reduces the loss. The journal entry at the time of loss: ```
Abnormal Loss A/c Dr. (Cost of goods lost) To Trading A/c (Cost of goods lost)
``` When insurance claim is admitted: ```
Insurance Company A/c Dr. (Claim admitted) To Abnormal Loss A/c (Claim admitted)
``` If claim is received: ```
Bank A/c Dr. (Cash received) To Insurance Company A/c (Cash received)
``` The net abnormal loss transferred to P&L = Cost of goods lost – Insurance claim admitted. This ensures the trading result reflects only normal business operations while the extraordinary loss is disclosed separately.
steps: Let’s walk through an abnormal loss step by step, using a familiar Indian shop — Ramesh Kirana Stores in Mumbai. 1.
Event occurs – A short‑circuit fire destroys 50 kg of sugar costing ₹40/kg (total ₹2,000).
This is abnormal because fire is not a routine part of selling sugar. 2.
Remove from Trading – The Trading Account must show only the cost of goods actually available for sale.
So we credit Trading Account (or Purchases) with ₹2,000 and debit a new Abnormal Loss Account.
The gross profit now reflects the true cost of goods sold. 3.

cards.title: Adjusted purchases is the corrected gross purchases figure used in the Trading…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Adjusted purchases is the corrected gross purchases figure used in the Trading Account when the closing stock appears in the Trial Balance. In such a case the purchases amount in the Trial Balance is net of closing stock (i.e., purchases – closing stock). To arrive at the gross purchases that must be matched against sales, the closing stock value is added back to the purchases figure. The resulting amount is called Adjusted Purchases. Relationship with other concepts: - Closing Stock in Trial Balance (covered in node) signals that purchases have already been reduced. - Cost of Goods Sold (node) is then computed as Opening Stock + Adjusted Purchases – Closing Stock (which simplifies to Opening Stock + Net Purchases). - Trading Account (node) uses Adjusted Purchases on the debit side instead of the raw purchases figure. - Marshalling (node) does not affect the calculation but determines the order of presentation in the Balance Sheet. The adjustment ensures the matching principle: revenue of the period is matched with the cost of goods actually sold, not with a purchases figure that has been artificially lowered by an asset (closing stock) that belongs to the next period.
steps: Let’s walk through the idea step by step, using a small Indian kirana store as our example.
Step 1 – Spot the clue in the Trial Balance.
At 31 March 2025 the Trial Balance of “Sharma & Sons” shows: - Purchases … ₹ 4,80,000 - Closing Stock … ₹ 1,20,000 (appears on the debit side as an asset).
Because closing stock is listed inside the Trial Balance, the accountant has already credited the Trading Account with ₹ 1,20,000 and debited Closing Stock.
That means the Purchases figure of ₹ 4,80,000 is after deducting the closing stock.
In other words, the store actually bought goods worth ₹ 4,80,000 + ₹ 1,20,000 = ₹ 6,00,000 during the year.

cards.title: Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) represents the total cost incurred by a sole‑trader…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) represents the total cost incurred by a sole‑trader to acquire or produce the goods that were actually sold during an accounting period. In the Trading Account it is deducted from Net Sales to arrive at Gross Profit. COGS links three key elements: (1) Opening Stock – the value of inventory at the beginning of the period; (2) Net Purchases plus Direct Expenses (carriage inwards, wages, import duty) – the cost of goods added during the period, adjusted for purchase returns and allowances; (3) Closing Stock – the value of unsold inventory at period‑end. The standard formula is COGS = Opening Stock + Net Purchases + Direct Expenses – Closing Stock. An alternative route uses Adjusted Purchases (Net Purchases + Direct Expenses) so that COGS = Adjusted Purchases + Opening Stock – Closing Stock. Adjustments such as abnormal loss, free samples, drawings of goods, and goods given as charity reduce the cost available for sale and therefore lower COGS. The concept is confined to the Trading Account; it does not include indirect expenses (rent, salaries) which belong to the Profit & Loss Account. Mastery of COGS is essential because it feeds directly into gross profit, which in turn influences net profit, tax liability, and managerial decisions on pricing and inventory control.
steps: Let’s walk through COGS as if we are preparing the Trading Account for “Shree Textiles”, a sole‑trader in Surat.
Step 1 – Gather the building blocks.
From the trial balance we pick Opening Stock (₹1,20,000), Purchases (₹8,50,000), Purchase Returns (₹30,000), Carriage Inwards (₹15,000), Wages (₹25,000), and Closing Stock (₹1,80,000).
Step 2 – Compute Net Purchases.
Net Purchases = Purchases – Purchase Returns = ₹8,50,000 – ₹30,000 = ₹8,20,000.
Step 3 – Add Direct Expenses.

cards.title: GST offset (or GST set‑off) is the mechanism in the final accounts of a sole…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: GST offset (or GST set‑off) is the mechanism in the final accounts of a sole trader where the Input Tax Credit (ITC) on eligible purchases is deducted from the Output GST collected on sales to arrive at the net GST liability payable to the government. In the horizontal format of the Trading and Profit & Loss Account, the gross purchases and sales are shown inclusive of GST; the adjustment for GST offset appears as a separate line item — “Less: GST Set‑off (ITC)” under purchases (or as a reduction from “GST Payable” on the liability side of the Balance Sheet). The offset ensures that tax is paid only on the value added by the trader. It links directly to the Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) because the GST embedded in opening stock, purchases, and closing stock determines the eligible ITC. The offset does not affect gross profit; it only changes the net tax payable and the current liability shown in the Balance Sheet.
steps: The GST offset is the net tax liability calculated by subtracting eligible Input Tax Credit (ITC) from the total Output GST collected.
This calculation ensures that the business only pays tax on the value it adds, rather than the total turnover.
Supporting arguments:
GST paid on purchases is a recoverable asset (ITC), not an expense, meaning it does not reduce Gross Profit.
The offset mechanism prevents the "cascading effect" of taxes by allowing traders to reclaim tax paid on inputs.
Netting the tax ensures that the Balance Sheet accurately reflects the actual liability owed to the government or the credit due from them.

cards.title: Marshalling is the systematic arrangement of assets and liabilities in a…
cards.subject: Accountancy
cards.definition: Marshalling is the systematic arrangement of assets and liabilities in a Balance Sheet according to a prescribed sequence. Under the order of permanence (also called order of liquidity for assets), items are listed from the most permanent/least liquid to the least permanent/most liquid. For a sole trader’s horizontal Balance Sheet (as per CISCE ISC), the typical sequence for assets is: 1. Fixed Assets (Land, Building, Plant & Machinery, Furniture, Vehicles) – most permanent. 2. Intangible Assets (Goodwill, Patents, Trademarks). 3. Investments (long‑term). 4. Current Assets (Closing Stock, Sundry Debtors, Bills Receivable, Accrued Income, Prepaid Expenses, Cash at Bank, Cash in Hand) – most liquid. For liabilities, the order of permanence runs from the most permanent source of funds to the most immediate obligation: 1. Capital (opening capital + net profit – drawings). 2. Long‑term Liabilities (Long‑term Loans, Debentures, Mortgage). 3. Current Liabilities (Sundry Creditors, Bills Payable, Outstanding Expenses, Income Received in Advance, Bank Overdraft, Short‑term Provisions). Marshalling ensures comparability across periods and between firms, satisfies the going concern assumption, and meets the disclosure requirements of the Companies Act, 2013 (Schedule III) and the Accounting Standards (AS‑1) adopted by CISCE. It is distinct from grouping (which clusters similar items) because marshalling imposes a strict hierarchical order within each group.
steps: Marshalling arranges Balance Sheet items from the most permanent to the most liquid so that the financial position reflects the going concern reality.

Here is why: the going concern assumption presumes the business will continue indefinitely; therefore, resources that support long‑term operations (land, building) are shown first, while resources that will be converted…
This order lets a bank manager instantly gauge the proportion of fixed versus current assets, aiding credit decisions.

Building 8,00,000;
Plant & Machinery 5,00,000;
