cards.title: Data collection is the systematic process of acquiring raw observations from…
cards.subject: Artificial Intelligence
cards.definition: Data collection is the systematic process of acquiring raw observations from primary or secondary sources to build a dataset for analysis or model training. Primary collection involves direct capture — surveys, IoT sensor streams, camera feeds, or manual entry — while secondary collection reuses existing repositories such as government open data portals, Kaggle datasets, or organisational databases. The process defines the population, sampling strategy (random, stratified, convenience), frequency (batch vs. streaming), and metadata (timestamps, source identifiers, consent flags). Quality attributes — completeness, timeliness, relevance, and bias — are established at this stage and propagate through cleaning and preprocessing. In the AI pipeline, collection feeds the raw dataframe that cleaning (node) will sanitise and preprocessing (node) will transform.
steps: Effective data collection determines the ceiling of any AI system — garbage in, garbage out. Here is why: first, the source dictates the nature of noise; a temperature sensor in a Mumbai local train yields different…
Second, sampling method controls representativeness; a convenience sample of urban college students will not generalise to rural healthcare needs.

Third, streaming vs. batch decides infrastructure; real‑time traffic feeds from Delhi’s ITS require Kafka‑style pipelines, while annual census data fits a nightly batch job. Fourth, metadata (timestamp, device ID…
Fifth, bias audits at collection time — checking gender balance in a hiring dataset — prevent costly rework later.
Consider a project predicting monsoon onset for Maharashtra farmers.
You would collect primary data from IMD weather stations (API, hourly), secondary satellite imagery (NASA MODIS, daily), and farmer SMS reports (opt‑in, weekly).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., choosing A) reveals the misconception that any digital file counts as primary data — confusing access with origin.

Evaluate the claim: “Streaming ingestion is always better than batch ingestion for AI data collection.”.

cards.title: Data cleaning is the systematic process of detecting, diagnosing…
cards.subject: Artificial Intelligence
cards.definition: Data cleaning is the systematic process of detecting, diagnosing, and correcting or removing errors, inconsistencies, and irrelevant entries in a raw dataset so that subsequent preprocessing and modelling steps operate on reliable, uniform information. It sits between data collection and data preprocessing in the pipeline. Core sub‑tasks include: (1) handling missing values — imputation, deletion, or flagging; (2) removing duplicates — exact or near‑duplicate rows; (3) correcting structural errors — inconsistent capitalisation, whitespace, or delimiter misuse; (4) type conversion — ensuring each column matches its intended datatype (numeric, categorical, datetime); (5) outlier treatment — winsorisation, capping, or domain‑based removal; and (6) standardising units and formats — e.g., converting all dates to ISO‑8601, all currency to INR. Each action is logged to maintain reproducibility. The output of cleaning is a tidy dataset where every variable is a column, every observation a row, and each cell holds a single atomic value, ready for feature engineering in the next node.
steps: Cleaning transforms a noisy raw file into a trustworthy analytical asset; without it, every downstream model inherits the garbage‑in‑garbage‑out flaw.
Here is why: (1) Missing values bias estimates — mean imputation restores sample size but shrinks variance; median is robust to skew.
(2) Duplicates inflate confidence — dropping exact copies preserves information content.
(3) Inconsistent types break vectorised operations — explicit casting prevents silent coercion errors.
(4) Mixed units (kg vs g, ₹ vs $) distort distance‑based algorithms — conversion to a single standard restores comparability.
(5) Outliers can dominate loss functions — IQR‑based capping limits influence while retaining bulk structure.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “to increase the size of the dataset”) reveals the misconception that cleaning is about quantity rather than quality — confusing data augmentation with error remediation.
remember: What is the primary purpose of data cleaning in the AI pipeline.
A dataset contains a column “Age” with values “25”, “thirty”, “”, “200”. Which cleaning actions are appropriate for each entry.
Explain why mean imputation reduces variance in a numeric column.

cards.title: Preprocessing transforms cleaned raw data into a format suitable for…
cards.subject: Artificial Intelligence
cards.definition: Preprocessing transforms cleaned raw data into a format suitable for machine‑learning algorithms. It follows data cleaning and precedes model training. Core steps include: (1) Feature scaling — min‑max normalization or z‑score standardization to bring numeric attributes onto a common range; (2) Categorical encoding — one‑hot, label, or target encoding to convert nominal/ordinal text into numbers; (3) Feature engineering — deriving new columns (e.g., extracting month from a date, computing BMI from height/weight) to expose hidden patterns; (4) Dimensionality reduction — techniques like PCA (introduced later) to compress correlated features; (5) Handling class imbalance — resampling or synthetic generation (SMOTE) so the learner sees balanced classes. Each step is reversible only with stored parameters (scaler min/max, encoder mapping) to apply identically on test data. Preprocessing pipelines (e.g., scikit‑learn Pipeline) chain these operations, ensuring reproducibility and preventing data leakage.
steps: Rigorous machine learning preprocessing requires transforming a human-readable table into a model-ready tensor while strictly guarding against data leakage through proper sequencing and pipelining.
First, separate the target variable from features and perform an 80-20 train-test split before any scaling to ensure the test set remains completely unseen.

Second, apply min-max scaling exclusively on the training set to prevent features with larger numeric ranges from dominating distance-based algorithms, and reuse those stored parameters for the test set. Third, convert…
Fourth, wrap all these sequential transformation steps into a Pipeline object to guarantee that future deployment data automatically undergoes the exact same preprocessing.
Imagine you have a spreadsheet of 500 students from a Delhi school: columns are Name, Class, Gender, Height_cm, Weight_kg, DOB, and Exam_Score.
After cleaning (node 003) you removed duplicate rows, fixed a few impossible heights, and imputed missing weights with the class median.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "it makes the code faster") reveals the misconception that preprocessing is only about computational efficiency, ignoring the statistical integrity of model evaluation.

cards.title: Feature engineering is the process of transforming raw…
cards.subject: Artificial Intelligence
cards.definition: Feature engineering is the process of transforming raw, cleaned data into informative attributes (features) that improve the performance of machine learning models. It builds directly on the output of preprocessing (node), where missing values are handled, outliers treated, and scales normalized. The main sub‑tasks are: (1) Feature extraction – deriving new variables from existing ones (e.g., extracting “month” from a timestamp); (2) Feature construction – creating composite features by mathematical or logical combination (e.g., “total rooms per household” = total rooms / households); (3) Feature encoding – converting categorical variables into numeric form (one‑hot, label, target encoding); (4) Feature scaling – ensuring all numeric features lie on comparable ranges (standardization, min‑max); (5) Feature selection – choosing a subset of relevant features to reduce dimensionality and avoid overfitting. Good feature engineering captures domain knowledge (e.g., knowing that “festival season” boosts sales in India) and directly influences model accuracy, training time, and interpretability. It sits between preprocessing and data splitting (next node), providing the final feature matrix that feeds into model training.
steps: Let’s walk through feature engineering as if we are preparing a dataset for predicting house prices in Bengaluru.
After preprocessing (node 004), we have a clean DataFrame with columns: `area_sqft`, `bedrooms`, `bathrooms`, `location`, `age_years`, `price`.
Stage 1 – Feature Extraction We notice `location` is a high‑cardinality categorical variable.

Instead of one‑hot encoding all 200+ neighborhoods (which would explode dimensionality), we extract a new feature `location_tier` by mapping each neighborhood to a tier (Tier‑1, Tier‑2, Tier‑3) based on average price…

This captures domain knowledge: prime areas like Indiranagar are Tier‑1, upcoming areas are Tier‑2, etc. Stage 2 – Feature Construction We create `area_per_room = area_sqft / (bedrooms + bathrooms)` to reflect…
We also compute `house_age_category` by binning `age_years` into “new (0‑5)”, “mid (6‑15)”, “old (16+)”.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “feature engineering is only about scaling numbers”) reveals the misconception that it is a single mechanical step rather than a creative, domain‑driven process.
remember: What is the primary goal of feature engineering in a machine learning pipeline.
Why is it important to fit scalers (e.g., StandardScaler) only on the training split and not on the whole dataset.
Evaluate the claim: “One‑hot encoding should always be used for categorical variables because it preserves all information.”.

cards.title: Data transformation is the process of converting cleaned and preprocessed data…
cards.subject: Artificial Intelligence
cards.definition: Data transformation is the process of converting cleaned and preprocessed data into a suitable format for machine learning algorithms. It follows data collection, cleaning, and preprocessing in the pipeline. Key sub-concepts include scaling (normalization and standardization) to bring numerical features to a common range, encoding (label encoding, one-hot encoding) to convert categorical variables into numbers, and discretization to turn continuous variables into intervals. Normalization (min-max) rescales values to [0,1] using feature minimum and maximum. Standardization (z-score) centres data around mean zero with unit variance, making it robust to outliers. Encoding choices depend on whether categorical data is nominal (one-hot) or ordinal (label encoding). Proper transformation ensures distance-based algorithms (k-NN, SVM, neural networks) converge faster and treat features equitably. It does not handle missing values or noise — those are addressed in cleaning.
steps: Data transformation reshapes existing information so algorithms can process features equally without creating new data.
First, feature scaling prevents large numerical ranges like carpet area from dominating distance-based algorithms over smaller ranges like bedroom counts.
Second, min-max normalization squashes values between 0 and 1, ensuring features contribute equally when data lacks extreme values.
Third, standardization uses mean and standard deviation to handle outliers better than min-max without compressing normal data.
Fourth, one-hot encoding prevents false numerical hierarchy in categorical data like localities by creating separate binary columns.
Let's walk through a real Indian scenario: predicting flat prices in Mumbai.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., X' = (X - mean) / std) reveals the misconception that normalization and standardization are the same — confusing range-based scaling with distribution-based scaling.
remember: What is the formula for min-max normalization of a value X given feature minimum X_min and maximum X_max.
Why is standardization preferred over min-max normalization when the dataset contains significant outliers.
A student applies min-max normalization to a feature with values [10, 12, 14, 1000]. Evaluate the effect on the first three values.

cards.title: This node covers the stage after data cleaning: data transformation…
cards.subject: Artificial Intelligence
cards.definition: This node covers the stage after data cleaning: data transformation, feature engineering, and data splitting. Data transformation converts cleaned data into a format suitable for modelling — scaling numerical features (e.g., min‑max normalization, z‑score standardization), encoding categorical variables (one‑hot, label encoding), and handling skewed distributions (log, Box‑Cox). Feature engineering creates new predictive attributes from existing ones — e.g., extracting day‑of‑week from a timestamp, combining “area” and “rooms” into “area_per_room”, or generating polynomial features. Data splitting partitions the dataset into training, validation, and test sets (commonly 70/15/15 or 80/10/10) using stratified sampling to preserve class distribution. These steps are interdependent: transformation must be fitted only on training data to avoid leakage; engineered features must be validated for relevance; and splitting must be reproducible (fixed random seed). Together they turn raw cleaned data into a modelling‑ready pipeline, ensuring the AI system learns generalisable patterns rather than memorising noise.
steps: The key takeaway: every transformation, feature creation, and split decision must be learned solely from the training partition to prevent data leakage and ensure realistic model evaluation.
Here is why: if we compute the mean for standardization using the whole dataset, the test set influences the scaling parameters, leaking future information into the model.
Similarly, creating a feature like “average sales per store” using test data would give the model an unfair advantage.
Stratified splitting preserves the original class ratio, which is critical for imbalanced datasets like fraud detection where fraud cases may be <1%.
Consider a practical Indian example: predicting house prices in Bengaluru.
After cleaning (removing duplicates, imputing missing balcony counts), we have numerical features (area_sqft, bhk, bath) and categorical (location, society).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “stratified splitting makes the model train faster”) reveals the misconception that stratification is about computational efficiency rather than statistical representativeness.
remember: What is the primary purpose of stratified splitting in a classification dataset with imbalanced classes.
A student applies `StandardScaler` on the entire dataset (including test set) before….
Given a numerical feature “annual_income” with a heavy right skew (few very high incomes), which transformation would most effectively reduce skewness for a linear regression….

cards.title: Data processing for AI is a sequential pipeline comprising three interdependent…
cards.subject: Artificial Intelligence
cards.definition: Data processing for AI is a sequential pipeline comprising three interdependent stages: collection, cleaning, and preprocessing. Collection involves acquiring raw data from diverse sources such as sensors, surveys, web scraping, or existing databases, ensuring relevance, legality, and sufficient volume. Cleaning detects and corrects errors — missing values, duplicates, outliers, inconsistent formats — to improve data quality without introducing bias. Preprocessing transforms cleaned data into a format suitable for modelling: scaling numerical features, encoding categorical variables, handling class imbalance, and splitting into train-test sets. Each stage feeds the next; poor collection cannot be fully remedied by cleaning, and inadequate cleaning undermines preprocessing. The pipeline must be documented and reproducible, adhering to privacy norms (e.g., India’s DPDP Act) and ethical guidelines. In the CISCE ISC AI (866) syllabus, students must understand the purpose, techniques, and typical pitfalls of each stage, and be able to design or critique a pipeline for a given problem.
steps: The data processing pipeline — collection, cleaning, preprocessing — must be executed sequentially with careful documentation to ensure reliable AI model inputs.
Here is why: each stage addresses distinct quality dimensions; skipping or reordering stages propagates errors that degrade model performance.
Consider a project predicting Delhi air quality index (AQI) from sensor data.
Collection: you gather hourly PM2.5, temperature, humidity from government portals and low-cost sensors.

If you ignore sensor calibration differences, you introduce systematic bias no cleaning can fix. Cleaning: you find missing hours due to power cuts, duplicate timestamps from overlapping sensors, and outliers like PM2.5…
You impute missing values using linear interpolation, drop exact duplicates, and cap outliers at the 99th percentile.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "preprocessing, cleaning, collection") reveals the misconception that data can be transformed before errors are fixed, ignoring the dependency chain.
remember: List the three main stages of data processing in the correct order.
Why is cleaning performed before preprocessing? Explain with one concrete example.

cards.title: Chapter 6 introduces data modelling through simple linear regression…
cards.subject: Artificial Intelligence
cards.definition: Chapter 6 introduces data modelling through simple linear regression, a supervised learning technique that models the relationship between a single independent variable (predictor) and a dependent variable (response) with a straight line: ŷ = β₀ + β₁x. The chapter covers three core sub‑concepts: (1) regression basics — understanding the linear model, assumptions (linearity, independence, homoscedasticity, normality of residuals), and interpretation of slope and intercept; (2) fitting — estimating β₀ and β₁ using the ordinary least squares (OLS) criterion that minimises the sum of squared residuals, and implementing the calculation in Python with libraries such as NumPy, pandas, and scikit‑learn; (3) evaluation — quantifying model quality via coefficient of determination (R²), mean squared error (MSE), root mean squared error (RMSE), and residual analysis to detect violations of assumptions. Together these pieces enable a student to move from raw bivariate data to a validated predictive model, forming the foundation for multiple regression and more advanced algorithms later in the syllabus.
steps: The chapter equips you to turn two‑column data into a trustworthy straight‑line predictor and to judge its reliability.
Here is why: (1) Simple linear regression is the gateway to all supervised modelling; mastering its mechanics makes later topics intuitive.
(2) The OLS fitting procedure is a concrete optimisation problem — minimise Σ(yᵢ − ŷᵢ)² — that can be solved analytically and programmatically, reinforcing both algebra and coding skills.
(3) Evaluation metrics translate abstract fit quality into numbers (R², MSE) and visual diagnostics (residual plots), teaching you to question a model rather than accept it blindly.
(4) The assumptions checklist (linearity, independence, homoscedasticity, normality) is a reusable mental model for any regression task.
(5) A common exam trap is reporting a high R² while ignoring a curved residual pattern; the chapter explicitly warns against this.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “carpet area”) reveals the misconception that the variable on the x‑axis is always the dependent one, confusing the roles of predictor and response.
remember: What is the dependent variable in a simple linear regression model that predicts house rent from carpet area.
Explain why the ordinary least squares method minimises the sum of squared residuals rather than the sum of absolute residuals.
A student obtains R² = 0.92 for a regression of exam marks on study hours but the residual plot shows a clear U‑shape. Evaluate the model’s adequacy.

cards.title: Simple linear regression is a statistical method that models the relationship…
cards.subject: Artificial Intelligence
cards.definition: Simple linear regression is a statistical method that models the relationship between a single explanatory variable (independent variable, denoted x) and a response variable (dependent variable, denoted y) by fitting a straight line y = a + bx to observed data pairs (xᵢ, yᵢ). The parameters a (intercept) and b (slope) are estimated using the ordinary least squares (OLS) criterion, which minimises the sum of squared vertical residuals Σ(yᵢ − ŷᵢ)² where ŷᵢ = a + bxᵢ. The slope b quantifies the average change in y for a one‑unit increase in x; the intercept a is the predicted y when x = 0. Key assumptions include linearity, independence of errors, homoscedasticity (constant error variance), and normality of residuals. The coefficient of determination R² = 1 − SS_res/SS_tot measures the proportion of variance in y explained by x. Regression does not imply causation; it only describes association. This node covers the conceptual foundation, the OLS derivation, interpretation of parameters, and the distinction between correlation and regression. Fitting algorithms, diagnostic plots, and model evaluation are treated in subsequent nodes.
steps: The one thing to remember: simple linear regression finds the straight line that minimises the sum of squared vertical distances between observed points and the line.

Here is why: the line y = a + bx is chosen so that the total squared error Σ(yᵢ − a − bxᵢ)² is as small as possible; this criterion yields unique formulas for a and b that depend only on the data’s means, variances, and…
Consider a Class 11 student recording weekly study hours (x) and test scores (y) for ten weeks.
First, compute the means x̄ and ȳ.
Next, find the deviations (xᵢ − x̄) and (yᵢ − ȳ).
The slope b equals the covariance of x and y divided by the variance of x: b = Σ(xᵢ − x̄)(yᵢ − ȳ) / Σ(xᵢ − x̄)².
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “minimise the sum of absolute residuals”) reveals the misconception that least squares and least absolute deviations are the same; they differ in sensitivity to outliers and mathematical tractability.
remember: What is the ordinary least squares (OLS) objective function minimised in simple linear regression.
Given a dataset with Σ(xᵢ − x̄)(yᵢ − ȳ) = 120 and Σ(xᵢ − x̄)² = 30, compute the OLS slope estimate b and explain its meaning.
A student claims that a high R² value (close to 1) proves that x causes y. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Fitting in simple linear regression is the process of estimating the two…
cards.subject: Artificial Intelligence
cards.definition:
Fitting in simple linear regression is the process of estimating the two parameters of the model y = β_0 + β_1 x + — the intercept β_0 and the slope β_1 — from a given data set {(x_i, y_i)}_i=1^n. The ordinary least squares (OLS) criterion chooses β_0, β_1 that minimise the sum of squared residuals S(β_0,β_1)=Σ_i=1^n (y_i - β_0 - β_1 x_i)^2. Setting the partial derivatives to zero yields the normal equations, whose closed‑form solution is β_1 = Σ_i=1^n (x_i- x)(y_i- y)Σ_i=1^n (x_i- x)^2
= Cov(x,y) Var(x), β_0 = y - β_1 x. Fitting therefore converts raw paired observations into a predictive rule. The fitted line y = β_0 + β_1 x is the unique line that makes the vertical distances (residuals) squared and summed as small as possible. This node covers the derivation, interpretation of β_1 as the average change in y per unit change in x, and a practical Python implementation using NumPy or scikit‑learn. Evaluation of goodness‑of‑fit (R², residual plots) belongs to the next node.
steps: The OLS method identifies the unique line that minimizes the total squared vertical error, providing a mathematically optimal predictive rule.
Squaring residuals ensures that large errors are penalized more heavily than small ones.
The squaring process makes the function differentiable, allowing for a precise, closed-form algebraic solution.
The resulting line is guaranteed to pass through the centroid of the data, ( x, y).
The slope β_1 provides a clear, interpretable measure of the average change in y for every unit change in x. To fit a line to temperature vs. ice-cream sales data: 1.
Gather data: Collect paired observations for temperature (x) and sales (y).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer such as “minimise the sum of absolute residuals” reveals the misconception that OLS uses absolute deviations; in fact OLS uses squares because squares lead to differentiable normal equations and a unique closed‑form solution, whereas absolute…
remember: What is the ordinary least squares (OLS) criterion for fitting a simple linear regression line.
Given the data points (1,2), (2,3), (3,5), compute the OLS slope β_1 manually.
Explain why the fitted regression line always passes through the point ( x, y).

cards.title: Evaluation in simple linear regression quantifies how well the fitted line…
cards.subject: Artificial Intelligence
cards.definition: Evaluation in simple linear regression quantifies how well the fitted line y=b_0+b_1x reproduces the observed data. The core sub‑concepts are residuals e_i=y_i-y_i, loss functions (Mean Absolute Error MAE, Mean Squared Error MSE, Root Mean Squared Error RMSE), and the coefficient of determination R^2. MAE averages absolute residuals, MSE averages squared residuals (penalising large errors), RMSE returns the error to the original unit, and R^2 expresses the proportion of variance in y explained by x. Residual plots (residuals versus fitted values or versus x) reveal non‑linearity, heteroscedasticity, or outliers. Together these tools let a practitioner decide whether the linear model is adequate or whether a more complex model is required.
steps: Evaluation is the process of quantifying prediction error and inspecting residual patterns to determine if a model is fit for purpose.
This process is essential because a line can be mathematically fitted to any data, but it may not accurately represent the underlying relationship.
Compute predicted values y_i for every observation to establish the baseline for comparison.
Calculate residuals e_i = y_i - y_i to identify the vertical distance between actual data and the model.
Apply loss functions (MAE, MSE, RMSE) to summarize the magnitude of errors, with RMSE providing a unit-consistent measure of typical error.
Determine the coefficient of determination R^2 to assess the proportion of variance explained by the model.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “residual is the horizontal distance from the point to the line”) reveals the misconception that residuals are measured along the x-axis, confusing the geometry of least‑squares which minimises vertical distances.
remember: What does a residual represent in simple linear regression.
Given the residuals [-2, 4, -1, 3] for a fitted model, compute the MAE and MSE.
A student claims that a higher R^2 always means a better model. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: This node covers the four classical assumptions of simple linear regression…
cards.subject: Artificial Intelligence
cards.definition: This node covers the four classical assumptions of simple linear regression — linearity, independence, homoscedasticity, and normality of residuals — and the diagnostic tools used to verify them. Linearity means the true relationship between the predictor (X) and response (Y) is well approximated by a straight line. Independence requires that residuals are not correlated, often checked with the Durbin‑Watson statistic. Homoscedasticity demands constant variance of residuals across all fitted values; a funnel‑shaped residual plot signals violation. Normality assumes residuals follow a Gaussian distribution, assessed via Q‑Q plots or Shapiro‑Wilk test. Residual analysis — plotting residuals versus fitted values, leverage, and Cook’s distance — identifies outliers, high‑leverage points, and influential observations that can distort the fitted line. Understanding these checks ensures the model’s inference (confidence intervals, p‑values) and predictions are trustworthy. This node builds directly on the evaluation metrics (R², MSE, MAE) from the previous node and prepares for multiple regression and regularisation in later nodes.
steps: The validity of a regression model depends on meeting four core assumptions: linearity, independence, homoscedasticity, and normality.
Linearity ensures the straight-line model captures the actual trend; if points curve, the model is misspecified.
Independence ensures each observation provides unique information; correlated residuals invalidate standard error calculations.
Homoscedasticity ensures the model's precision is consistent across the entire range of data.
Normality ensures that hypothesis tests and confidence intervals are mathematically sound.
To verify these, first check linearity by plotting raw data; if points curve, consider a polynomial or log transformation.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “R² tests normality”) reveals the misconception that goodness‑of‑fit metrics replace assumption diagnostics — confusing model fit with model validity.
remember: List the four classical assumptions of simple linear regression and state one diagnostic plot or test for each.
A residual‑versus‑fitted plot shows a clear U‑shaped pattern. Which assumption is violated, and what are two possible remedies.
You compute the Durbin‑Watson statistic for a dataset of 30 observations and obtain d = 1.2. Interpret this value and state the implication for regression inference.

cards.title: Residual analysis is the process of examining the differences between observed…
cards.subject: Artificial Intelligence
cards.definition: Residual analysis is the process of examining the differences between observed values and predicted values (residuals) to validate the assumptions of simple linear regression. Key sub-concepts include: raw residuals (e_i = y_i - ŷ_i), standardized residuals (scaled by estimated standard deviation), residual plots (residuals vs fitted values, residuals vs predictor, normal Q-Q plot), and influence diagnostics (leverage h_i, Cook's distance D_i). These tools detect violations of linearity, homoscedasticity, normality, and independence, and identify outliers or influential points that disproportionately affect the fitted line. Residual analysis directly builds on the fitting (node 003) and evaluation (node 004) stages: after estimating coefficients and computing metrics like R², we must verify that the model's assumptions hold; otherwise, inference and predictions may be unreliable. The relationship is diagnostic: residuals reveal what aggregate metrics hide.
steps: Residual analysis is the essential final step to verify that a model captures the true underlying pattern rather than being misled by noise or outliers.
A residual is the vertical distance from a data point to the fitted line: e = y_observed - y_predicted.
If the model is correct, these residuals should appear as random noise with constant spread and a normal distribution. 1.
Compute residuals for every observation.
In Python, after `model = sm.OLS(y, X).fit()`, you access these via `model.resid`.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "residual is the horizontal distance from the point to the line") reveals the misconception that residuals are measured perpendicular to the line or horizontally, confusing orthogonal regression with ordinary least squares which…
remember: What is a residual in the context of simple linear regression, and what does it represent geometrically.
A student plots residuals versus fitted values and sees a distinct U-shaped pattern. What does this indicate about the model, and which assumption is violated.
In a residual vs predictor plot, the residuals fan out — spread increases as the predictor increases. What assumption is violated, and what are two possible remedies.

cards.title: In simple linear regression, influential observations are data points whose…
cards.subject: Artificial Intelligence
cards.definition: In simple linear regression, influential observations are data points whose removal substantially changes the estimated regression coefficients (slope and intercept). Leverage quantifies how far an independent variable value (x) lies from the mean of x; high leverage points have unusual x-values and can pull the regression line toward themselves. Cook’s distance combines leverage and residual size to measure the overall influence of a point on all fitted values. It is computed as D_i = (r_i^2)/(p · MSE) · h_ii(1-h_ii)^2 where r_i is the residual, p=2 (number of parameters), MSE is mean squared error, and h_ii is the leverage (diagonal of the hat matrix). Points with D_i > 4/n or D_i > 1 are often flagged as influential. This concept extends residual analysis (covered in) by quantifying influence rather than just flagging large residuals. It connects to model robustness: a model driven by few points may not generalize. Understanding influence helps decide whether to investigate, transform, or remove such points before finalising the model.
steps: Let’s continue from where we left off: we have a fitted line y = b_0 + b_1 x and we examined residuals.
Now we ask: Does any single observation control the line?
Step 1 – Leverage (the “pull” of x).
In simple linear regression, leverage for observation i is h_ii = (1)/(n) + ((x_i - x)^2)/(Σ (x_j - x)^2).

The first term 1/n is the average leverage; the second term grows as x_i moves away from x. Think of a seesaw: the pivot is x. A child sitting far from the pivot (extreme study hours) exerts more torque on the…
High leverage alone doesn’t mean the point is bad — it just means the line is sensitive to that x-location.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., (c) Both x_i and y_i) reveals the misconception that leverage measures overall “unusualness” of a point, confusing it with influence which combines leverage and residual.
