cards.title: Simple linear regression models the relationship between a single predictor…
cards.subject: Artificial Intelligence
cards.definition: Simple linear regression models the relationship between a single predictor variable x (independent) and a response variable y (dependent) with a straight line ŷ = a + bx. The slope b quantifies the average change in y per unit change in x; the intercept a is the expected y when x = 0. Parameters are estimated by ordinary least squares (OLS), minimising the sum of squared residuals Σ(yᵢ – ŷᵢ)². Model evaluation uses the coefficient of determination R² (proportion of variance explained), mean squared error (MSE), root mean squared error (RMSE), and mean absolute error (MAE). Residual analysis (plots of residuals vs fitted values, normal Q‑Q plot) checks linearity, homoscedasticity, independence, and normality — assumptions required for valid inference. In the CISCE ISC syllabus, students must derive a and b from raw data, compute R², interpret the slope in context, and answer short‑answer and numerical questions on fitting, evaluation, and assumption diagnostics.
steps: The single most important takeaway for the ISC exam is that every regression question — whether it asks for the line, the goodness‑of‑fit, or a residual check — starts with the same three sums: Σx, Σy, Σxy, Σx², Σy²…
Here is why: the OLS formulas for slope b and intercept a are algebraic rearrangements of those five sums;
R² is a ratio of explained to total variation, both expressed with the same sums; residuals are simply yᵢ – (a + bxᵢ), so once a and b are known, every diagnostic follows mechanically.

Consider a typical ISC 3‑mark question: “Given the data (x, y) = (1,2), (2,3), (3,5), (4,4), (5,6), find the regression line of y on x and compute R².” The student first builds a table with columns x, y, xy, x², y²…
With a and b in hand, predicted values ŷᵢ are generated, residuals eᵢ = yᵢ – ŷᵢ are listed, and R² = 1 – Σeᵢ² / Σ(yᵢ – ȳ)² is computed.
A common exam trap is to confuse the regression of y on x with that of x on y; the slope formulas differ (the denominator uses Σx² vs Σy²).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., b = Σxy / Σx²) reveals the misconception that the regression line passes through the origin, ignoring the intercept term and the correction for means.
remember: Write the ordinary least squares formula for the slope b in simple linear regression of y on x using the five summary sums Σx, Σy, Σxy, Σx², Σy² and sample size n.
Given the data points (2,5), (4,7), (6,10), (8,12), compute the intercept a of the regression line ŷ = a + bx. Show all intermediate sums.
A student calculates R² = 0.85 for a fitted model and claims “the model explains 85 % of the variance in x”. Evaluate this statement.

cards.title: Chapter 7, “Ethical Practices in AI,” introduces the three pillars that every…
cards.subject: Artificial Intelligence
cards.definition: Chapter 7, “Ethical Practices in AI,” introduces the three pillars that every trustworthy AI system must address: bias, privacy, and responsible AI. Bias refers to systematic errors that cause a model to favour or disadvantage certain groups — for example, a credit-scoring model trained mostly on urban applicants may unfairly reject rural borrowers. Privacy concerns the protection of personal data throughout the AI lifecycle, from collection and storage to inference and sharing; Indian contexts such as Aadhaar-linked health apps make this especially salient. Responsible AI is the overarching governance framework that ties bias mitigation and privacy protection together with transparency, accountability, and societal impact assessment. The chapter is organised into eight nodes: this overview (001), three concept nodes that each deep-dive into one pillar (002-004), three further concept nodes that extend the discussion (005-007), and a final synthesis node (008) that maps the material to CISCE exam patterns. Understanding the overview lets students see how the later nodes interlock — bias detection informs privacy-preserving design, and both feed into a responsible-AI checklist — so that the ethical analysis becomes a coherent workflow rather than isolated topics.
steps: Deploying artificial intelligence safely requires systematically evaluating system bias, protecting user privacy, and enforcing clear accountability for outcomes.
First, systems reflect input data, meaning uncalibrated models inherit and amplify real-world inequalities.
Second, digital tracking without consent creates severe surveillance and data-linking vulnerabilities.
Third, algorithmic failures demand explicit ownership structures and accessible public grievance channels.
An AI system functions like a new traffic signal installed at a busy Delhi intersection.
Before it goes live, engineers must address three requirements.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “fairness, transparency, accountability”) reveals the misconception that the chapter’s pillars are the same as generic AI-ethics principles, ignoring the specific CISCE syllabus structure.
remember: What are the three ethical pillars introduced in this chapter.
Why is bias considered a foundational issue before privacy in the chapter sequence.
Assess whether a facial-recognition system deployed in a Mumbai railway station can be ethical if it only addresses privacy but ignores bias.

cards.title: Bias in artificial intelligence refers to systematic and repeatable errors that…
cards.subject: Artificial Intelligence
cards.definition: Bias in artificial intelligence refers to systematic and repeatable errors that cause a model to produce unfair outcomes for certain individuals or groups. It arises when the data used to train a model does not represent the real‑world population, when the labeling process reflects human prejudices, or when the algorithmic design amplifies existing disparities. Bias can be categorized as data bias (sampling, measurement, or label bias), algorithmic bias (objective functions that favour majority classes), and deployment bias (context shift between training and real use). These sub‑concepts interact: biased data feeds a biased algorithm, which in turn reinforces biased decisions when deployed. Detecting bias requires evaluating performance metrics — accuracy, precision, recall, false‑positive/negative rates — separately for each protected attribute (gender, caste, region, language). Mitigation strategies include re‑sampling, re‑weighting, adversarial debiasing, and fairness‑aware constraints. Understanding bias is foundational for responsible AI because it directly impacts privacy (through profiling) and the broader ethical framework covered in later nodes.
steps: Let’s walk through bias step by step, using an Indian context you know.
Step 1 – Data collection.
Suppose a bank wants an AI model to approve home loans.
They gather past loan records from their branches in Mumbai, Delhi, and Bengaluru.
Most applicants are salaried IT professionals; few are farmers from rural Maharashtra.
The dataset therefore under‑represents rural applicants.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “algorithmic bias because the model uses a decision tree”) reveals the misconception that bias originates only from the algorithm, ignoring that the data itself can be…
remember: What is the primary source of data bias in a machine‑learning model trained on historical hiring records from a single large corporation.
A model predicting student dropout risk shows a false‑negative rate of 10 % for urban students and 30 % for rural….
Evaluate the claim: “If we remove the ‘gender’ column from the training data, the model cannot be gender‑biased.”.

cards.title: Privacy in AI refers to the set of principles, techniques…
cards.subject: Artificial Intelligence
cards.definition: Privacy in AI refers to the set of principles, techniques, and legal safeguards that ensure personal or sensitive data is collected, stored, processed, and shared only with the explicit, informed consent of the data subject and strictly for the declared purpose. Core sub‑concepts include data minimisation (collect only what is needed), purpose limitation (use data only for the stated aim), consent management (clear opt‑in/opt‑out mechanisms), anonymisation and pseudonymisation (removing or masking identifiers), access control and encryption (protecting data at rest and in transit), and data retention and deletion policies (erasing data when no longer required). In the Indian context, the Information Technology Act, 2000 (as amended) and the forthcoming Personal Data Protection framework provide the statutory backbone. Privacy interacts closely with bias because biased datasets often arise from non‑representative or improperly consented data, and with responsible AI where privacy is a non‑negotiable pillar of trustworthy systems.
steps: Let’s walk through privacy as if we are building a school health‑survey app that collects students’ height, weight, and allergy information.
Stage 1 – Data Collection (Minimisation & Purpose Limitation).
Before writing any code, ask: What is the minimum data needed?
The school nurse only needs height, weight, and known allergies to plan a nutrition programme.
We must not collect parents’ income, Aadhaar numbers, or full medical histories.
This is data minimisation.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Encryption is the same as anonymisation”) reveals the misconception that protecting data and removing identifiers are…
remember: List the six core privacy principles that must guide any AI data pipeline, and give a one‑sentence Indian example for each.
A student writes a Python script that reads a CSV of student health data, prints the first five rows to the console, and then writes the entire DataFrame to a public GitHub….
Evaluate the claim: “If we encrypt the database with AES‑256, we have fully satisfied the privacy requirement for the health‑survey app.” Provide a reasoned judgement.

cards.title: Responsible AI is a governance framework that ensures artificial‑intelligence…
cards.subject: Artificial Intelligence
cards.definition: Responsible AI is a governance framework that ensures artificial‑intelligence systems are designed, developed, deployed, and monitored in ways that respect human rights, legal obligations, and societal values. It integrates the principles studied in earlier nodes — bias mitigation, privacy protection, transparency, accountability, fairness, robustness, and explainability — into every stage of the AI lifecycle: problem definition, data collection, model training, validation, deployment, and post‑deployment monitoring. A responsible AI system must (1) detect and reduce unfair bias against protected groups, (2) safeguard personal and sensitive data through privacy‑by‑design and compliance with regulations such as the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, (3) provide clear, understandable explanations for its outputs so that users and regulators can scrutinise decisions, (4) establish clear ownership and audit trails for accountability, and (5) maintain performance and safety under changing real‑world conditions. These sub‑concepts are inter‑dependent: privacy‑preserving data practices reduce bias risk; transparency enables bias audits; accountability mechanisms enforce privacy and fairness commitments. Responsible AI therefore acts as the overarching “guardrail” that turns isolated ethical checks into a continuous, organisation‑wide discipline.
steps: We have already seen how bias can creep into a model when training data reflects historic prejudice, and how privacy can be violated if personal identifiers leak into datasets.
Responsible AI stitches those lessons together into a single, repeatable process.
Stage 1 – Problem framing.
Before writing any code, the team asks: “Who will be affected?
What harms could arise?” For a crop‑yield advisory bot used by farmers in Maharashtra, the team lists stakeholders: smallholder farmers, agronomists, local banks.
Potential harms: wrong advice causing loss, exclusion of women farmers who lack smartphones, misuse of soil‑data.
remember: Recall: List the five core pillars of responsible AI as defined in the CISCE ISC Class 11 curriculum.
Reasoning: A school project builds a facial‑recognition attendance system using photos of students taken without explicit….
Evaluate: An agritech startup claims its yield‑prediction model is “responsible” because it achieves 92 % accuracy on a national test set. Critique this claim using responsible‑AI….

cards.title: Transparency in AI refers to the openness of a system’s design, data sources…
cards.subject: Artificial Intelligence
cards.definition: Transparency in AI refers to the openness of a system’s design, data sources, training process, and decision‑making logic to stakeholders (developers, regulators, users). Explainability (or interpretability) is the ability to present the reasons behind a specific output in human‑understandable terms. Together they form a pillar of responsible AI: transparency enables auditability, while explainability supports trust, debugging, and legal compliance (e.g., the right to explanation under data‑protection laws). They relate to bias (transparent data pipelines reveal skewed samples), privacy (explanations must not leak personal data), and accountability (clear logic lets owners be held responsible). Techniques include model cards, datasheets, feature‑importance plots, surrogate models, and counterfactual explanations. The goal is not full disclosure of proprietary code but sufficient insight for meaningful oversight.
steps: Let’s walk through transparency and explainability as if we are building a loan‑approval AI for a regional rural bank in Maharashtra.
Stage 1 – Data transparency.

Before training, we publish a datasheet (Gebru et al., 2021) that lists: source of applicant data (bank records, credit bureau), collection period (Jan 2020‑Dec 2023), preprocessing steps (removing duplicate PAN…
This mirrors the “nutrition label” on a packet of Amul butter — you see ingredients, allergens, and expiry.
Stage 2 – Model transparency.

After training a gradient‑boosted tree, we create a model card (Mitchell et al., 2019) stating: intended use (small‑ticket agri loans), performance metrics (AUC 0.87, false‑negative rate 4 % for women applicants)…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “They are synonyms”) reveals the misconception that openness of process equals clarity of individual decisions — confusing systemic visibility with local interpretability.
remember: What is the primary difference between transparency and explainability in AI systems.
A bank uses a neural network to approve credit….
Evaluate the claim: “If a model card reports high overall accuracy, the system is sufficiently transparent for deployment in a public‑health triage tool.”.

cards.title: Transparency, explainability, and accountability form the trust infrastructure…
cards.subject: Artificial Intelligence
cards.definition: Transparency, explainability, and accountability form the trust infrastructure of responsible AI. Transparency refers to the openness of an AI system’s design, data sources, training process, and decision logic to relevant stakeholders. Explainability is the ability of the system to provide human-understandable reasons for its specific outputs, often through post-hoc methods (e.g., SHAP, LIME) or inherently interpretable models (e.g., decision trees, linear models). Accountability establishes clear ownership for AI outcomes across the lifecycle — from data collection to deployment — including audit trails, human-in-the-loop checkpoints, and redress mechanisms. These three concepts interlink: transparency enables scrutiny, explainability turns scrutiny into understanding, and accountability ensures consequences for harm. In the Indian context, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 and the proposed IndiaAI framework emphasize explainable decisions for high-risk sectors like credit scoring (CIBIL), healthcare diagnostics, and agricultural advisory. This node builds on bias, privacy, and responsible AI principles and the fairness-metrics slice to show how transparent, explainable, and accountable systems operationalize ethical AI.
steps: Let’s walk through the three pillars using an Indian agricultural AI that recommends fertilizer doses to smallholder farmers in Maharashtra. 1.

Transparency — the “glass box” Before the model runs, the development team publishes a model card (like a nutrition label) listing: training data (soil sensor readings from 2018‑2022, covering 5 districts), intended use…
This card is shared in Marathi with farmer cooperatives.
Transparency also means the code repository is accessible to auditors, and the data provenance log shows each sensor’s calibration date.
In class, you saw bias node where skewed training data caused unfair loan denials.
Transparency prevents that by exposing data gaps early. 2.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “transparency means open‑sourcing the code”) reveals the misconception that transparency equals full public code release, ignoring that transparency can be selective (shared with auditors, regulators) and includes documentation artifacts…
remember: Define transparency, explainability, and accountability in AI. Give one distinct Indian example for each.
Why is explainability necessary for high‑stakes AI decisions even when the model achieves high accuracy? Reason with reference to the bias‑fairness concepts from earlier nodes.
Compare SHAP and LIME for explaining a gradient‑boosted tree ensemble used in a loan‑approval system for a regional rural bank. Which would you recommend and why.

cards.title: Transparency and explainability in AI refer to the principle that AI systems…
cards.subject: Artificial Intelligence
cards.definition: Transparency and explainability in AI refer to the principle that AI systems must make their decision-making processes understandable to humans. Transparency involves openness about data sources, model architecture, training objectives, and deployment context. Explainability goes further: it requires that individual predictions or behaviors can be interpreted in human-meaningful terms (e.g., feature importance, counterfactuals, or rule extraction). These concepts are distinct from but complementary to bias mitigation (which ensures fairness across groups) and privacy protection (which safeguards data). Responsible AI frameworks (such as those from NITI Aayog or IEEE) treat transparency as a prerequisite for accountability — without it, audits, redressal, and public trust are impossible. Sub-concepts include global interpretability (understanding the whole model), local interpretability (explaining a single prediction), and model-agnostic methods (e.g., LIME, SHAP) that work across algorithms. In the Indian context, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 emphasizes purpose limitation and consent, which align with transparent data usage. This node focuses on the technical and governance mechanisms that enable stakeholders — developers, regulators, users — to scrutinize AI systems.
steps: Let’s walk through transparency and explainability step by step, connecting to what you already know about bias and privacy.
Stage 1: Why do we need to see inside the black box?
In earlier nodes you learned that biased models can discriminate (e.g., a loan approval AI rejecting applicants from certain pin codes) and that privacy laws require knowing what data is used.
But even if a model is fair and privacy-compliant, stakeholders still ask: “How did it reach this decision?” Imagine a hospital AI that flags a patient as high-risk for diabetes.
The doctor needs to know why — is it BMI, family history, or a spurious correlation with zip code?
Without an explanation, the doctor cannot validate, the patient cannot consent meaningfully, and the hospital cannot be held accountable.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “they both just mean open source”) reveals the misconception that transparency only means code availability, ignoring the need for human-understandable reasoning per decision.
remember: A student says, "Transparency and explainability are the same thing — both mean showing how the AI works." Is this….
Why is a model card (as recommended by NITI Aayog) considered a transparency artifact but not an explainability artifact.
Evaluate this claim: "If a model is highly accurate, we don’t need explainability because the results speak for themselves." Use a healthcare example.

cards.title: This synthesis node integrates the three core ethical pillars — bias, privacy…
cards.subject: Artificial Intelligence
cards.definition: This synthesis node integrates the three core ethical pillars — bias, privacy, and responsible AI — into a single framework that mirrors CISCE ISC Class 11 Artificial Intelligence (866) assessment patterns. Bias refers to systematic deviations in data or algorithmic outcomes that favour or disfavour specific groups; privacy concerns the protection of personal and sensitive information throughout the AI lifecycle; responsible AI denotes the governance, transparency, accountability, and fairness mechanisms that ensure systems operate ethically. The node demonstrates how these sub‑concepts interact: biased training data can violate privacy when proxy attributes reveal protected characteristics, and responsible‑AI practices (audit trails, impact assessments, diverse development teams) mitigate both. It maps each concept to typical CISCE question types — short‑answer definitions, case‑study analysis, diagram labelling, and extended‑response design tasks — and provides practice items that require students to evaluate, apply, and create ethical safeguards in realistic Indian contexts (e.g., Aadhaar‑linked health diagnostics, regional language NLP models, agricultural yield prediction for smallholder farmers).
steps: The takeaway is that every CISCE AI ethics case study must be evaluated through the three-pillar lens of bias, privacy, and responsible AI to ensure a comprehensive, high-scoring response.
Supporting arguments:
CISCE examiners look for the integration of all three pillars; addressing only one or two results in significant mark deductions.
Indian contexts, such as Aadhaar-linked systems or regional language models, are essential for demonstrating the practical application of ethical principles.
A structured approach—defining the pillar, analysing the specific case, and recommending a concrete mitigation—is the standard for securing full marks.
Timed practice with past-paper scenarios builds the speed and precision required for the board exam.
remember: List the three ethical pillars that must be analysed together in every CISCE ISC AI ethics case study.
A student writes: “If a model has 95 % accuracy, it is ethically sound.” Using the three pillars, explain why this statement is insufficient for a CISCE 6‑mark answer.
Evaluate the following mitigation for a biased language model: “Add more English sentences to the training corpus.” Is this….

cards.title: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a branch of computer science concerned with…
cards.subject: Artificial Intelligence
cards.definition: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a branch of computer science concerned with creating systems that can perform tasks normally requiring human intelligence. These tasks include perception (recognising images or speech), reasoning (solving puzzles, planning), learning (improving from experience), and natural language understanding. An AI system typically consists of three intertwined components: data (the raw material), algorithms (the procedures that process data), and models (the learned representations that enable prediction or decision‑making). Unlike traditional software where rules are hard‑coded, AI systems adjust their internal parameters based on exposure to data, a process called training. The field spans symbolic AI (logic‑based reasoning), machine learning (statistical pattern recognition), and deep learning (multi‑layer neural networks). Key relationships: data feeds algorithms; algorithms produce models; models drive decisions; decisions generate new data, closing the loop. AI is not a single algorithm but a framework that integrates data handling, model building, evaluation, and deployment. Understanding this definition sets the foundation for later topics such as the role of data, evolution of AI, decision‑making overview, project framework components, and data representation.
steps: Let’s start with something you already know: a calculator app. You type 12 × 15 and it instantly shows 180.
The calculator follows a fixed set of instructions written by a programmer — it never “learns” a new way to multiply.
Now think of a music‑recommendation app like Gaana or JioSaavn.
The first time you open it, it suggests popular Bollywood tracks.
As you listen, skip, or like songs, the app starts offering tracks that match your taste.
That change happens because the system analyses your listening history (data), runs a learning algorithm, builds a model of your preferences, and then uses that model to decide what to play next.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., choosing C) reveals the misconception that AI equals deep learning only, ignoring symbolic AI, statistical learning, and other paradigms.
remember: Recall: Which of the following best describes the fundamental difference between a traditional rule‑based program and an AI….
Reasoning: In the music‑recommendation example, identify the data, algorithm, and model components. Explain how the feedback loop operates when a user skips a suggested song.
Evaluate: “An AI system that has been trained once on a static dataset will continue to perform optimally forever without further data.” Assess this statement.

cards.title: Data refers to raw, unprocessed facts such as numbers, text, images…
cards.subject: Artificial Intelligence
cards.definition: Data refers to raw, unprocessed facts such as numbers, text, images, or sensor readings that have no inherent meaning on their own. Information is data that has been organized, structured, or interpreted to give it context and purpose, enabling decisions or actions. In Artificial Intelligence, data serves as the foundational fuel: models learn patterns from historical data, and the quality, quantity, and relevance of that data directly determine model accuracy, fairness, and robustness. The transformation from data to information involves steps like cleaning (removing errors), integration (combining sources), feature engineering (creating meaningful attributes), and labeling (assigning target values). High‑quality data is accurate, complete, consistent, timely, and representative of the problem domain. Poor data — noisy, biased, incomplete, or outdated — leads to unreliable predictions, a phenomenon often summarized as “garbage in, garbage out.” Understanding the role of data and information also includes recognizing ethical considerations: privacy, consent, and bias mitigation are integral to responsible AI development. This node focuses on these concepts, linking them to the AI project lifecycle covered in later nodes.
steps: Data becomes actionable information for AI through a systematic pipeline of collection, cleaning, integration, engineering, and labeling.
First, raw data must be gathered from diverse sources like farm sensors, user clicks, or hospital records, which initially lack context.
Second, rigorous cleaning eliminates messy issues such as missing values, duplicates, and inconsistent units like Celsius versus Fahrenheit.
Third, integration and feature engineering combine multiple datasets and transform daily readings into predictive attributes like average weekly rainfall.
Fourth, proper labeling assigns target outcomes, such as high or low yield, enabling supervised models to learn accurately.
Finally, ethical checks ensure proper consent and representation across all groups, preventing biased or faulty predictions.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “data and information are synonyms”) reveals the misconception that the terms are interchangeable, ignoring the crucial processing step that adds context and utility.
remember: What is the primary distinction between data and information in the context of Artificial Intelligence.
A student claims that “more data always improves an AI model.” Using the concept of data quality, evaluate this claim.
Consider a dataset of customer reviews for a Hindi‑language e‑commerce….

cards.title: The evolution of Artificial Intelligence traces the historical progression from…
cards.subject: Artificial Intelligence
cards.definition: The evolution of Artificial Intelligence traces the historical progression from symbolic reasoning to statistical learning and finally to representation learning. The first wave (1950s‑1970s) focused on symbolic AI — hand‑crafted rules, logic programming, and search algorithms (e.g., the Logic Theorist, General Problem Solver). The second wave (1980s‑1990s) introduced expert systems that encoded domain knowledge as if‑then rules (e.g., MYCIN for medical diagnosis) and early neural networks limited by hardware. The third wave (2000s‑present) is driven by machine learning, where algorithms learn patterns from data; key milestones include Support Vector Machines, Random Forests, and the resurgence of neural networks as deep learning after 2012 (AlexNet on ImageNet). Each wave retains useful ideas — search, knowledge representation, gradient‑based optimisation — while discarding bottlenecks such as manual feature engineering. The evolution also reflects shifting data availability, compute capacity, and algorithmic insight, forming a feedback loop: more data enables larger models, which demand more compute, which spurs hardware innovation (GPUs, TPUs). Understanding this trajectory helps students situate current AI techniques (transformers, reinforcement learning) within a continuum rather than as isolated inventions.
steps: The evolution of AI is a three‑wave progression where each wave solves the bottlenecks of its predecessor by leveraging more data, more compute, and better algorithms.

Here is why: the first wave relied on explicit human‑written rules, which scaled poorly; the second wave encoded expert knowledge but still required manual feature design; the third wave lets machines discover features…
Consider the task of recognising handwritten Devanagari digits.
In the 1960s a symbolic program would need handcrafted stroke detectors for each character — brittle and labour‑intensive.
In the 1990s an expert system could store rules from calligraphers, yet still failed on noisy scans.
After 2012 a convolutional neural network trained on millions of labelled images learns edge, curve, and loop detectors automatically, achieving >99 % accuracy on the MNIST‑Devanagari benchmark.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “ELIZA”) reveals the misconception that early AI was only about natural language conversation, confusing a later 1960s chatbot with the foundational theorem‑proving work.
remember: Which landmark program, developed in 1956, is widely regarded as the first AI system to prove mathematical theorems using symbolic logic.
Explain why expert systems of the 1980s, despite capturing domain knowledge, could not scale to complex perception tasks such as image recognition.
Evaluate the claim: “The resurgence of neural networks after 2012 was solely due to the invention of the back‑propagation algorithm.”.

cards.title: Decision making in Artificial Intelligence refers to the systematic process by…
cards.subject: Artificial Intelligence
cards.definition: Decision making in Artificial Intelligence refers to the systematic process by which an intelligent agent selects a course of action from a set of alternatives to achieve a defined objective. The process comprises four tightly coupled components: (1) Perception – acquiring raw data from sensors or databases; (2) Representation – structuring that data into a formal state space (features, variables, constraints); (3) Evaluation – applying a model (rule‑based, probabilistic, or learned) to estimate the utility, risk, or reward of each feasible action; and (4) Selection – choosing the action that optimises the evaluation criterion (e.g., maximum expected utility, minimum loss, highest confidence). The quality of the decision hinges on the fidelity of the data (covered in node), the expressive power of the representation (previewed in node), and the suitability of the evaluation model (which evolves from simple heuristics to sophisticated learning algorithms as described in node). Decision making can be reactive (instantaneous, rule‑driven), deliberative (planning over a horizon), or adaptive (updating the model online). In the CISCE ISC AI curriculum, this node provides the conceptual scaffold; concrete algorithms such as decision trees, Markov decision processes, or reinforcement learning are reserved for later chapters.
steps: Let’s walk through the decision‑making loop as if we are designing an AI that helps a Delhi‑based food‑delivery startup assign orders to riders.
Step 1 – Perception (Data Acquisition).
The system continuously receives streams: rider GPS locations, restaurant preparation times, traffic feeds from Google Maps, and customer ratings.
This mirrors the “Role of data and information” node — without clean, timely data the downstream steps crumble.
Step 2 – Representation (State Space).

Raw streams are transformed into a structured state: each rider becomes a feature vector (current location, load, average speed, rating), each order a vector (pickup point, drop point, promised delivery time, food type).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Evaluation → Perception → Representation → Selection”) reveals the misconception that the model can evaluate before data is structured — confusing the need for a defined state space prior to scoring.
remember: Recall the four core components of the AI decision‑making loop in the correct order.
A student claims that a reactive decision‑making system always outperforms a deliberative one because it is….
Evaluate the statement: “Improving data quality alone guarantees better AI decisions, regardless of representation or model choice.”.

cards.title: The AI project framework is a structured…
cards.subject: Artificial Intelligence
cards.definition: The AI project framework is a structured, iterative lifecycle that guides the development of an artificial intelligence system from conception to maintenance. Its core components are: (1) Problem Definition – translating a business or research need into a clear, measurable objective (e.g., “predict crop yield for Maharashtra farmers”). (2) Data Acquisition – identifying, collecting, and storing relevant data from sources such as sensors, public repositories, or manual entry, ensuring legal and ethical compliance. (3) Data Preparation – cleaning, transforming, augmenting, and splitting data into training, validation, and test sets; handling missing values, class imbalance, and feature engineering. (4) Model Selection & Architecture Design – choosing algorithms (e.g., decision trees, neural networks) and defining hyper‑parameters, guided by problem type (classification, regression, clustering) and resource constraints. (5) Training – fitting the model on training data, using techniques like cross‑validation, regularisation, and early stopping to avoid over‑fitting. (6) Evaluation – measuring performance with domain‑appropriate metrics (accuracy, F1‑score, RMSE, AUC) on unseen test data, and conducting error analysis. (7) Deployment – packaging the model (e.g., as a REST API, edge device binary) and integrating it into the target environment with monitoring hooks. (8) Monitoring & Maintenance – tracking data drift, model decay, and operational metrics; scheduling retraining cycles. The framework emphasises version control (code, data, model), reproducibility (experiment tracking), and responsible AI practices (bias audit, privacy, explainability) throughout. Each component feeds into the next, and feedback loops allow returning to earlier stages — making the process cyclic rather than linear.
steps: The AI project framework is a repeatable, eight‑stage cycle that turns a vague idea into a reliable, maintainable intelligent system.
Here is why: each stage produces a concrete artefact that the next stage consumes, and feedback from later stages forces revisiting earlier ones, preventing costly rework.
Consider a team building a Hindi‑language chatbot for a rural e‑governance portal.

First, Problem Definition frames the goal: “Answer 90 % of farmer queries about MSP rates within 2 seconds.” Next, Data Acquisition gathers query logs, government PDFs, and crowd‑sourced translations, storing them in a…
Data Preparation then cleans the text (removing OCR errors), tokenises using Indic‑NLP, balances intent classes, and splits 70/15/15.
Model Selection compares a lightweight Bi‑LSTM against a distilled mBERT, choosing the former for low‑latency edge deployment.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Model Selection”) reveals the misconception that model‑related decisions include data partitioning — confusing algorithm choice with data engineering.
remember: Which component of the AI project framework is responsible for splitting the dataset into training, validation, and test sets.
A team has trained a model and obtained high accuracy on the validation set but poor performance on the test set. Which framework component should they revisit first to diagnose….
In the AI project framework, which component explicitly addresses legal and ethical compliance during data gathering.

cards.title: Data representation in artificial intelligence refers to the systematic methods…
cards.subject: Artificial Intelligence
cards.definition: Data representation in artificial intelligence refers to the systematic methods used to convert raw observations — text, images, audio, sensor readings, categorical labels — into structured numerical forms that algorithms can process. The core sub‑concepts include: 1. Data types – primitive (integer, float, boolean) and composite (strings, arrays). 2. Encoding schemes – one‑hot encoding for nominal categories, label encoding for ordinal categories, tokenisation and embedding for text, pixel‑intensity matrices for images, spectrograms for audio. 3. Vector / tensor representation – arranging encoded values into 1‑D vectors, 2‑D matrices, or higher‑order tensors so that linear‑algebra operations (dot product, matrix multiplication) become possible. 4. Normalization / scaling – min‑max scaling, z‑score standardisation, or robust scaling to bring disparate features onto a comparable range, preventing domination by large‑magnitude attributes. 5. Dimensionality reduction – techniques such as PCA or auto‑encoders that compress high‑dimensional vectors while preserving variance, useful for visualisation and computational efficiency. These elements relate hierarchically: raw data → encoding → numeric array → scaling → optional dimensionality reduction → model‑ready tensor. The choice of representation directly influences model performance, training speed, and interpretability, making it a foundational design decision in every AI project.
steps: Let’s walk through the journey of a single observation — a student’s record from a school in Bengaluru — from paper to a tensor ready for a classifier that predicts whether the student will opt for the science stream.
Step 1 – Identify raw fields.
The register holds: name (text), age (integer), gender (Male/Female), mother‑tongue (Kannada, Hindi, English, …), previous‑year‑percentage (float), and extracurricular‑activity (Yes/No).

Step 2 – Choose encodings. - Name is high‑cardinality text; we drop it or hash it — not used for prediction. - Age and percentage are already numeric → keep as floats. - Gender is binary → label‑encode (Male = 0, Female…
Step 3 – Assemble the feature vector.
After encoding, each student becomes a 1‑D vector of length 8: [age, percentage, gender, extracurricular, tongue_Kannada, tongue_Hindi, tongue_English, tongue_Other].
remember: What is the primary reason for converting categorical variables such as “mother‑tongue” into one‑hot vectors instead of using label encoding.
A dataset contains a feature “annual family income” ranging from ₹50,000 to….
Explain why z‑score standardisation is preferred over min‑max scaling when the data contains significant outliers, such as a few families earning ₹50,000,000.

cards.title: Chapter 9 of the ISC Class 11 Artificial Intelligence (866) syllabus provides a…
cards.subject: Artificial Intelligence
cards.definition: Chapter 9 of the ISC Class 11 Artificial Intelligence (866) syllabus provides a panoramic view of the field by organizing content into four tightly linked subtopics. The first, Brief history and primary elements of AI, traces the evolution from early symbolic programs to modern machine-learning paradigms and identifies the core building blocks — search, knowledge representation, learning, and reasoning — that every AI system relies upon. The second, Domain of Natural Language Processing, narrows the focus to the specialized branch that enables machines to comprehend, generate, and translate human language, showing how the primary elements (especially learning and representation) are instantiated in linguistic tasks. The third, Potential uses of AI, surveys concrete application domains — agriculture (crop-disease detection), healthcare (diagnostic imaging), finance (fraud detection), education (adaptive tutoring) — and demonstrates how the capabilities described in the first two subtopics translate into societal value. The fourth, AI and society, examines ethical, legal, and economic implications such as bias, privacy, job displacement, and regulatory frameworks, encouraging students to evaluate technology through a responsible lens. Together, the four subtopics form a logical narrative: history supplies context, elements supply mechanisms, NLP supplies a flagship capability, uses supply deployment scenarios, and society supplies critical reflection. This structure ensures that learners progress from foundational concepts to real-world impact without gaps.
steps: This chapter is a roadmap for the whole AI journey you will take in Class 11.
In Class 10 you already met the idea that a computer can “think” in a narrow sense — like a chess engine that searches moves.
Chapter 9 starts by asking how we got here.
You will walk through the Dartmouth workshop of 1956, the rise and fall of expert systems, the “AI winter”, and the resurgence powered by data and GPUs.
This history is not a list of dates; it explains why today’s AI relies on learning from data rather than hand-crafted rules.
Next, the syllabus isolates the primary elements — search, knowledge representation, learning, reasoning — and shows how each element is a reusable component.
remember: Which four subtopics constitute Chapter 9 of the ISC Class 11 Artificial Intelligence syllabus.
Why does the syllabus place “Brief history and primary elements of AI” before “Domain of Natural Language Processing”.
Assess whether the inclusion of “AI and society” as the final subtopic is pedagogically sound.

cards.title: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is the branch of computer science that creates…
cards.subject: Artificial Intelligence
cards.definition: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is the branch of computer science that creates systems capable of performing tasks that normally require human intelligence. Its brief history begins with Alan Turing’s 1950 paper proposing a test for machine intelligence, followed by the 1956 Dartmouth Conference where John McCarthy coined the term “Artificial Intelligence.” Early work focused on symbolic reasoning (Logic Theorist, General Problem Solver) and rule‑based expert systems in the 1970s‑80s. The “AI winter” periods saw reduced funding when expectations outpaced hardware. From the 1990s, machine learning — especially statistical learning and neural networks — revived progress, culminating in deep learning breakthroughs after 2012. The primary elements of AI, often called its “core capabilities,” are: (1) Learning – algorithms that improve performance from data (supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement). (2) Reasoning – logical inference, planning, and problem solving using knowledge representation. (3) Perception – interpreting sensory input such as images (computer vision) and sound (speech recognition). (4) Natural Language Processing – understanding and generating human language (covered in detail in the next node). (5) Robotics/Actuation – physical interaction with the world. These elements interact: learning feeds reasoning, perception supplies data to learning, and language bridges human‑machine communication. The node focuses on this historical arc and the five pillars, leaving deeper NLP, applications, and societal impact to subsequent nodes.
steps: Let’s walk through the story of AI as if we are flipping through a family album. 1.
The Spark (1950‑1956).
Alan Turing, a British mathematician, asked “Can machines think?” and proposed the Imitation Game — now called the Turing Test.
Six years later, John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester and Claude Shannon gathered at Dartmouth College for a summer workshop.
They wrote a proposal that first used the phrase “Artificial Intelligence.” Think of this as the moment a group of friends decided to build a “thinking machine” club. 2.
Symbolic Era (late 1950s‑1970s).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., choosing A) reveals the misconception that Turing’s test was proposed earlier than it actually was, confusing the 1948 “Intelligent Machinery” report with the 1950 Mind paper.
