Industrially, lactic acid fermentation acidifies foods, preserving them and imparting flavor, while alcohol fermentation produces ethanol for beverages and fuel, with CO₂ as a useful by‑product in baking. Physiologically, lactic acid accumulation lowers muscle pH, contributing to fatigue, whereas ethanol is toxic at high concentrations, limiting yeast tolerance.
steps: Takeaway: Anaerobic fermentation is a universal, oxygen‑independent strategy that recycles NADH to NAD⁺ so glycolysis can keep producing a small but vital supply of ATP when oxidative phosphorylation is unavailable.
Supporting argument 1 – The NAD⁺ bottleneck: Glycolysis generates 2 NADH per glucose.
Without a way to re‑oxidize NADH, the glyceraldehyde‑3‑phosphate dehydrogenase step halts, stopping ATP synthesis.
Fermentation solves this by using an endogenous organic molecule (pyruvate or its derivative) as the final electron acceptor.
Supporting argument 2 – Two distinct enzymatic routes: In lactic acid fermentation, a single enzyme (lactate dehydrogenase) transfers electrons from NADH directly to pyruvate, forming lactate.
In alcohol fermentation, two enzymes act sequentially: pyruvate decarboxylase removes CO₂ to make acetaldehyde, then alcohol dehydrogenase reduces acetaldehyde to ethanol using NADH.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “oxygen” or “acetaldehyde”) reveals the misconception that fermentation uses an external electron acceptor or confuses the two fermentation types.
remember: What is the immediate electron acceptor that regenerates NAD⁺ in lactic acid fermentation.
Why does yeast produce ethanol and CO₂ instead of lactate during anaerobic glucose metabolism.
Evaluate the statement: “Lactic acid fermentation yields more ATP per glucose than alcohol fermentation.”.

cards.title: Mutation is a permanent alteration in the nucleotide sequence of an organism’s…
cards.subject: Biotechnology
cards.definition: Mutation is a permanent alteration in the nucleotide sequence of an organism’s genome. Causes of mutation are broadly classified into spontaneous and induced categories. Spontaneous mutations arise from intrinsic cellular processes: errors during DNA replication (e.g., tautomeric shifts causing base mispairing), spontaneous hydrolytic deamination of cytosine to uracil or 5‑methylcytosine to thymine, depurination leading to apurinic sites, and oxidative damage from reactive oxygen species generated during normal metabolism. Induced mutations result from exposure to external mutagens. Physical mutagens include ionising radiation (X‑rays, γ‑rays, α/β particles) that cause single‑ and double‑strand breaks, and non‑ionising UV radiation (especially UV‑B, 280–315 nm) that forms cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers and 6‑4 photoproducts. Chemical mutagens encompass base analogues (5‑bromouracil, 2‑aminopurine) that mispair during replication, alkylating agents (ethyl methanesulfonate, nitrosoguanidine) that add alkyl groups altering base‑pairing, intercalating agents (acridine orange, ethidium bromide) that insert between bases causing frameshifts, and oxidative chemicals (hydrogen peroxide) that modify bases. Biological mutagens include transposon insertion, viral integration, and errors by error‑prone DNA polymerases (e.g., Pol ζ, Pol η) during translesion synthesis. The relationship between cause and mutation type is direct: replication errors and deamination mainly produce point mutations (gene mutations), while strand breaks and misrepair generate chromosomal mutations (deletions, duplications, translocations, inversions). Understanding these causes underpins the classification of mutations into somatic vs. germinal, spontaneous vs. induced, and gene vs. chromosomal — each addressed in subsequent concept nodes.
steps: The one essential takeaway: Mutations arise either from inevitable imperfections in the cell’s own DNA‑handling machinery (spontaneous) or from external agents that damage DNA (induced), and the nature of the cause…
Here is why: DNA replication, though highly accurate, occasionally misincorporates bases because tautomeric forms of bases pair incorrectly; this yields point mutations.
Spontaneous hydrolytic reactions — deamination of cytosine to uracil and depurination creating baseless sites — also produce single‑base alterations if not repaired before the next replication round.
Endogenous reactive oxygen species oxidise guanine to 8‑oxoguanine, which mispairs with adenine, again a point mutation.
These three mechanisms together account for the bulk of spontaneous mutations in every dividing cell.
Induced mutations, by contrast, are triggered by agents we encounter.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “UV radiation causes spontaneous point mutations”) reveals the misconception that any point mutation is spontaneous — UV is an external physical mutagen, not an intrinsic cellular error.
remember: Name two spontaneous molecular events that can change a single DNA base without any external mutagen.
Explain why ionising radiation predominantly causes chromosomal mutations rather than only point mutations.
A researcher treats a bacterial culture with ethyl methanesulfonate (EMS) and observes a high frequency of G·C → A·T….

cards.title: Somatic mutations are alterations in the nucleotide sequence of DNA that occur…
cards.subject: Biotechnology
cards.definition: Somatic mutations are alterations in the nucleotide sequence of DNA that occur in any cell of the body except the germ cells (sperm or ova). Because they arise after fertilisation, they are present only in the descendant cells of the mutated cell, creating a mosaic organism where some cells carry the change and others do not. These mutations can be caused by endogenous factors such as replication errors, oxidative stress, or exogenous agents like UV radiation, tobacco carcinogens, and certain chemicals. They are not transmitted to the next generation, distinguishing them from germinal mutations. Somatic mutations underlie many cancers (e.g., TP53, KRAS), contribute to ageing, and can produce visible mosaicism such as sectorial pigmentation in skin or sectorial variegation in plants. The functional impact depends on the gene affected, the type of alteration (point mutation, insertion, deletion, chromosomal rearrangement), and the developmental stage at which the mutation occurs. Early embryonic somatic mutations affect a larger proportion of tissues than those arising later. Detection often requires deep sequencing of affected tissue because the mutant allele frequency may be low.
steps: Somatic mutations are DNA changes confined to body cells and therefore cannot be inherited.
Here is why: they arise after the zygote forms, so only the lineage of the mutated cell carries the alteration, producing a genetic mosaic.
First, endogenous sources such as spontaneous depurination, oxidative damage from reactive oxygen species, and replication slippage introduce errors during normal metabolism.
Second, exogenous agents like ultraviolet B radiation from sunlight, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in tobacco smoke, and alkylating chemicals directly modify bases or cause strand breaks.
Third, if a mutation hits a gene controlling cell division (e.g., TP53), the affected clone may expand uncontrollably, forming a tumour — this is the somatic mutation theory of cancer.

Fourth, early embryonic somatic mutations affect many tissues, creating widespread mosaicism (e.g., McCune‑Albright syndrome), whereas late mutations affect only a small patch (e.g., a pigmented naevus).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “both can be inherited if they happen early”) reveals the misconception that any early mutation automatically enters the germline, confusing developmental timing with cell lineage.
remember: What is the fundamental difference between a somatic mutation and a germinal mutation regarding inheritance.
Explain how oxidative stress can lead to a somatic point mutation in a liver cell.
Evaluate the statement: “All somatic mutations cause cancer.”.

cards.title: A germinal mutation is a permanent alteration in the nucleotide sequence of DNA…
cards.subject: Biotechnology
cards.definition: A germinal mutation is a permanent alteration in the nucleotide sequence of DNA that occurs in germ‑line cells (spermatogonia, oogonia, or their meiotic products). Because these cells give rise to gametes, the mutation is transmitted to the next generation and becomes part of the offspring’s constitutional genome. Germinal mutations contrast with somatic mutations (node), which arise in non‑reproductive cells and are not inherited. They may be spontaneous (arising from replication errors, tautomeric shifts, or endogenous DNA damage) or induced (caused by external mutagens such as radiation or chemicals) — concepts covered in nodes and. At the molecular level a germinal mutation can be a gene mutation (single‑base change, small insertion/deletion) or a chromosomal mutation (large‑scale rearrangements, aneuploidy, polyploidy) — detailed in nodes and. The key relationship: germinal → heritable → appears in every cell of the offspring → can affect phenotype, disease risk, and evolutionary change.
steps: Only mutations in the germ line enter the gene pool; they are the ones that matter for heredity, genetic counselling, and long‑term species change.

This is supported by the fact that gametes are the sole transmitters of genetic information to the next generation, DNA copying errors during gametogenesis become permanent if uncorrected, the resulting zygote…
Every human starts as a single fertilised egg — a zygote formed by the fusion of a sperm and an ovum.
Those two gametes are the only cells that pass genetic information to the next generation.
During gametogenesis (spermatogenesis in testes, oogenesis in ovaries) the germ‑line cells undergo many rounds of mitosis followed by meiosis.
Each division copies the entire genome; occasionally the DNA polymerase inserts a wrong base, a strand slips, or a reactive oxygen species damages a base.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “germinal mutations are only those caused by radiation”) reveals the misconception that mutagen source defines germinal status, confusing origin with cell type.
remember: What is the defining feature that makes a mutation germinal rather than somatic.
A researcher sequences DNA from a patient’s blood lymphocytes and finds a single‑base substitution absent in the patient’s parents’ blood DNA. The same substitution is also found….
Evaluate the statement: “All hereditary diseases are caused by germinal mutations, so somatic mutations have no clinical relevance.”.

cards.title: A spontaneous mutation is a permanent alteration in the DNA sequence that…
cards.subject: Biotechnology
cards.definition: A spontaneous mutation is a permanent alteration in the DNA sequence that arises without exposure to an external mutagen. It originates from intrinsic cellular processes such as errors during DNA replication, spontaneous chemical changes in bases (tautomeric shifts, depurination, deamination, oxidative damage), and faulty DNA repair. Spontaneous mutations can be point mutations (single‑base substitutions, insertions, or deletions) or frameshift mutations when the reading frame is altered. They may occur in somatic cells (affecting only the individual) or germinal cells (heritable). Unlike induced mutations, which require an external agent (UV, chemicals, radiation), spontaneous mutations reflect the baseline error rate of the replication‑repair machinery. In the CISCE ISC syllabus they are classified alongside somatic, germinal, induced, gene‑level, and chromosomal mutations, and they provide the raw material for evolution and genetic disease.
steps: Let’s walk through a spontaneous mutation as if we were watching a cell divide in a mango tree’s meristem. 1.
DNA replication begins — the double helix unwinds and each strand serves as a template.
DNA polymerase adds complementary nucleotides. 2.
A rare mistake occurs — polymerase may insert a wrong base (e.g., A opposite C) because the template base momentarily adopts a rare tautomeric form (keto ↔ enol, amino ↔ imino).
This fleeting shape change alters hydrogen‑bonding preferences, so the wrong nucleotide fits. 3.
Chemical instability of bases — a purine (adenine or guanine) can lose its bond to the sugar (depurination), leaving an apurinic site.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “spontaneous mutations are caused by radiation”) reveals the misconception that all mutations need an outside trigger, confusing the baseline error rate with mutagen‑induced damage.
remember: What is the fundamental difference between a spontaneous mutation and an induced mutation.
Which of the following molecular events is a classic example of a spontaneous mutation….
Evaluate the statement: “Spontaneous mutations are always harmful to the organism.”.

cards.title: Induced mutation refers to a heritable alteration in the nucleotide sequence of…
cards.subject: Biotechnology
cards.definition: Induced mutation refers to a heritable alteration in the nucleotide sequence of DNA that results from exposure to an external mutagenic agent. Mutagens are classified into three broad categories: physical (e.g., ionizing radiation such as X‑rays and gamma rays, non‑ionizing UV radiation), chemical (e.g., alkylating agents like ethyl methanesulfonate (EMS), base analogues such as 5‑bromouracil, intercalating agents like ethidium bromide), and biological (e.g., transposable elements, viral integration). Each class damages DNA through distinct mechanisms: UV radiation induces cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers, ionizing radiation causes single‑ and double‑strand breaks, alkylating agents add methyl or ethyl groups to bases leading to mispairing, and transposons insert themselves into genes disrupting function. Induced mutations can be gene‑level (point mutations, small insertions/deletions) or chromosomal (large deletions, duplications, inversions, translocations). They differ from spontaneous mutations, which arise from endogenous errors during replication or repair. In biotechnology, induced mutagenesis is a deliberate tool — chemical or radiation treatment of seeds or cell cultures creates genetic variation for crop improvement (e.g., dwarf wheat, disease‑resistant rice) and functional genomics (e.g., TILLING, transposon tagging). Understanding the dose‑response relationship, mutation spectrum, and repair pathways is essential for both risk assessment (carcinogenesis, occupational exposure) and harnessing mutagenesis for beneficial traits.
steps: Induced mutations are heritable changes in DNA sequence that arise from exposure to external mutagens, and understanding their mechanisms is essential for both risk assessment and biotechnological applications.

First, mutagens are grouped into physical, chemical, and biological agents, each leaving a signature lesion on DNA. Physical mutagens like X‑rays and gamma rays deposit high energy, causing single‑ and double‑strand…
UV radiation, though non‑ionizing, forms cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers that stall replication.
Chemical mutagens such as EMS alkylate the O⁶ position of guanine, causing GC→AT transitions, while base analogues like 5‑bromouracil mispair during replication.
Biological mutagens include transposable elements that insert into genes, disrupting function, and viral integrases that randomly integrate into host genomes.
Second, the type of DNA damage determines whether the mutation is a point change (gene mutation) or a large‑scale chromosomal aberration.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “EMS and nitrous acid are physical mutagens”) reveals the misconception that chemical agents belong to the physical category, confusing chemical structure with energy‑based classification.
remember: Define induced mutation and name two physical mutagens.
Explain why UV radiation primarily causes thymine dimers rather than other base modifications.
A student claims that all chemical mutagens are carcinogens. Evaluate this statement.

cards.title: A gene mutation is a permanent alteration in the nucleotide sequence of a…
cards.subject: Biotechnology
cards.definition: A gene mutation is a permanent alteration in the nucleotide sequence of a single gene. It involves changes at the DNA level — substitution, insertion, or deletion of one or a few base pairs — that can modify the codon sequence during transcription and translation. Gene mutations are classified by their molecular nature: Point mutations – replacement of a single base pair. Subtypes: - Silent – codon change does not alter the amino acid (degeneracy of genetic code). - Missense – codon change leads to a different amino acid, potentially affecting protein function. - Nonsense – codon becomes a stop codon, truncating the protein. Frameshift mutations – insertion or deletion of a number of bases not divisible by three, shifting the reading frame and altering all downstream amino acids. In‑frame insertions/deletions – addition or loss of three‑base multiples; reading frame preserved but protein length changes. Gene mutations may be spontaneous (errors during DNA replication, tautomeric shifts) or induced (chemical mutagens, radiation). Their phenotypic impact ranges from neutral to lethal, depending on the gene’s role, the mutation type, and whether the allele is dominant or recessive. In the ISC syllabus, gene mutations are contrasted with chromosomal mutations (large‑scale changes) covered in the next concept node. Understanding gene mutations provides the molecular basis for inborn errors of metabolism such as albinism, sickle‑cell anaemia, and alkaptonuria.
steps: Let’s walk through a gene mutation step by step, using an Indian kitchen analogy. 1.
The recipe (gene) – A gene is a stretch of DNA that codes for one protein.
Think of it as a handwritten recipe for dal makhani written in a language where every three letters (a codon) stands for one ingredient (an amino acid). 2.
Copying the recipe (DNA replication) – When a cell divides, the recipe is copied.
Occasionally the scribe (DNA polymerase) makes a mistake: a single letter is swapped (substitution), an extra letter slips in (insertion), or a letter is omitted (deletion). 3.
Reading the recipe (transcription & translation) – The ribosome reads the mRNA copy three letters at a time.
remember: Which type of gene mutation is most likely to produce a completely non‑functional protein if it occurs near the start of the coding sequence.
A single‑base substitution changes the codon GAA (glutamate) to GUA (valine) in the β‑globin….
Evaluate the statement: “All frameshift mutations are more harmful than any point mutation.”.

cards.title: Chromosomal mutations are large‑scale alterations that affect the structure or…
cards.subject: Biotechnology
cards.definition: Chromosomal mutations are large‑scale alterations that affect the structure or number of whole chromosomes rather than a single gene. They arise from errors in DNA replication, repair, or segregation during meiosis and mitosis. Structural chromosomal mutations include deletions (loss of a segment), duplications (gain of a segment), inversions (reversal of a segment), and translocations (exchange of segments between non‑homologous chromosomes). Numerical chromosomal mutations involve changes in chromosome count: euploidy (gain or loss of complete chromosome sets, e.g., polyploidy) and aneuploidy (gain or loss of individual chromosomes, such as monosomy, trisomy, or tetrasomy). These mutations can be somatic (occurring in body cells, not transmitted) or germinal (occurring in gametes, heritable). They may be spontaneous (random) or induced (by radiation, chemicals). Chromosomal mutations often have profound phenotypic consequences because they alter the dosage of many genes simultaneously, unlike gene mutations that affect a single locus. They are central to understanding syndromes such as Down’s (trisomy 21), Turner’s (monosomy X), and Klinefelter’s (XXY), and to plant breeding where polyploidy is exploited for crop improvement.
steps: Chromosomal mutations are large-scale genetic alterations that rewrite, delete, duplicate, or reshuffle entire chapters of the genome, whereas gene mutations are merely spelling mistakes in a single word.
This distinction is critical because chromosomal changes affect hundreds of genes simultaneously, upsetting delicate gene networks and regulatory environments.
Structural changes involve the physical rearrangement of chromosome segments:
Deletion: A segment snaps off, resulting in the permanent loss of those genes.
Duplication: A segment is copied and inserted, increasing gene dosage and potentially disrupting cellular balance.
Inversion: A segment flips end-to-end; while the genes remain, their reversed order can move them away from their original promoters, causing regulatory failure.
remember: Which of the following best describes a chromosomal mutation as opposed to a gene….
A researcher treats onion root tips with colchicine and observes cells with 16 chromosomes instead of the normal….
Evaluate the statement: “All aneuploidies are lethal in humans.” Provide two examples to support your evaluation.

cards.title: Euploidy is a chromosomal condition in which the total chromosome number of a…
cards.subject: Biotechnology
cards.definition: Euploidy is a chromosomal condition in which the total chromosome number of a cell or organism is an exact integer multiple of the basic haploid number (n) characteristic of that species. The haploid number (n) represents the number of chromosomes in a gamete; the diploid number (2n) is the typical somatic chromosome complement formed by the fusion of two gametes. Euploid categories include haploid (n), diploid (2n), and polyploid states such as triploid (3n), tetraploid (4n), pentaploid (5n), hexaploid (6n), etc. Euploidy arises from whole‑genome duplication events — either through failure of chromosome segregation during meiosis (producing unreduced gametes) or through somatic chromosome doubling. In contrast, aneuploidy involves gain or loss of individual chromosomes, not whole sets. Euploidy is a major driver of speciation and crop improvement in plants (e.g., Triticum aestivum wheat is hexaploid, 6n = 42), while in animals it is rare and often lethal beyond the diploid state. The concept links directly to the earlier node on chromosomal mutations and sets the foundation for understanding aneuploidy and specific syndromes caused by non‑disjunction.
steps: Euploidy means the chromosome complement is an exact multiple of the species’ haploid number (n).

Here is why: the haploid set (n) is the fundamental unit of genetic information packaged into chromosomes; any whole‑number multiple of this set preserves the stoichiometric balance of all genes, whereas adding or…
First, consider the normal human life cycle: gametes are haploid (n = 23), fertilisation restores diploidy (2n = 46).
This 2n state is the baseline euploid condition for humans.
Second, if meiosis fails to reduce chromosome number, an unreduced (2n) gamete forms; fusion with a normal n gamete yields a triploid (3n) zygote.
In animals, 3n embryos usually abort, but in many flowering plants triploids survive and are often sterile — a trait exploited for seedless fruits like watermelon.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “euploidy means having 46 chromosomes”) reveals the misconception that euploidy is synonymous with diploidy, ignoring haploid and polyploid multiples.

cards.title: Aneuploidy is a chromosomal mutation in which the total chromosome number…
cards.subject: Biotechnology
cards.definition: Aneuploidy is a chromosomal mutation in which the total chromosome number deviates from an exact multiple of the haploid set (n). Unlike euploidy — where the genome contains complete sets of chromosomes (e.g., 2n, 3n) — aneuploidy involves the gain or loss of individual chromosomes, producing karyotypes such as 2n + 1 (trisomy), 2n − 1 (monosomy), 2n − 2 (nullisomy) or 2n + 2 (tetrasomy). The primary mechanism is non‑disjunction: failure of homologous chromosomes (meiosis I) or sister chromatids (meiosis II/mitosis) to separate, yielding gametes with an abnormal chromosome complement. When such a gamete fuses with a normal one, the resulting zygote carries an extra or missing chromosome. Aneuploidy can be autosomal (e.g., trisomy 21 → Down syndrome) or sex‑chromosomal (e.g., 45,X → Turner syndrome; 47,XXY → Klinefelter syndrome). It generally disrupts gene dosage balance, causing developmental abnormalities, reduced viability, or lethality. In plants, aneuploidy is often tolerated better and exploited for breeding. This node defines the overarching concept; specific types (monosomy, nullisomy, trisomy, tetrasomy) and syndrome‑level details are covered in sibling nodes‑016.
steps: A single segregation error rewrites the chromosome count, and that count change rewrites the phenotype. - Aneuploidy is a numerical change in chromosomes, distinct from structural changes like deletions.
Non‑disjunction acts as a "traffic jam" at the metaphase plate where chromosomes fail to part, creating gametes with n+1 or n-1 counts.
Gene‑dosage imbalance occurs because genes on the affected chromosome are present in three copies instead of two, or one instead of two, disrupting developmental pathways.
Autosomal trisomies are often lethal, except for trisomy 21, which is gene‑poor; sex‑chromosome aneuploidies are more viable due to X‑inactivation.
Plants tolerate aneuploidy better than animals, allowing breeders to use monosomic or trisomic lines to map genes to specific chromosomes.
In a normal diploid state (2n=46), meiosis produces gametes with n=23.

cards.title: Monosomy is a type of aneuploidy in which a diploid cell lacks one chromosome…
cards.subject: Biotechnology
cards.definition: Monosomy is a type of aneuploidy in which a diploid cell lacks one chromosome from a homologous pair, giving a chromosome complement of 2n‑1. It arises when homologous chromosomes or sister chromatids fail to separate during meiosis I or II (non‑disjunction), producing a gamete that is null for that chromosome. Fertilisation of such a gamete with a normal haploid gamete yields a zygote with a single copy of the affected chromosome. The most viable human monosomy is Turner syndrome (45,X), where the missing sex chromosome leads to characteristic phenotypes such as short stature, ovarian dysgenesis, and cardiovascular anomalies. Autosomal monosomies (e.g., loss of chromosome 21) are usually lethal early in embryogenesis. Monosomy differs from nullisomy (loss of both homologues, 2n‑2) and from trisomy (gain of one chromosome, 2n+1). It is a subset of chromosomal mutations, distinct from gene‑level mutations, and is classified under structural/numerical abnormalities covered in this chapter. Understanding monosomy requires prior knowledge of euploidy, aneuploidy, and the mechanics of meiotic segregation.
steps: Monosomy is the simplest form of aneuploidy where a cell has 45 chromosomes instead of the standard 46, because one chromosome from a homologous pair is missing (2n-1).
Aneuploidy represents any deviation from the exact multiple of the haploid number.
Non-disjunction during meiosis causes this condition when spindle fibers fail to separate chromosomes correctly.
A null gamete (lacking a chromosome) fuses with a normal haploid gamete to create a monosomic zygote.
Most autosomal monosomies are lethal due to the loss of essential genes, while Turner syndrome (45,X) is the only viable full monosomy in humans.
A normal human somatic cell is diploid (2n = 46) with 23 homologous pairs.

cards.title: Nullisomy is a type of aneuploidy in which an organism or cell lacks both…
cards.subject: Biotechnology
cards.definition: Nullisomy is a type of aneuploidy in which an organism or cell lacks both homologous chromosomes of a particular pair, giving a chromosome complement of 2n‑2. It arises when non‑disjunction occurs in both homologous chromosomes during meiosis I or when a gamete missing one chromosome fuses with another gamete also missing the same chromosome. The resulting zygote is missing an entire chromosome pair, leading to loss of all genes on that chromosome. In diploid animals, nullisomy is usually lethal early in development because essential genes are absent; in plants, especially polyploid species like wheat (hexaploid, 2n=6x=42), nullisomic lines are viable and are powerful cytogenetic tools for assigning genes to chromosomes. Nullisomy differs from monosomy (loss of a single chromosome, 2n‑1) and from euploidy (exact multiples of the basic set). It is a chromosomal‑level mutation, not a gene‑level change, and is classified under structural/numerical abnormalities caused by errors in cell division.
steps: Nullisomy is the loss of both homologous chromosomes of a pair, resulting in a chromosome count of 2n-2.
This condition is distinct from monosomy (2n-1) and trisomy (2n+1) because it involves the total absence of a specific chromosome pair. 1.
Nullisomy represents a severe chromosomal imbalance, reducing the total chromosome count by two.
It occurs through non-disjunction during meiosis I, where both homologues migrate to the same pole, or through the fusion of two gametes that are both missing the same chromosome.

cards.title: Trisomy is a type of aneuploidy in which a diploid cell contains three copies…
cards.subject: Biotechnology
cards.definition: Trisomy is a type of aneuploidy in which a diploid cell contains three copies of a particular chromosome instead of the normal two. It arises when homologous chromosomes or sister chromatids fail to separate during meiosis I or II (non‑disjunction), producing a gamete with an extra chromosome. Fertilisation of such a gamete with a normal haploid gamete yields a zygote with 2n + 1 chromosomes for that specific chromosome. The extra genetic material disrupts gene dosage balance, leading to developmental abnormalities. In humans, the most common viable trisomies are chromosome 21 (Down syndrome), chromosome 18 (Edwards syndrome), chromosome 13 (Patau syndrome), and the sex‑chromosome trisomies XXY (Klinefelter syndrome) and XXX (Triple‑X syndrome). Trisomy differs from monosomy (one copy), nullisomy (zero copies), and tetrasomy (four copies) — all are aneuploidies but with distinct chromosome counts. The phenotypic severity correlates with the size and gene density of the trisomic chromosome; larger chromosomes with many genes (e.g., chromosome 21) produce more pronounced effects. Trisomy can be constitutional (present in all cells) or mosaic (present in a subset of cells due to post‑zygotic non‑disjunction). Diagnosis is by karyotyping, fluorescence in situ hybridisation (FISH), or non‑invasive prenatal testing (NIPT). Understanding trisomy links the mechanics of chromosome segregation to clinical genetics and underpins counselling for chromosomal disorders.
steps: Trisomy is the gain of an entire chromosome, resulting in a total of 47 chromosomes in humans, which disrupts the cell's gene dosage balance. - The primary cause is meiotic non-disjunction, where chromosomes fail to…
The extra genetic material forces the cell to produce 1.5 times the normal amount of gene products, which triggers developmental abnormalities.
Phenotypic severity is determined by the specific chromosome involved; larger, gene-dense chromosomes cause more severe syndromes like Patau or Edwards.
Sex-chromosome trisomies are often less severe due to X-inactivation, which partially compensates for the extra genetic material.
Modern diagnostics, including karyotyping, FISH, and NIPT, allow for the precise identification of these chromosomal gains.

cards.title: Tetrasomy is a type of aneuploidy in which a particular chromosome is present…
cards.subject: Biotechnology
cards.definition: Tetrasomy is a type of aneuploidy in which a particular chromosome is present in four copies instead of the normal diploid number of two. It arises when non‑disjunction occurs during meiosis I or II (or during early mitotic divisions), producing a gamete with two copies of the same chromosome; fertilisation with a normal gamete yields a zygote with four copies. Tetrasomy can be complete (entire chromosome) or partial (segmental duplication). The condition is usually lethal in early embryogenesis for most autosomes, but viable cases such as tetrasomy 12p (Pallister‑Killian syndrome), tetrasomy 18p, and tetrasomy X (XXXX) are documented. Phenotypic consequences stem from gene dosage imbalance: over‑expression of genes on the extra chromosome disrupts developmental pathways. Tetrasomy is distinct from trisomy (three copies) and polyploidy (whole‑genome duplication). It is classified under chromosomal mutations (see sibling nodes,).
steps: Tetrasomy is a chromosome‑number abnormality where one chromosome exists in four copies, caused by non‑disjunction during gamete formation.
Here is why: 1.
Normal diploid cells have two homologues of each chromosome (2n).
During meiosis, homologous pairs separate (meiosis I) and sister chromatids separate (meiosis II).
If either division fails, a gamete receives two copies of the same chromosome. 2.
Fertilisation of such a gamete (n+1) with a normal gamete (n) yields a zygote with 2n+2 = four copies of that chromosome — tetrasomy. 3.

cards.title: Turner syndrome is a sex‑chromosome aneuploidy caused by non‑disjunction of the…
cards.subject: Biotechnology
cards.definition: Turner syndrome is a sex‑chromosome aneuploidy caused by non‑disjunction of the X chromosome during meiosis I or II in either parent, producing a gamete lacking an X. Fertilisation of such a gamete by a normal X‑bearing sperm yields a 45,X zygote (monosomy X). The condition is classified under monosomy (see node) and is a specific instance of aneuploidy (node). Clinically, the loss of one X leads to haploinsufficiency of pseudo‑autosomal genes (e.g., SHOX) causing short stature, gonadal dysgenesis (streak ovaries), webbed neck, low‑set ears, lymphedema at birth, and increased risk of cardiovascular and renal anomalies. Diagnosis is confirmed by karyotyping (45,X or mosaics such as 45,X/46,XX). Management includes growth‑hormone therapy, estrogen replacement at puberty, and regular cardiac/renal monitoring. The syndrome illustrates how a single chromosome segregation error propagates to a recognizable phenotype, linking the molecular mechanism (non‑disjunction) to organism‑level consequences.
steps: Let’s walk through Turner syndrome step by step, linking what you already know about chromosome behaviour. 1.
Recall normal meiosis – In oogenesis, a primary oocyte (46,XX) undergoes meiosis I to separate homologous X chromosomes, then meiosis II to separate sister chromatids.

Each mature ovum should receive one X. In spermatogenesis, a primary spermatocyte (46,XY) separates X and Y in meiosis I, then sister chromatids in meiosis II, producing X‑bearing and Y‑bearing sperm. 2.

Where non‑disjunction occurs – If homologous X chromosomes fail to separate in meiosis I (maternal) or sister chromatids fail to separate in meiosis II (maternal or paternal), an ovum or sperm ends up with no sex…
Fertilisation of a nullisomic gamete by a normal X‑bearing gamete gives a 45,X zygote.
This is the classic non‑disjunction route to Turner syndrome. 3.

cards.title: Klinefelter’s syndrome is a sex‑chromosome aneuploidy characterised by the…
cards.subject: Biotechnology
cards.definition: Klinefelter’s syndrome is a sex‑chromosome aneuploidy characterised by the presence of one or more extra X chromosomes in a phenotypic male, most commonly a 47,XXY karyotype. It arises from non‑disjunction of the X chromosomes during meiosis I or II in either parent, producing a gamete with two X chromosomes (or an X and a Y) that fuses with a normal gamete. The additional X chromosome carries genes that escape X‑inactivation, leading to dosage‑sensitive effects on testicular development, hormone production, and neurodevelopment. Clinically, individuals present with small firm testes, hypergonadotropic hypogonadism (elevated FSH and LH, low testosterone), gynecomastia, tall stature with eunuchoid proportions, reduced facial and body hair, and variable cognitive‑behavioural profiles (often language‑based learning difficulties). The syndrome is not inherited in a Mendelian fashion; recurrence risk for siblings is low unless a parental mosaicism or translocation exists. Diagnosis is confirmed by peripheral blood karyotyping or chromosomal microarray. Management includes testosterone replacement from puberty onward, fertility counselling (assisted reproductive technologies such as TESE‑ICSI may retrieve sperm), and educational support. Klinefelter’s is the most common sex‑chromosome disorder in males and a classic example of how non‑disjunction produces aneuploidy, linking directly to the concepts of euploidy, aneuploidy, trisomy, and non‑disjunction covered in earlier nodes.
steps: Klinefelter’s syndrome is the classic male sex‑chromosome aneuploidy caused by an extra X chromosome, most often 47,XXY.

Here is why: the extra X arises when homologous X chromosomes fail to separate during meiosis I or sister chromatids fail to separate during meiosis II in either the mother or the father, producing a gamete with two sex…
First, the non‑disjunction event creates a diploid gamete (XX or XY) instead of a haploid one; fertilisation with a normal haploid gamete (X or Y) yields a zygote with three sex chromosomes.
Second, the additional X chromosome carries many genes that escape X‑inactivation, so their expression is increased by 50 %, disrupting testicular development and androgen production.
Third, the hormonal imbalance (low testosterone, high gonadotropins) drives the physical phenotype: small testes, gynecomastia, tall stature with long legs, sparse facial hair.
Fourth, neurodevelopmental effects include delayed speech, reading difficulties, and executive‑function challenges, which are variable and not universal.

cards.title: Down’s syndrome (Trisomy 21) is a chromosomal aneuploidy where an individual…
cards.subject: Biotechnology
cards.definition: Down’s syndrome (Trisomy 21) is a chromosomal aneuploidy where an individual possesses three copies of chromosome 21 instead of the usual two. It arises primarily through non‑disjunction during meiosis I or II in gametogenesis, producing a gamete with 24 chromosomes (two chromosome 21s). Fertilisation with a normal gamete yields a zygote with 47 chromosomes (47,XX,+21 or 47,XY,+21). Three cytogenetic forms exist: 1. Standard trisomy 21 (~95 % of cases) – full extra chromosome 21 from meiotic non‑disjunction. 2. Robertsonian translocation (~3‑4 %) – the long arm of chromosome 21 fuses to chromosome 14 (or another acrocentric), so the karyotype is 46,XX,der(14;21)(q10;q10),+21. 3. Mosaicism (~1‑2 %) – non‑disjunction occurs post‑zygotically, giving a mixture of 46 and 47‑chromosome cell lines. Clinical hallmarks include intellectual disability (variable severity), characteristic facial dysmorphism (epicanthic folds, flat nasal bridge), congenital heart defects (especially atrioventricular septal defect), hypotonia, and increased risk of leukaemia and early‑onset Alzheimer’s disease. Maternal age is the strongest epidemiological correlate; incidence rises from ~1/1500 at age 20 to ~1/30 at age 45. Prenatal screening (combined first‑trimester test, NIPT) and diagnostic karyotyping (amniocentesis, CVS) enable detection. Management is multidisciplinary: cardiac surgery, early intervention therapies, thyroid monitoring, and regular haematological surveillance.
steps: Takeaway: Down’s syndrome is caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21, most often due to meiotic non‑disjunction, and its three cytogenetic forms dictate different recurrence risks.
Here is why: 1.
Meiotic non‑disjunction — During oogenesis (especially in older oocytes) or spermatogenesis, homologous chromosomes or sister chromatids fail to separate, producing a gamete with two chromosome 21s.
Fertilisation adds a third copy.
This explains the steep maternal‑age curve. 2.
Robertsonian translocation — A break‑fusion event joins the long arms of chromosome 21 and another acrocentric (usually 14).

cards.title: A chromosomal deletion is a structural abnormality in which a segment of a…
cards.subject: Biotechnology
cards.definition: A chromosomal deletion is a structural abnormality in which a segment of a chromosome is lost during DNA replication, repair, or meiotic/mitotic division. The breakage occurs at two points on the same chromosome arm (interstitial deletion) or at one point near the end (terminal deletion), and the intervening fragment fails to reattach, resulting in a chromosome that is shorter than normal. Because genes are linearly arranged, any deletion removes all loci within the missing interval; the phenotypic effect depends on the size of the deleted segment, the number and function of genes lost, and whether the deletion is heterozygous (one homologue affected) or homozygous (both homologues affected, usually lethal). Deletions can arise spontaneously through errors in DNA double‑strand break repair (non‑homologous end joining) or be induced by ionising radiation, chemical mutagens, or replication stress. In humans, well‑characterised deletion syndromes include Cri‑du‑chat (5p‑), Wolf‑Hirschhorn (4p‑), and DiGeorge/22q11.2 deletion syndrome. Cytogenetically, deletions are detected by G‑banding, high‑resolution microarray comparative genomic hybridisation (aCGH), or fluorescence in situ hybridisation (FISH) using locus‑specific probes. The concept links to earlier nodes on chromosomal mutations and non‑disjunction syndromes (‑016) because both involve altered chromosome structure or number, but deletions specifically change the gene dosage without altering chromosome count. Understanding deletions also sets the stage for studying duplications, where extra copies of a segment produce a complementary dosage imbalance.
steps: A chromosomal deletion removes a contiguous block of genes from one homologue, creating a dosage imbalance that underlies several well‑known human syndromes.

Here is why: first, deletions arise when two double‑strand breaks occur on the same chromosome arm and the fragment between them is lost during faulty repair, most often by non‑homologous end joining; ionising…

Second, the position of the breaks defines the class — terminal deletions delete the chromosome tip including the telomere, while interstitial deletions remove an internal segment leaving both telomeres intact; both…

Third, the phenotypic severity scales with the number and haploinsufficiency of genes lost; for example, a 5‑Mb terminal deletion of 5p15.2 (Cri‑du‑chat) eliminates the TERT and CTNND2 genes, producing the…

Fourth, cytogenetic diagnosis proceeds from conventional G‑banding (which reveals a visibly shortened band) to high‑resolution aCGH or FISH with locus‑specific probes that map the exact breakpoints; the International…

Fifth, understanding deletions prepares you for the next node on duplications, where an extra copy of a segment creates the opposite dosage effect; together they illustrate how structural rearrangements reshape the…

cards.title: A duplication is a structural chromosomal abnormality in which a contiguous…
cards.subject: Biotechnology
cards.definition: A duplication is a structural chromosomal abnormality in which a contiguous segment of DNA is present in two copies on the same chromosome or on a homologous chromosome. The duplicated segment may be arranged in the same orientation (tandem duplication), in reverse orientation (inverted or reverse duplication), or displaced to a non‑homologous location (displaced duplication). Duplications arise mainly through unequal crossing‑over between misaligned homologous chromosomes during prophase I of meiosis, through replication slippage at repetitive sequences, or via erroneous repair of double‑strand breaks. The extra genetic material alters gene dosage: genes within the duplicated region are expressed at higher levels, which can disrupt developmental pathways, cause metabolic imbalances, or predispose to disease. Phenotypic consequences depend on the size of the duplicated segment, the genes it contains, and whether the duplication is heterozygous (one chromosome carries the extra copy) or homozygous. In humans, a well‑studied example is the 1.4 Mb tandem duplication on chromosome 17p12 that includes the PMP22 gene, causing Charcot‑Marie‑Tooth disease type 1A. In Drosophila, the Bar mutation results from a tandem duplication of the 16A region, reducing eye size. Duplications are detected by karyotyping (banding patterns), fluorescence in situ hybridisation (FISH), array comparative genomic hybridisation (aCGH), and next‑generation sequencing read‑depth analysis. They differ from deletions (loss of material) and from whole‑genome polyploidy, which involves complete chromosome sets.
steps: A duplication is an extra copy of a chromosomal segment that changes gene dosage and can cause disease.

Here is why: the cell’s DNA‑copying and recombination machinery sometimes misaligns homologous chromosomes or slips on repetitive DNA, producing two copies of a region instead of one. First, during meiotic prophase I…
Crossing‑over between these misaligned chromatids yields one chromatid with a deletion and the other with a duplication — this is unequal crossing‑over.
Second, during DNA replication, the polymerase can slip on tandem repeats, causing the newly synthesised strand to loop out and re‑anneal, duplicating the repeat unit — replication slippage.
Third, erroneous non‑homologous end joining after a double‑strand break can stitch a fragment back in twice, creating a displaced duplication.
The duplicated segment may sit next to the original (tandem), be inverted (reverse), or jump to another chromosome (displaced).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “replication slippage during S‑phase”) reveals the misconception that all duplications arise from replication errors, ignoring the major meiotic recombination pathway.

cards.title: Carbohydrates are polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones…
cards.subject: Biotechnology
cards.definition: Carbohydrates are polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones, or substances that yield them on hydrolysis. They are classified by the number of monomeric units: monosaccharides (one unit), disaccharides (two units linked by a glycosidic bond), and polysaccharides (many units). Glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆) is an aldohexose — a six-carbon monosaccharide with an aldehyde group at C-1. In solution it exists predominantly as two cyclic hemiacetals, α-D-glucopyranose and β-D-glucopyranose, which interconvert via the open-chain form (mutarotation). The configuration at the anomeric carbon (C-1) determines α/β designation. Two glucose units can condense, eliminating water, to form the disaccharide maltose (α-1,4-glycosidic bond). Repeated condensation yields polysaccharides such as starch (α-1,4 and α-1,6 branches) and cellulose (β-1,4). Glucose thus sits at the hub of carbohydrate chemistry: it is the building block for larger saccharides, a primary energy metabolite, and a structural precursor when polymerised with β-linkages.
steps: Glucose is the central monomer whose stereochemistry dictates whether a polymer functions as energy-dense food or rigid structural fibre.
This distinction arises from the orientation of the hydroxyl group at the anomeric carbon, which determines the geometry of the glycosidic bond.
Glucose is an aldohexose, containing a six-carbon chain with an aldehyde group at C-1 and hydroxyl groups on the remaining carbons.
In aqueous solution, the aldehyde reacts with the C-5 hydroxyl to form a stable six-membered ring (pyranose), creating a new chiral centre at C-1 called the anomeric carbon.
The two possible configurations at C-1, α (hydroxyl pointing down) and β (hydroxyl pointing up), interconvert through the open-chain form in a process known as mutarotation.
Condensation reactions link these units: α-1,4-linkages form digestible energy stores like starch, while β-1,4-linkages create indigestible structural materials like cellulose.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer suggests a misunderstanding of the structural components, such as confusing it with a ketose (like fructose) or a pentose (like ribose).
