cards.title: The modern periodic law states that the physical and chemical properties of the…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: The modern periodic law states that the physical and chemical properties of the elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers (Z). Atomic number equals the number of protons in the nucleus and uniquely identifies an element. When elements are arranged in order of increasing Z, elements with similar valence‑electron configurations recur at regular intervals, producing the periodic table’s groups and periods. This law supersedes Mendeleev’s original formulation based on atomic mass, because atomic mass does not always increase monotonically with chemical similarity (e.g., Ar (39.9) before K (39.1)). Henry Moseley’s 1913 X‑ray spectroscopy work showed that the square‑root of the frequency of characteristic K‑α X‑rays varies linearly with Z (√ν = a(Z – b)), providing experimental proof that Z, not mass, is the fundamental ordering parameter. The law underpins the long form of the periodic table (18 groups, 7 periods) and all subsequent periodic trends — atomic radius, ionisation enthalpy, electron gain enthalpy, electronegativity, and valence — which are explored in the following nodes.
steps: Let’s walk through the modern periodic law as if we are rebuilding the periodic table from scratch.
Step 1 – Recall the old problem.
In Class 10 you learned Mendeleev arranged elements by increasing atomic mass.
He left gaps for undiscovered elements and even swapped a few (like Te and I) to keep chemical families together.
But anomalies remained: argon (Ar, 39.9 u) comes before potassium (K, 39.1 u) though K is an alkali metal and Ar a noble gas. Mass alone cannot explain why chemical properties repeat.
Step 2 – Enter Henry Moseley (1913).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “properties are periodic functions of atomic mass, proved by Mendeleev”) reveals the misconception that the modern law is merely a restatement of Mendeleev’s mass‑based law, ignoring Moseley’s nuclear‑charge evidence.
remember: State the modern periodic law in your own words and name the scientist whose experimental work provided its strongest evidence.
Explain why arranging elements by atomic number resolves the Ar–K anomaly that persisted in Mendeleev’s mass‑based table.
A student claims: “Moseley’s law is just a mathematical fit; it doesn’t prove that atomic number is the cause of periodicity.” Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: The long form of the periodic table is the modern tabular arrangement of all…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: The long form of the periodic table is the modern tabular arrangement of all known elements in order of increasing atomic number (Z). It consists of seven horizontal rows called periods and eighteen vertical columns called groups. Elements are further classified into four blocks — s, p, d, and f — based on the subshell that receives the last electron according to the Aufbau principle. The s‑block comprises Groups 1‑2, the p‑block Groups 13‑18, the d‑block Groups 3‑12 (transition metals), and the f‑block contains the lanthanides and actinides placed separately below the main table to preserve its compact shape. Each period corresponds to the filling of a principal quantum shell (n = 1 to 7), while each group shares a common valence‑electron configuration, giving rise to similar chemical properties. The table thus embodies the modern periodic law: the physical and chemical properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers.
steps: Let’s build the long form periodic table step by step, just as you would organise a school timetable.
Step 1 – The guiding principle Recall the modern periodic law (from the previous node): properties repeat periodically when elements are arranged by atomic number, not atomic mass.
So the very first column of our table is simply Z = 1, 2, 3 … up to 118.
Step 2 – Periods = principal quantum shells Each new period starts when a new principal quantum number (n) begins to fill.
Period 1 has only the 1s subshell (2 elements).
Period 2 fills 2s and 2p (8 elements).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “8 groups because of the old A/B notation”) reveals the misconception that the older group‑labeling system is still the standard, ignoring the current IUPAC convention.
remember: How many periods and groups are present in the long form periodic table, and what is the basis for the 18‑group numbering.
Why are the lanthanides and actinides placed separately at the bottom of the periodic table instead of being inserted in the main body.
Evaluate the statement: “In the long form periodic table, elements are arranged strictly in order of increasing atomic mass.”.

cards.title: Atomic radius is the distance from the nucleus to the outermost electron cloud…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Atomic radius is the distance from the nucleus to the outermost electron cloud boundary. Because electron clouds are fuzzy, three operational definitions are used: covalent radius (half the internuclear distance in a homonuclear covalent bond), metallic radius (half the distance between nuclei in a metallic crystal), and van der Waals radius (half the distance between nuclei of non‑bonded atoms in a solid). The periodic trend arises from two competing factors: effective nuclear charge (Z_eff) and principal quantum number (n). Across a period, Z_eff increases because protons are added while shielding by inner electrons remains nearly constant; the stronger pull contracts the electron cloud, decreasing radius. Down a group, a new principal shell (higher n) is added, increasing the average distance of valence electrons from the nucleus despite a higher Z_eff; the radius therefore increases. The relationship can be expressed qualitatively as r ∝ n²/Z_eff. Isoelectronic species (same electron count) show radius decreasing with increasing nuclear charge because Z_eff rises while n stays fixed. These trends underpin subsequent properties such as ionisation enthalpy, electron gain enthalpy, and electronegativity.
steps: Atomic radius decreases across a period and increases down a group because effective nuclear charge rises across a period while principal quantum number increases down a group.
Here is why: 1.
Radius definitions matter – Covalent radius applies to non‑metals (e.g., Cl–Cl bond), metallic radius to metals (e.g., Na in bcc lattice), van der Waals radius to noble gases and non‑bonded contacts.
All are measured in picometres (1 pm = 10⁻¹² m). 2.
Effective nuclear charge (Z_eff) is the net pull – Z_eff = Z – σ, where Z is atomic number and σ is shielding constant from inner electrons (Slater’s rules).
Across period 2, Li (Z=3) has Z_eff ≈ 1.3 for its 2s electron, while Ne (Z=10) has Z_eff ≈ 5.8 for its 2p electrons; the stronger pull shrinks the cloud. 3.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “atomic radius is the size of the nucleus”) reveals the misconception that the nucleus defines atomic size, confusing nuclear radius (~fm) with atomic radius (~pm).
remember: Define atomic radius and name the three operational types used in periodic trends.
Explain why atomic radius decreases from lithium to neon across period 2, referencing effective nuclear charge and shielding.
Evaluate the statement: “In the isoelectronic series N³⁻, O²⁻, F⁻, Ne, Na⁺, Mg²⁺, the ionic radius increases with increasing nuclear charge.”.

cards.title: Ionisation enthalpy (ΔH_ion) is the standard enthalpy change when one mole of…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Ionisation enthalpy (ΔH_ion) is the standard enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous atoms loses one mole of electrons to form one mole of gaseous cations: M(g) → M⁺(g) + e⁻. It is always positive because energy must be supplied to overcome the electrostatic attraction between the nucleus and the electron. The first ionisation enthalpy (IE₁) refers to removal of the outermost electron; successive ionisation enthalpies (IE₂, IE₃…) correspond to removal from increasingly positively charged ions and are progressively larger. Trends: across a period, IE generally increases due to rising effective nuclear charge (Z_eff) and decreasing atomic radius; down a group, IE decreases because the outermost electron occupies a higher principal quantum shell, experiences greater shielding, and is farther from the nucleus. Exceptions arise from stable electronic configurations (e.g., half‑filled or fully filled subshells) which raise IE relative to neighbours. Units: kilojoules per mole (kJ mol⁻¹). Ionisation enthalpy is a key indicator of metallic character, reactivity, and the ease of cation formation.
steps: Let’s start from what you already know: atomic radius shrinks across a period because the nucleus pulls the electron cloud tighter (higher Z_eff) and expands down a group because a new shell is added.
Ionisation enthalpy is the energetic counterpart of that size trend.
Picture a sodium atom (Na) in the gas phase.
Its single 3s electron feels a net pull of about +1 from the nucleus after shielding by the 1s²2s²2p⁶ core.
To pluck that electron away you must supply energy — that’s the first ionisation enthalpy, 496 kJ mol⁻¹.
Now move to magnesium (Mg) next door: the 3s² pair feels a larger Z_eff (~+2), so IE₁ jumps to 738 kJ mol⁻¹.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “IE₁ is negative because energy is released”) reveals the misconception that ionisation is exothermic, confusing it with electron gain enthalpy.
remember: State the definition of first ionisation enthalpy, including its sign convention and SI unit.
Explain why the first ionisation enthalpy generally increases across a period from left to right, referencing effective nuclear charge and atomic radius.
Evaluate the statement: “The first ionisation enthalpy of oxygen is higher than that of nitrogen because oxygen has more protons.” Provide a correct explanation.

cards.title: Electron gain enthalpy (ΔₑgH) is the enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Electron gain enthalpy (ΔₑgH) is the enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous atoms each accepts one electron to form one mole of gaseous anions under standard conditions (298 K, 1 bar). The process is: X(g) + e⁻ → X⁻(g). By convention, ΔₑgH is negative when energy is released (exothermic) and positive when energy must be supplied (endothermic). Its SI unit is kilojoule per mole (kJ mol⁻¹). Trends: across a period, ΔₑgH generally becomes more negative because increasing nuclear charge attracts the incoming electron more strongly; down a group, ΔₑgH becomes less negative (or even positive) because the added electron occupies a larger, more diffuse orbital and experiences greater shielding. Exceptions arise from stable half‑filled or fully‑filled subshells (e.g., N, Be, Mg) where adding an electron forces pairing, making ΔₑgH less exothermic. The magnitude of ΔₑgH influences chemical reactivity, especially the tendency to form anions and the strength of ionic bonds.
steps: Let’s walk through electron gain enthalpy step by step, linking it to what you already know from ionisation enthalpy. 1.
Set the stage – Picture a single gaseous sodium atom, Na(g).
It has one valence electron in the 3s orbital.
If we bring a free electron close, the nucleus (11 protons) pulls it in. The electron settles into the 3s orbital, forming Na⁻(g).
Energy is released because the electron moves to a lower‑energy, more stable arrangement.
That released energy per mole of atoms is the electron gain enthalpy, ΔₑgH(Na). 2.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “down a group ΔₑgH becomes more negative because there are more protons”) reveals the misconception that only nuclear charge matters, ignoring orbital size and shielding.
remember: State the sign convention for electron gain enthalpy and give its SI unit.
Explain why electron gain enthalpy generally becomes more negative across a period but less negative down a group.
Chlorine has ΔₑgH = –349 kJ mol⁻¹; fluorine has ΔₑgH = –328 kJ mol⁻¹. Evaluate which halogen forms its anion more readily and why the trend deviates from the simple group trend.

cards.title: Electronegativity (χ) is a dimensionless relative scale that quantifies the…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Electronegativity (χ) is a dimensionless relative scale that quantifies the ability of an atom in a chemical bond to attract shared electrons toward itself. It is not a directly measurable physical quantity like ionisation enthalpy; instead it is derived from thermochemical data (bond dissociation energies) or from atomic properties (ionisation energy and electron affinity). The most widely used scale in the ISC curriculum is the Pauling scale, where fluorine is assigned χ = 3.98 (≈4.0) and values decrease down a group and increase across a period. Electronegativity correlates with other periodic trends: high ionisation enthalpy and high electron gain enthalpy generally give high electronegativity. The difference Δχ between two bonded atoms predicts bond character: Δχ < 0.4 → non‑polar covalent; 0.4–1.7 → polar covalent; >1.7 → predominantly ionic. Because it is a relative scale, electronegativity has no SI unit; it is reported as a pure number.
steps: Electronegativity merges the atomic tendencies of ionisation enthalpy and electron gain enthalpy into a single measure of an atom’s electron-attracting power within a chemical bond.
Supporting arguments:
It provides a quantitative basis for predicting bond polarity using the difference in electronegativity (Δχ) between bonded atoms.
It explains the physical nature of chemical bonds by quantifying the unequal sharing of electrons.
It follows consistent periodic trends driven by effective nuclear charge and atomic radius.
It allows for the classification of bonds into ionic or covalent categories based on empirical thresholds.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “electronegativity is the energy released when an atom gains an electron”) reveals confusion between electron gain enthalpy (a measurable thermodynamic quantity with units kJ mol⁻¹) and electronegativity (a relative, unit‑less scale).
remember: Define electronegativity and state the reference element and its value on the Pauling scale.
Explain why electronegativity generally increases across a period from left to right.
Compare the electronegativity of oxygen (χ = 3.44) and sulfur (χ = 2.58). Which factor dominates the difference.

cards.title: Valence (or valency) of an element is the combining capacity of its atoms…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Valence (or valency) of an element is the combining capacity of its atoms, expressed as the number of hydrogen atoms (or electrons) that one atom can combine with, lose, gain, or share to achieve a stable noble‑gas configuration. For main‑group elements it equals the number of valence electrons (group number for groups 1‑2 and 13‑18) or eight minus that number for non‑metals. Transition metals show variable valence because (n‑1)d and ns electrons can both participate. Valence is closely linked to oxidation state — the charge an atom would have if all bonds were ionic — but valence is a whole‑number combining capacity, whereas oxidation state can be fractional in complexes. Periodic trends: valence generally increases across a period (1 → 4 then decreases to 0) and remains constant down a group for main‑group elements. The concept underpins formula writing, stoichiometry, and the prediction of molecular geometry.
steps: Let’s start from what you already know: every atom wants a full outer shell like the nearest noble gas. In Class 10 you learned that sodium (2,8,1) loses one electron to become Na⁺ (2,8) — that loss of one electron is…
Chlorine (2,8,7) gains one electron to become Cl⁻ (2,8,8) — valence 1 again, but as a gain.
Carbon (2,4) cannot easily lose or gain four electrons, so it shares four electrons — valence 4.
Now look at the periodic table.
For groups 1 and 2 the valence equals the group number (1, 2).
For groups 13‑18 the valence is usually 8 − group number (e.g., group 15 → 3, group 16 → 2, group 17 → 1, group 18 → 0).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “manganese has more protons so it can lose more electrons”) reveals the misconception that nuclear charge alone determines valence, ignoring the role of d‑orbital energy and electron availability.
remember: State the valence of phosphorus (atomic number 15) and justify it using its group number.
Explain why transition metals such as manganese show variable valence while sodium does not.
In the compound Fe₂O₃, what is the oxidation state of iron? Is this the same as its valence? Explain.

cards.title: The Kossel‑Lewis approach, also called the electronic theory of valency…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: The Kossel‑Lewis approach, also called the electronic theory of valency, postulates that chemical bonding arises from the tendency of atoms to acquire a stable noble‑gas electron configuration, typically an octet (eight electrons) in the valence shell. Atoms achieve this by either transferring electrons completely (ionic bond) or sharing electron pairs (covalent bond). Lewis symbols represent valence electrons as dots around the element symbol; the number of dots equals the group number for main‑group elements. When atoms combine, the total valence‑electron count is conserved and redistributed so that each atom (except hydrogen, which seeks a duet) is surrounded by eight electrons. The approach introduces the concepts of lone pairs, bonding pairs, formal charge, and the octet rule, and it provides a systematic way to draw Lewis structures for molecules and polyatomic ions. It also highlights limitations: electron‑deficient species (e.g., BF₃), expanded octets (e.g., SF₆), and odd‑electron molecules (e.g., NO) cannot be fully described. This node links directly to the next node on ionic bond Lewis structures and underpins all subsequent bonding theories (VSEPR, valence bond, molecular orbital, etc.).
steps: Atoms bond to achieve a stable noble-gas configuration by ensuring every atom is surrounded by eight valence electrons.
This process is governed by the need to reach the "octet" state, which mirrors the electronic stability of noble gases.
Electron Accounting: Atoms use valence electrons to form bonds, and these electrons are represented as dots in Lewis symbols based on their group number.
Ionic Transfer: When one atom has excess electrons and another lacks them, complete transfer occurs, creating ions held together by electrostatic attraction.
Covalent Sharing: When atoms have similar needs, they share electron pairs to ensure each atom "sees" eight electrons (or two for hydrogen).
Formal Charge Audit: Formal charge acts as a bookkeeping tool to determine the most stable structure by comparing an atom's valence electrons to those it "owns" in a molecule.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the octet rule means every atom must have exactly eight protons”) reveals the misconception that the rule concerns nuclear particles rather than valence electrons, confusing atomic number with electron count.
remember: State the octet rule as proposed by Kossel and Lewis, and give one example of a molecule that follows it.
Explain why noble gases are chemically inert according to the Kossel‑Lewis approach.
A student draws the Lewis structure of CO₂ with a single bond between C and each O and two lone pairs on each O. Evaluate the correctness of this structure.

cards.title: An ionic bond forms when one or more electrons are transferred from a metal…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: An ionic bond forms when one or more electrons are transferred from a metal atom (low ionisation energy) to a non‑metal atom (high electron affinity), producing oppositely charged ions that attract each other electrostatically. The Lewis structure (dot‑and‑cross diagram) represents this transfer: valence electrons of the metal are shown as dots, those of the non‑metal as crosses. After transfer, the cation has a complete octet (or duplet for H⁺) with no valence dots, while the anion displays a full octet of dots and crosses. The overall charge balance requires that total positive charge equals total negative charge, determining the stoichiometric formula (e.g., Na⁺Cl⁻ → NaCl, Mg²⁺O²⁻ → MgO, Al³⁺₃O²⁻₂ → Al₂O₃). This visualisation links the Kossel‑Lewis octet rule to the formation of a crystal lattice, where each ion is surrounded by counter‑ions in a repeating pattern. The diagram does not show three‑dimensional geometry or bond lengths; those are covered in later nodes on VSEPR and bond parameters.
steps: The Lewis structure of an ionic compound is a dot‑and‑cross diagram that shows complete electron transfer from metal to non‑metal so both ions achieve a stable octet.
Here is why: the octet rule drives atoms to gain or lose electrons until they have eight valence electrons (or two for hydrogen).
Metals in Groups 1‑3 lose 1‑3 electrons to form cations with empty valence shells; non‑metals in Groups 15‑17 gain 1‑3 electrons to fill their valence shell.
The diagram uses dots for the metal’s original electrons and crosses for the non‑metal’s electrons, making the transfer visible.
After transfer, the cation is drawn with its charge and no dots; the anion shows a full octet of mixed dots and crosses.
Charge balance then fixes the formula: total positive charge must equal total negative charge.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “It shows shared electron pairs between the ions”) reveals the misconception that ionic bonds involve electron sharing like covalent bonds, confusing the two bonding types.
remember: What does a Lewis structure for an ionic compound primarily represent.
Why are dots used for one element and crosses for the other in a dot‑and‑cross diagram of an ionic compound.
A student draws the Lewis structure of NaCl with eight dots around both Na and Cl. Evaluate this drawing.

cards.title: Covalent bond parameters are quantitative descriptors that characterise the…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Covalent bond parameters are quantitative descriptors that characterise the strength, geometry and electronic distribution in a covalent bond. Bond length (r) is the equilibrium distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms, measured in picometres (pm) or ångströms (Å). Bond angle (θ) is the angle formed by three nuclei (A–B–C) and defines molecular shape; it is expressed in degrees (°). Bond energy (or bond dissociation enthalpy, ΔH_diss) is the enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous bonds is broken homolytically, units kJ mol⁻¹. Bond order (BO) indicates the number of electron‑pair bonds between two atoms; for a single Lewis structure it is an integer (1, 2, 3), while for resonance hybrids it is the average over all contributing structures (BO = Σb / n). Bond polarity arises from unequal sharing of electrons due to electronegativity difference (Δχ) and is quantified by dipole moment μ = q·d (C·m). These parameters are inter‑related: higher bond order generally shortens bond length, increases bond energy, and reduces bond angle strain. Experimental techniques such as X‑ray diffraction, microwave spectroscopy, and thermochemistry provide these values. Understanding them allows prediction of reactivity, stability, and physical properties of covalent compounds.
steps: Bond parameters provide the numerical foundation for understanding molecular stability and geometry. - Higher bond order leads to shorter bond lengths and higher bond energies because increased electron density between…
Bond length acts as the equilibrium distance where attractive and repulsive forces balance; shorter bonds are generally stiffer and stronger.
Bond energy represents the work required to break a bond; it is higher for multiple bonds (e.g., C≡C at 839 kJ mol⁻¹ vs C–C at 347 kJ mol⁻¹) due to the cumulative strength of σ and π components.
Bond order is determined by counting shared electron pairs in Lewis structures, using averaging for resonance hybrids like ozone (BO = 1.5).
Bond polarity arises from electronegativity differences, creating a dipole moment (μ = q·d) that dictates how molecules interact with electric fields.
To determine these values, chemists use X-ray diffraction for solids and microwave spectroscopy for gases to find bond lengths, while calorimetry measures bond energies.
remember: Define bond length, bond angle, bond energy, bond order, and bond polarity. State the SI unit for each quantity.
Explain why bond length decreases and bond energy increases as bond order increases from single to double to triple bond, using the concept of electron density between nuclei.
Evaluate the statement: “The bond energy of a C=C double bond is exactly twice the bond energy of a C–C single bond.” Use typical values (C–C ≈ 347 kJ mol⁻¹, C=C ≈ 614 kJ mol⁻¹)….

cards.title: The octet rule states that atoms tend to gain, lose…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: The octet rule states that atoms tend to gain, lose, or share electrons to achieve a noble‑gas configuration with eight electrons in the valence shell. Octet deviations occur in three categories: 1. Electron‑deficient species – central atom has fewer than eight electrons (e.g., BF₃, BeCl₂). 2. Expanded octet – central atom accommodates more than eight electrons using available d‑orbitals (e.g., PF₅, SF₆, ClF₃). 3. Odd‑electron species – molecules with an odd number of valence electrons (e.g., NO, NO₂). Fajan’s rules predict the degree of covalent character in an ionic bond by comparing the polarizing power of the cation with the polarizability of the anion. Polarizing power (PP) ∝ charge of cation / ionic radius of cation; polarizability (Pol) ∝ charge of anion × ionic radius of anion. The rules state: - Higher cationic charge and smaller cationic radius increase PP. - Higher anionic charge and larger anionic radius increase Pol. - Cations with pseudo‑noble‑gas configuration (18‑electron) polarize more than those with noble‑gas configuration (8‑electron) of the same size and charge. When PP ≫ Pol, the electron cloud of the anion is distorted toward the cation, creating covalent character (e.g., AlCl₃, AgI).
steps: Takeaway: Octet deviations and Fajan’s rules together explain why many “ionic” compounds show covalent traits and why some molecules violate the eight‑electron guideline.
Here is why: the octet rule is a useful first approximation, but real atoms often need fewer or more electrons for stability.
Electron‑deficient molecules like BF₃ achieve stability by accepting a lone pair from a donor (forming coordinate bonds, later node).
Expanded‑octet species such as SF₆ use vacant 3d orbitals of sulfur to accommodate twelve electrons, a possibility only for period‑3 and heavier elements.
Odd‑electron radicals like NO remain paramagnetic because pairing all electrons would require an unfavorable promotion.
Fajan’s rules translate these ideas into a predictive framework for ionic compounds.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “expanded octet includes BeCl₂”) reveals the misconception that any molecule with less than eight electrons is expanded octet, confusing electron‑deficiency with expansion.
remember: State the three categories of octet rule deviations and give one example for each.
Explain why BeCl₂ is electron‑deficient and describe how it attains stability in the solid state.
Assess whether the statement “All compounds of third‑period elements obey the octet rule” is true. Justify your answer.

cards.title: VSEPR (Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion) theory is a model used to predict…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: VSEPR (Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion) theory is a model used to predict the three‑dimensional geometry of molecules from the arrangement of electron domains around a central atom. An electron domain is either a bonding pair (single, double, or triple bond counted as one domain) or a lone pair. The steric number (SN) equals the total number of electron domains: SN = number of σ bonds + number of lone pairs on the central atom. Electron domains adopt an arrangement that minimises repulsion, following the order: lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bonding pair > bonding pair–bonding pair. The resulting electron‑domain geometry (linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, octahedral) determines the molecular geometry when lone pairs are ignored. The AXE notation (A = central atom, X = bonded atoms, E = lone pairs) succinctly captures this: e.g., AX₄ = tetrahedral, AX₃E = trigonal pyramidal, AX₂E₂ = bent. VSEPR builds directly on Lewis structures (from the Kossel‑Lewis and covalent bond nodes) because correct Lewis structures provide the count of bonding and lone pairs. It does not predict bond lengths or energies, only approximate bond angles. Deviations from ideal angles are explained by the greater repulsive strength of lone pairs. The theory applies reliably to main‑group compounds with up to six electron domains; transition‑metal complexes and systems with strong π‑delocalisation are treated in later chapters.
steps: Electron pairs repel each other and adopt the arrangement that maximises separation to minimize repulsion.
This is the fundamental principle of VSEPR theory.
Lewis Structure Accuracy: The foundation of VSEPR is a correct Lewis structure, where each line or pair of dots represents an electron domain.
Steric Number Calculation: The steric number (SN = X + E) determines the electron-domain geometry, where X is the number of bonded atoms and E is the number of lone pairs.
Repulsion Minimization: Lone pairs occupy more space than bonding pairs, creating a hierarchy of repulsion (lp-lp > lp-bp > bp-bp) that forces bond angles to deviate from ideal values.
Geometry Distinction: Electron-domain geometry accounts for all pairs, while molecular geometry describes only the positions of the atoms, effectively "hiding" the lone pairs.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "bonding pair–bonding pair > lone pair–bonding pair > lone pair–lone pair") reveals the misconception that shared electron pairs repel more because they are involved in bonding, confusing bond strength with spatial repulsion.
remember: State the order of repulsion between electron pairs according to VSEPR theory.
Why does the H–O–H bond angle in water (104.5°) deviate from the ideal tetrahedral angle (109.5°).
A student predicts that SF₄ has a trigonal bipyramidal molecular geometry. Evaluate this prediction.

cards.title: Valence bond (VB) theory is a quantum‑mechanical model that explains covalent…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Valence bond (VB) theory is a quantum‑mechanical model that explains covalent bond formation through the overlap of half‑filled atomic orbitals on adjacent atoms. Each overlapping orbital contributes one electron; the paired electrons occupy the region of overlap, lowering the system’s potential energy. The theory introduces the overlap integral (S), a dimensionless measure of orbital overlap (0 ≤ S ≤ 1); larger S gives a stronger bond. VB theory also accounts for spin pairing — electrons must have opposite spins (Pauli principle) to occupy the same overlapping region. It predicts bond directionality because orbitals have specific shapes (s, p, d) and orientations; maximum overlap occurs along the orbital axis, giving rise to σ (sigma) bonds (head‑on overlap) and π (pi) bonds (side‑on overlap). The theory further explains bond length and bond energy trends: shorter bonds correspond to larger overlap integrals. VB theory is the conceptual precursor to hybridisation (node), which mixes atomic orbitals to produce equivalent hybrid orbitals for molecules like CH₄, NH₃, and H₂O. It does not treat electron delocalisation across the whole molecule — that is the domain of molecular orbital theory (node).
steps: Valence bond theory explains covalent bonding as the result of maximum overlap between half‑filled atomic orbitals with opposite‑spin electrons.
Here is why: the quantum‑mechanical wavefunctions of two approaching atoms begin to interfere constructively in the region between the nuclei.
When the orbitals are half‑filled, each contributes one electron; the Pauli principle forces the two electrons to adopt opposite spins, allowing them to occupy the same spatial region.
This shared electron density screens the nuclear repulsion and lowers the total energy — the hallmark of bond formation.
Consider the hydrogen molecule (H₂).
Each H atom has a 1s orbital with one electron.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “S can be negative or greater than 1”) reveals the misconception that S behaves like a probability amplitude rather than a positive‑definite overlap magnitude.
remember: Define the overlap integral (S) in valence bond theory and state its allowed range of values.
Explain why a σ bond is generally stronger than a π bond formed between the same two atoms.
A student claims that valence bond theory can fully explain the paramagnetism of O₂. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Hybridisation is a model within valence bond theory where atomic orbitals of…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Hybridisation is a model within valence bond theory where atomic orbitals of comparable energy on the same atom combine to form an equal number of new hybrid orbitals that are degenerate, directional, and oriented to minimise electron‑pair repulsion. The number and type of hybrid orbitals equal the number of atomic orbitals mixed. The steric number (σ‑bonds + lone pairs on the central atom) determines the hybridisation: steric number 2 → sp (linear, 180°), 3 → sp² (trigonal planar, 120°), 4 → sp³ (tetrahedral, 109.5°), 5 → sp³d (trigonal bipyramidal, 90°/120°), 6 → sp³d² (octahedral, 90°). Hybrid orbitals form σ‑bonds; unhybridised p (or d) orbitals form π‑bonds. This concept links the Lewis‑structure electron‑pair count (node 002, 005) to the directional overlap described in valence bond theory (node 006) and provides a predictive framework for molecular geometry before molecular orbital theory (node 008) offers a more quantitative picture.
steps: Hybridisation is a mathematical bookkeeping tool used to explain how atoms form equivalent bonds at specific angles, despite their ground-state orbitals having different energies and orientations.
Conservation of orbitals: The number of hybrid orbitals produced is always equal to the number of atomic orbitals mixed.
Directional geometry: Hybrid orbitals are oriented to minimise repulsion, dictating the shape of the molecule.

Predictive framework: The steric number (sum of σ-bonds and lone pairs) acts as a reliable recipe for determining the hybridisation state. π-bond formation: Unhybridised p or d orbitals remain available to form π-bonds…
To determine hybridisation, calculate the steric number by adding the number of σ-bonds and lone pairs on the central atom.
For a steric number of 2, one s and one p orbital mix to form two sp hybrids (linear, 180°, e.g., BeCl₂).
remember: What is the hybridisation of carbon in methane (CH₄).
Explain why the hybridisation of boron in BF₃ is sp² and not sp³.
A student claims that the hybridisation of sulfur in SF₆ is sp³d² because sulfur uses its 3d orbitals. Evaluate this claim in light of modern understanding.

cards.title: Molecular orbital (MO) theory describes electrons in a molecule as occupying…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Molecular orbital (MO) theory describes electrons in a molecule as occupying orbitals that extend over the entire nuclear framework, formed by the linear combination of atomic orbitals (LCAO). Each atomic orbital contributes to a set of molecular orbitals: bonding orbitals (lower energy, electron density between nuclei) and antibonding orbitals (higher energy, nodal plane between nuclei). Electrons fill these MOs following the Aufbau principle, Pauli exclusion principle, and Hund’s rule. The bond order, defined as half the difference between the number of electrons in bonding (Nb) and antibonding (Na) orbitals, quantifies bond strength and predicts stability; a bond order of zero indicates no net bonding. MO theory also explains magnetic properties: species with unpaired electrons in degenerate MOs are paramagnetic, while those with all electrons paired are diamagnetic. The theory successfully accounts for the paramagnetism of O₂, the bond orders of homonuclear and heteronuclear diatomics, and the electronic spectra of molecules, linking quantum‑mechanical orbital mixing to observable chemical behaviour.
steps: The central takeaway is that molecular orbitals are delocalised over the whole molecule and their filling determines both bond strength (bond order) and magnetic properties.
Here is why: (1) Atomic orbitals combine mathematically (LCAO) to give an equal number of molecular orbitals — bonding and antibonding pairs.
(2) Electrons occupy the lowest‑energy MOs first, obeying Pauli and Hund rules, just as in atoms.
(3) Bond order = (Nb – Na)/2 directly follows from this filling; a positive bond order means a stable bond, zero means no bond, and fractional values appear in ions.
(4) Unpaired electrons in degenerate π or σ orbitals make a species paramagnetic, a hallmark prediction of MO theory that valence bond theory misses.
(5) For heteronuclear diatomics like CO, the energy ordering shifts but the same principles apply.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Bond order = Nb + Na”) reveals the misconception that both bonding and antibonding electrons strengthen the bond, confusing electron count with net bonding effect.
remember: State the formula for bond order in molecular orbital theory and define each term.
Explain why O₂ is paramagnetic according to MO theory.
A student claims that a molecule with bond order zero cannot exist. Evaluate this claim with an example.

cards.title: A coordinate bond (also called a dative covalent bond) is a covalent bond in…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: A coordinate bond (also called a dative covalent bond) is a covalent bond in which both shared electrons originate from the same atom. The donor atom possesses a lone pair of electrons in its valence shell; the acceptor atom has an empty orbital of suitable energy. When the lone pair is donated, a shared pair forms, giving each atom a stable octet (or duet for hydrogen). The bond is represented by an arrow (→) pointing from donor to acceptor. Unlike a normal covalent bond where each atom contributes one electron, the coordinate bond involves a one‑sided electron donation. After formation, the bond is indistinguishable from a regular covalent bond in terms of length, strength, and polarity. Common examples include the formation of ammonium ion (NH₄⁺) from ammonia (NH₃) and a proton (H⁺), and the hydration of metal ions such as [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺. Coordinate bonds are central to complex ion formation, Lewis acid‑base adducts, and many biological molecules (e.g., haemoglobin). They obey the octet rule (or expanded octet for heavier elements) and are described within valence bond theory as sigma bonds formed by overlap of a filled donor orbital with an empty acceptor orbital.
steps: A coordinate bond forms when one atom provides both electrons for a shared pair, functioning exactly like a normal covalent bond once established. - The donor atom acts as a Lewis base by providing a lone pair of…
The acceptor atom acts as a Lewis acid by providing an empty orbital.
The resulting bond is a stable, shared electron pair that satisfies the octet rule for both atoms.
The arrow notation (→) is merely a bookkeeping tool to track the electron origin, not a sign of different bond strength. 1.
Identify the donor: Look for atoms with non-bonding electron pairs, such as Nitrogen in NH₃ or Oxygen in H₂O.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., choosing Cl₂) reveals the misconception that any covalent bond with equal sharing is a coordinate bond, ignoring the one‑sided electron donation characteristic.
remember: Which of the following species contains a coordinate bond? A) Cl₂ B) NH₄⁺ C) CH₄ D) O₂.
In the formation of the hydronium ion (H₃O⁺) from water and a proton, which atom acts as the Lewis base and which as the Lewis acid.
Explain why the coordinate bond in NH₄⁺ is indistinguishable from a normal covalent N–H bond after formation.

cards.title: Resonance (mesomerism) describes the delocalisation of π‑electrons or lone…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Resonance (mesomerism) describes the delocalisation of π‑electrons or lone pairs over two or more adjacent atoms when a single Lewis structure cannot represent the true electron distribution. A set of contributing (canonical) structures, each obeying the octet rule and differing only in the placement of electrons (not nuclei), are combined to give a resonance hybrid. The hybrid has lower energy (greater stability) than any individual contributor; the energy difference is the resonance energy (RE). Key criteria: (1) same atomic positions, (2) same number of unpaired electrons, (3) similar energy among contributors. Formal charges guide the relative importance — structures with minimal charge separation and negative charge on more electronegative atoms contribute more. Resonance explains bond‑length equalisation (e.g., C–C in benzene = 1.39 Å), reactivity patterns, and acid‑base strengths (e.g., carboxylate anion stabilisation).
steps: The one thing to remember: Resonance is not a rapid flipping between structures; it is a single, blended electron distribution that is more stable than any individual Lewis drawing.
Here is why: 1.
Electron delocalisation lowers energy — spreading charge over a larger volume reduces electron‑electron repulsion. 2.
Canonical structures are bookkeeping tools — they differ only in electron placement; nuclei stay fixed. 3.
Formal charge guides contributor importance — structures with zero or minimal formal charges, and negative charge on electronegative atoms, dominate the hybrid. 4.
Resonance energy quantifies the stabilisation — it is the difference between the energy of the best canonical form and the real hybrid. 5.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “two structures”) reveals the misconception that only two distinct arrangements are possible, ignoring the symmetry‑equivalent third oxygen.
remember: How many canonical resonance structures can be drawn for the nitrate ion (NO₃⁻) that satisfy the octet rule and have the same atomic connectivity.
Why does the carbonate ion (CO₃²⁻) have three equivalent resonance structures, and what is the formal charge on carbon in each.
Evaluate the statement: “The resonance hybrid of benzene has alternating single and double bonds that rapidly interconvert.”.

cards.title: Hydrogen bonding is a strong dipole‑dipole interaction that occurs when a…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Hydrogen bonding is a strong dipole‑dipole interaction that occurs when a hydrogen atom covalently bonded to a highly electronegative atom (nitrogen, oxygen, or fluorine) experiences an electrostatic attraction toward a lone pair on another nearby electronegative atom. The donor atom (N, O, F) withdraws electron density from the H–X bond, creating a partial positive charge (δ+) on hydrogen; the acceptor atom bears a partial negative charge (δ−) due to its lone pairs. This interaction is directional, typically 10–40 kJ mol⁻¹, stronger than van der Waals forces but weaker than covalent or ionic bonds. Hydrogen bonds can be intermolecular (between separate molecules, e.g., H₂O, HF, NH₃) or intramolecular (within a single molecule, e.g., o‑nitrophenol). They dictate anomalous properties of water: high specific heat, high latent heat of vaporisation, density maximum at 4 °C, and the open hexagonal lattice of ice. In biological systems, hydrogen bonds stabilise DNA double helices (base‑pairing) and protein secondary structures (α‑helices, β‑sheets). The concept links to earlier topics: electronegativity and bond polarity (covalent bond parameters), molecular geometry (VSEPR), and resonance (delocalisation can enhance acceptor ability). It does not involve electron sharing or transfer, so it is classified as a non‑covalent interaction.
steps: Let’s build the idea step by step, linking what you already know.
In the covalent bond node you learned that when two atoms share electrons unequally, a dipole forms — think of the O–H bond in water.
Oxygen (EN = 3.44) pulls the shared pair toward itself, leaving hydrogen electron‑deficient (δ+).
At the same time, oxygen carries two lone pairs, regions of high electron density (δ−).
Now picture a second water molecule approaching: its oxygen lone pair can electrostatically attract the δ+ hydrogen of the first molecule.
This attraction is the hydrogen bond.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., choosing HCl because chlorine is electronegative) reveals the misconception that any highly electronegative atom can serve as a donor — the syllabus restricts donors to N, O, F only.

cards.title: In chemical thermodynamics a system is the specific portion of matter chosen…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: In chemical thermodynamics a system is the specific portion of matter chosen for study — a reaction mixture, a gas in a cylinder, or a solution in a beaker. The surroundings comprise everything external to the system that can exchange energy or matter with it. The boundary separates system from surroundings; it may be real (container wall) or imaginary (a geometric surface). The universe = system + surroundings. A system is described by state variables (pressure P, volume V, temperature T, amount n, internal energy U, enthalpy H, entropy S, Gibbs energy G) which have definite values at equilibrium and are independent of the path taken to reach that state. The choice of system determines which energy transfers (heat q, work w) are counted as entering or leaving. All subsequent laws — first law (energy conservation), second law (entropy increase) — are applied to the defined system. Precise definition of system, surroundings, and boundary is therefore the prerequisite for any quantitative thermodynamic analysis.
steps: Let’s start with a familiar Indian kitchen scene: a steel handi (pot) of dal simmering on a gas stove.
The dal plus the water and spices inside the handi is the system — we want to know how its temperature changes.
The flame, the metal of the handi, the air in the kitchen, the cook — all of that is the surroundings.

The inner wall of the handi is the boundary; heat flows across it from flame to dal, but the dal cannot jump out unless the lid is off. If we put a tight lid, the boundary becomes closed to matter but still allows heat…
Now imagine we draw an imaginary sphere around a gas expanding in a piston.
The gas is the system; the piston, cylinder, and outside atmosphere are surroundings.

cards.title: A thermodynamic system is the part of the universe under study…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: A thermodynamic system is the part of the universe under study, separated from the surroundings by a real or imaginary boundary, and classified by what can cross this boundary. An open system permits both mass and energy (heat, work) to be exchanged with surroundings, such as a beaker of boiling water open to air or a continuous flow reactor. A closed system permits energy (heat and work) to be exchanged while mass remains constant, though chemical reactions may change the number of moles of individual species, as seen in a reaction in a sealed rigid container that is not thermally insulated. An isolated system permits neither mass nor energy to cross the boundary, resulting in strictly constant total energy and mass, though perfect isolation is an idealisation approximated by a well‑insulated calorimeter (bomb + water + jacket). This classification determines the form of the first law: mass‑flow terms appear for open systems, ΔU = q + w for closed systems, and ΔU = 0 for isolated systems, making system type understanding essential before defining state functions and applying the first law.
steps: The type of thermodynamic system is determined by whether mass and energy pass through the boundary separating the chosen study system from its surroundings.

Thermodynamic classification relies on four key supporting arguments: mass transfer determines open systems, thermal or mechanical transfer creates closed systems, complete containment defines isolated systems, and…
First, systems that allow atoms or molecules to enter or leave are open, such as a kitchen pressure cooker venting steam or a continuous‑flow reactor.
Second, systems that stop matter while allowing heat or work to pass are closed, such as a sealed glass ampoule in an oil bath or a gas cylinder with a movable piston.
Third, systems that block both mass and energy are isolated, which is an idealisation best approximated in practice by a bomb calorimeter.
Fourth, the system type dictates the specific energy-balance equation required, such as enthalpy terms for open systems, ΔU = q + w for closed systems, and ΔU = 0 for isolated systems.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., choosing (b) because the container is sealed) reveals the misconception that “sealed” automatically means isolated, ignoring thermal conductivity of the container walls.

cards.title: A state function (or state variable) is a thermodynamic quantity whose value is…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: A state function (or state variable) is a thermodynamic quantity whose value is determined solely by the current equilibrium state of the system, independent of the history or pathway by which that state was reached. Mathematically, for any state function X, the change between two states 1 and 2 is Δ X = X_2 - X_1. Because Δ X depends only on the endpoints, the cyclic integral of an exact differential vanishes: dX = 0. In contrast, path functions (heat q and work w) depend on the specific process; their cyclic integrals are generally non‑zero. The principal state functions encountered in Class 11 ISC Physical Chemistry are: - Temperature (T) – SI unit kelvin (K) - Pressure (p) – SI unit pascal (Pa) - Volume (V) – SI unit cubic metre (m³) - Internal energy (U) – SI unit joule (J) - Enthalpy (H = U + pV) – SI unit joule (J) - Entropy (S) – SI unit joule per kelvin (J K⁻¹) - Gibbs energy (G = H – TS) – SI unit joule (J) Relationships: H, S and G are defined from the primitive state functions U, p, V, T. The first law ( Δ U = q + w ) combines a state function (U) with path functions (q,w). Hess’s law and calorimetry later exploit the path‑independence of Δ H and Δ U. The second law introduces entropy S as a state function whose change for a reversible process is Δ S = dq_revT. Gibbs energy G combines H and S to predict spontaneity at constant T and p.
steps: The one thing to remember: a state function’s change depends only on the initial and final states, never on the path taken.
Here is why: 1.
Exact differential – If a quantity X is a state function, its infinitesimal change dX is an exact differential.
This means the mixed partial derivatives of its natural variables are equal (e.g., for U(S,V), (∂^2 U)/(∂ S ∂ V) = (∂^2 U)/(∂ V ∂ S)).
Consequently, the line integral _1^2 dX = X_2 - X_1 is path‑independent. 2.
Cyclic integral zero – Because the integral depends only on endpoints, going around a closed loop (state 1 → 2 → 1) gives dX = 0.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., choosing heat) reveals the misconception that any energy transfer quantity is a state function, confusing energy transfer with energy content.

cards.title: The first law of thermodynamics is the principle of energy conservation applied…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: The first law of thermodynamics is the principle of energy conservation applied to thermodynamic systems. For a closed system, the change in internal energy (ΔU) equals the heat supplied to the system (q) plus the work done on the system (w): ΔU = q + w. Internal energy (U) is a state function — its value depends only on the current state (temperature, pressure, composition) and not on the path taken. Heat (q) and work (w) are path functions; their magnitudes depend on how the process is carried out. By convention, q is positive when heat enters the system (endothermic) and negative when heat leaves (exothermic). Work done on the system (e.g., compression) is positive; work done by the system (e.g., expansion) is negative. For pressure–volume work at constant external pressure, w = –PΔV. The SI unit for all energy terms is the joule (J). This law connects the microscopic concept of internal energy (kinetic and potential energy of molecules) with macroscopic measurable quantities q and w, and it underpins later concepts such as enthalpy (H = U + pV) and Hess’s law.
steps: The first law tells us that energy cannot be created or destroyed in a thermodynamic process — it is conserved as the sum of heat and work crossing the system boundary.
Here is why: (1) Internal energy U is a property of the system’s state; any change ΔU depends only on initial and final states.
(2) Heat q and work w are energy transfers that depend on the pathway; different routes between the same states give different q and w but the same ΔU.
(3) The sign convention (q positive into system, w positive onto system) ensures ΔU = q + w holds universally.
(4) For expansion work against constant pressure, w = –PΔV, linking macroscopic pressure‑volume changes to energy.
(5) A cyclic process returns to its initial state, so ΔU = 0, yet net q and w can be non‑zero — this is the basis of heat engines.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., ΔU = q – w) reveals the misconception that the sign convention for work is universal — confusing the chemistry convention (work on system positive) with the physics convention (work by system positive).
remember: State the mathematical expression of the first law of thermodynamics for a closed system, defining each term and its SI unit.

A student claims that in an isothermal expansion of an ideal gas, ΔU = 0, so q = –w. Is this statement correct? Justify.

cards.title: Internal energy (U) is the sum of all microscopic kinetic and potential…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Internal energy (U) is the sum of all microscopic kinetic and potential energies of the particles constituting a thermodynamic system. It is a state function, meaning its value depends only on the current equilibrium state (temperature, pressure, volume, composition) and not on the path taken to reach that state. The First Law of Thermodynamics quantifies its change: ΔU = q + w, where q is the heat transferred to the system (positive when absorbed) and w is the work done on the system (positive when work is done on the system). For an ideal gas, internal energy depends solely on temperature (Joule’s law), so ΔU = nCᵥ,mΔT for a constant‑volume process. In real substances, intermolecular forces contribute a potential‑energy component, making U a function of both temperature and volume. Because U is a state function, cyclic processes return the system to its initial U, giving ∮dU = 0. The SI unit of internal energy and its change is the joule (J). This concept links the microscopic molecular picture to macroscopic thermodynamic measurements and underpins the definition of enthalpy (H = U + pV) in the next node.
steps: Internal energy is the total microscopic energy of a system and its change equals the heat added plus the work done on the system.
First, internal energy gathers every molecular motion — translational, rotational, vibrational — and every intermolecular potential interaction into a single thermodynamic property.
Because it is a state function, only the initial and final equilibrium states matter; the path taken (whether you heat quickly or slowly, compress reversibly or irreversibly) does not alter ΔU.
Second, the First Law gives the operational rule: ΔU = q + w. Heat q is energy transferred due to temperature difference; work w is energy transferred by macroscopic forces (e.g., pΔV work).
The sign convention used in ISC chemistry is that q > 0 when heat enters the system and w > 0 when work is done on the system.
Third, for an ideal gas the potential‑energy part is zero, so U depends only on temperature.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “internal energy is the heat content of a system, measured in calories”) reveals the misconception that heat and internal energy are identical — confusing a path‑dependent transfer quantity with a state property.
remember: Define internal energy and state its SI unit.
A gas expands adiabatically into vacuum (free expansion). What is ΔU? Explain.
Evaluate the statement: “For an ideal gas, internal energy depends only on temperature.”.

cards.title: Enthalpy (symbol H) is a thermodynamic state function defined for any system as…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Enthalpy (symbol H) is a thermodynamic state function defined for any system as the sum of its internal energy U and the product of its pressure p and volume V: H = U + pV Because U, p, and V are state functions, H is also a state function; its value depends only on the current equilibrium state, not on the path taken to reach it. The SI unit of enthalpy is the joule (J); in chemistry the kilojoule (kJ) is customary. For a process occurring at constant pressure (the most common laboratory condition), the heat exchanged with the surroundings, q_p, equals the change in enthalpy: Δ H = q_p This relationship follows from the first law Δ U = q + w and the definition of pressure‑volume work w = -pΔ V (only expansion work considered). Substituting q = Δ U - w and w = -pΔ V gives q_p = Δ U + pΔ V = Δ(U + pV) = Δ H Thus, at constant pressure, the enthalpy change directly measures the heat absorbed or released. Enthalpy changes are classified as exothermic (Δ H < 0, heat released) or endothermic (Δ H > 0, heat absorbed). Standard enthalpy changes (ΔH°) refer to reactions carried out at 1 bar and a specified temperature (usually 298 K) with all reactants and products in their standard states. Because enthalpy is a state function, Hess’s law applies: the total enthalpy change for a reaction is the sum of enthalpy changes for any series of steps that lead from the same reactants to the same products. This property makes enthalpy a central quantity in thermochemistry, calorimetry, and the prediction of reaction spontaneity when combined with entropy (ΔS) to give Gibbs energy (ΔG = ΔH – TΔS). In the ISC syllabus, enthalpy is introduced after internal energy (node) and before Hess’s law (node). It connects the microscopic concept of internal energy to the macroscopic, experimentally measurable heat at constant pressure.
steps: Enthalpy is the heat content of a system at constant pressure, defined as H = U + pV, so that any heat exchanged at constant pressure equals the change in enthalpy (ΔH = q_p).

Here is why: the first law tells us Δ U = q + w. For a process where the only work is expansion against a constant external pressure, w = -pΔ V. Rearranging gives q = Δ U + pΔ V. Notice that Δ U + pΔ V is exactly the…
Because H is a state function, its change depends only on initial and final states, not on the path.
Consider a simple experiment: 1 mol of ice at 0 °C melts in a beaker open to the atmosphere (constant pressure).
The system absorbs 6.01 kJ of heat from the surroundings.
Since the pressure is constant, this heat is precisely ΔH for the melting process.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “enthalpy is the heat content at constant volume”) reveals the misconception that enthalpy and internal energy are interchangeable, confusing the conditions (constant pressure vs. constant volume) under which each equals heat.

cards.title: Hess’s law states that the total enthalpy change for a chemical reaction is…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Hess’s law states that the total enthalpy change for a chemical reaction is independent of the pathway taken, provided the initial and final states are the same. Because enthalpy (H) is a state function, ΔH for an overall reaction equals the algebraic sum of ΔH values for each step in any thermochemical cycle that connects reactants to products. This principle allows calculation of reaction enthalpies that are difficult to measure directly by combining known enthalpies of formation (ΔH_f°), combustion (ΔH_c°), or bond dissociation (ΔH_bond). The law follows directly from the first law of thermodynamics and the definition of enthalpy as H = U + pV. In practice, one writes a target reaction, identifies a series of intermediate reactions with known ΔH values, manipulates them (reverse, multiply) to cancel intermediates, and sums the ΔH values to obtain the desired ΔH_rxn. Standard conditions (298 K, 1 bar) are used for tabulated data; the sign convention is that exothermic steps have negative ΔH. Hess’s law underpins calorimetric determinations (see node) and the construction of Born–Haber cycles, which are treated in higher classes.
steps: The takeaway: Because enthalpy is a state function, the net enthalpy change of a reaction depends only on the initial and final states, not on the intermediate steps.
Here is why: (1) The first law guarantees energy conservation;
(2) Enthalpy, defined as H = U + pV, inherits the state‑function property from internal energy U;
(3) Any cyclic process returns the system to its original state, so the sum of ΔH around the cycle must be zero;
(4) Therefore, a reaction carried out in one step or in several steps must have the same overall ΔH.
Consider the formation of carbon dioxide from graphite and oxygen.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Hess’s law says heat is conserved in a reaction”) reveals the misconception that the law is about heat conservation rather than the state‑function nature of enthalpy.

cards.title: Calorimetry is the experimental technique for measuring the quantity of heat…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Calorimetry is the experimental technique for measuring the quantity of heat (q) transferred during a physical or chemical process. It relies on the first law: ΔU = q + w. At constant pressure (open container) the heat exchanged equals the enthalpy change, qₚ = ΔH; at constant volume (sealed bomb) it equals the internal energy change, qᵥ = ΔU. The fundamental relation is q = m c ΔT for a substance of mass m, specific heat capacity c (SI unit J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ or J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹), and temperature change ΔT. For the calorimeter itself, q_cal = C_cal ΔT where C_cal (J K⁻¹) is the calorimeter constant (heat capacity of the vessel, stirrer, thermometer, etc.). In a coffee‑cup (constant‑pressure) calorimeter the system is the reaction mixture; the surroundings are the solution and the cup, so ΔH_rxn = –(q_soln + q_cal). In a bomb (constant‑volume) calorimeter the reaction occurs in a steel vessel immersed in a known mass of water; the heat released raises the temperature of water and the bomb, giving ΔU_comb = –(m_w c_w ΔT + C_cal ΔT). Calorimetry thus provides the experimental ΔH and ΔU values that feed into Hess’s law cycles and later into entropy and Gibbs‑energy calculations.
steps: Calorimetry is the laboratory method used to measure the heat changes associated with chemical and physical processes, grounded in the first law of thermodynamics.
Calorimetry quantifies energy transfer by measuring temperature changes in a controlled environment.
The heat exchanged is calculated by accounting for the energy absorbed by the reaction mixture and the calorimeter vessel itself.
Experimental conditions dictate the thermodynamic state function measured: constant pressure yields enthalpy (ΔH), while constant volume yields internal energy (ΔU).
Data obtained from calorimetry serves as the empirical foundation for applying Hess’s Law to determine reaction enthalpies that are otherwise difficult to measure.
In practice, calorimetry involves tracking heat flow through temperature monitoring.

cards.title: The Second Law of Thermodynamics governs the direction of spontaneous processes…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: The Second Law of Thermodynamics governs the direction of spontaneous processes and sets limits on the conversion of heat into work. It is expressed through two classical statements: the Kelvin‑Planck statement — no cyclic process can convert heat entirely into work without rejecting some heat to a colder reservoir — and the Clausius statement — heat cannot spontaneously flow from a colder body to a hotter body without external work. These statements are equivalent and lead to the concept of a reversible Carnot engine operating between two temperatures T_H (hot) and T_C (cold). The maximum possible efficiency of any heat engine is the Carnot efficiency _Carnot = 1 - (T_C)/(T_H). The law also introduces entropy S as a state function; for any reversible process dS = δ Q_revT, and for any real (irreversible) process dS > (δ Q)/(T). The Second Law thus quantifies the degradation of energy quality and provides the criterion for spontaneity: the total entropy of an isolated system never decreases (Δ S_univ ≥ 0). This node covers the statements, Carnot cycle, efficiency limit, and the Clausius inequality; detailed entropy calculations and Gibbs energy are reserved for the next node.
steps: The Second Law tells us that energy has a quality — heat at a higher temperature can do more work than the same amount of heat at a lower temperature — and that every real process degrades some energy into unusable…
Here is why: (1) The Kelvin‑Planck statement forbids a 100 % efficient heat engine; any engine must reject heat to a cold reservoir.
(2) The Clausius statement forbids spontaneous heat flow from cold to hot; refrigerators need work input.
(3) These two statements are logically equivalent — violating one allows constructing a device that violates the other.
(4) The Carnot engine, an ideal reversible cycle of two isotherms and two adiabats, sets the upper efficiency bound = 1 - T_C/T_H.
(5) The Clausius inequality δ Q/T ≤ 0 generalises this limit to any cycle, introducing entropy as the quantity whose change is δ Q_rev/T.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “heat can be fully converted to work in a cyclic process”) reveals the misconception that the First Law alone governs energy conversion, ignoring the directionality imposed by the Second Law.
remember: State the Kelvin‑Planck statement of the Second Law of Thermodynamics.
Explain why the Clausius statement (“heat cannot spontaneously flow from a colder body to a hotter body”) is equivalent to the Kelvin‑Planck statement.
A cyclic engine operates between reservoirs at 500 K and 300 K. In one cycle it absorbs 2000 J from the hot reservoir, performs 800 J of work, and rejects 1200 J to the cold….

cards.title: Entropy (S) is a state function quantifying the number of microscopic…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Entropy (S) is a state function quantifying the number of microscopic configurations (microstates) corresponding to a macroscopic state; its change for a reversible process is ΔS = q_rev/T, with SI unit J K⁻¹. The Second Law states that for any spontaneous process in an isolated system, ΔS_universe > 0. Gibbs free energy (G) combines enthalpy (H) and entropy to predict spontaneity at constant temperature and pressure: G = H – TS, so ΔG = ΔH – TΔS. A process is spontaneous if ΔG < 0, non‑spontaneous if ΔG > 0, and at equilibrium ΔG = 0. Standard Gibbs energy of formation (Δ_fG°) and standard entropy (S°) are tabulated for elements and compounds at 298 K, 1 bar. The relationship ΔG° = –RT ln K links thermodynamics to equilibrium constants. These concepts extend the First Law (energy conservation) and Second Law (entropy direction) to practical chemical predictions.
steps: Spontaneity is determined by the balance between energy release and the increase in system disorder. - Entropy measures the dispersal of energy and matter; for a reversible change, the entropy change is defined as ΔS =…
For phase transitions at constant temperature, such as ice melting, this simplifies to ΔS = ΔH_fus/T.
Absolute entropies are tabulated as standard molar entropies (S°), allowing the calculation of reaction entropy via ΔS° = ΣνS°(products) – ΣνS°(reactants).
Gibbs free energy (ΔG = ΔH – TΔS) serves as the definitive scoreboard for spontaneity at constant temperature and pressure, where ΔG < 0 corresponds to a spontaneous process (ΔS_univ > 0).
Standard conditions allow for the calculation of ΔG° using tabulated Δ_fH° and S° values, or directly from Δ_fG° values, where ΔG° = ΣνΔ_fG°(products) – ΣνΔ_fG°(reactants).
The equilibrium constant K is linked to standard Gibbs energy by the equation ΔG° = –RT ln K, where a large negative ΔG° indicates a product-favored equilibrium.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “entropy is heat” or “unit is J”) reveals the misconception that entropy equals heat rather than heat divided by temperature, confusing energy with energy dispersal.
remember: Define entropy and state its SI unit.

cards.title: Chemical equilibrium is the state of a reversible reaction in which the rate of…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Chemical equilibrium is the state of a reversible reaction in which the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction, so the macroscopic concentrations of all species remain constant with time. The law of mass action, formulated by Guldberg and Waage, states that for a generic equilibrium aA + bB cC + dD the equilibrium constant in terms of molar concentrations (Kc) is K_c = ([C]^c[D]^d)/([A]^a[B]^b) where [X] denotes the equilibrium molar concentration (mol L⁻¹) of species X, and a, b, c, d are the stoichiometric coefficients from the balanced equation. For gas‑phase equilibria an analogous constant Kp uses partial pressures (bar) K_p = ((p_C)^c(p_D)^d)/((p_A)^a(p_B)^b) and the two are related by K_p = K_c(RT)^Δ n_g where Δ n_g = (c+d)-(a+b), R = 0.08314 L bar K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, and T is the absolute temperature (K). The equilibrium constant is temperature‑dependent only; it does not change with initial concentrations, pressure (for Kc), or the presence of a catalyst. A large K (≫1) indicates product‑favoured equilibrium; a small K (≪1) indicates reactant‑favoured equilibrium. The reaction quotient Q has the same algebraic form as K but uses instantaneous concentrations; comparing Q with K predicts the direction in which the system will shift to reach equilibrium.
steps: The one thing to remember: At equilibrium the ratio of product concentrations (each raised to its stoichiometric coefficient) to reactant concentrations (each raised to its coefficient) is a constant, Kc, that depends…
Here is why: Consider the reversible synthesis of ammonia, N_2(g) + 3H_2(g) 2NH_3(g).
Initially only N₂ and H₂ are present.
As the reaction proceeds, NH₃ forms and its concentration rises while N₂ and H₂ fall.
The forward rate is proportional to [N_2][H_2]^3 (law of mass action for elementary steps) and the reverse rate to [NH_3]^2.
When the two rates become equal, the concentrations stop changing — equilibrium is reached.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., K_c = ([SO_3])/([SO_2][O_2])) reveals the misconception that coefficients are ignored or that only one power is used, confusing the exponent rule with simple concentration ratios.

For the equilibrium H_2(g) + I_2(g) 2HI(g) at 500 K, Kc =….

cards.title: Le Chatelier’s principle states that if a dynamic equilibrium is subjected to a…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Le Chatelier’s principle states that if a dynamic equilibrium is subjected to a change in concentration, pressure (or volume), or temperature, the position of equilibrium moves in the direction that counteracts the imposed change. For a generic reaction aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD, the reaction quotient Q = ([C]^c[D]^d)/([A]^a[B]^b) (or the analogous pressure expression) is compared with the equilibrium constant K. If Q < K the forward reaction is favoured; if Q > K the reverse reaction is favoured. Increasing the concentration of a reactant (or decreasing a product) lowers Q, driving the net reaction forward. Raising total pressure (or decreasing volume) shifts the equilibrium toward the side with fewer gas moles. For an exothermic reaction (ΔH < 0), raising temperature increases K for the endothermic direction, so equilibrium shifts left; for an endothermic reaction it shifts right. A catalyst speeds both forward and reverse rates equally, so it does not alter the equilibrium position, only the time to reach it. The principle links directly to the law of mass action (node) and underpins later ionic‑equilibrium topics (acids, bases, buffers, solubility product).
steps: Takeaway: Le Chatelier’s principle lets you foresee how any equilibrium will respond to a disturbance by comparing the reaction quotient Q with the equilibrium constant K. Supporting argument 1 – Concentration changes…
Because Q < K, the system consumes the added reactant, forming more products until Q = K again.
Removing a product has the same effect.
Supporting argument 2 – Pressure/volume changes (gaseous systems): For N₂(g) + 3 H₂(g) ⇌ 2 NH₃(g), the forward side has 2 gas moles, the reverse side 4.
Compressing the vessel (raising total pressure) favours the side with fewer moles — the forward reaction — so more NH₃ forms.
Adding an inert gas at constant volume does not change partial pressures, so no shift occurs.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer such as “the equilibrium constant changes to accommodate the disturbance” reveals the misconception that K is variable with concentration or pressure, whereas K only changes with temperature.
remember: State Le Chatelier’s principle in one sentence.
For the equilibrium 2 SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2 SO₃(g) (ΔH = ‑198 kJ mol⁻¹), predict the effect of (a) increasing total pressure by halving the volume, (b) raising the temperature, (c)….
A student argues that adding an inert gas at constant pressure to the equilibrium N₂(g) + 3 H₂(g) ⇌ 2 NH₃(g) will shift the equilibrium toward products because total pressure….

cards.title: Ionic equilibrium of acids concerns the reversible dissociation of an acid HA…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Ionic equilibrium of acids concerns the reversible dissociation of an acid HA in water: HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻. At constant temperature, the ratio of product concentrations to reactant concentration reaches a fixed value, the acid dissociation constant Ka = [H⁺][A⁻]/[HA]. Ka quantifies acid strength: larger Ka means greater tendency to donate protons, lower pH for a given concentration. The equilibrium position obeys the law of mass action and shifts according to Le Chatelier’s principle when [H⁺] or [HA] is changed. Percent ionization = ([H⁺]eq / C₀)×100, where C₀ is the initial acid concentration. Relationships: pH = –log₁₀[H⁺]; for weak acids, [H⁺] ≈ √(Ka·C₀) when ionization <5%. Strong acids are treated as completely dissociated (Ka → ∞). This node focuses on monoprotic acids; polyprotic systems and salt hydrolysis are reserved for later nodes.
steps: The strength of an acid in aqueous solution is quantified by its acid dissociation constant Ka, which determines the equilibrium concentration of hydrogen ions.
Here is why: 1.
Law of mass action gives Ka = [H⁺][A⁻]/[HA] at equilibrium, linking molecular concentrations to a constant. 2.
Le Chatelier’s principle predicts that increasing [H⁺] (e.g., by adding a strong acid) shifts the equilibrium left, suppressing dissociation of HA. 3.

Approximation validity: for weak acids with Ka·C₀ < 10⁻⁴, the change in [HA] is negligible, allowing [H⁺] ≈ √(Ka·C₀). 4. pH connection: pH = –log₁₀[H⁺] translates the equilibrium [H⁺] into the familiar acidity scale.
Consider a student preparing a 0.10 M solution of acetic acid (CH₃COOH) in a kitchen vinegar experiment.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Ka has unit mol L⁻¹”) reveals the misconception that equilibrium constants retain the units of concentration, confusing Kc with Ka.
remember: Write the expression for the acid dissociation constant Ka of a generic monoprotic acid HA and state its SI unit.
Acid X has Ka = 2.0×10⁻⁴ and acid Y has Ka = 5.0×10⁻⁶. Which acid is stronger and why.
Evaluate the statement: “A 0.01 M solution of a weak acid always has a higher pH than a 0.01 M solution of a strong acid.”.

cards.title: A base, in the Brønsted–Lowry sense…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: A base, in the Brønsted–Lowry sense, is a species that accepts a proton (H⁺) from a donor (acid). In aqueous solution the acceptance of H⁺ by a base B produces its conjugate acid BH⁺ and releases hydroxide ion: B + H₂O ⇌ BH⁺ + OH⁻. The equilibrium constant for this reaction is the base dissociation constant, Kb = [BH⁺][OH⁻]/[B] (activities approximated by molar concentrations, mol L⁻¹). The strength of a base is quantified by Kb or its negative logarithm pKb = –log₁₀Kb. For any conjugate acid–base pair, Ka × Kb = Kw, where Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ (at 298 K) is the ionic product of water. Strong bases (e.g., NaOH, KOH) dissociate completely, giving very large Kb (effectively infinite) and pKb ≈ 0; weak bases (e.g., NH₃, CH₃NH₂) have finite Kb (10⁻⁵–10⁻⁹) and pKb 5–9. The hydrolysis of salts of weak bases (e.g., NH₄Cl) produces acidic solutions because the conjugate acid BH⁺ donates H⁺ to water. Understanding Kb, pKb, and the Ka–Kb–Kw relationship is essential for predicting pH of basic solutions and for designing buffer systems (covered in the next node).
steps: The one thing to remember: A base’s strength is quantified by Kb, and for any conjugate pair Ka × Kb = Kw, so knowing one constant gives the other.
Here is why: 1.
Proton acceptance creates OH⁻ — When a base B accepts H⁺ from water, the equilibrium B + H₂O ⇌ BH⁺ + OH⁻ shifts right for strong bases, producing high [OH⁻]. 2.

Kb measures the equilibrium position — Kb = [BH⁺][OH⁻]/[B]; a large Kb means the numerator dominates, i.e., the base is largely protonated. 3. pKb = –log Kb converts the scale — Just as pH = –log[H⁺], pKb makes…
Ka–Kb–Kw link — For conjugate acid BH⁺, Ka = [B][H⁺]/[BH⁺].
Multiplying Ka and Kb cancels [B] and [BH⁺] leaving [H⁺][OH⁻] = Kw. Thus, if Ka of NH₄⁺ is 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁰, Kb of NH₃ = Kw/Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵. 5.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Kb = [B]/[BH⁺][OH⁻]”) reveals the misconception that the equilibrium constant is written with reactants over products, confusing Kb with the reciprocal expression.
remember: Define the base dissociation constant Kb for a generic weak base B in water and state its SI units.
Explain why the conjugate acid of a strong base has a negligible Ka, using the Ka × Kb = Kw relationship.
A student claims that a 0.01 M solution of a weak base with Kb = 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ has pH = 7. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: A buffer solution is a homogeneous mixture that maintains an approximately…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: A buffer solution is a homogeneous mixture that maintains an approximately constant pH when small quantities of strong acid or strong base are added. It consists of a weak acid (HA) and its conjugate base (A⁻) — typically supplied as a salt such as NaA — or a weak base (B) and its conjugate acid (BH⁺) supplied as a salt such as BH⁺Cl⁻. The buffer action arises from the equilibrium HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻ (or B + H₂O ⇌ BH⁺ + OH⁻) and Le Chatelier’s principle: added H⁺ is consumed by A⁻ forming HA; added OH⁻ is consumed by HA forming A⁻ and water. The quantitative relationship between pH and the component concentrations is given by the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation: pH = pKₐ + log₁₀([A⁻]/[HA]) for acidic buffers, and pOH = pK_b + log₁₀([BH⁺]/[B]) for basic buffers.
