Why did Muslim leaders feel the need to form a separate political organisation in 1906.
Assess whether the initial objectives of the Muslim League were primarily communal or loyalist in nature.

cards.title: The Morley‑Minto Reforms (Indian Councils Act 1909) expanded the central and…
cards.subject: History
cards.definition: The Morley‑Minto Reforms (Indian Councils Act 1909) expanded the central and provincial legislative councils and introduced separate electorates for Muslims. The Act increased the number of additional members in the Imperial Legislative Council from 16 to 60 and allowed provincial councils to have non‑official majorities. Crucially, it accepted the Muslim League’s 1906 demand for separate electorates, meaning only Muslims could vote for Muslim candidates in reserved seats. This institutionalised communal representation, giving the League a constitutional foothold while the Indian National Congress opposed the principle as divisive. The reforms also retained official majorities at the centre, limiting real power. They marked the first statutory recognition of religion as a basis for political representation in India, shaping future constitutional negotiations and deepening Hindu‑Muslim political divergence.
steps: The Morley‑Minto Reforms of 1909 were the first British law to embed religion into India’s electoral architecture by granting Muslims separate electorates.

Here is why: the Muslim League, founded in 1906, had explicitly demanded separate representation to safeguard Muslim interests; the British, seeking to widen their legislative base while containing nationalist unity…
Second, it reserved seats for Muslims to be filled only by Muslim voters, a mechanism that gave the League a guaranteed platform but denied cross‑communal voting.
Third, the official majority at the centre remained intact, so real executive power stayed with the Viceroy.
Fourth, the Congress condemned separate electorates as a “divide and rule” tactic, while the League welcomed them as a political victory.
Fifth, the reforms set a precedent: every subsequent constitutional scheme (1919, 1935) retained and expanded communal electorates, entrenching identity‑based politics.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “it gave Muslims reserved seats elected by all voters”) reveals the misconception that separate electorates are the same as reserved seats with joint electorates — confusing exclusive communal voting with mere seat reservation.
remember: What was the primary constitutional innovation introduced by the Indian Councils Act 1909 regarding Muslim representation.
Why did the Indian National Congress oppose the separate electorates introduced in 1909.
Evaluate the extent to which the Morley‑Minto Reforms satisfied the Muslim League’s objectives.

cards.title: The Indian Councils Act 1909, known as the Morley‑Minto Reforms…
cards.subject: History
cards.definition: The Indian Councils Act 1909, known as the Morley‑Minto Reforms, was a British constitutional measure that expanded the size and functions of central and provincial legislative councils in India. It introduced the principle of separate electorates for Muslims, reserving seats to be filled exclusively by Muslim voters. The Act increased the number of non‑official members, allowed limited discussion of the budget, and permitted members to ask questions and move resolutions. However, the executive remained unaccountable to the legislature, and the franchise stayed extremely restricted (based on property, education, and tax payment). The reforms were a direct response to the Swadeshi agitation and the Muslim League’s 1906 demand for safeguards. They institutionalised communal representation, giving the Muslim League a structural foothold while the Indian National Congress opposed separate electorates as divisive. This Act marks the first statutory recognition of communal politics in modern India and set a precedent for the 1919 and 1935 Acts.
steps: The Morley‑Minto Reforms of 1909 institutionalised communal representation through separate electorates, embedding a structural divide that shaped Indian politics until Partition.

Here is why: first, the British used the reforms to appease moderate opinion after the Swadeshi upheaval while simultaneously cultivating Muslim loyalty by granting the League’s demand for separate electorates.

Second, the Act enlarged legislative councils at both centre and provinces, increased non‑official members, and allowed limited financial discussion — but real power stayed with the Viceroy’s executive council, exposing…

Third, the Congress, dominated by moderates at the time, opposed separate electorates as a “divide and rule” tactic, yet could not prevent their implementation; the Muslim League welcomed them as a political safeguard.
Fourth, the separate electorate system meant Muslim candidates only needed Muslim votes, encouraging communal mobilisation over cross‑communal alliances — a pattern that intensified in later decades.

Fifth, an exam trap: students often confuse the 1909 separate electorates with the 1919 dyarchy or the 1932 Communal Award; remember that 1909 introduced the principle for Muslims only, while later acts extended it to…

cards.title: This node examines the constitutional and repressive measures of 1919 that…
cards.subject: History
cards.definition: This node examines the constitutional and repressive measures of 1919 that marked a decisive shift from elite petitioning to mass civil resistance in the growth of Indian nationalism. The Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms (Government of India Act, 1919) introduced dyarchy in provinces, transferring subjects like education and health to elected Indian ministers while keeping finance, law, and order under British-appointed governors. Simultaneously, the Rowlatt Act (Anarchical and Revolutionary Crimes Act, 1919) extended wartime emergency powers — detention without trial, censorship, and special courts — into peacetime. The Jallianwala Bagh massacre (13 April 1919) in Amritsar, where General Dyer ordered troops to fire on an unarmed crowd, became the symbol of British brutality. In response, Mahatma Gandhi launched the Rowlatt Satyagraha (April 1919), the first all-India hartal and civil disobedience campaign, signalling the advent of Gandhian mass nationalism. These events are causally linked: the reforms disappointed nationalist aspirations for responsible government; the Rowlatt Act betrayed wartime promises of reform; the massacre radicalised moderate opinion; and Gandhi’s satyagraha provided a new methodology that would define the next phase (Non-Cooperation Movement). The node connects the constitutional trajectory (Morley-Minto 1909 → Montagu-Chelmsford 1919) with the shift from constitutional agitation to extra-legal mass mobilisation.

Here is why: First, the 1919 Act introduced dyarchy — a half-measure that gave Indians control over “transferred” subjects like education and public health but kept “reserved” subjects (finance, law, police, land…
This fell far short of the “responsible government” promised in the 1917 August Declaration, disappointing both Moderates and Extremists who had united in the Lucknow Pact.

Second, the Rowlatt Act, passed in March 1919 despite unanimous Indian opposition in the Imperial Legislative Council, extended the Defence of India Act’s wartime powers — detention without trial, in-camera trials…
It was perceived as a betrayal of Indian war support (1.3 million soldiers, £100 million contribution).

Third, the Jallianwala Bagh massacre on 13 April 1919, where Brigadier-General Dyer ordered 50 soldiers to fire 1,650 rounds into a trapped crowd of 15,000–20,000 unarmed civilians (official toll 379 dead, 1,200 wounded;

cards.title: The synthesis node integrates three pivotal developments in early Indian…
cards.subject: History
cards.definition: The synthesis node integrates three pivotal developments in early Indian nationalism: the 1905 Partition of Bengal and the ensuing anti‑partition agitation; the Swadeshi and Boycott Movement (1905‑1908) that turned economic self‑reliance into a political weapon; and the foundation of the All‑India Muslim League at Dhaka in December 1906 with objectives of safeguarding Muslim political interests, promoting loyalty to the British Crown, and fostering Muslim unity. The Partition, announced by Lord Curzon, was officially justified on administrative grounds but widely seen as a “divide and rule” tactic splitting the Bengali‑speaking population along religious lines. The anti‑partition protests — led by Surendranath Banerjea, Rabindranath Tagore, and others — introduced mass mobilisation techniques: public meetings, processions, and the singing of “Vande Mataram.” Swadeshi (indigenous production) and Boycott (rejection of British goods) expanded the struggle beyond petitions into everyday life, encouraging national schools, arbitration courts, and indigenous industries. The Muslim League, founded by Nawab Salimullah, Aga Khan III, and others, initially sought separate electorates and safeguards for Muslims, reflecting a distinct political trajectory that later shaped communal politics. Together, these events mark the transition from elite petitioning to mass‑based nationalist politics and the emergence of communal identity as a political factor.

Here is why: first, the 1905 Partition was a deliberate British “divide and rule” act that split the Bengali‑speaking region into East Bengal (Muslim‑majority) and West Bengal (Hindu‑majority), turning administrative…

Second, the anti‑partition protests introduced mass mobilisation — public meetings, processions, and the singing of “Vande Mataram” — that brought students, women, and merchants into politics for the first time.

Third, Swadeshi and Boycott turned economic self‑reliance into a political weapon: indigenous textile mills, national schools, and arbitration courts sprang up, linking everyday consumption to national sovereignty.

Fourth, the Muslim League’s formation in December 1906 at Dhaka, led by Nawab Salimullah and Aga Khan III, articulated a separate Muslim political identity, demanding safeguards and separate electorates, which the…

Fifth, these strands interacted: the League’s loyalty to the Crown contrasted with the Congress’s increasingly radical Swadeshi rhetoric, while the Partition’s communal logic fed both Hindu and Muslim separatist…

cards.title: Gandhian Nationalism (1916‑1922) marks the first mass‑based…
cards.subject: History
cards.definition: Gandhian Nationalism (1916‑1922) marks the first mass‑based, non‑violent struggle for Indian self‑government under Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi’s leadership. It begins with the Rowlatt Act (1919), a wartime emergency law that allowed detention without trial, provoking nationwide hartals. The Jallianwala Bagh massacre (13 April 1919) in Amritsar, where General Dyer ordered troops to fire on an unarmed gathering, turned constitutional protest into a moral crusade. Simultaneously, the Khilafat Movement (1919‑1924), led by the Ali brothers, sought to protect the Ottoman Caliphate, giving Gandhi a platform to forge Hindu‑Muslim unity. Gandhi merged the two causes into the Non‑Cooperation Movement (1920‑1922), calling for surrender of titles, boycott of government schools, courts, legislative councils, and foreign cloth, and promotion of swadeshi and khadi. The movement spread to peasants, workers, students, and women, making nationalism a lived experience. It was suspended on 12 February 1922 after the Chauri Chaura incident, where a mob burnt a police station killing 22 constables; Gandhi insisted that non‑violence could not be compromised. The chapter therefore covers: (1) the legislative trigger (Rowlatt Act), (2) the pivotal massacre (Jallianwala Bagh), (3) the dual‑track Khilafat‑Non‑Cooperation alliance, its course, and its abrupt suspension. Understanding this period is essential because it establishes the template of mass civil disobedience, the strategy of moral authority over physical force, and the enduring challenge of communal unity — themes that reappear in the Civil Disobedience and Quit India movements.
steps: The single most important takeaway is that Gandhian nationalism turned abstract demands for self‑rule into a disciplined, mass, non‑violent campaign that could be started and stopped on moral grounds.
Here is why: first, the Rowlatt Act gave the British legal cover to arrest anyone without trial, turning law into an instrument of terror; this made civil liberties a concrete rallying point.

Second, the Jallianwala Bagh massacre transformed legal protest into a moral outrage — Indians saw that the empire would kill unarmed civilians to protect its authority, so the only credible response was a moral weapon…
Third, the Khilafat issue supplied a ready‑made Muslim constituency;
Gandhi’s genius was to link the Caliphate’s fate with India’s freedom, creating a rare Hindu‑Muslim united front.
Fourth, the Non‑Cooperation programme translated lofty ideals into everyday acts — spinning khadi, leaving government schools, refusing titles — so that every household could participate.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “it imposed heavy taxes on Indian merchants”) reveals the misconception that the Rowlatt Act was an economic measure rather than a repressive security law.

cards.title: The Rowlatt Act (officially the Anarchical and Revolutionary Crimes Act…
cards.subject: History
cards.definition: The Rowlatt Act (officially the Anarchical and Revolutionary Crimes Act, 1919) was enacted by the Imperial Legislative Council on 18 March 1919 on the recommendations of the Rowlatt Committee (chaired by Sir Sidney Rowlatt). Its reasons were: (1) the British feared a post‑war revolutionary upsurge, especially after the 1915‑16 Ghadar conspiracy and the 1918‑19 labour strikes; (2) the Montagu‑Chelmsford Reforms (1919) promised limited self‑government, but the government wanted emergency powers to suppress dissent before the new legislatures could function; (3) wartime Defence of India Act (1915) was expiring, so a permanent replacement was sought. Its main terms included: - Detention without trial – any person suspected of “revolutionary” or “terrorist” activity could be arrested and detained for up to two years without a warrant, magistrate’s order, or right to legal counsel. - In‑camera trials – if a trial was held, it could be conducted in secret, with no jury and limited defence rights. - Press censorship – publications deemed “seditious” could be banned, and editors could be prosecuted without normal judicial safeguards. - Extension of wartime ordinances – the Act made permanent many provisions of the Defence of India Act, such as restrictions on public meetings and movement. The Act applied to all of British India and was seen as a direct betrayal of the promises of responsible government, galvanising the Indian National Congress, the Muslim League, and emerging mass leaders like Gandhi into a nationwide Rowlatt Satyagraha (April 1919). The legislation therefore sits at the intersection of constitutional reform, wartime emergency law, and the rise of Gandhian mass civil disobedience.
steps: The Rowlatt Act was a repressive law that gave the British unlimited power to detain Indians without trial, sparking the first all‑India Gandhian mass protest.
Here is why: 1.
Post‑war anxiety – After 1918 the British feared a revolutionary wave fuelled by returning soldiers, labour unrest, and the Russian Revolution’s example. 2.
Legislative vacuum – The Defence of India Act (1915) lapsed in 1919; the government wanted a permanent substitute before the new dyarchy legislatures could meet. 3.
Montagu‑Chelmsford promise – The 1919 Reforms offered limited self‑rule, but the Act undermined that promise by retaining emergency powers. 4.
Rowlatt Committee’s mandate – Chaired by Sir Sidney Rowlatt, it recommended “preventive detention” to nip conspiracies in the bud. 5.

cards.title: The Jallianwala Bagh massacre (13 April 1919) was a deliberate…
cards.subject: History
cards.definition: The Jallianwala Bagh massacre (13 April 1919) was a deliberate, unprovoked firing by British Indian Army troops under Brigadier‑General Reginald Dyer on a non‑violent assembly of 15 000–20 000 Indians in the enclosed garden of Jallianwala Bagh, Amritsar, Punjab. The crowd had gathered to celebrate Baisakhi and to protest the Rowlatt Act (1919), which allowed detention without trial. Dyer, citing martial law, ordered 50 riflemen to fire 1 650 rounds into the trapped crowd for ten minutes, killing an official 379 (Indian estimates exceed 1 000) and wounding over 1 200. The event exposed the brutality of colonial rule, galvanised the Indian National Congress, prompted the Hunter Commission inquiry, and became the immediate catalyst for Mahatma Gandhi’s launch of the Non‑Cooperation Movement (1920‑22). It also intensified the Khilafat agitation, linking Hindu‑Muslim unity to the broader nationalist struggle. The massacre is therefore a pivotal turning point that transformed constitutional protest into mass civil disobedience.
steps: The Jallianwala Bagh massacre was the moment British moral authority in India collapsed, turning constitutional protest into mass civil disobedience.
Here is why: first, the Rowlatt Act (1919) gave the colonial state draconian powers to arrest without trial, inflaming a population already strained by wartime inflation and recruitment.

Second, the Punjab administration, fearing a repeat of the 1857 uprising, imposed martial law and banned public meetings, yet allowed a Baisakhi fair to proceed, creating a volatile mix of celebration and protest.

Third, Brigadier‑General Dyer, convinced that a “moral lesson” was needed, sealed the only exit of the walled garden and ordered sustained rifle fire into the unarmed crowd, ignoring the principle of minimum force.

Fourth, the official Hunter Commission (1919‑20) condemned Dyer’s “error of judgment” but stopped short of criminal prosecution, while Indian leaders — from Motilal Nehru to Gandhi — denounced the massacre as “a crime…
Consider the scene: a narrow lane, high brick walls, a single gate locked from outside; the sound of 1 650 rounds echoing for ten minutes; bodies piling near the well where many jumped to escape.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the Defence of India Act 1915”) reveals the misconception that wartime emergency legislation alone caused the protest, ignoring the specific post‑war Rowlatt Act that directly triggered the 1919 agitation.

cards.title: The Khilafat and Non‑Cooperation Movements (1919‑1922) were two linked…
cards.subject: History
cards.definition: The Khilafat and Non‑Cooperation Movements (1919‑1922) were two linked campaigns that marked the first nationwide, Hindu‑Muslim united effort under Mahatma Gandhi’s leadership to achieve swaraj (self‑rule) through peaceful non‑cooperation. The Khilafat Movement, launched by the Ali brothers (Maulana Mohammad Ali and Shaukat Ali) in 1919, sought to protect the Ottoman Caliphate after World War I and attracted Muslim support. Gandhi, seeing an opportunity for Hindu‑Muslim unity, allied the Khilafat cause with his Non‑Cooperation Movement, which he announced at the Calcutta Congress in September 1920. Non‑cooperation entailed surrendering government titles, boycotting official schools, courts, and legislative councils, rejecting foreign cloth, and promoting swadeshi (indigenous) goods and khadi. The movement spread rapidly: students left government schools, lawyers gave up practice, and peasants refused to pay taxes in some areas. Its course was marked by peaceful protests, processions, and the growth of khadi centres. The movement was suspended abruptly after the Chauri Chaura incident on 5 February 1922, when a crowd burned a police station, killing 22 policemen. Gandhi, believing that violence violated the core principle of satyagraha, called off the movement on 12 February 1922. Thus, the node covers the alliance’s formation, the methods and spread of non‑cooperation, the role of Khilafat leadership, and the reasons for its suspension, setting the stage for later phases of Gandhian nationalism.

Here is why: 1.
Shared grievance created a platform for unity – Post‑WWI Muslims feared the abolition of the Ottoman Caliphate;
Gandhi saw this as a chance to bring Hindus and Muslims together under a common nationalist goal. 2.

Non‑cooperation offered a concrete, peaceful programme – By surrendering titles, boycotting government institutions, and promoting khadi, the movement gave people a clear way to resist without arms. 3.

Mass participation demonstrated its reach – Students left schools, lawyers gave up practice, merchants boycotted foreign cloth, and peasants in Awadh and Malabar refused to pay taxes, showing nationwide uptake. 4.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “April 1919”) reveals the misconception that the movement began immediately after the Rowlatt Act, confusing the timing of the Rowlatt protests with the formal launch of non‑cooperation.

cards.title: The assessment of the Non‑Cooperation Movement (1920‑1922) examines how Gandhi…
cards.subject: History
cards.definition: The assessment of the Non‑Cooperation Movement (1920‑1922) examines how Gandhi merged the Khilafat demand for the Ottoman Caliphate with the Congress goal of Swaraj, launching a nationwide campaign of non‑violent non‑cooperation. Its social base expanded beyond traditional elites to include peasants (e.g., Awadh kisan sabhas), industrial workers (Ahmedabad mill strikes), students (boycott of government colleges), women (picketing liquor and foreign‑cloth shops), and the middle class (resignation from titles and legislative councils). Economically, the boycott of foreign cloth boosted khadi production and indigenous industry. Politically, it forged a temporary Hindu‑Muslim unity symbolised by joint hartals and the Ali brothers’ leadership alongside Gandhi. However, the movement’s reliance on Gandhi’s moral authority meant that any outbreak of violence — most famously the Chauri Chaura incident (5 February 1922) where a police station was burnt — forced an immediate suspension. The abrupt halt disappointed many participants, leading to a split in the Congress: the “No‑Changers” (Gandhi’s followers) insisted on constructive work, while the “Pro‑Changers” (Motilal Nehru, C.R. Das) formed the Swaraj Party to contest elections and obstruct the 1919 Act from within. The legacy thus includes the template for future mass civil disobedience, the politicisation of new social groups, and the strategic debate between extra‑parliamentary struggle and council entry that shaped nationalist politics until 1930.
steps: The Non‑Cooperation Movement turned Indian nationalism into a mass struggle, but its sudden suspension exposed the tension between moral purity and political effectiveness.

Here is why: first, the movement recruited peasants, workers, students and women who had never before participated in politics — for example, the Awadh kisan sabhas refused to pay illegal levies, and women in Bombay…
Second, the economic boycott of foreign cloth made khadi a symbol of self‑reliance; hand‑spun yarn production rose sharply, hitting British textile imports.
Third, the Khilafat alliance created a rare Hindu‑Muslim unity, visible in joint processions and the shared leadership of Gandhi and the Ali brothers.

Fourth, the movement’s insistence on absolute non‑violence meant that the Chauri Chaura violence (a mob burning a police station, killing 22 policemen) compelled Gandhi to call off the campaign, arguing that a violent…

Fifth, the suspension split the Congress: “No‑Changers” focused on constructive work (spinning, Harijan uplift), while “Pro‑Changers” formed the Swaraj Party to enter legislatures and wreck the 1919 reforms from inside.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “only lawyers and merchants joined”) reveals the misconception that the movement remained an upper‑class affair, ignoring Gandhi’s deliberate outreach to the masses.

Assess the view that the Non‑Cooperation Movement failed because it did not achieve Swaraj.

cards.title: The Non‑Cooperation Movement (1920‑22) expanded Gandhian nationalism beyond…
cards.subject: History
cards.definition: The Non‑Cooperation Movement (1920‑22) expanded Gandhian nationalism beyond elite petitions into mass civil disobedience. Its constructive programme — boycott of British goods (especially cloth), renunciation of titles, resignation from government service, withdrawal of students from colonial schools, and promotion of khadi — linked political resistance with economic self‑reliance and social reform. The movement drew peasants, artisans, merchants, students, and women into a unified struggle, forging Hindu‑Muslim unity through the Khilafat alliance. British repression (arrests, police firings) and the Chauri Chaura incident (February 1922) led Gandhi to suspend the movement, but the experience reshaped Indian nationalism by proving that non‑violent mass mobilisation could challenge imperial authority.
steps: The Non‑Cooperation Movement turned ordinary economic choices into political weapons, making every Indian a potential soldier of freedom.

Here is why: first, the boycott of foreign cloth and promotion of khadi hit British textile profits while reviving village industries; second, resignation from government posts and surrender of titles stripped the…
Consider a merchant in Bombay who burns his stock of Manchester cloth and switches to khadi — his loss becomes a political statement.

In Punjab, students form volunteer corps to enforce boycott.
The British respond with mass arrests (over 30,000 by early 1922) and police firings, yet the movement spreads.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the boycott targeted British tea exports”) reveals the misconception that any British product was equally targeted, ignoring Gandhi’s strategic focus on cloth because of its visibility, employment impact, and symbolic value.

cards.title: The Chauri Chaura incident (5 February 1922) was a violent clash in Gorakhpur…
cards.subject: History
cards.definition: The Chauri Chaura incident (5 February 1922) was a violent clash in Gorakhpur district, United Provinces, where a crowd of non‑cooperation volunteers set fire to a police station, killing 22 policemen. The incident occurred during the Non‑Cooperation Movement (1920‑22), which combined the Khilafat cause with Gandhi’s call for swadeshi, boycott of British institutions, and non‑violent non‑cooperation. Gandhi, adhering strictly to ahimsa, viewed the violence as a betrayal of the movement’s moral foundation. On 12 February 1922 he unilaterally suspended the Non‑Cooperation Movement, arguing that the people were not yet ready for mass civil disobedience. This decision split nationalist opinion: some (like C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru) later formed the Swaraj Party to work within legislatures, while others (like Jawaharlal Nehru) accepted the pause. The suspension marked a strategic shift from mass non‑cooperation to constructive programme (spinning, Hindu‑Muslim unity, removal of untouchability) and set the stage for the next phase of nationalist struggle.
steps: The single governing takeaway is that grassroots tactical violence forces a leadership pivot from mass civil disobedience to moral self-purification and alternative organisational structures.

First, the Rowlatt Act sparked nationwide protests, and Jallianwala Bagh showed British brutality, which led Gandhi to launch the Non‑Cooperation Movement merged with the Khilafat cause to unite Hindus and Muslims.

Second, people boycotted schools, courts, and foreign cloth while students left colleges, lawyers gave up practice, and peasants refused taxes under largely peaceful conditions with simmering tensions.

Third, in early February 1922, volunteers in Chauri Chaura marched to the local police station demanding release of arrested leaders, prompting police firing, crowd retaliation, and the torching of the station resulting…

Fourth, news reached Gandhi at Bardoli who wrote in Young India that the movement had “lost its non‑violent character” and called for immediate suspension, much like a cricket match captain calling off a game when…
Fifth, Gandhi’s decision shocked leaders where C.R.

cards.title: The Constructive Programme (1920‑1922) was Gandhi’s parallel agenda of…
cards.subject: History
cards.definition: The Constructive Programme (1920‑1922) was Gandhi’s parallel agenda of nation‑building activities that ran alongside the Non‑Cooperation Movement. It comprised eighteen items — most famously khadi spinning, village sanitation, basic education (Nai Talim), removal of untouchability, Hindu‑Muslim unity, prohibition, and uplift of women and tribals. Unlike the political non‑cooperation (boycott of courts, schools, legislatures), the Constructive Programme aimed to create the social and economic foundations of Swaraj by making communities self‑sufficient and morally disciplined. It linked the political struggle to everyday life, turning abstract nationalism into tangible work. The programme was administered through the All‑India Spinners’ Association, the Harijan Sevak Sangh, and local Congress committees. Its success was measured not in arrests but in the spread of charkhas, the opening of national schools, and the erosion of caste barriers. While the Non‑Cooperation Movement was suspended after Chauri Chaura (1922), the Constructive Programme continued, becoming the core of Gandhi’s strategy until independence.
steps: The Constructive Programme was Gandhi’s blueprint for turning political independence into social self‑rule, because he believed that merely expelling the British would not end exploitation if Indians remained divided…

Here is why: first, the programme translated the abstract demand for Swaraj into daily acts — spinning one hour a day, cleaning a village lane, teaching a child in the mother tongue — making nationalism participatory.
Second, it provided a non‑violent, constructive outlet for energy when mass civil disobedience was suspended, keeping the Congress organisation alive.
Third, it attacked the internal structures of oppression (untouchability, communal mistrust, alcoholism) that the British exploited.
Fourth, it created alternative institutions — national schools, khadi bhandars, village panchayats — that pre‑figured a self‑governing India.
Fifth, it broadened the political constituency by drawing in women, merchants, and peasants who might not join street protests but would spin or donate.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “boycott of legislatures, courts, and schools”) reveals confusion between the political Non‑Cooperation programme and the constructive social programme.

cards.title: The Kheda Satyagraha (1918) was a peasant-led non-violent resistance in Kheda…
cards.subject: History
cards.definition: The Kheda Satyagraha (1918) was a peasant-led non-violent resistance in Kheda district, Gujarat, against the British insistence on collecting full land revenue despite widespread crop failure and a plague epidemic. Mahatma Gandhi, invited by local leaders such as Vallabhbhai Patel and Indulal Yagnik, transformed the grievance into a structured satyagraha: peasants pledged non-payment of revenue, endured confiscation of property and arrest, and maintained strict non-violence. The British administration, initially dismissive, eventually suspended the revenue demand for the year and returned confiscated lands. This episode demonstrated that satyagraha could mobilise rural masses, established Gandhi’s credibility among peasants, and provided a template for later mass movements like Non-Cooperation. It also highlighted the role of regional lieutenants (Patel) in translating Gandhi’s strategy into local organisation, linking the earlier Champaran experiment to the forthcoming Rowlatt Act protests.
steps: The Kheda Satyagraha proved that disciplined non-violent non-cooperation could compel a colonial state to retreat, creating a replicable model for mass civil resistance.
Here is why: 1.
Agrarian crisis as catalyst – In 1917‑18, Kheda suffered a near‑total crop failure compounded by a plague outbreak.
The Bombay Presidency refused to suspend the land revenue assessment, demanding full payment.
This injustice gave Gandhi a concrete, relatable issue around which peasants could unite. 2.

Gandhi’s strategic entry – Gandhi arrived in March 1918 after local leaders (Patel, Yagnik, Shankarlal Banker) appealed to him. He insisted on a formal pledge of non‑payment, turning spontaneous anger into a disciplined…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “complete independence” or “abolition of zamindari”) reveals the misconception that every Gandhian movement aimed at political sovereignty; Kheda was a targeted economic relief campaign, not a demand for self‑rule.
remember: What was the primary demand of the peasants during the Kheda Satyagraha of 1918.
Why did Gandhi choose to intervene in Kheda rather than leave the issue to local leaders alone.
Assess the effectiveness of the Kheda Satyagraha in achieving its immediate goals.

cards.title: The Constructive Programme (1920‑1922) was Gandhi’s parallel strategy to mass…
cards.subject: History
cards.definition: The Constructive Programme (1920‑1922) was Gandhi’s parallel strategy to mass civil disobedience, comprising eighteen items that aimed at social, economic, and moral regeneration. Core components included khadi (hand‑spun, hand‑woven cloth) to boycott British textiles and revive village industry; Hindu‑Muslim unity through joint prayers and shared festivals; removal of untouchability by opening temples and wells to Dalits; village sanitation and basic education (Nai Talim) centred on productive crafts; prohibition of alcohol; and promotion of indigenous languages. Unlike the Non‑Cooperation Movement’s confrontational boycott of schools, courts, and legislatures, the Constructive Programme worked within communities to build the material and moral capacity for self‑rule. It linked political independence to social reform, arguing that a free India required a reformed society. The programme was administered through the All‑India Spinners’ Association, the Harijan Sevak Sangh, and local Congress committees, making it a grassroots network that survived the 1922 suspension of Non‑Cooperation.
steps: The Constructive Programme was Gandhi’s blueprint for turning political resistance into everyday nation‑building.

Here is why: it translated the abstract ideal of swaraj into concrete tasks — spinning, cleaning, teaching — that every Indian could perform, thereby widening the nationalist base beyond elite petitioners.
First, khadi linked economic self‑reliance to political boycott; each spindle became a symbol of defiance against Lancashire mills.

Second, Hindu‑Muslim unity was pursued not through abstract declarations but through shared community work — joint spinning bees, inter‑dining, and common festivals — directly countering the communal tensions that the…
Third, the attack on untouchability via temple entry and well‑access campaigns gave Dalits a tangible stake in the freedom struggle, aligning social justice with national liberation.
Fourth, Nai Talim (basic education) fused literacy with vocational training, producing citizens capable of sustaining a free economy.

cards.title: The aftermath of the Non‑Cooperation Movement’s suspension (February 1922)…
cards.subject: History
cards.definition: The aftermath of the Non‑Cooperation Movement’s suspension (February 1922) marks a pivotal transition in Gandhian nationalism. Following the Chauri Chaura incident, Gandhi halted mass civil disobedience, was arrested on 10 March 1922, tried for sedition, and sentenced to six years’ imprisonment (released early in 1924). The Indian National Congress, meeting at Gaya in December 1922, fractured over strategy: the Swaraj Party (led by Motilal Nehru and C. R. Das) advocated council‑entry to wreck the reforms from within, while the No‑Changers (C. Rajagopalachari, Vallabhbhai Patel, Rajendra Prasad) insisted on continued boycott and constructive programme — khadi, village sanitation, Hindu‑Muslim unity, removal of untouchability. This split shaped Congress politics until the 1929 Lahore session. Simultaneously, Gandhi’s constructive programme laid organisational groundwork for future mass movements, and the British exploited the division through the 1923 elections and the 1924‑25 “Reforms” debates. The node therefore covers: Gandhi’s arrest and trial; the Gaya Congress split; Swarajist vs No‑Changer ideologies; the constructive programme’s content and impact; and the immediate political consequences up to the 1924 Belgaum Congress where Gandhi resumed leadership.
steps: The 1922 suspension of Non-Cooperation was a strategic retreat that converted a tactical pause into an organisational re-orientation, keeping the nationalist movement alive through diversified tactics and grassroots…

Supporting this claim are four key arguments: first, Gandhi's arrest and trial removed the central leader but preserved the movement's moral integrity; second, the Gaya Congress split generated parallel strategies of…
The narrative unfolds through distinct stages.
The Chauri Chaura violence led directly to Gandhi suspending the movement on 12 February 1922.
Subsequently, the British arrested Gandhi at Sabarmati Ashram on 10 March 1922, sentencing him to six years in Yerwada jail for sedition.

cards.title: The Non‑Cooperation Movement (1920‑1922) was a nationwide mass…
cards.subject: History
cards.definition: The Non‑Cooperation Movement (1920‑1922) was a nationwide mass civil‑disobedience campaign launched by the Indian National Congress under Gandhi’s leadership, merging the Khilafat demand for Ottoman caliphate protection with the goal of swaraj. Its social composition was remarkably broad: peasants refusing revenue, artisans boycotting foreign goods, students leaving government schools, lawyers surrendering practices, women picketing liquor and toddy shops, and industrial workers striking in Bombay and Ahmedabad. Regionally, the movement manifested differently — Bengal saw massive hartals and bonfires of foreign cloth; Punjab witnessed the Akali Sikh gurdwara reform agitation merging with non‑cooperation; Madras presidency experienced widespread boycott of legislative councils; the United Provinces saw peasant no‑rent campaigns; and Bombay mill workers staged prolonged strikes. The British responded with repression (arrests, press censorship, the Seditious Meetings Act) but also with limited concessions (Montagu‑Chelmsford reforms already in place). The movement’s suspension after Chauri Chaura (February 1922) revealed strategic tensions between Gandhi’s insistence on non‑violence and the radicalising grassroots. This node analyses the patterns of mobilisation, the interplay of local grievances with the national call, and the limits of a unified non‑violent mass struggle in a diverse colony.
steps: The Non‑Cooperation Movement succeeded because it translated an abstract demand for swaraj into concrete, everyday acts of refusal that diverse Indians could perform.

Here is why: first, the programme targeted institutions that touched daily life — schools, courts, councils, foreign cloth, liquor — allowing peasants, artisans, and urban poor to participate without needing political…

Second, local leaders adapted the national call to regional grievances: in Bengal, the boycott of British textiles resonated with a strong swadeshi tradition; in Punjab, the Akali movement for gurdwara control fused…

Third, women entered public politics unprecedentedly — Basanti Devi in Bengal, Sarojini Naidu in the Deccan, and thousands of ordinary women picketing toddy shops — expanding the movement’s moral authority.

Fourth, the British response — mass arrests (over 30,000 by 1921), the Seditious Meetings Act, and the banning of Congress volunteer corps — radicalised many participants, pushing some toward violence, which culminated…
Fifth, Gandhi’s unilateral suspension shocked leaders like C.R.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “only peasants and workers joined”) reveals the misconception that the movement was narrowly class‑based, ignoring the broad cross‑class alliance Gandhi forged.

cards.title: The Non‑Cooperation Movement (1920‑1922) was the first nationwide mass campaign…
cards.subject: History
cards.definition: The Non‑Cooperation Movement (1920‑1922) was the first nationwide mass campaign led by Mahatma Gandhi under the Indian National Congress, merging the Khilafat cause with the demand for swaraj. It urged Indians to boycott government schools, courts, legislative councils, foreign cloth, and titles, and to adopt swadeshi goods and national education. The movement’s suspension after the Chauri Chaura incident (February 1922) marked a strategic pivot: Gandhi prioritised non‑violent discipline over mass momentum. This node evaluates the movement’s outcomes — expansion of political participation to peasants, workers, women, and students; the British response of repression and limited reforms (e.g., the 1923 Indian Finance Act); and the internal Congress debate between “no‑changers” (who wanted to continue boycott) and “pro‑changers” (who entered legislatures). It connects these outcomes to the later Civil Disobedience Movement, showing how the 1922 suspension shaped Gandhi’s emphasis on constructive programme and the Congress’s eventual acceptance of council entry.
steps: The Non‑Cooperation Movement turned elite petitioning into a mass struggle, yet its abrupt halt forced Indian leaders to rethink the relationship between moral purity and political effectiveness.

Here is why: first, the boycott of schools, courts, and foreign cloth drew peasants, artisans, women, and students into political action for the first time, creating a new political vocabulary of “swadeshi” and “hartal”.

Second, the British responded with a dual strategy — repression (arrests, press censorship) and limited concessions (the 1923 Indian Finance Act, modest expansion of electorates) — showing that mass pressure could…
Third, the Chauri Chaura violence gave Gandhi a moral reason to suspend the movement, but it also exposed the difficulty of controlling decentralized mass action.
Fourth, the 1922 Gaya and 1923 Cocanada Congress sessions revealed a split: “no‑changers” (C.
R. Das, Motilal Nehru) wanted to continue boycott, while “pro‑changers” (Vithalbhai Patel, Rajagopalachari) argued for council entry to obstruct colonial legislation from within.

cards.title: The core truth is that the Constructive Programme (1916-1922) was Gandhi’s…
cards.subject: History
cards.definition: The core truth is that the Constructive Programme (1916-1922) was Gandhi’s comprehensive agenda for social, economic, and moral regeneration that ran parallel to political agitations such as the Non-Cooperation Movement. Its seven core components were: khadi and village industries for hand-spinning to boycott British textiles; removal of untouchability by opening temples and wells to Harijans; Hindu-Muslim unity through joint festivals and shared leadership; prohibition to protect poor families; village sanitation and hygiene for basic health; basic education (Nai Talim) linking manual work with literacy; and women’s participation in spinning and public meetings. Gandhi viewed these not as charity but as the foundation of Swaraj because disciplined, united, and economically independent citizens are capable of self-government. This programme linked directly to the Rowlatt Act protests, Jallianwala Bagh aftermath, and the Non-Cooperation Movement by providing a constructive outlet for mass energy when political protest was suspended, while anticipating the later Civil Disobedience phase through voluntary, non-confrontational work.
steps: The core truth is that political freedom without social discipline is hollow, making the Constructive Programme the essential kitchen garden that sustained the household of Indian nationalism.
The first supporting argument is that Gandhi insisted political high-points like the Rowlatt Act, Jallianwala Bagh, and Non-Cooperation needed a social safety net of self-reliance.
The second is that pilot projects in Champaran, Kheda, and Ahmedabad proved constructive work could mobilise people who feared direct politics.
The third is that the 1920 Nagpur Congress session made the programme a mandatory condition for membership.
The fourth is that during the 1921-1922 peak, khadi became the national uniform while sanitation committees and anti-untouchability efforts spread nationwide.
The narrative steps unfolded across three distinct stages: Stage 1 – Seeds (1916-1918).

cards.title: This synthesis node integrates the three pivotal strands of Gandhian…
cards.subject: History
cards.definition: This synthesis node integrates the three pivotal strands of Gandhian nationalism (1916‑1922): the Rowlatt Act’s repressive legal framework, the Jallianwala Bagh massacre’s shock to public conscience, and the Khilafat‑Non‑Cooperation alliance that translated communal grievance into a mass civil‑disobedience campaign. It maps the causal chain — wartime emergency powers → indiscriminate violence → pan‑Indian protest — and highlights Gandhi’s strategic use of religious symbolism (Khilafat) to broaden the nationalist base beyond elite petitioning. The node also distils CISCE ISC examination patterns: typical 4‑mark “explain” questions on Rowlatt provisions, 6‑mark “assess” items on Jallianwala’s political fallout, and 8‑mark “evaluate” essays on the movement’s suspension after Chauri Chaura. By linking factual recall to structured answer templates, the node equips students to move from isolated event knowledge to analytical synthesis required in the board paper.
steps: The Gandhian nationalism phase (1916‑1922) demonstrates how a series of repressive colonial measures — Rowlatt Act, Jallianwala Bagh massacre, and the Khilafat grievance — were woven by Gandhi into a unified…

First, the Rowlatt Act (1919) extended wartime emergency powers into peacetime, allowing detention without trial and press censorship; this legal assault on civil liberties gave Gandhi a concrete issue to mobilise…
Second, the Jallianwala Bagh massacre (13 April 1919) turned legal oppression into visceral horror, galvanising provincial leaders like Motilal Nehru and Lala Lajpat Rai to endorse mass protest.
Third, the Khilafat issue (1919‑1920) supplied a pan‑Islamic cause that Gandhi linked to swaraj, creating a Hindu‑Muslim united front unprecedented in scale.
The Non‑Cooperation Movement (1920‑1922) then operationalised this unity through boycott of schools, courts, and foreign cloth, turning abstract nationalism into daily practice.

The movement’s abrupt suspension after the Chauri Chaura incident (5 February 1922) illustrates Gandhi’s strategic insistence on non‑violence over momentum — a decision that examiners frequently test.

cards.title: The chapter “Gandhian Nationalism (1927‑1937)” surveys the decisive decade when…
cards.subject: History
cards.definition: The chapter “Gandhian Nationalism (1927‑1937)” surveys the decisive decade when Mahatma Gandhi’s non‑violent mass mobilisation became the principal engine of Indian nationalism. It begins with the Simon Commission (1927), an all‑British statutory body whose exclusion of Indians sparked a nationwide boycott and the demand for an Indian‑drafted constitution. The Nehru Report (1928), prepared by a cross‑party committee under Motilal Nehru, articulated a dominion‑status framework with fundamental rights and a federal structure, but was rejected by the Muslim League and radical nationalists. At the Lahore Session (December 1929) the Indian National Congress, under Jawaharlal Nehru’s presidency, passed the Poorna Swaraj Resolution, declaring 26 January 1930 as Independence Day and committing to complete sovereignty. The Civil Disobedience Movement (1930‑1934), launched with the Dandi Salt March, turned non‑cooperation into mass civil resistance — illegal salt production, boycott of foreign cloth, refusal to pay taxes — drawing global attention and forcing the British to negotiate. The Gandhi‑Irwin Pact (March 1931) suspended the movement and secured Gandhi’s participation in the Second Round Table Conference (1931) in London, where deadlock over communal representation persisted. The Poona Pact (September 1932), negotiated between Gandhi and B.R. Ambedkar, replaced separate electorates for Depressed Classes with reserved seats within a joint electorate, shaping future electoral politics. The Government of India Act 1935, the longest British statute for India, introduced provincial autonomy, a federal centre (never fully implemented), and expanded the franchise to about 14 % of adults. Finally, the 1937 provincial elections under the 1935 Act saw Congress win majorities in seven provinces and form ministries, demonstrating Indian capacity for self‑government and setting the stage for the 1940s demand for Pakistan and the Quit India Movement. The chapter links each episode causally: constitutional proposals → mass mobilisation → negotiation → constitutional reform → electoral practice.
steps: The decade 1927‑1937 is the hinge on which Indian nationalism turned from elite petitioning to mass civil resistance and finally to electoral self‑government.

Here is why: each British constitutional gesture — Simon Commission, Round Table Conferences, 1935 Act — was met by an Indian response that widened participation, sharpened demands, and forced the next British…

First, the Simon Commission’s all‑white composition (1927) insulted Indian political opinion, producing a unified boycott that brought students, merchants, and peasants onto the streets — a rehearsal for mass…

Second, the Nehru Report (1928) showed Indians could draft their own constitution, yet its dominion‑status ceiling and failure to satisfy Muslim League’s “Fourteen Points” exposed communal fault‑lines.

Third, the Lahore Session (1929) converted the Congress goal to Poorna Swaraj, making independence non‑negotiable and giving a symbolic date (26 January) that later became Republic Day. Fourth, the Civil Disobedience…

Fifth, the Gandhi‑Irwin Pact (1931) and the Second Round Table Conference revealed the limits of British willingness to concede; the deadlock on communal representation led directly to the Communal Award and the Poona…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Indians welcomed the Commission as a step toward reform”) reveals the misconception that British‑initiated constitutional bodies were generally accepted — ignoring the principle that legitimacy required Indian representation.

cards.title: The Simon Commission (officially the Indian Statutory Commission) was appointed…
cards.subject: History
cards.definition: The Simon Commission (officially the Indian Statutory Commission) was appointed by the British Government in November 1927 under Sir John Simon to examine the working of the Government of India Act 1919 and suggest constitutional reforms. Its composition — seven British MPs and no Indian — violated the principle of self‑representation that Indian nationalists had demanded since the Montagu‑Chelmsford Reforms. The Commission’s arrival in Bombay on 3 February 1928 triggered a nationwide boycott organised by the Indian National Congress, the Muslim League, the Hindu Mahasabha and other groups. Protesters greeted the Commission with black flags, hartals and the slogan “Simon Go Back.” The boycott demonstrated a rare unity across communal lines and forced the British to concede that any future constitutional scheme must involve Indian opinion, paving the way for the Nehru Report (1928) and the demand for Dominion Status. The episode also exposed the limits of British willingness to devolve power, radicalising younger leaders like Jawaharlal Nehru and Subhas Chandra Bose toward complete independence.
steps: The Simon Commission’s all‑British makeup turned a routine constitutional review into a flashpoint for Indian nationalism.
Here is why: the British refused to include any Indian voice, signalling that they still viewed Indians as subjects rather than partners in governance.
First, the Commission was announced in November 1927, two years ahead of the statutory ten‑year review, suggesting a pre‑emptive move to control the reform agenda.

Second, when the Commission landed in Bombay on 3 February 1928, a complete hartal paralysed the city; black flags flew from homes and offices, and the slogan “Simon Go Back” echoed in every province.
Third, the boycott united the Congress, the Muslim League (under Jinnah), the Hindu Mahasabha, the Liberal Federation and regional parties — a rare moment of cross‑communal solidarity.
Fourth, the police lathi‑charge on demonstrators in Lahore on 30 October 1928 killed Lala Lajpat Rai, turning him into a martyr and intensifying anti‑British sentiment.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the Commission proposed harsh taxes”) reveals the misconception that the boycott was about specific policy proposals rather than the fundamental denial of Indian participation.
remember: What was the primary reason Indian nationalists boycotted the Simon Commission.
Explain how the Simon Commission boycott demonstrated unity among Indian political groups.
Evaluate the immediate political impact of the Simon Commission boycott on British policy.

cards.title: The Nehru Report (1928) was the first comprehensive constitutional draft…
cards.subject: History
cards.definition: The Nehru Report (1928) was the first comprehensive constitutional draft prepared entirely by Indians, produced by a committee chaired by Motilal Nehru under the auspices of the All Parties Conference (called after the boycott of the Simon Commission). Its central demand was Dominion Status for India within the British Commonwealth, implying full internal self‑government with the British Crown as symbolic head. Key recommendations included: a federal structure with strong provinces, a bicameral legislature at the centre, fundamental rights (freedom of speech, equality before law), universal adult suffrage, and separation of powers between executive and legislature. The report also proposed joint electorates with reserved seats for minorities, rejecting separate electorates. The Muslim League, led by Jinnah, responded with the Delhi Proposals (1927) demanding safeguards; when these were not fully incorporated, the League rejected the report. The British government did not accept the report, but it shifted the nationalist discourse from petitioning to self‑authored constitutionalism, paving the way for the Lahore Session (1929) and the Poorna Swaraj resolution.
steps: The Nehru Report was the first Indian‑drafted constitutional blueprint demanding Dominion Status, marking a shift from petitioning the British to self‑authored constitutionalism.
Here is why: 1.
All Parties Conference catalyst – After the 1927 Simon Commission boycott, Indian leaders convened the All Parties Conference (May 1928) to produce an indigenous constitution.
The conference appointed a committee under Motilal Nehru, signalling unity across Congress, Liberals, and some regional parties. 2.

Dominion Status as pragmatic goal – The report asked for “Dominion Status” (the same status enjoyed by Canada, Australia, New Zealand, and South Africa) rather than full independence, because leaders judged it…
The phrase “within the British Commonwealth” was explicit. 3.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Jawaharlal Nehru”) reveals the misconception that the younger Nehru authored the report, confusing the 1928 committee with his later role in the 1929 Lahore Session.

cards.title: The Lahore Session (29‑31 December 1929) of the Indian National Congress…
cards.subject: History
cards.definition: The Lahore Session (29‑31 December 1929) of the Indian National Congress, presided by Jawaharlal Nehru, marked the formal adoption of the Poorna Swaraj (Complete Independence) Resolution. It replaced the earlier demand for Dominion Status (as articulated in the Nehru Report, 1928) with an unequivocal call for total sovereignty. The resolution declared 26 January 1930 as “Independence Day,” urged a boycott of British institutions, and authorised the launch of a civil‑disobedience campaign. The session also saw the unfurling of the tricolour flag on the banks of the Ravi, symbolising the new goal. This shift reflected the growing influence of younger leaders (Nehru, Subhas Chandra Bose) and the frustration with the Simon Commission’s all‑British composition and the British government’s refusal to concede even dominion status. The Lahore decision directly precipitated the Civil Disobedience Movement (1930‑34) and set the ideological benchmark for all subsequent nationalist negotiations.
steps: The Lahore Session of December 1929 was the turning point where the Indian National Congress abandoned the goal of Dominion Status and demanded Poorna Swaraj — complete independence.

Here is why: the Simon Commission (1927) had excluded Indians, sparking a nationwide boycott; the Nehru Report (1928) then offered a constitutional scheme for Dominion Status, but the British government ignored it, and…
At Lahore, Nehru, as president, moved the Poorna Swaraj Resolution, which passed unanimously on 31 December 1929.

The resolution declared 26 January 1930 as “Independence Day,” called for a boycott of legislatures, courts, and schools, and authorised Mahatma Gandhi to launch a civil‑disobedience campaign at his discretion.
The tricolour was hoisted on the Ravi’s banks, becoming the visual emblem of the new aim. This decision directly led to the Salt Satyagraha (March 1930) and the broader Civil Disobedience Movement.

An exam trap: students often confuse the 1929 Lahore demand with the 1942 Quit India call; the former was a formal Congress resolution, the latter a mass movement launched during World War II. Remember: Lahore = first…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Dominion Status”) reveals the misconception that the Congress never shifted its aim after the Nehru Report — confusing the 1928 report’s recommendation with the 1929 resolution’s decisive break.
remember: What was the primary demand of the Indian National Congress at its Lahore Session in December 1929.

Evaluate the significance of declaring 26 January 1930 as Independence Day.

cards.title: The Civil Disobedience Movement (1930‑1934) was a nationwide…
cards.subject: History
cards.definition: The Civil Disobedience Movement (1930‑1934) was a nationwide, non‑violent campaign launched by the Indian National Congress under Mahatma Gandhi to oppose British colonial laws, especially the salt tax. It began with the Dandi March (12 March – 6 April 1930) where Gandhi and 78 followers walked 385 km to produce salt illegally. The movement expanded to include: (1) refusal to pay land revenue and other taxes; (2) boycott of British goods, especially cloth, and promotion of khadi; (3) picketing of liquor shops and foreign‑cloth shops; (4) mass arrests — over 60,000 volunteers, including women like Sarojini Naidu and Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay, were jailed. The British responded with the Gandhi‑Irwin Pact (5 March 1931), which suspended the movement and allowed Gandhi to attend the Second Round Table Conference in London. When the conference failed, the movement resumed (January 1932) but was severely repressed; the Congress was declared illegal, leaders arrested, and the movement formally withdrawn in May 1934. The episode demonstrated the power of mass civil resistance, forced the British to negotiate, and set the stage for the Government of India Act 1935 and the 1937 provincial elections.
steps: The Civil Disobedience Movement (1930‑1934) turned the abstract demand for Poorna Swaraj into concrete, everyday defiance that ordinary Indians could join.

Here is why: the salt tax was a universally felt burden, the Dandi March gave a visual symbol of resistance, and the British choice to negotiate rather than crush the movement proved that mass non‑violence could extract…

First, the Lahore Congress (December 1929) declared Poorna Swaraj and fixed 26 January 1930 as Independence Day. Gandhi chose the salt law — a monopoly that taxed a basic necessity — as the target because it affected…
On 12 March 1930 he set out from Sabarmati Ashram with 78 satyagrahis; the 24‑day march to Dandi attracted global press attention, turning a local act into an international spectacle.

Second, once Gandhi broke the salt law on 6 April, the movement spread spontaneously: coastal villages produced salt, inland towns boycotted foreign cloth, peasants refused land revenue, and women picketed liquor shops.
The Congress organized “Salt Satyagraha” committees in every province; by May 1930 over 60,000 arrests were recorded, including prominent leaders like Jawaharlal Nehru and Vallabhbhai Patel.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the Simon Commission’s arrival in 1928”) reveals the misconception that the Simon Commission boycott directly started civil disobedience, confusing the earlier protest phase with the 1930 movement.

cards.title: The Gandhi‑Irwin Pact (5 March 1931) was a bilateral agreement between Mahatma…
cards.subject: History
cards.definition: The Gandhi‑Irwin Pact (5 March 1931) was a bilateral agreement between Mahatma Gandhi and Viceroy Lord Irwin that suspended the Civil Disobedience Movement. Its key terms: release of all political prisoners not convicted of violence, permission for peaceful picketing of liquor and foreign‑cloth shops, restoration of confiscated property, and the right to make salt for personal use. In return, Gandhi agreed to attend the Second Round Table Conference in London as the sole Congress representative. The Round Table Conferences (1930‑1932) were three British‑convened sessions in London to discuss constitutional reforms for India. The First (Nov 1930‑Jan 1931) proceeded without Congress; the Second (Sep‑Dec 1931) included Gandhi but deadlocked over minority safeguards and the demand for Poorna Swaraj; the Third (Nov‑Dec 1932) excluded Congress and produced the basis for the Government of India Act 1935. Together, the Pact and the Conferences mark the shift from mass non‑violent resistance to negotiated constitutional politics, revealing both the limits of British willingness to concede dominion status and the internal divisions among Indian leaders over communal representation.
steps: The Gandhi‑Irwin Pact and the Round Table Conferences together illustrate how a mass movement was channelled into formal negotiations, yet the British retained control over the constitutional agenda.

Here is why: the Pact was a tactical pause, not a surrender; the Conferences were British‑designed forums that exposed Indian disunity; and the failure to achieve Poorna Swaraj pushed the nationalist leadership toward…
First, the Civil Disobedience Movement (1930‑34) had mobilised millions through salt satyagraha, boycott, and non‑payment of taxes.
British repression — arrests, ordinances, press censorship — created a stalemate.

Viceroy Irwin, seeking to restore order before the London conferences, offered concessions that Gandhi accepted to keep the moral high ground and to represent Congress at the Second Round Table Conference.
Second, the First Round Table Conference (1930‑31) proceeded without Congress; it gathered princes, landlords, and minority leaders who favoured a federal structure with strong safeguards.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the British granted dominion status”) reveals the misconception that the Pact was a major constitutional breakthrough rather than a limited truce.

cards.title: The Poona Pact (24 September 1932) was an agreement between Mahatma Gandhi and…
cards.subject: History
cards.definition: The Poona Pact (24 September 1932) was an agreement between Mahatma Gandhi and Dr B.R. Ambedkar, negotiated in Yerwada Central Jail, Poona, to modify the British Communal Award of August 1932. The Award had granted separate electorates to the Depressed Classes (Scheduled Castes), a provision Gandhi opposed because he believed it would fracture Hindu unity and perpetuate untouchability. Gandhi undertook a fast‑unto‑death; Ambedkar, under pressure to save Gandhi’s life and secure political safeguards, accepted a compromise. The Pact provided for reserved seats for Depressed Classes in provincial legislatures (148 seats) and a central legislature (18 seats), elected through a two‑stage process: a primary election among Depressed Class voters to choose a panel of candidates, followed by a general election in which all voters chose the final representatives. It also guaranteed adequate representation in public services and educational grants. The Pact thus replaced separate electorates with joint electorates plus reservation, influencing the Government of India Act 1935 and setting the template for later affirmative‑action policies in independent India.
steps: The Poona Pact of 1932 replaced separate electorates for Depressed Classes with reserved seats in joint electorates, shaping Indian constitutional representation.

Here is why: first, the British Communal Award of August 1932 granted separate electorates to Depressed Classes, a move Gandhi saw as a British divide‑and‑rule tactic that would cement untouchability; he began a…

Second, Dr Ambedkar, the leading Depressed Class leader, negotiated under immense moral pressure to save Gandhi’s life while securing tangible political safeguards; the result was a compromise signed on 24 September…

Third, the Pact’s terms created 148 reserved provincial seats and 18 central seats, filled through a two‑stage election: Depressed Class voters first chose a panel of four candidates per seat (primary), then the general…
Fourth, the Pact also promised fair representation in public services and educational grants, linking political rights to socio‑economic uplift.
Fifth, the arrangement was incorporated into the Government of India Act 1935, establishing the principle of reserved seats in joint electorates that independent India later expanded.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the Pact kept separate electorates but increased the number of seats”) reveals the misconception that the Pact merely modified seat numbers without altering the electoral structure — confusing reservation with separate electorates.

Why did Gandhi undertake a fast‑unto‑death against the Communal Award’s provision for separate electorates for Depressed Classes.
Assess the impact of the Poona Pact on Dalit political representation in the 1930s.

cards.title: The Government of India Act 1935 was the longest and most detailed…
cards.subject: History
cards.definition: The Government of India Act 1935 was the longest and most detailed constitutional statute passed by the British Parliament for India. It introduced provincial autonomy, replacing dyarchy with responsible government in eleven provinces, each with an elected legislature and a council of ministers accountable to it. At the centre, it proposed a federation of British Indian provinces and princely states, but the federal part never came into force because the princely states refused to join. The Act retained the Viceroy’s overriding powers in defence, external affairs, and minority safeguards, and it entrenched separate electorates and weightage for minorities (Muslims, Sikhs, Europeans, etc.) based on the Communal Award as modified by the Poona Pact. It also established a Federal Court (precursor to the Supreme Court) and a Reserve Bank of India. The Act’s provincial provisions were implemented after the 1937 elections, leading to Congress ministries in most provinces, while the federal scheme remained a dead letter until the 1947 Independence Act adapted its framework.
steps: The Government of India Act 1935 was the British attempt to devolve power to Indian provinces while keeping strategic control at the centre.

Here is why: the Act replaced dyarchy with full provincial autonomy, giving elected ministers control over all provincial subjects except law and order, which remained with the governor; it designed a federal structure…

Consider the 1937 elections: Congress won majorities in seven provinces and formed ministries, demonstrating that provincial autonomy worked in practice, yet the Viceroy’s veto and the governor’s special powers limited…

The Act’s legacy is dual — it gave Indians their first taste of responsible government at the provincial level, but its federal blueprint became the template for the 1947 transfer of power, showing how a failed…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the 1935 Act kept dyarchy but added more transferred subjects”) reveals the misconception that the 1935 Act was merely an incremental tweak rather than a structural shift to responsible government.
remember: What was the principal change the Government of India Act 1935 introduced at the provincial level compared with the 1919 Act.
Why did the federal part of the 1935 Act never come into operation.
Evaluate the significance of the Federal Court established under the 1935 Act.

cards.title: The Elections of 1937 were held under the Government of India Act 1935…
cards.subject: History
cards.definition: The Elections of 1937 were held under the Government of India Act 1935, which introduced provincial autonomy and a limited franchise (about 11 % of adults). The Indian National Congress contested the elections, winning absolute majorities in five provinces (Madras, Bombay, Central Provinces, United Provinces, Bihar) and emerging as the largest party in three others. Congress formed ministries in July 1937, marking its first experience of responsible government. The ministries undertook social reforms (temple entry, tenancy laws, prohibition), released political prisoners, and promoted civil liberties. However, they faced constraints: governors retained special powers, finances were controlled by the centre, and the British could dismiss ministries. The experience sharpened Congress’s administrative capacity, exposed communal tensions (Muslim League’s poor performance), and influenced the 1939 resignation over war policy. This node links the 1935 Act to the subsequent wartime politics and the demand for a constituent assembly.
steps: The 1937 elections gave Congress its first taste of governing, proving Indians could administer provinces despite British-imposed limits.
Here is why: the Government of India Act 1935 created provincial autonomy with a restricted electorate;

Congress, after initial hesitation, contested and swept the polls, forming ministries in seven provinces; these ministries passed progressive laws on tenancy, labour, and social reform, but governors’ veto powers and…
Consider the sequence: the 1935 Act introduced dyarchy at the centre and autonomy in provinces;

Congress debated participation, finally deciding to contest to expose the Act’s inadequacies; the election results (February 1937) gave Congress clear majorities in Madras, Bombay, Central Provinces, United Provinces…
This episode sharpened Congress’s demand for a constituent assembly and highlighted communal divisions, as the Muslim League’s “Day of Deliverance” celebrated the resignations.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “universal adult franchise”) reveals the misconception that the 1935 Act introduced full democracy; in reality, it retained a highly restricted electorate.
remember: What was the approximate percentage of the adult population enfranchised under the Government of India Act 1935 for the 1937 provincial elections.
Why did the Congress initially hesitate to contest the 1937 elections but later decide to participate.
Evaluate the significance of the Congress ministries’ legislative record (1937‑39) for the nationalist movement.

cards.title: The Congress Ministries (1937‑1939) were the first popularly elected Indian…
cards.subject: History
cards.definition: The Congress Ministries (1937‑1939) were the first popularly elected Indian governments in British India, formed after the 1937 provincial elections under the Government of India Act 1935. Congress secured majorities in seven of eleven provinces — Madras, Bombay, Central Provinces, United Provinces, Bihar, Orissa, and Assam — and headed coalition ministries in two others. These ministries exercised limited legislative and executive powers subject to the Governor’s special responsibilities and veto, and they operated within a financial framework controlled by the centre. Their tenure (July 1937 – November 1939) is significant for three interconnected dimensions: (1) Social and administrative reforms — they introduced temple‑entry legislation for Dalits, prohibition, free primary education, tenancy reforms, debt‑relief acts, and labour welfare measures; (2) Constitutional constraints — the Governor’s discretionary powers, the need for central approval for financial bills, and the lack of control over defence and foreign affairs curtailed their autonomy; (3) Political consequences of resignation — when the Viceroy Lord Linlithgow declared India a belligerent in World War II (September 1939) without consulting Indian leaders, Congress ministries resigned en masse on the instruction of the Working Committee. This resignation demonstrated the hollowness of provincial autonomy, galvanised the demand for Poorna Swaraj, and provided the Muslim League an opportunity to observe a “Day of Deliverance” (22 December 1939), accelerating communal polarisation that culminated in the Lahore Resolution (1940). The episode bridges the constitutional experiment of 1935 and the mass mobilisation of the Quit India Movement (1942).
steps: The Congress ministries of 1937‑39 proved that Indians could govern responsibly but also exposed the 1935 Act’s built‑in brakes that made real self‑rule impossible.

Here is why: first, the ministries enacted progressive social laws — temple‑entry bills in Madras and Bombay, the Bombay Prohibition Act, the Bihar Tenancy Amendment Act, and free primary education schemes — showing the…

Second, every major bill required the Governor’s assent; financial bills needed the Governor‑General’s prior sanction, and subjects like law‑and‑order, finance, and irrigation remained “reserved” under British…

Third, the Viceroy’s unilateral declaration of war in September 1939 violated the federal spirit of the Act and the Congress demand for a constituent assembly; the Working Committee ordered ministries to resign rather…

Fourth, the resignation handed the Muslim League a propaganda victory — Jinnah declared 22 December 1939 a “Day of Deliverance” from “Congress tyranny” — deepening the Hindu‑Muslim divide and paving the way for the…

Fifth, the episode convinced Congress that provincial autonomy under British paramountcy was a dead end, hardening the resolve for complete independence and setting the stage for the 1942 Quit India Movement.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Punjab and Bengal”) reveals the misconception that Congress dominated all provinces — in fact, the Unionist Party ruled Punjab and the Krishak Praja Party led Bengal.
remember: Which seven provinces saw Congress form ministries after the 1937 elections.
Explain why the Governor’s veto power under the 1935 Act limited the effectiveness of Congress ministries.
Evaluate the significance of the Congress ministries’ resignation in 1939 for the nationalist movement.

cards.title: The Constructive Programme (1920s‑1930s) was Gandhi’s systematic plan for…
cards.subject: History
cards.definition: The Constructive Programme (1920s‑1930s) was Gandhi’s systematic plan for social and economic self‑reliance that ran parallel to political agitations like the Civil Disobedience Movement. Its core components were: (1) Khadi and village industries — spinning and weaving hand‑spun cloth to boycott British textiles and revive rural employment; (2) Harijan (Dalit) uplift — temple entry, removal of untouchability, and education for depressed classes; (3) Communal harmony — Hindu‑Muslim unity through joint prayers, inter‑dining, and opposition to separate electorates; (4) Prohibition — campaign against liquor to improve public health and morality; (5) Basic education (Nai Talim) — craft‑centred learning linking manual work with literacy; (6) Women’s participation — encouraging women to join picketing, spinning, and public meetings; (7) Village sanitation and health — latrines, clean water, and preventive care. The programme was not merely welfare; it was a political strategy to expand the Congress’s social base, demonstrate Indian capacity for self‑governance, and create a disciplined cadre for mass movements. It linked directly to the Poona Pact (1932) (Harijan representation), the 1937 Congress ministries (implementation of prohibition, khadi subsidies, Harijan welfare), and the Government of India Act 1935 (provincial autonomy gave Congress a platform to enact constructive policies). Unlike the overtly confrontational boycotts, the Constructive Programme built long‑term organisational strength and moral authority, making the nationalist movement resilient even when political negotiations stalled.
steps: The Constructive Programme was Gandhi’s parallel track of nation‑building that turned everyday activities into political acts.
Here is why: it transformed spinning, cleaning, and teaching into instruments of anti‑colonial resistance, making the freedom struggle a daily habit for millions.

First, khadi linked economic boycott (rejecting Lancashire cloth) with village employment; the All India Spinners Association (1925) and later the All India Village Industries Association (1934) created a nationwide…

Second, Harijan uplift after the Poona Pact (1932) institutionalised the fight against untouchability through the Harijan Sevak Sangh, turning temple‑entry campaigns (e.g., Guruvayur 1931‑32) into mass mobilisation…

Third, communal harmony efforts — joint Hindu‑Muslim prayers, opposition to the Communal Award — aimed to pre‑empt the divisive politics that the British encouraged through separate electorates; however, the programme’s…

Fourth, prohibition became a signature policy of the 1937 Congress ministries (e.g., Madras, Bombay), demonstrating that self‑governance could deliver social reform, yet it also alienated toddy‑tapping communities and…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “land redistribution, nationalisation of industries, universal suffrage”) reveals the misconception that the Constructive Programme was a socialist economic manifesto rather than a moral‑organisational framework centred on self‑reliance…
remember: List the seven pillars of Gandhi’s Constructive Programme as implemented between 1927 and 1937.
Explain how the khadi programme functioned simultaneously as an economic boycott and a tool for mass mobilisation during the Civil Disobedience Movement (1930‑34).
Evaluate the extent to which the Harijan uplift component of the Constructive Programme succeeded in integrating Dalits into the nationalist movement by 1937.

cards.title: The Congress Socialist Party (CSP) emerged in October 1934 at the Bombay…
cards.subject: History
cards.definition: The Congress Socialist Party (CSP) emerged in October 1934 at the Bombay session of the Indian National Congress as a left‑wing ginger group committed to achieving complete independence (Poorna Swaraj) through mass civil disobedience combined with a socialist transformation of Indian society.
