The sub‑concepts are linked: sample spaces provide the universe for events; classical counting supplies probabilities for equally likely spaces; axioms extend probability to any space; conditional probability and Bayes connect prior and posterior knowledge. Mastery requires moving fluently among these representations.
steps: Mastering ISC Probability requires fluently moving between classical counting, axiomatic rules, and conditional reasoning to solve multi‑step problems under timed conditions.
Here is why: the ISC paper tests not only formula recall but the ability to choose the right model for a described experiment.
First, recognise the experiment type — coins, dice, cards, balls, or real‑world scenarios — and write the sample space explicitly; this prevents hidden assumptions about equally likely outcomes.

Second, decide whether events are mutually exclusive, independent, or neither; the addition rule simplifies only for mutually exclusive events, while the multiplication rule needs conditional probability when draws are…
Third, practice the two classic ISC patterns: (a) “Find the probability that exactly k successes occur in n draws” — use combinations for without replacement, binomial for with replacement;
(b) “Given that B occurred, find the probability of A” — apply Bayes’ theorem with a clear partition of the sample space.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “P(E)=(n(S))/(n(E))”) reveals the misconception that probability is the ratio of total to favourable outcomes, confusing numerator and denominator.
remember: State the classical definition of probability for an event E in a finite sample space S.
If a die is rolled twice, explain why the sample space has 36 equally likely outcomes.
A student claims that for any two events A and B, P(A∪ B)=P(A)+P(B). Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Physics is the fundamental science that investigates the nature and behavior of…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Physics is the fundamental science that investigates the nature and behavior of matter and energy across all scales, from subatomic particles (10⁻¹⁵ m) to the observable universe (10²⁶ m). Its scope encompasses classical mechanics, electromagnetism, thermodynamics, quantum mechanics, and relativity, each governed by unifying principles such as conservation laws and symmetry. The excitement of physics arises from its predictive power: a few equations can describe phenomena as diverse as planetary orbits, semiconductor operation, and nuclear fusion in stars. This predictive capability drives technological innovation — lasers, MRI scanners, satellite communication, and renewable energy systems all stem from physical principles. Quantification is central to physics; therefore, the discipline relies on a coherent system of units (SI), dimensional consistency, and rigorous treatment of measurement uncertainty, significant figures, precision, and accuracy. These measurement concepts (covered in subsequent nodes) provide the language that translates qualitative observations into testable, reproducible results. In essence, physics connects the microscopic and macroscopic, the theoretical and the applied, making it the bedrock of modern science and engineering.
steps: Physics provides a universal framework to describe nature from the smallest particles to the largest galaxies, and its excitement comes from turning curiosity into predictive power and technology.
Here is why: first, physics spans an enormous range of scales — from quarks inside a proton (10⁻¹⁵ m) to galaxy clusters (10²⁴ m) — yet uses the same fundamental laws.
Second, diverse phenomena unify under principles like energy conservation and gauge symmetry; the same Maxwell equations govern lightning, radio waves, and the light from a diya.

Third, this unification yields predictive technology: the semiconductor physics behind every smartphone chip, the nuclear physics behind cancer radiotherapy, and the fluid dynamics that shape monsoon forecasts.
Fourth, measurement is the bridge between theory and reality; without agreed units, dimensions, and error analysis, physics would be mere speculation.

Fifth, Indian context makes it tangible — the pressure cooker’s whistle illustrates thermodynamics, the swing of a cricket ball demonstrates Magnus effect, and Chandrayaan’s orbit insertion showcases orbital mechanics.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "physics only studies motion and forces") reveals the misconception that physics is limited to mechanics, ignoring fields like electromagnetism, quantum physics, and thermodynamics.
remember: Name the two fundamental aspects that define the scope of physics.
Why is physics considered a foundational science for engineering and technology.
Evaluate the statement: "Physics only deals with theoretical concepts and has no practical relevance.".

cards.title: Units are standardized quantities used to express the magnitude of a physical…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Units are standardized quantities used to express the magnitude of a physical quantity. The International System of Units (SI) defines seven base units: metre (m) for length, kilogram (kg) for mass, second (s) for time, ampere (A) for electric current, kelvin (K) for thermodynamic temperature, mole (mol) for amount of substance, and candela (cd) for luminous intensity. All other units are derived by algebraic combination of these base units; for instance, the newton (N) = kg·m·s⁻². Dimensions describe the nature of a physical quantity in terms of the base quantities, independent of the numerical value or the unit chosen. The dimensional formula of a quantity Q is written as [Q] = M^a L^b T^c I^d Θ^e N^f J^g, where the exponents a…g are integers (positive, negative, or zero) indicating how many times each base quantity appears. For example, velocity has dimension [v] = L T⁻¹, force [F] = M L T⁻², and energy [E] = M L² T⁻². Dimensional homogeneity requires that every term in a physically meaningful equation have identical dimensions; this principle allows us to check the correctness of equations, derive relationships between quantities, and convert values from one unit system to another without memorising separate conversion factors. The node also introduces the concept of a dimensionless quantity (dimension 1) such as refractive index or strain, which carries no unit but may have a numerical value.
steps: Every physical quantity can be expressed as a product of powers of the seven base SI units, and this dimensional identity lets us check equations and convert units without memorising separate formulas.
Here is why: the SI system was built so that each base unit is independent; any derived unit is a unique algebraic combination of them.
Consider the equation for kinetic energy, E = ½ mv².
The dimension of mass is M, velocity is L T⁻¹, so v² carries L² T⁻²; multiplying gives M L² T⁻², which matches the known dimension of energy.
If a student wrote E = mv, the right‑hand side would be M L T⁻¹ — a mismatch that instantly flags the error.
Next, unit conversion becomes a matter of writing the same dimension in two different unit sets.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., listing “newton” as a base unit) reveals the misconception that any commonly used unit is a base unit, confusing derived units with the fundamental set.
remember: State the seven SI base units and their symbols.
Why can a quantity with dimension of length not be added to a quantity with dimension of time.
A student writes the dimensional formula of force as M L T⁻¹. Identify the error and give the correct formula.

cards.title: Dimensional analysis is a systematic method that uses the dimensions of…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Dimensional analysis is a systematic method that uses the dimensions of physical quantities — expressed as powers of the seven base dimensions (mass M, length L, time T, electric current I, thermodynamic temperature Θ, amount of substance N, luminous intensity J) — to verify the consistency of equations, derive relationships between quantities, and convert units between systems. The principle of homogeneity states that in any physically valid equation, every term must have identical dimensional formula; for example, in v = u + at, the dimensions of velocity [LT^-1] match those of u and at. A dimensional formula writes a quantity Q as [Q] = M^αL^βT^γI^δ ^ N^ J^, where the exponents are determined from the definition of Q. This tool links directly to the concepts of units and dimensions (node) because dimensions are independent of the chosen unit system, while units provide the numerical scale. It also underpins error analysis (node) and significant figures (node) by ensuring that only dimensionally consistent quantities are added or subtracted, and that derived results carry correct units. Limitations include inability to determine dimensionless constants, handle trigonometric, exponential, or logarithmic functions, or distinguish between quantities with same dimensions (e.g., work and torque). Mastery of dimensional analysis enables quick sanity checks of formulas, derivation of scaling laws (e.g., period of a pendulum T ∝ √(l/g)), and unit conversions such as joules to ergs.
steps: Dimensional analysis lets you check whether a physics equation is dimensionally consistent and derive relationships between physical quantities without knowing the exact numerical constants.

Here is why: every physical quantity can be expressed as a product of powers of the seven base dimensions; the principle of homogeneity demands that each term in an equation share the same dimensional formula; this…
Consider the equation for the period T of a simple pendulum.

We suspect T depends on length l, gravitational acceleration g, and mass m. Write the dimensional formulas: [T] = T, [l] = L, [g] = LT^-2, [m] = M. Assume a power-law relation T = k\, l^a g^b m^c where k is…
Equating dimensions: T = (L)^a(LT^-2)^b(M)^c = M^cL^a+bT^-2b.
Matching exponents gives c=0, a+b=0, -2b=1 → b=-1/2, a=1/2.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., M L^2 T^-2) reveals the misconception that force has the same dimensions as energy or work, confusing force with the product of force and distance.
remember: What is the dimensional formula of force in terms of base dimensions M, L, T.
An equation is given as P = (1)/(2)ρ v^2 + ρ g h. Using dimensional analysis, verify whether this equation is dimensionally….
Evaluate the claim: “Dimensional analysis can determine the exact numerical value of the constant in the formula for the period of a simple pendulum.”.

cards.title: Significant figures (SF) are the digits in a measured or calculated quantity…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Significant figures (SF) are the digits in a measured or calculated quantity that convey meaningful precision. The rules for counting SF are: (1) All non‑zero digits are significant. (2) Zeros between non‑zero digits are significant (e.g., 1002 has four SF). (3) Leading zeros are never significant; they only locate the decimal point (e.g., 0.0045 has two SF). (4) Trailing zeros in a number with a decimal point are significant (e.g., 12.300 has five SF). (5) Trailing zeros in a whole number without a decimal point are ambiguous; scientific notation removes the ambiguity (e.g., 1.20 × 10³ has three SF). When performing arithmetic, the result must be rounded to reflect the least precise operand: addition/subtraction uses the fewest decimal places; multiplication/division uses the fewest SF. Rounding follows the “round‑to‑even” rule for a final digit of 5. These conventions ensure that reported values never imply greater certainty than the original measurements.
steps: The result of any calculation can never be more precise than the least precise measurement used.
Here is why: every measuring instrument has a smallest division; the last digit you read is an estimate.
If you combine measurements, the combined uncertainty is governed by the weakest link.
First, identify the significant figures in each datum using the five rules above.
For example, a length recorded as 0.004560 m has four SF because the leading zeros are placeholders, while the trailing zero after the 6 is significant due to the decimal point.
Second, apply the arithmetic rule: in addition or subtraction, align decimal points and keep only as many decimal places as the term with the fewest decimal places.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “six significant figures because there are six digits”) reveals the misconception that every written digit counts, ignoring the role of leading zeros as mere placeholders.
remember: How many significant figures are in the measurement 0.004560 kg.
Why is the number 100 ambiguous in terms of significant figures, and how can scientific notation resolve the ambiguity.
A student records the mass of a copper block as 12.345 g using a balance that reads to the nearest 0.01 g. Evaluate the correctness of this reported value.

cards.title: Error in measurement quantifies the deviation of a measured value from the true…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Error in measurement quantifies the deviation of a measured value from the true (or accepted) value. The absolute error Δx = |x_measured – x_true| has the same unit as the quantity. Relative error = Δx / x_true (dimensionless) and percentage error = relative error × 100 %. When a result is calculated from several measured quantities, errors propagate: for addition/subtraction, absolute errors add; for multiplication/division, relative errors add in quadrature (√(Σ(Δxi/xi)²)); for a power xⁿ, relative error multiplies by |n|. Systematic errors shift all readings in one direction (zero error, calibration drift) while random errors scatter readings about the mean. The final reported value is expressed as x ± Δx, rounded so that the uncertainty has one or two significant figures and the measured value matches that decimal place. This node builds on significant figures and prepares for precision/accuracy.
steps: Every measurement carries an uncertainty that must be quantified and propagated to give a reliable result.
Here is why: a single reading like “mass = 150 g” is meaningless without knowing how far it could be from the true mass.
Consider a kitchen scale that reads 150 g for a bag of rice; if the scale’s least count is 1 g, the absolute error is ±0.5 g (half the least count).
The relative error is 0.5/150 ≈ 0.33 %, small enough for cooking but unacceptable for a pharmacy.
First, identify the type of error.
A zero error on a vernier caliper (systematic) shifts every reading by a fixed amount; you correct it by subtracting the zero error.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “absolute error is the ratio of error to true value”) reveals the misconception that absolute error is dimensionless — confusing it with relative error.
remember: Define absolute error and state its SI unit.
A student records three readings for the time period of a pendulum: 2.05 s, 2.07 s, 2.03 s. The accepted value is 2.00 s. Calculate the mean absolute error.
Instrument A gives length = 10.00 ± 0.01 cm; Instrument B gives 10.0 ± 0.1 cm. True length = 10.00 cm. Which instrument is more precise? Which is more accurate.

cards.title: Precision quantifies the repeatability of a set of measurements…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Precision quantifies the repeatability of a set of measurements — how close the individual readings are to each other — and is expressed by statistical spread such as standard deviation (σ) or range. Accuracy quantifies the closeness of the mean of those measurements to the accepted true value and is expressed by percent error or absolute error. A measurement can be precise but inaccurate (systematic error), accurate but imprecise (large random error), both, or neither. The relationship is captured by the error model: measured value = true value + systematic error + random error. Reducing systematic error improves accuracy; reducing random error improves precision. Both concepts rely on the treatment of significant figures and error propagation covered in earlier nodes.
steps: Takeaway: Precision describes how tightly repeated measurements group together, while accuracy describes how close their average is to the true value; both must be evaluated to judge data quality.
Here is why: 1.
Statistical spread — The standard deviation (σ) of a data set numerically captures precision; a smaller σ means tighter clustering. 2.
Bias detection — Percent error = |(mean − true)/true| × 100 % reveals systematic bias; a large percent error signals inaccuracy even if σ is tiny. 3.
Error decomposition — Measured = true + systematic + random.
Systematic shifts the whole cluster (affects accuracy); random widens the cluster (affects precision). 4.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “precision means the instrument is expensive”) reveals the misconception that cost or brand determines measurement quality rather than statistical spread.
remember: Define precision and accuracy in your own words and give one everyday example for each.
A student records the length of a rod five times: 12.34 cm, 12.36 cm, 12.35 cm, 12.33 cm, 12.37 cm. The true length is 12.30 cm. Calculate the mean, standard deviation, and….
Explain why increasing the number of trials reduces random error but does not eliminate systematic error.

cards.title: A frame of reference is a coordinate system
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: A frame of reference is a coordinate system (usually three mutually perpendicular axes x, y, z with an origin O) together with a clock that records time t. It provides the standard against which the position vector r(t) of any particle is measured. The SI unit of position is the metre (m) and of time is the second (s). Frames are classified as inertial (Newton’s first law holds; a free particle moves with constant velocity) and non‑inertial (accelerated or rotating; fictitious forces appear). The choice of frame determines the numerical values of displacement, velocity, and acceleration, but the physical laws retain their form only in inertial frames (Galilean relativity). All subsequent kinematic quantities — distance, displacement, velocity, acceleration — are defined relative to a chosen frame. Relationship to sub‑concepts: - Distance and displacement (node) are measured along the axes of the selected frame. - Velocity and acceleration (node) are time derivatives of the position vector in that frame. - Uniform / non‑uniform motion (node) and graphs of motion (node) are plotted using coordinates from the frame. - Equations of uniformly accelerated motion (node) assume an inertial frame with constant acceleration.
steps: A frame of reference is a coordinate system with a clock that lets us assign numbers to where and when an object is. Here is why: every measurement of position, velocity, or acceleration is meaningless unless we say…

First, the origin O fixes the zero of position; the three axes give direction; the clock gives the time coordinate t. Second, if the frame moves with constant velocity (inertial), Newton’s first law works — a free…
Third, if the frame accelerates or rotates (non‑inertial), fictitious forces such as the Coriolis or centrifugal force must be added to explain observed motion.

Fourth, the same physical event — a ball dropped inside a moving train — looks like a straight vertical fall in the train’s frame but a parabola in the ground frame; both descriptions are correct once the frame is…
Fifth, in kinematics we always begin by declaring the frame; the next nodes (distance/displacement, velocity/acceleration, graphs, equations) all inherit that choice.
Consider a car turning a circular track.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Earth is perfectly inertial”) reveals the misconception that Earth’s rotation and orbital motion are negligible for all classroom problems — ignoring the small but real Coriolis effect.
remember: Define a frame of reference and list its three essential components.
Explain the difference between an inertial and a non‑inertial frame of reference. Give one everyday example of each.
A student claims: “The Earth’s surface is an inertial frame for all mechanics problems in Class 11.” Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Distance (s) is the total length of the actual path travelled by a particle…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Distance (s) is the total length of the actual path travelled by a particle, irrespective of direction. It is a scalar quantity, always non‑negative, measured in metres (m) in the SI system. Displacement (Δr) is the vector drawn from the initial position rᵢ to the final position r_f; its magnitude is the shortest straight‑line distance between the two points and its direction points from start to finish. Displacement can be zero, positive, or negative depending on the chosen coordinate axis. The relationship between the two is: distance ≥ |displacement|, with equality only when motion occurs along a straight line without reversal. In a chosen frame of reference (see node), position vectors r(t) describe the particle’s location at time t; distance is the integral of speed |v| over time, while displacement is r(t_f) − r(t_i). Both quantities are foundational for defining average speed (distance/time) and average velocity (displacement/time) in the next node.
steps: Takeaway: Distance measures the total path length travelled, while displacement measures the straight‑line change in position; distance is a scalar, displacement a vector, and distance is always at least as large as the…
Here is why: 1.
Path dependence vs. end‑point dependence – Distance accumulates every segment of the journey; displacement cares only about the initial and final coordinates. 2.
Scalar vs. vector – Distance has magnitude only; displacement has magnitude and direction, so it can be negative along a chosen axis. 3.
Triangle inequality – The straight line between two points is the shortest possible path, guaranteeing distance ≥ |displacement|. 4.
Zero displacement with non‑zero distance – A round trip returns to the start, giving zero displacement but positive distance. 5.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “distance = 0 m because it ends where it started”) reveals the misconception that distance depends only on the final position, confusing it with displacement.
remember: A particle moves 10 m east, then 10 m west. What are its total distance travelled and its displacement.
Explain why distance can never be less than the magnitude of displacement for any motion.
A car travels along a semicircular track of radius 50 m from point A to point B (diametrically opposite). Calculate the distance travelled and the magnitude of displacement.

cards.title: Velocity (symbol v) is a vector quantity defined as the rate of change of…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Velocity (symbol v) is a vector quantity defined as the rate of change of displacement s with respect to time t: v = (ds)/(dt) Its SI unit is metre per second (m s⁻¹). The magnitude of velocity is speed, a scalar measured in the same unit. Acceleration (symbol a) is the rate of change of velocity with respect to time: a = (dv)/(dt) Its SI unit is metre per second squared (m s⁻²). Both quantities are vectors; direction matters. For motion along a straight line we can treat them as signed scalars: positive in the chosen reference direction, negative opposite. Relationships: - Average velocity over interval Δt: v = (Δ s)/(Δ t). - Instantaneous velocity is the limit of average velocity as Δt → 0. - Average acceleration: a = (Δ v)/(Δ t). - Instantaneous acceleration is the limit of average acceleration as Δt → 0. Uniform motion ⇒ a = 0, v = constant. Non‑uniform motion ⇒ a ≠ 0. The sign of a relative to v indicates speeding up (same sign) or slowing down (opposite sign).
steps: Velocity and acceleration are the two fundamental descriptors of how an object’s position changes in time; velocity tells how fast and in which direction the displacement changes, while acceleration tells how fast the…
Here is why: velocity is the first time‑derivative of displacement, and acceleration is the first time‑derivative of velocity (or the second derivative of displacement).
This derivative relationship means that if you know the displacement function s(t), you can obtain v(t) by differentiating once and a(t) by differentiating twice.
Consider a car moving along a straight road with displacement given by s(t) = 2t^3 - 9t^2 + 12t metres, where t is in seconds.
Differentiating once gives v(t) = 6t^2 - 18t + 12 m s⁻¹.
Differentiating again gives a(t) = 12t - 18 m s⁻².
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “velocity is distance divided by time”) reveals the misconception that velocity is a scalar average quantity, confusing it with speed and ignoring the vector nature and the limiting process.
remember: Define instantaneous velocity and state its SI unit.
A particle moves along a straight line with displacement s(t) = 4t^2 - 3t + 5 m. Find its velocity at t = 2 s.
Explain why a particle can have zero velocity but non‑zero acceleration at an instant.

cards.title: Uniform motion is defined as motion in which a body covers equal displacements…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Uniform motion is defined as motion in which a body covers equal displacements in equal intervals of time, irrespective of how small the interval. Consequently, its velocity v is constant (both magnitude and direction) and its acceleration a is zero. Non‑uniform motion occurs when displacements in equal time intervals are unequal; the velocity changes with time, so the acceleration is non‑zero. The average velocity over a finite interval Δt is v_avg = Δx/Δt (SI unit m s⁻¹), while the instantaneous velocity is the time derivative v = dx/dt. Similarly, average acceleration is a_avg = Δv/Δt (SI unit m s⁻²) and instantaneous acceleration is a = dv/dt = d²x/dt². Uniform motion is a special case of non‑uniform motion where a = 0 at all instants. The distinction relies on the frame of reference (node) and the vector nature of displacement (node); speed alone cannot decide uniformity because a body moving in a circle at constant speed has changing velocity.
steps: Uniform motion means constant velocity and zero acceleration, while non‑uniform motion involves changing velocity and non‑zero acceleration.
Here is why: 1.
In uniform motion the displacement‑time graph is a straight line with constant slope; the slope gives the constant velocity. 2.
In non‑uniform motion the displacement‑time graph curves because the slope (velocity) changes at each instant. 3.
The velocity‑time graph for uniform motion is a horizontal line (zero slope → zero acceleration); for non‑uniform motion it slopes upward or downward, and its slope equals acceleration. 4.
Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity; zero acceleration is the hallmark of uniform motion, non‑zero acceleration defines non‑uniform motion. 5.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “acceleration is constant but not zero”) reveals the misconception that constant acceleration implies uniform motion — confusing uniformly accelerated motion with uniform motion.
remember: Define uniform motion and state the value of its acceleration.
A car travels 30 km in the first hour, 30 km in the second hour, and 30 km in the third hour. Is its motion uniform? Justify your answer.
A student claims that if speed is constant, motion must be uniform. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Graphs of motion are visual representations that relate the kinematic…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Graphs of motion are visual representations that relate the kinematic quantities — position (x), velocity (v) and acceleration (a) — to time (t) for a particle moving in a straight line. In a position‑time (x‑t) graph the vertical axis is displacement (metre, m) and the horizontal axis is time (second, s); the slope at any point, Δx/Δt, gives the instantaneous velocity (m s⁻¹). In a velocity‑time (v‑t) graph the vertical axis is velocity (m s⁻¹); its slope, Δv/Δt, yields acceleration (m s⁻²), while the signed area between the curve and the time axis, ∫v dt, equals the displacement (m) over that interval. In an acceleration‑time (a‑t) graph the vertical axis is acceleration (m s⁻²); the area under the curve, ∫a dt, gives the change in velocity (m s⁻¹). For uniform motion the x‑t graph is a straight line (constant slope), the v‑t graph is a horizontal line (zero slope), and the a‑t graph lies on the time axis. For uniformly accelerated motion the x‑t graph is a parabola, the v‑t graph is a straight line with non‑zero slope, and the a‑t graph is a horizontal line at the constant acceleration value. These graphical relationships are the geometric counterparts of the differential and integral definitions of velocity and acceleration and provide a method to extract quantitative kinematic data without algebraic manipulation.
steps: The slope of a position‑time graph gives velocity, the slope of a velocity‑time graph gives acceleration, and the area under a velocity‑time graph gives displacement.
First, graphs turn an abstract motion into a visual record that can be read at a glance.

Second, uniform motion produces straight‑line graphs: a constant slope on x‑t means constant velocity, a horizontal v‑t line means zero acceleration, and a flat a‑t line on the time axis confirms no acceleration.
Third, uniformly accelerated motion yields a straight line on the v‑t graph (constant slope = constant acceleration) and a parabola on the x‑t graph (changing slope).
Fourth, the area under the v‑t curve — whether a rectangle, triangle or trapezoid — equals the displacement because integration of velocity over time is exactly the definition of displacement.
Fifth, the area under the a‑t curve gives the change in velocity, linking acceleration directly to the velocity graph.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the slope gives speed”) reveals the misconception that slope yields a scalar quantity; velocity is a vector and the sign of the slope indicates direction.
remember: What does the slope of a position‑time graph represent.
A velocity‑time graph is a straight line with a positive constant slope. What does this indicate about the particle’s acceleration.
A student claims that the area under an acceleration‑time graph gives displacement. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Uniformly accelerated motion occurs when a particle moves along a straight line…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Uniformly accelerated motion occurs when a particle moves along a straight line and its acceleration a remains constant in magnitude and direction. Let the initial velocity at time t = 0 be u (m s⁻¹), the velocity after time t be v (m s⁻¹), and the displacement during that interval be s (m). The four kinematic equations relate these five quantities: 1. v = u + a t – velocity after time t. 2. s = u t + ½ a t² – displacement after time t. 3. v² = u² + 2 a s – velocity‑displacement relation, independent of t. 4. s = (u + v)/2 × t – displacement using average velocity. All quantities are vectors along the chosen axis; sign conventions (positive direction) must be kept consistent. The equations are derived from the definitions a = dv/dt and v = ds/dt by integrating with constant a. They apply only when acceleration is uniform; for non‑uniform acceleration the graphical or calculus methods (covered in later nodes) are required.
steps: The four kinematic equations are the complete algebraic toolkit for any straight‑line motion with constant acceleration.
Here is why: they are direct consequences of the definition a = (v‑u)/t and the fact that the velocity‑time graph is a straight line, so the area under it (displacement) is a trapezium.
First, start from a = (v‑u)/t → v = u + at (Equation 1).
Second, the average velocity during the interval is (u+v)/2; multiplying by t gives s = (u+v)/2 × t (Equation 4).
Third, substitute v from Equation 1 into Equation 4: s = (u + u + at)/2 × t = ut + ½at² (Equation 2).
Fourth, eliminate t between Equation 1 and Equation 2: t = (v‑u)/a; insert into Equation 2 and simplify to obtain v² = u² + 2as (Equation 3).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., writing s = vt) reveals the misconception that displacement equals final velocity times time, ignoring the initial velocity and acceleration contributions.
remember: State the four kinematic equations for uniformly accelerated motion and list the symbols with their SI units.
A car accelerates uniformly from 10 m s⁻¹ to 30 m s⁻¹ in 5 s. Which single equation directly gives the displacement without first finding acceleration? Show the calculation.
Evaluate the claim: “If a particle’s acceleration is zero, the equation v² = u² + 2as reduces to v = u, so displacement must be zero.” Explain why this reasoning is flawed.

cards.title: Kinematics in a plane extends one‑dimensional motion to two dimensions by…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Kinematics in a plane extends one‑dimensional motion to two dimensions by introducing vectors — quantities with both magnitude and direction (e.g., displacement, velocity, acceleration) — and scalars — quantities with only magnitude (e.g., distance, speed, time). Vector addition follows the triangle or parallelogram law, allowing resultant displacement or velocity to be found geometrically or analytically using components. Projectile motion analyses the trajectory of an object launched into the air under gravity, treating horizontal and vertical motions as independent: horizontal velocity remains constant (neglecting air resistance) while vertical velocity changes uniformly due to g = 9.8 m s⁻². Uniform circular motion describes an object moving at constant speed along a circular path; although speed is constant, the velocity vector changes direction continuously, producing a centripetal acceleration a_c = v²/r directed toward the centre. These four sub‑concepts are linked: vectors provide the mathematical framework, vector addition combines component motions, projectile motion applies independent component analysis, and uniform circular motion illustrates continuous vector change. Mastery of this chapter enables prediction of range, maximum height, time of flight, and centripetal force requirements in real‑world situations such as sports, satellite orbits, and mechanical design.
steps: This chapter equips you with vector tools to analyse any motion that occurs on a flat surface, from a thrown ball to a rotating wheel.
First, vectors replace simple numbers because direction matters: a 5 km walk north is not the same as 5 km east.
Second, vector addition (triangle or parallelogram law) lets you combine multiple displacements or velocities into a single resultant — essential for navigation and engineering.
Third, projectile motion splits into two independent one‑dimensional motions: horizontal (constant velocity) and vertical (uniform acceleration due to gravity).
This separation simplifies calculating range, height, and flight time — think of a cricket ball lofted at 30° during an IPL match.

Fourth, uniform circular motion shows that constant speed does not mean zero acceleration; the velocity vector turns continuously, creating a centripetal acceleration toward the centre — like a stone whirled on a string…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “both have unit metre so both are vectors”) reveals the misconception that identical units imply identical vector nature — confusing magnitude‑only quantities with those needing direction.
remember: State the SI unit of displacement and explain why displacement is a vector while distance is a scalar.
A student adds two displacement vectors of 3 m east and 4 m north by simply adding their magnitudes to get 7 m. Identify the error and give the correct resultant magnitude.
Evaluate the statement: “In projectile motion, the horizontal velocity decreases because gravity pulls the object down.”.

cards.title: A scalar is a physical quantity completely described by a magnitude
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: A scalar is a physical quantity completely described by a magnitude (numerical value) and a unit, with no direction. Examples: mass (kg), time (s), temperature (K), speed (m s⁻¹), energy (J). Scalars obey ordinary algebraic addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division. A vector is a physical quantity that requires both magnitude and a specific direction in space for complete description. It is represented by a directed line segment (arrow) whose length is proportional to the magnitude and whose arrowhead indicates direction. Examples: displacement (m), velocity (m s⁻¹), acceleration (m s⁻²), force (N), momentum (kg m s⁻¹). Vectors follow the triangle (or parallelogram) law of addition: the resultant vector is the diagonal of the parallelogram formed by the two vectors placed tail‑to‑tail. Key relationships: - The magnitude of a vector A is a scalar denoted |A|. - Multiplying a vector by a scalar changes its magnitude (and possibly reverses direction if the scalar is negative) but does not alter its inherent vector nature. - The zero vector (null vector) has zero magnitude and undefined direction; it is the additive identity for vectors. - Unit vectors (î, ĵ, k̂) have magnitude 1 and point along the positive x, y, z axes; any vector can be expressed as a linear combination of these. In the CISCE ISC Class 11 syllabus, scalars and vectors form the foundation for subsequent topics: vector addition (node), projectile motion (node), and uniform circular motion (node). Mastery of scalar‑vector distinction, representation, and basic operations is essential for analysing two‑dimensional motion.
steps: Scalars have only magnitude; vectors have both magnitude and direction — this single distinction governs every subsequent operation in two‑dimensional kinematics.
Here is why: 1.
Physical meaning – When a cricket ball is thrown, the distance it travels (scalar) tells how much ground it covered, but the displacement (vector) tells where it landed relative to the bowler.
The direction component is crucial for field placement. 2.
Mathematical representation – A vector A in three‑dimensional space is written as A = Aₓî + Aᵧĵ + A_zk̂, where Aₓ, Aᵧ, A_z are scalar components.
The magnitude |A| = √(Aₓ² + Aᵧ² + A_z²) is a scalar derived from the components. 3.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., choosing (a) temperature) reveals the misconception that any measurable quantity with a unit is a vector, confusing the presence of a unit with the need for direction.
remember: Which of the following quantities is a vector? (a) Temperature of a room (b) Mass of a textbook (c) Velocity of a train (d) Time taken for a journey.
A vector A = 3î + 4ĵ is given. What is its magnitude? Show the calculation.
Evaluate the statement: “Multiplying a vector by a negative scalar only changes its magnitude.” Is it true or false? Justify.

cards.title: Vector addition is the process of combining two or more vectors to obtain a…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Vector addition is the process of combining two or more vectors to obtain a single resultant vector that has the same effect as the original set. The triangle law states that if two vectors A and B are represented as two sides of a triangle taken in order, the third side taken in the opposite order represents the resultant R = A + B. The parallelogram law gives the same resultant as the diagonal of the parallelogram formed by A and B as adjacent sides. Analytically, any vector can be resolved into rectangular components (Ax, Ay) along mutually perpendicular axes; the resultant’s components are the algebraic sums Rx = ΣAx, Ry = ΣAy. The magnitude of the resultant is R = √(Rx² + Ry²) and its direction θ = tan⁻¹(Ry/Rx) measured from the positive x‑axis. Vector addition is commutative (A + B = B + A) and associative ((A + B) + C = A + (B + C)). These properties hold for any number of vectors and form the mathematical basis for analysing projectile motion, uniform circular motion, and equilibrium of forces in later nodes.
steps: The resultant of two vectors is obtained by placing them tip‑to‑tail (triangle law) or by adding their rectangular components; both give the same magnitude and direction.
Here is why: 1.
Triangle law visualises addition as a path — walk along A, then along B; the straight line from start to finish is R. 2.
Parallelogram law shows the same resultant as the diagonal when A and B originate from the same point. 3.
Component method breaks each vector into perpendicular parts (Ax, Ay); adding components separately (Rx = Ax + Bx, Ry = Ay + By) turns a geometric problem into simple algebra. 4.
Commutative and associative nature means the order of addition does not affect the final resultant, allowing flexible grouping of many vectors. 5.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the resultant is the sum of the magnitudes”) reveals the misconception that vectors add like scalars, ignoring direction.
remember: State the triangle law of vector addition.
Two vectors of magnitudes 5 N and 12 N act at an angle of 90°. Find the magnitude of the resultant.
A student adds two vectors by adding their magnitudes directly. Explain why this is incorrect except when vectors are collinear and in the same direction.

cards.title: Projectile motion is the two‑dimensional motion of an object launched with an…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Projectile motion is the two‑dimensional motion of an object launched with an initial velocity u at an angle θ to the horizontal, moving under the sole influence of gravity g (≈ 9.8 m s⁻²) near Earth’s surface, with air resistance neglected. The motion separates into independent horizontal and vertical components: - Horizontal: constant velocity uₓ = u cosθ, displacement x = u cosθ · t. - Vertical: uniformly accelerated motion with initial velocity uᵧ = u sinθ, acceleration −g, displacement y = u sinθ · t − ½ g t². Eliminating t gives the trajectory equation y = x tanθ − (g x²)/(2 u² cos²θ), a parabola. Key derived quantities: time of flight T = 2u sinθ/g, maximum height H = u² sin²θ/(2g), horizontal range R = u² sin2θ/g. These relations hold for launch and landing at the same vertical level; different levels require solving the quadratic in t from the vertical displacement equation.
steps: The single most important takeaway: Projectile motion is the superposition of a constant‑velocity horizontal motion and a uniformly accelerated vertical motion, and every projectile quantity can be obtained by treating…
Here is why: the gravitational force acts only vertically, so there is no horizontal acceleration (neglecting air drag).
This independence lets us write x(t) and y(t) separately, then eliminate t to get the path.
Consider a stone thrown from a rooftop at 20 m s⁻¹, 30° above horizontal.
First, resolve the velocity: uₓ = 20 cos30° ≈ 17.3 m s⁻¹, uᵧ = 20 sin30° = 10 m s⁻¹.
The horizontal motion is x = 17.3 t. The vertical motion follows y = 10 t − 4.9 t² (taking roof as y = 0, upward positive).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., uₓ = u sinθ, uᵧ = u cosθ) reveals the misconception that the angle is measured from the vertical instead of the horizontal, confusing the sine and cosine assignments.
remember: State the horizontal and vertical components of the initial velocity for a projectile launched with speed u at angle θ to the horizontal.
Explain why the horizontal velocity of a projectile remains constant (ignoring air resistance) while the vertical velocity changes.
A projectile is launched from ground level with speed u at angle θ. Evaluate the claim: “The maximum height reached depends only on the vertical component of the initial velocity.”.

cards.title: Uniform circular motion is the motion of a particle along a circular path with…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Uniform circular motion is the motion of a particle along a circular path with constant speed. Although the speed is constant, the velocity vector changes direction at every instant; therefore the particle experiences an acceleration directed radially inward toward the centre of the circle. This acceleration is called centripetal acceleration (a_c) and its magnitude is given by a_c = v²/r = ω²r, where v is the linear speed, r the radius, and ω the angular velocity. The net force required to produce this acceleration is the centripetal force F_c = m a_c = m v²/r = m ω²r, where m is the mass of the particle. Angular velocity ω (rad s⁻¹) relates to linear speed by v = ωr. The period T (s) is the time for one complete revolution, T = 2π/ω, and frequency f (Hz) is the reciprocal, f = 1/T. All quantities are defined in SI units: v in m s⁻¹, r in m, ω in rad s⁻¹, a_c in m s⁻², F_c in N, T in s, f in Hz. Uniform circular motion is a special case of planar motion where the tangential acceleration is zero and the only acceleration is the centripetal component.
steps: The key takeaway is that in uniform circular motion the speed is constant but the velocity changes because its direction changes, producing a centripetal acceleration always directed toward the centre.
Here is why: (1) Velocity is a vector; a change in direction alone constitutes a change in velocity, so acceleration exists.
(2) The acceleration is perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work and cannot change the kinetic energy, keeping the speed constant.
(3) The magnitude of this acceleration follows from the geometry of the velocity triangle: for a small time Δt the change in velocity Δv points toward the centre, and |Δv|/Δt → v²/r as Δt → 0.
(4) Newton’s second law then requires a net inward force F_c = m v²/r, which must be supplied by a physical interaction such as tension, friction, or gravity.
(5) Angular quantities simplify many problems: ω = v/r, T = 2π/ω, f = 1/T.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “centripetal acceleration is tangential to the path”) reveals the misconception that acceleration always aligns with velocity, confusing speed change with direction change.
remember: Define uniform circular motion and state the direction of centripetal acceleration.
Explain why a particle in uniform circular motion has acceleration even though its speed is constant.
A student claims that centripetal force is a new type of force like gravity or friction. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Relative motion in a plane describes how the velocity and acceleration of one…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Relative motion in a plane describes how the velocity and acceleration of one object appear when observed from another moving object. The relative velocity of object A with respect to object B is the vector difference v_AB = v_A - v_B, where v_A and v_B are velocities measured in a common inertial frame (usually ground). In two dimensions, each velocity is resolved into rectangular components (e.g., east and north) before subtraction. Relative acceleration follows the same rule: a_AB = a_A - a_B. This concept builds directly on vector addition and subtraction and is essential for analysing projectile motion from a moving frame and for understanding the apparent motion in uniform circular motion when the observer is also moving. Applications include river‑crossing problems, rain‑man problems, aircraft navigation with wind, and collision avoidance. The key principle is that only relative quantities are physically observable; absolute motion depends on the chosen reference frame.
steps: The takeaway: Relative motion in a plane is found by vector subtraction of the observer’s velocity from the object’s velocity, and every classic two‑dimensional kinematics problem (river, rain, aircraft) is just an…
Here is why: (1) Velocity is a vector; changing reference frames means adding the negative of the observer’s velocity.
(2) In a plane, subtraction is done component‑wise, so east‑west and north‑south parts are treated independently.
(3) The same rule holds for acceleration because acceleration is the time derivative of velocity.
(4) All “moving medium” problems — boat in river, rain on running man, plane in wind — reduce to finding the resultant of two perpendicular or angled vectors.
(5) The magnitude and direction of the relative velocity give the apparent speed and direction seen by the moving observer.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “relative velocity is the difference of speeds”) reveals the misconception that velocity is a scalar and direction can be ignored.
remember: Define relative velocity of object A with respect to object B in a plane and state its SI unit.
Two cars move on a flat road. Car A travels north at 20 m/s. Car B travels east at 15 m/s. Explain why the velocity of A relative to B is not simply 35 m/s.
A boat crosses a river of width 200 m. The boat’s speed in still water is 4 m/s directed perpendicular to the….

cards.title: Relative motion in a plane analyses the velocity of an object as observed from…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Relative motion in a plane analyses the velocity of an object as observed from a moving reference frame. If object A has velocity v_A and object B has velocity v_B (both measured in a common inertial frame, usually ground), the velocity of A relative to B is v_AB = v_A − v_B. This vector subtraction follows the triangle or parallelogram law of vector addition. The magnitude is |v_AB| = √(v_A² + v_B² − 2 v_A v_B cos θ), where θ is the angle between v_A and v_B. The direction is given by tan α = (v_A sin θ)/(v_A cos θ − v_B) for the angle α that v_AB makes with v_A. This concept extends projectile motion and uniform circular motion by allowing analysis of motion from non‑stationary frames — e.g., rain appearing slanted to a running person, or a boat’s resultant path in a flowing river. It connects vector addition (node) and projectile motion (node) because the relative trajectory is often a straight line or a parabola in the moving frame. It also underpins the concept of relative angular velocity in non‑uniform circular motion, which is reserved for higher classes.
steps: The velocity of an object depends entirely on the observer’s frame of reference; relative velocity in a plane is the vector difference v_AB = v_A − v_B.
Here is why: motion is not absolute — a passenger on a bus sees a fellow passenger at rest, while a pedestrian sees both moving at the bus’s speed.
To analyse such situations, we subtract the observer’s velocity vector from the object’s velocity vector.
First, represent both velocities as vectors in a common coordinate system (usually east‑north).

Second, reverse the observer’s vector and add it tip‑to‑tail to the object’s vector — this is the triangle law. Third, compute the resultant’s magnitude using the cosine rule and its direction using the sine rule or…
For example, rain falls vertically at 10 m/s; a man runs east at 5 m/s.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “relative velocity is the sum of the two velocities”) reveals the misconception that relative motion adds speeds regardless of direction, confusing vector subtraction with scalar addition.
remember: Define relative velocity of object A with respect to object B in a plane and state its SI unit.
Two cars move on perpendicular roads: Car A travels north at 20 m/s, Car B travels east at 15 m/s. Explain why the magnitude of the velocity of A relative to B is not 35 m/s.
A student claims: “If rain falls vertically and a man runs horizontally, the rain appears to come at an angle whose tangent is (man’s speed)/(rain’s speed).” Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Kinematics in a plane deals with motion described by two perpendicular…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Kinematics in a plane deals with motion described by two perpendicular components. Scalars (e.g., speed, distance) have only magnitude; vectors (e.g., displacement, velocity, acceleration) have magnitude and direction and obey the triangle or parallelogram law of addition. Vector addition resolves a vector into rectangular components (x and y) using trigonometric functions. Projectile motion is the superposition of uniform horizontal velocity (no air resistance) and uniformly accelerated vertical motion under gravity (g = 9.8 m s⁻²). Its key parameters — time of flight, maximum height, range — are derived from the component equations. Uniform circular motion describes a particle moving at constant speed along a circle; its velocity vector changes direction continuously, producing a centripetal acceleration a_c = v²/r directed toward the centre. The angular velocity ω = v/r links linear and angular quantities. All these sub‑concepts connect through vector algebra: the same component method solves projectile and circular problems, and the concept of relative velocity extends vector addition to moving frames.
steps: The single most important takeaway is that every planar motion problem reduces to independent one‑dimensional motions along chosen axes, and the final answer is the vector sum of those independent results.
Here is why: the superposition principle holds because forces (gravity, tension) act independently in perpendicular directions.
Consider a stone thrown from a 20 m high tower at 30° with 25 m s⁻¹.
First, resolve the initial velocity: u_x = u cosθ = 25 cos30° ≈ 21.65 m s⁻¹, u_y = u sinθ = 25 sin30° = 12.5 m s⁻¹.
The horizontal motion has no acceleration, so x = u_x t. The vertical motion follows y = u_y t – ½gt² with y = –20 m (downward displacement).
Solving the quadratic gives t ≈ 4.2 s (positive root).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “radian per second squared”) reveals the misconception that angular acceleration and centripetal acceleration share units — confusing angular quantities (rad s⁻²) with linear acceleration.
remember: State the SI unit of centripetal acceleration and write its dimensional formula.
A projectile is launched at 45° with speed 20 m s⁻¹ from ground….
Evaluate the statement: “In uniform circular motion, the acceleration vector is constant because the speed is constant.”.

cards.title: Newton’s three laws of motion form the axiomatic basis of classical mechanics.
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Newton’s three laws of motion form the axiomatic basis of classical mechanics. First Law (Law of Inertia): A body remains at rest or in uniform motion in a straight line unless acted upon by a net external force. This law defines an inertial reference frame — any frame in which a free particle moves with constant velocity. Inertia is the intrinsic property of matter that resists changes in its state of motion; mass is the quantitative measure of inertia. Second Law (Law of Acceleration): The rate of change of linear momentum of a body is directly proportional to the net external force applied and occurs in the direction of that force. For a body of constant mass m, F = dp/dt = ma, where p = mv is linear momentum, a is acceleration, and F is the vector sum of all forces. The SI unit of force is the newton (N), defined as the force that gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m s⁻². Third Law (Action–Reaction): For every force F₁₂ exerted by body 1 on body 2, there exists an equal‑in‑magnitude, opposite‑in‑direction force F₂₁ exerted by body 2 on body 1: F₁₂ = –F₂₁. These forces act on different bodies, so they never cancel for a single free‑body diagram. Together the three laws allow us to construct free‑body diagrams, write equations of motion, and predict the trajectory of any system of particles provided all forces are known.
steps: Newton’s three laws form the complete logical framework that predicts how any object changes its motion when forces act on it. First supporting argument – the first law defines the arena.
An inertial frame is one in which a free particle (no net force) moves with constant velocity.
In a moving train that suddenly brakes, a standing passenger lurches forward because the train’s frame becomes non‑inertial; the passenger’s inertia keeps him moving at the original velocity.

This everyday Indian railway experience illustrates why we must identify the correct reference frame before applying the second law. Second supporting argument – the second law quantifies the interaction.
Force is not a vague “push”; it is the agent that changes momentum.

For a constant‑mass cricket ball of 0.16 kg bowled at 30 m s⁻¹, the bowler’s hand exerts an average force of about 80 N over 0.06 s, giving an impulse of 4.8 N s and a momentum change of 4.8 kg m s⁻¹.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “an object at rest stays at rest unless a force acts on it”) reveals the misconception that the law only applies to stationary objects, ignoring uniform motion and the vector nature of velocity.
remember: State Newton’s first law of motion in vector form and name the type of reference frame it defines.
A passenger in a bus moving at constant speed suddenly lurches forward when the driver applies….
Evaluate the statement: “If the net force on an object is zero, the object must be at rest.”.

cards.title: Inertia is the intrinsic property of matter that resists any change in its…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Inertia is the intrinsic property of matter that resists any change in its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line. It is quantitatively measured by mass (symbol m, SI unit kilogram kg). Newton’s first law formally states this property: a body remains at rest or in uniform motion unless acted upon by a net external force. Inertia manifests in three forms: inertia of rest (resistance to starting motion), inertia of motion (resistance to stopping or changing speed), and inertia of direction (resistance to changing direction). Because inertia is a scalar property, it has no direction; only its magnitude (mass) matters. A larger mass possesses greater inertia, requiring a larger force to produce the same acceleration (Newton’s second law, F = m a). Inertia is not a force — it does not cause motion but opposes changes in motion. It underpins the concept of momentum (p = m v) and is the reason why momentum is conserved in isolated systems. In the CISCE ISC curriculum, inertia is introduced after Newton’s three laws (node) and before momentum (node), providing the qualitative foundation for quantitative dynamics.
steps: Inertia is the inherent property of matter that resists any change in its state of rest or uniform motion, and it is quantitatively measured by mass.

First, inertia appears in three distinct forms: inertia of rest (a stationary object stays stationary), inertia of motion (a moving object keeps moving at constant speed), and inertia of direction (a moving object keeps…
Second, mass is the sole measure of inertia; a 10 kg stone has ten times the inertia of a 1 kg stone, so it needs ten times the force for the same acceleration.
Third, Newton’s first law is simply the formal statement of inertia — no net force means no change in velocity.
Fourth, inertia is not a force; it does not push or pull, it only describes how stubbornly matter holds onto its current motion.
Fifth, everyday Indian scenes illustrate each type: a book on a desk (rest), a rolling cricket ball on a pitch (motion), a passenger leaning sideways when a train turns (direction).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “inertia is a force measured in newtons”) reveals the misconception that inertia is an active push or pull rather than a passive property of mass.
remember: Define inertia and state its SI unit.
Explain why a heavier cricket ball is harder to stop than a lighter one when both move at the same speed.
A student says “Inertia is the force that keeps an object moving.” Evaluate this statement.

cards.title: Momentum (symbol p) is a vector quantity defined as the product of an object’s…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Momentum (symbol p) is a vector quantity defined as the product of an object’s mass m (kilogram) and its velocity v (metre per second): p = m v. Its direction is the same as the velocity vector. The SI unit is kilogram‑metre per second (kg·m s⁻¹). Momentum quantifies the resistance of a body to a change in its motion; a larger momentum means a larger force or a longer time is required to bring the body to rest. It is directly linked to Newton’s second law: the net external force on a body equals the rate of change of its momentum (F = dp/dt). Unlike kinetic energy (a scalar), momentum adds vectorially, so the total momentum of a system is the vector sum of individual momenta. This concept bridges inertia (mass) and motion (velocity) and is the precursor to impulse (change in momentum) and the law of conservation of momentum for isolated systems.
steps: Momentum is the product of an object's mass and its velocity, a vector quantity that quantifies how difficult it is to stop a moving body.
Here is why: first, momentum inherits direction from velocity, so two identical balls moving opposite ways have momenta that cancel when added vectorially.

Second, Newton’s second law in its original form states that force equals the rate of change of momentum, not merely mass times acceleration; this form remains valid even when mass varies (e.g., rockets).
Third, the SI unit kg·m s⁻¹ directly reflects the multiplication of kg and m s⁻¹, making dimensional checks straightforward.

Fourth, everyday Indian examples clarify the concept: a 5 kg sack of rice sliding at 2 m s⁻¹ has the same momentum as a 0.5 kg cricket ball bowled at 20 m s⁻¹ (both 10 kg·m s⁻¹), yet the ball’s higher speed makes it…
Fifth, a common exam trap is treating momentum as a scalar; students must always resolve velocities into components before adding momenta.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “momentum is measured in newtons”) reveals the misconception that momentum and force share units, confusing the rate of change of momentum (force) with momentum itself.
remember: Define momentum and state its SI unit.
A 1500 kg car moves at 20 m s⁻¹ east. A 1000 kg truck moves at 15 m s⁻¹ west. Which has greater magnitude of momentum? Show the calculation.
Evaluate the statement: “Momentum is always conserved in any collision.”.

cards.title: Impulse (symbol I) is the integral of the net force F acting on a body over the…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Impulse (symbol I) is the integral of the net force F acting on a body over the time interval Δt during which the force acts: I = ∫ F dt. It is a vector quantity, directed along the net force. The SI unit of impulse is the newton‑second (N·s), which is dimensionally equivalent to kilogram‑metre per second (kg·m/s). From Newton’s second law, F = dp/dt, where p = mv is linear momentum. Integrating both sides over the same interval gives ∫ F dt = Δp, so impulse equals the change in momentum of the body. For a constant force, I = F Δt = m Δv. Graphically, impulse is the area under the force‑time curve. Impulse connects the dynamical concept of force (a rate) with the kinematic concept of momentum (a state), and it is the foundation for analysing collisions, rocket propulsion, and safety devices such as airbags and helmets.
steps: Impulse is the measure of the total effect of a force acting over a time interval, and it equals the change in momentum of the body.
Here is why: (1) Newton’s second law states F = dp/dt; integrating over time converts the instantaneous rate into a finite change.
(2) The integral ∫ F dt is exactly the area under the force‑time graph, making impulse a geometric quantity that can be found even when force varies.
(3) Because Δp = mΔv for constant mass, impulse directly tells us how much the velocity changes, regardless of how the force varied during the interval.
(4) The vector nature of impulse means direction matters; a force that reverses direction produces a negative impulse relative to the initial motion.
(5) Practical safety devices exploit the inverse relationship F_avg = I/Δt: for a fixed impulse (fixed momentum change), lengthening Δt reduces the average force.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “impulse is the same as force”) reveals the misconception that impulse and force are interchangeable, confusing a rate (force) with its accumulated effect (impulse).
remember: Define impulse and state its SI unit.
A constant force of 10 N acts on a 2 kg body initially at rest for 3 s. Calculate the impulse delivered and the final velocity of the body.
Two forces produce the same impulse on a 1 kg mass: Force A = 5 N for 4 s, Force B = 20 N for 1 s. Which force causes the greater acceleration? Explain.

cards.title: Conservation of linear momentum states that for an isolated system…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Conservation of linear momentum states that for an isolated system — one on which no net external force acts — the vector sum of the momenta of all constituent particles remains constant in time. Mathematically, Σ p_initial = Σ p_final, where p = m v for each particle. This principle follows directly from Newton’s third law (action–reaction pairs are equal and opposite) and the second law (F = dp/dt); internal forces cancel pairwise, leaving only external forces to change the total momentum. Momentum is a vector quantity (SI unit kg·m·s⁻¹), so direction must be accounted for in one‑dimensional and multi‑dimensional problems. The law applies to collisions (elastic and inelastic), explosions, recoil, and any interaction where the system can be treated as isolated. It is closely linked to the impulse–momentum theorem (Δp = J) covered in the previous node: when the net external impulse is zero, the total momentum change is zero. In the ISC curriculum, the law is used to solve one‑dimensional collision problems, to analyse rocket propulsion, and to understand why friction (an external force) breaks momentum conservation unless the Earth is included in the system.
steps: In any isolated system, the total linear momentum remains constant before and after an interaction.
Here is why: (1) Newton’s third law guarantees that every internal force has an equal and opposite counterpart, so the vector sum of internal forces is zero.
(2) Newton’s second law in momentum form (F_net = dp/dt) then gives dp_total/dt = 0 when F_net,external = 0, so p_total is constant.
(3) Because momentum is a vector, the conservation equation must be applied component‑wise; in one dimension this reduces to algebraic sums with signs for direction.
(4) The law holds for all types of collisions — elastic, inelastic, perfectly inelastic — and for explosions where internal forces push fragments apart.
(5) If external forces such as friction or air resistance act, the system is not isolated; momentum changes by the external impulse.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “momentum is conserved in every collision”) reveals the misconception that momentum conservation is universal, ignoring the requirement of zero external force.
remember: State the law of conservation of linear momentum for an isolated system.
Explain why momentum is conserved in a collision between two billiard balls on a frictionless table.
A student says momentum is conserved in a car crash even though the cars deform. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Static friction (fₛ) is the resistive force that acts between two solid…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Static friction (fₛ) is the resistive force that acts between two solid surfaces in contact when there is no relative motion between them. It is a self‑adjusting force: its magnitude equals the applied tangential force F up to a maximum value fₛ(max) = μₛ N, where μₛ (coefficient of static friction) is a dimensionless constant depending only on the nature of the two surfaces, and N is the normal reaction force (perpendicular to the contact plane). The direction of static friction is always opposite to the impending motion (the direction the object would move if friction were absent). Key relationships: - fₛ ≤ μₛ N (inequality holds while the body remains at rest). - At the point of impending motion, fₛ = μₛ N (limiting static friction). - Once motion starts, static friction ceases and kinetic friction (fₖ = μₖ N, with μₖ < μₛ) takes over (covered in node). Static friction does no work because the point of application does not move relative to the surface. It is essential for equilibrium analysis in Newton’s first and second laws (nodes,) and for solving problems involving inclined planes, horizontal pulls, and systems on the verge of slipping.
steps: Static friction is a self‑adjusting force that prevents relative motion up to a maximum value μₛN, and its direction always opposes the impending motion.
Here is why: 1.
Self‑adjusting nature – When you push a block gently, the block stays still because static friction grows exactly to match your push.
If you push with 2 N, static friction is 2 N opposite to your push; with 5 N, it becomes 5 N. This continues until the push reaches the limiting value μₛN. 2.
Limiting value depends only on surfaces and normal force – μₛ is a property of the two materials (e.g., rubber on dry concrete ≈ 0.9, wood on wood ≈ 0.4).
The normal force N equals mg on a horizontal surface, or mg cosθ on an incline.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “fₛ = μₛN always”) reveals the misconception that static friction is always at its maximum, confusing it with kinetic friction which has a fixed magnitude μₖN.
remember: State the mathematical condition that static friction must satisfy for a body at rest on a rough horizontal surface.
A block of mass 5 kg rests on a rough horizontal table (μₛ =….
Evaluate the statement: “On an inclined plane, the coefficient of static friction can be found by measuring the angle at which the block just begins to slide.”.

cards.title: Kinetic friction (also called sliding friction) is the resistive force that…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Kinetic friction (also called sliding friction) is the resistive force that acts between two solid surfaces in relative motion. Its magnitude is given by f_k = μ_k N, where μ_k is the coefficient of kinetic friction (dimensionless) and N is the normal reaction force (newton, N). Unlike static friction, kinetic friction is essentially constant for a given pair of surfaces and does not vary with the applied force once motion has started. It always acts opposite to the direction of velocity of the moving body relative to the surface. The work done by kinetic friction is negative, converting mechanical energy into thermal energy. The coefficient μ_k is typically smaller than the corresponding static coefficient μ_s for the same materials, reflecting the fact that it is easier to keep an object moving than to start it. Kinetic friction is independent of the contact area (for rigid bodies) and of the sliding speed (within ordinary ranges). It plays a central role in dynamics problems involving blocks on rough planes, braking distances, and energy dissipation in machines.
steps: Kinetic friction is a constant‑magnitude force that always opposes the relative motion of two sliding surfaces.
Here is why: once motion begins, the microscopic interlocking of surface asperities is continuously broken and reformed, producing a steady resistive force proportional to the normal load.
Consider a block of mass m on a rough horizontal table.
The forces acting are weight mg downward, normal reaction N = mg upward, an applied horizontal push F, and kinetic friction f_k = μ_k N opposite to the velocity.
Applying Newton’s second law horizontally gives F - f_k = ma. If the block moves with constant velocity, F = f_k and the net force is zero.
On an inclined plane of angle θ, the normal force becomes N = mg θ and the component of weight down the plane is mg θ.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., writing f_k = μ_s N or omitting the normal force) reveals the misconception that static and kinetic friction share the same coefficient or that friction is independent of the normal load.
remember: State the formula for kinetic friction and name each symbol with its SI unit.
A 5 kg block slides on a horizontal rough surface with μ_k = 0.3. If a horizontal force of 20 N is applied, what is the block’s acceleration? (Take g = 9.8\ m/s^2.).
Evaluate the statement: “Kinetic friction does no work because the point of contact does not move relative to the surface.”.

cards.title: Rolling friction (rolling resistance) is the resistive force that opposes the…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Rolling friction (rolling resistance) is the resistive force that opposes the motion of a body rolling without slipping over a surface. It arises from microscopic deformations of the rolling body and the surface at the contact patch, causing a net torque opposite to the direction of rolling. The magnitude of the rolling friction force F_r is given by F_r = μ_r N, where μ_r is the coefficient of rolling friction (dimensionless) and N is the normal reaction. Unlike static or kinetic friction, μ_r is typically two orders of magnitude smaller (e.g., 10^-3–10^-2 for steel on steel). Rolling friction does no work in the ideal rigid‑body limit, but real materials dissipate energy as heat due to hysteresis losses. It is distinct from static friction (which prevents slipping) and kinetic friction (which acts during sliding). The rolling resistance torque about the centre is τ_r = F_r R for a wheel of radius R. In dynamics, rolling friction appears as a constant decelerating force F_r opposing translational motion, and as a resistive torque opposing rotation.
steps: Rolling friction is a resistive force proportional to the normal load, with a coefficient typically 100‑times smaller than kinetic friction.

Here is why: when a wheel rolls, the contact patch continuously forms and breaks; the leading edge compresses the surface while the trailing edge recovers, but the recovery is incomplete due to material hysteresis…
Consider a solid cylinder of mass m and radius R on a horizontal floor.

The normal force N = mg. The rolling resistance force is F_r = μ_r mg. This force acts at the contact point, opposite to the direction of motion, causing a translational deceleration a = F_r/m = μ_r g and a resistive…
The net acceleration down the plane becomes a = g( θ - μ_r θ).
A common exam trap: students confuse rolling friction with static friction and write f_s = μ_s N in the rolling equation.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., F_r = μ_k N) reveals the misconception that rolling friction uses the kinetic friction coefficient — confusing sliding resistance with rolling resistance.
remember: State the formula for rolling friction force and name each symbol with its SI unit.
Why is the coefficient of rolling friction typically two orders of magnitude smaller than the coefficient of kinetic friction for the same pair of materials.
Evaluate the statement: “Rolling friction is independent of the radius of the rolling body.”.

cards.title: Dynamics of circular motion deals with the forces that cause a particle to…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Dynamics of circular motion deals with the forces that cause a particle to follow a circular path. For uniform circular motion the speed is constant but the velocity vector changes direction continuously; therefore a centripetal acceleration a_c = v²/r = ω²r directed radially inward exists. By Newton’s second law, a net centripetal force F_c = m a_c = m v²/r = m ω²r must act on the body. This force is not a new fundamental force; it is the resultant of real forces such as tension, friction, normal reaction, or gravitational attraction, resolved toward the centre. In non‑uniform circular motion a tangential component of acceleration (and force) also appears, changing the speed. The banking of roads and railway tracks provides a component of normal reaction that supplies the required centripetal force without relying solely on friction. The angle of banking θ satisfies tan θ = v²/(rg) for ideal frictionless motion. All these relations connect the kinematic quantities (v, ω, r) with the dynamic quantities (F_c, a_c) and the applied forces.
steps: The essential takeaway: Any object moving in a circle must experience a net force directed toward the centre; this centripetal force equals mass times centripetal acceleration (m v²/r).
Here is why: 1.
Velocity changes direction — even at constant speed, the velocity vector rotates, producing an acceleration toward the centre. 2.
Newton’s second law demands a force — the inward acceleration requires an inward net force, which we call centripetal force. 3.
Real forces supply it — tension in a string, friction between tyres and road, normal reaction on a banked track, or gravity for satellites. 4.
Banking reduces reliance on friction — the normal reaction’s horizontal component provides the centripetal force; the vertical component balances weight. 5.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., a_c = v/r) reveals the misconception that acceleration equals speed divided by radius, confusing the dimensions of acceleration (m/s²) with those of angular speed (1/s).
remember: State the expression for centripetal acceleration of a particle moving uniformly in a circle of radius r with speed v.
A car of mass 1200 kg travels at 20 m/s on a flat circular track of radius 50 m. What is the minimum coefficient of static friction required to prevent skidding.
Evaluate the statement: “In a banked turn, the normal reaction alone provides the centripetal force; friction is never needed.”.

cards.title: Work done by a force is a scalar quantity defined as the dot product of the…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Work done by a force is a scalar quantity defined as the dot product of the force vector F and the displacement vector s of the point of application of the force. Mathematically, W = F · s = F s θ, where F is the magnitude of the force, s is the magnitude of the displacement, and θ is the angle between the force and displacement directions. The SI unit of work is the joule (J), equivalent to one newton‑metre (N·m). Work can be positive (force component along displacement), negative (force component opposite displacement), or zero (force perpendicular to displacement or no displacement). When multiple forces act, the total work is the algebraic sum of the work done by each force. Work is the mechanism by which energy is transferred between a system and its surroundings; it links directly to kinetic energy through the work‑energy theorem (covered in the next node) and to potential energy when conservative forces (e.g., gravity, spring) do work. The concept of work done by a variable force requires integration: W = F · ds. This node focuses on constant forces and the geometric interpretation of the dot product; variable‑force integration is reserved for later chapters.
steps: The one thing to remember: Work is the scalar product of force and displacement, so only the component of force along the displacement contributes.
Here is why: 1.
Force and displacement are vectors — they have magnitude and direction.
The dot product extracts the parallel component, automatically handling angle dependence. 2.

Sign of work tells energy flow — positive work adds energy to the object (e.g., pushing a cart forward), negative work removes energy (e.g., friction opposing motion), zero work means no energy transfer via that force…
Units unify mechanics — one joule = one newton‑metre, linking force (N) and distance (m) directly to energy. 4.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “Work is force times distance, unit newton”) reveals the misconception that work is a vector or that the angle between force and displacement can be ignored — confusing the scalar dot product with simple multiplication of magnitudes.
