remember: Define work done by a constant force and state its SI unit.
A 10 N force acts on a block that moves 5 m in a direction 30° away from the force. Is the work done positive, negative, or zero? Explain.
A student claims: “If a force acts on an object but the object does not move, the force still does work because effort is exerted.” Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Kinetic energy (K) is the energy a body possesses by virtue of its motion.
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Kinetic energy (K) is the energy a body possesses by virtue of its motion. For a particle of mass m moving with speed v, K = ½ m v². It is a scalar quantity; its SI unit is the joule (J = kg·m²·s⁻²). Potential energy (U) is the energy stored in a system due to the configuration of its parts in a force field. Two common forms in Class 11 are gravitational potential energy (U_g) and elastic potential energy (U_s). Near Earth’s surface, U_g = m g h, where g ≈ 9.8 m·s⁻² and h is height above a chosen reference level. For an ideal spring obeying Hooke’s law, U_s = ½ k x², where k is the spring constant (N·m⁻¹) and x is the extension or compression from natural length. Both kinetic and potential energies are measured in joules. They are interconvertible in isolated systems, a concept formalised in the work‑energy theorem and conservation of mechanical energy (covered in later nodes). The zero of potential energy is arbitrary; only differences matter. Kinetic energy depends on the square of speed, so doubling speed quadruples kinetic energy. Potential energy depends linearly on height (gravitational) or quadratically on displacement (elastic).
steps: The one thing to remember: kinetic energy depends on the square of speed, while gravitational potential energy depends linearly on height and elastic potential energy depends on the square of displacement — all are…
Here is why: kinetic energy quantifies how much work a moving object can do by virtue of its motion; the ½ mv² form emerges from integrating force over distance (covered in the work node).

Gravitational potential energy measures the work gravity can do when an object falls; choosing a reference level (ground, table top) sets U_g = 0 there, but only differences ΔU_g = mgΔh are physically observable.
Elastic potential energy stores work done in stretching or compressing a spring; the quadratic dependence on x follows from Hooke’s law (F = kx) and the work integral.
Consider a 0.5 kg ball thrown upward at 20 m·s⁻¹.

Its initial kinetic energy is ½ × 0.5 × 20² = 100 J. At the top of its flight, speed is zero, so kinetic energy is 0 J. If we set the launch point as h = 0, the gravitational potential energy at the top equals the…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “kinetic energy unit is newton”) reveals the misconception that force and energy share units — confusing force (N = kg·m·s⁻²) with energy (J = N·m).
remember: Define kinetic energy and state its SI unit.
Two objects have the same kinetic energy. Object A has mass 2 kg, object B has mass 8 kg. Which object has the greater speed, and by what factor.
A student says, “Gravitational potential energy is always positive because height is positive.” Evaluate this statement.

cards.title: The work‑energy theorem links the mechanical concept of work to the kinetic…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The work‑energy theorem links the mechanical concept of work to the kinetic energy of a particle. For a body of mass m moving along a straight line, the net work W<sub>net</sub> done by all forces acting on it during a displacement equals the change in its kinetic energy ΔK: W_net = Δ K = K_f - K_i = 12 m v_f^2 - 12 m v_i^2 W<sub>net</sub> is measured in joules (J), m in kilograms (kg), and the initial and final speeds v<sub>i</sub>, v<sub>f</sub> in metres per second (m/s). The theorem holds for any force profile – constant, variable, or even forces that do negative work (e.g., friction). It follows directly from Newton’s second law (F = ma) after integrating F·dx over the path. While kinetic energy depends only on speed, the theorem tells us that only the net work (the algebraic sum of works by individual forces) can change that speed; internal forces cancel out. Thus the work‑energy theorem provides a powerful shortcut: instead of solving F = ma for acceleration and then integrating to find velocity, we can equate total work to the kinetic‑energy change directly.
steps: The net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy.

Here is why: starting from Newton’s second law for a particle of mass m moving along the x‑axis, F<sub>net</sub> = m a. Multiply both sides by the infinitesimal displacement dx and integrate from the initial position…
Because a = dv/dt and dx = v dt, the right‑hand side becomes _t_i^t_f m v (dv)/(dt)\,dt = _v_i^v_f m v\,dv = 12 m v_f^2 - 12 m v_i^2.
The left‑hand side is, by definition, the work done by the net force: W<sub>net</sub> = ∫F<sub>net</sub>dx.
Hence W<sub>net</sub> = ΔK.
Supporting arguments 1.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “W = Fd is the work‑energy theorem”) reveals the misconception that the theorem reduces to the simple constant‑force formula, ignoring that net work must include the algebraic sum of works by all forces and that the theorem holds for any…
remember: State the work‑energy theorem and give the SI unit of each quantity involved.
Explain why the work done by internal forces does not appear in the work‑energy theorem for a system of particles.
A student claims that if the net work on an object is zero, its speed must remain unchanged. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Conservation of mechanical energy states that for an isolated system acted upon…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Conservation of mechanical energy states that for an isolated system acted upon only by conservative forces (gravity, spring force, electrostatic force), the total mechanical energy E = K + U remains constant with time. Here K = (1)/(2)mv^2 is kinetic energy (SI unit joule, J) and U is potential energy (gravitational U_g=mgh or elastic U_s=(1)/(2)kx^2, also in joule). The principle follows directly from the work‑energy theorem: the net work done by conservative forces equals the negative change in potential energy, W_c = -Δ U. Since W_net = Δ K and W_net=W_c when non‑conservative forces are absent, Δ K = -Δ U or Δ(K+U)=0. Thus K_i+U_i=K_f+U_f. The theorem applies only when dissipative forces (friction, air resistance) do zero work; otherwise mechanical energy decreases by the amount of work done by non‑conservative forces.
steps: Mechanical energy of an isolated system acted on only by conservative forces never changes; it merely transforms between kinetic and potential forms.
Here is why: the work‑energy theorem tells us that the net work on a body equals its change in kinetic energy.
When every force doing work is conservative, each force can be associated with a potential energy function such that the work done by that force equals the negative change in its potential energy.
Summing over all conservative forces gives W_net= -Δ U. Equating the two expressions for net work yields Δ K = -Δ U, or Δ(K+U)=0.
Therefore the total mechanical energy E=K+U is invariant.
Consider a 2 kg block released from rest at the top of a smooth 5 m high incline.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “mechanical energy is always conserved”) reveals the misconception that non‑conservative forces such as friction can be ignored in every situation; students forget the explicit requirement that dissipative forces must do zero work.
remember: State the principle of conservation of mechanical energy and the condition under which it holds.
A block slides down a rough inclined plane. Explain why mechanical energy is not conserved in this case.
A student claims that in a simple pendulum mechanical energy is conserved at all times. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: A collision in one dimension is an interaction where two bodies exert equal and…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: A collision in one dimension is an interaction where two bodies exert equal and opposite forces on each other for a short time, changing their velocities while moving along a single straight line. The law of conservation of linear momentum states that, in the absence of external forces, the total momentum before impact equals the total momentum after impact: m_1u_1+m_2u_2=m_1v_1+m_2v_2, where m is mass (kg), u and v are initial and final velocities (m s⁻¹). The coefficient of restitution e quantifies the “bounciness’’: e= v_2-v_1u_1-u_2, dimensionless, with 0≤ e≤1. For a perfectly elastic collision e=1 and kinetic energy is also conserved; for an inelastic collision 0<e<1 some kinetic energy transforms into internal energy (heat, sound, deformation); for a perfectly inelastic collision e=0 the bodies stick together and move with a common velocity, giving the maximum kinetic‑energy loss. These concepts link directly to the work‑energy theorem (change in kinetic energy equals net work) and to the conservation of mechanical energy when e=1.
steps: In any one‑dimensional collision with no external forces, the total linear momentum of the system stays constant.
Here is why: 1.
Newton’s third law guarantees the forces the bodies exert on each other are equal and opposite, so the internal impulses cancel when summing over the system. 2.
The impulse‑momentum theorem (Δ p = J) applied to each body shows that the change in momentum of one body is exactly the negative of the change in the other, leaving the sum unchanged. 3.
Consequently, the algebraic sum m_1u_1+m_2u_2 equals m_1v_1+m_2v_2 regardless of the nature of the forces during impact.
Consider a carom striker (mass 0.05 kg) hitting a stationary coin (mass 0.005 kg) along the board’s frictionless surface.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “kinetic energy is conserved in every collision”) reveals the misconception that momentum and kinetic energy are interchangeable, ignoring that only momentum is guaranteed when external forces are absent.
remember: State the law of conservation of linear momentum for a two‑body one‑dimensional collision.
Explain why kinetic energy may decrease in an inelastic collision, mentioning the role of internal energy.
A 0.20 kg ball moving at 5.0 m s⁻¹ strikes a stationary 0.30 kg ball and they stick together. Determine the type of collision and compute the common speed after impact.

cards.title: Power is the rate at which work is done or energy is transferred.
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Power is the rate at which work is done or energy is transferred. The average power over a time interval Δt is defined as P_avg = (W)/(Δ t) where W is the work done. Instantaneous power is the time derivative of work: P = (dW)/(dt). For a constant force F acting on a body moving with instantaneous velocity v, the instantaneous power equals the dot product P = F · v = F v θ, where θ is the angle between force and velocity. The SI unit of power is the watt (W), equivalent to one joule per second (J s⁻¹). Power connects directly to the work‑energy theorem: the net work done on a particle equals its change in kinetic energy, so the rate of change of kinetic energy is the net power delivered. In conservative systems, power can also be expressed as the negative rate of change of potential energy. While work and energy are scalar quantities, power is also scalar but can be positive, negative, or zero depending on whether energy is being supplied to, removed from, or not transferred to the system. This node builds on the concepts of work (node 001), kinetic and potential energy (node 002), the work‑energy theorem (node 003), conservation of mechanical energy (node 004), and collisions in one dimension (node 005) to quantify how quickly energy transformations occur.
steps: Power is the measure of how quickly energy is transferred or work is performed — the one thing you must remember is that power equals the time derivative of work, P = dW/dt, and for a constant force it simplifies to P =…

The average power over a finite interval is simply total work divided by total time, P_avg = W/Δ t. When the force or velocity varies, we need instantaneous power, obtained by differentiating work with respect to time.
Because dW = F · dr and dr/dt = v, we get P = F · v. This formula is powerful: it lets you compute power directly from force and velocity vectors without integrating.

Consider a 50 kg student running up a 10 m high staircase in 8 s. The work against gravity is mgh = 50 × 9.8 × 10 = 4900 J. Average power = 4900 J / 8 s = 612.5 W. If the same student walks up in 20 s, average power…
An exam trap: students often confuse power with energy, writing “power = 4900 J” instead of watts.
Another trap: using the angle between force and displacement in P = Fv θ when the force is not parallel to velocity; the correct angle is between force and velocity vectors.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “power is the same as energy measured in joules”) reveals the misconception that power and energy are interchangeable — confusing a quantity with its rate of change.
remember: Define power and state its SI unit.
A machine does 500 J of work in 10 s. What is its average power? If the same work is done in 5 s, how does the average power change.
A student claims that a 100 W bulb uses 100 J of energy every minute. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: The centre of mass (CM) of a system of particles is the unique point whose…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The centre of mass (CM) of a system of particles is the unique point whose position vector R satisfies R = Σ_i=1^n m_i r_iΣ_i=1^n m_i where m_i is the mass of the i^th particle and r_i its position vector measured from an arbitrary origin. For a continuous body the sum becomes an integral: R = (1)/(M) r\,dm, M= dm The CM behaves as if the total mass M of the system were concentrated there and all external forces acted at that point. Internal forces cancel in pairs (Newton’s third law), so the motion of the CM depends only on the net external force: Ma_CM = Σ F_ext If the net external force is zero, the CM moves with constant velocity (or remains at rest). The CM of a uniform symmetric body coincides with its geometric centre; for irregular bodies it must be calculated. The concept links directly to the next nodes: motion of the CM (node 002), torque and angular momentum about the CM (node 003), and conservation laws (node 004).
steps: The centre of mass is the single point that represents the entire mass distribution of a system for translational motion.

Here is why: internal forces between particles occur in equal‑and‑opposite pairs, so their vector sum is zero; only external forces change the total momentum, and that change is exactly what a single particle of mass M…

Consider a system of three particles of masses 2 kg, 3 kg and 5 kg placed at coordinates (0,0), (4,0) and (0,3) m. The CM coordinates are x_CM=(2(0)+3(4)+5(0))/(10)=1.2 m, y_CM=(2(0)+3(0)+5(3))/(10)=1.5 m If a 10 N…
A common exam trap: students treat the CM of a composite body as the average of the individual CMs without weighting by mass — always weight by mass.
The CM concept is the foundation for analysing collisions, rocket propulsion, and rotational dynamics in the subsequent nodes.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “R = (Σ r_i)/(n)”) reveals the misconception that the CM is a simple arithmetic mean of positions, ignoring mass weighting.
remember: State the vector formula for the centre of mass of a system of n particles and name each symbol with its SI unit.
A uniform rod of length 1.2 m and mass 4 kg lies along the x‑axis from x=0 to x=1.2 m. A point mass of 2 kg is attached at x=1.2 m. Find the x‑coordinate of the centre of mass of….
Explain why the centre of mass of a system moves as if all external forces act on a single particle of total mass placed at the CM, even when internal forces are large.

cards.title: The motion of the centre of mass (CM) of a system of particles or a rigid body…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The motion of the centre of mass (CM) of a system of particles or a rigid body is governed solely by the net external force acting on the system. For a system of total mass M with particles of masses m_i at position vectors r_i, the CM position is R_CM = (1)/(M)Σ m_ir_i. Differentiating gives the CM velocity V_CM = (1)/(M)Σ m_iv_i = P_totalM where P_total is the total linear momentum. The CM acceleration is A_CM = F_extM, where F_ext is the vector sum of all external forces; internal forces cancel by Newton’s third law. Thus the CM follows a trajectory identical to a single particle of mass M subjected to F_ext. This principle holds for any rigid body, deformable body, or collection of particles, and is independent of internal motions such as rotation or vibration.
steps: The centre of mass of any system moves as if all its mass were concentrated there and only external forces acted on it. Here is why: the total momentum of a system is the vector sum of individual momenta…
Consider a fireworks rocket that splits into two fragments mid‑air.
The fragments fly in different directions, but the CM continues along the original parabolic path because gravity is the only external force.
First, write the CM position vector R_CM = (1)/(M)Σ m_ir_i.
Differentiate once: V_CM = (1)/(M)Σ m_iv_i = P_totalM.
Differentiate again: A_CM = (1)/(M)Σ m_ia_i = F_extM.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., V_CM = (Σ v_i)/(N)) reveals the misconception that CM velocity is a simple arithmetic mean of velocities, ignoring mass weighting.
remember: State the expression for the velocity of the centre of mass of a system of particles in terms of total momentum and total mass.
A system of two particles of masses 2 kg and 3 kg moves with velocities 4i m/s and -2i m/s respectively. Calculate the velocity of the centre of mass.
Evaluate the statement: “If the net external force on a system is zero, the centre of mass must be at rest.”.

cards.title: Torque (τ) is the rotational analogue of force.
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Torque (τ) is the rotational analogue of force. For a particle at position vector r (measured from a chosen origin) acted upon by a force F, torque is defined as the vector cross product τ = r × F. Its magnitude is τ = r F sin θ, where θ is the angle between r and F. The SI unit is newton‑metre (N·m). Torque is a vector; its direction follows the right‑hand rule and is perpendicular to the plane formed by r and F. Angular momentum (L) of a particle about the same origin is L = r × p, where p = m v is the linear momentum. For a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis, L = I ω, where I is the moment of inertia about that axis and ω is the angular velocity vector. The SI unit of angular momentum is kilogram‑metre² per second (kg·m²·s⁻¹). The time derivative of angular momentum equals the net external torque: dL/dt = τ_ext. This is the rotational form of Newton’s second law. When the net external torque about a point (or axis) is zero, the total angular momentum about that point (or axis) is conserved. Torque and angular momentum are linked through the work‑energy theorem for rotation: the work done by a torque equals the change in rotational kinetic energy (½ I ω²). The concepts of centre of mass (node) and motion of centre of mass (node) provide the reference point for defining r and for separating translational and rotational motion. Moment of inertia (node) and radius of gyration (node) quantify how mass distribution affects L and τ. Rotational motion equations (node) give the kinematic relations among θ, ω, α, and t under constant angular acceleration.
steps: Torque and angular momentum are the rotational counterparts of force and linear momentum, and they obey the same cause‑effect structure: net torque changes angular momentum just as net force changes linear momentum.
Here is why: consider a particle of mass m moving in a plane.

Choose an origin O. The particle’s position vector is r, its velocity v, and its linear momentum p = m v. If a force F acts, the torque about O is τ = r × F. Taking the time derivative of L = r × p gives dL/dt = (dr/dt)…
The first term vanishes because v and p are parallel.
Thus the rate of change of angular momentum equals the applied torque — the exact rotational analogue of F = dp/dt.
Now extend to a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis (say the z‑axis).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “torque = force × distance” without the sine of the angle) reveals the misconception that torque is simply the product of force magnitude and distance, ignoring the directional nature and the angle between r and F.
remember: Define torque and state its SI unit.
A force F = (3 i + 4 j) N acts at a point with position vector r = (2 i – 1 j) m relative to the origin. Calculate the torque about the origin.
A uniform rod of mass 2 kg and length 1 m rotates about one end with angular velocity 4 rad/s. Compute its angular momentum about the rotation axis.

cards.title: Conservation laws for a system of particles or a rigid body state that certain…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Conservation laws for a system of particles or a rigid body state that certain total quantities remain constant when specific external influences are absent. Linear momentum p = Σ m_i v_i of the centre of mass is conserved when the net external force F_ext = 0. Angular momentum L = Σ r_i × p_i about a fixed point or axis is conserved when the net external torque τ_ext = 0. For a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis, L = Iω where I is the moment of inertia and ω the angular velocity. The two conservation principles are independent: a system may conserve linear momentum while angular momentum changes (if external torque acts) and vice‑versa. Internal forces and torques always occur in equal‑and‑opposite pairs (Newton’s third law) and therefore cannot alter the total momentum of the system. These laws connect directly to the earlier nodes: centre‑of‑mass motion (node 002) follows from linear‑momentum conservation; torque and angular momentum definitions (node 003) provide the dynamical variables whose constancy is now asserted. The next node (005) will supply the moment‑of‑inertia values needed to apply L = Iω in quantitative problems.
steps: The total angular momentum of an isolated system never changes; it can only be redistributed among its parts.
Here is why: (1) Torque is the rotational analogue of force, and angular momentum is the rotational analogue of linear momentum.

(2) Newton’s third law guarantees that internal torques cancel pairwise, so only external torques can change the system’s total L. (3) When τ_ext=0, the time derivative dL/dt = τ_ext vanishes, making L constant.
(4) For a rigid body about a fixed axis, L=Iω; if the body’s mass distribution changes (e.g., a skater pulling arms in), I changes and ω must adjust to keep L constant.
(5) The same logic applies to linear momentum: F_ext=0 ⇒ dp/dt=0.
Consider a classic Indian playground example: a child sits on a freely rotating merry‑go‑round holding two heavy bags.
remember: State the condition for conservation of angular momentum of a system.
A figure skater spins with arms extended, then pulls them in. Explain why her angular speed increases using conservation of angular momentum.
A student claims that linear momentum of a system is always conserved in any collision. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Moment of inertia (symbol I, SI unit kg·m^2) quantifies a rigid body’s…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Moment of inertia (symbol I, SI unit kg·m^2) quantifies a rigid body’s resistance to angular acceleration about a given axis. For a system of point masses m_i at perpendicular distances r_i from the axis, I = Σ_i m_i r_i^2. For a continuous mass distribution, I = r^2 \, dm, where r is the perpendicular distance of the mass element dm from the axis. It depends on both the total mass and its spatial distribution relative to the axis; the same mass shaped as a thin ring has larger I than a solid disc of equal mass and radius. Moment of inertia links torque τ and angular acceleration α through τ = Iα, analogous to F = ma in linear motion. It also appears in rotational kinetic energy K = 12 Iω^2 and angular momentum L = Iω. The concept extends the centre‑of‑mass framework (node) and the torque‑angular‑momentum relationship (node) by providing the rotational inertia term needed for dynamics of rotating systems.
steps: The moment of inertia is the rotational analogue of mass — it tells how much torque is needed for a given angular acceleration.
Here is why: mass resists linear acceleration; distributed mass resists angular acceleration in proportion to the square of its distance from the axis.
First, consider a point mass m on a light rod of length r rotating about the other end. Its I = mr^2.
If we double the distance, I quadruples, showing the r^2 dependence.

Second, for a continuous body we slice it into mass elements dm; each contributes r^2 dm. Integrating over the whole body yields the total I. Third, standard shapes are derived once and memorised: a thin ring of mass M…
Fourth, these formulas let us solve dynamics: a torque τ applied to a disc produces α = τ/I.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “kg·m” or “N·m”) reveals confusion between moment of inertia and torque or linear momentum, mixing up the physical quantities that share the same base units but different powers of length.
remember: State the SI unit of moment of inertia and write its dimensional formula.
A thin ring and a solid disc have the same mass M and radius R. Which has the larger moment of inertia about its central axis? Explain without calculation.
Evaluate the statement: “Moment of inertia is a scalar quantity, so it has no direction and is the same for any axis through the centre of mass.”.

cards.title: The radius of gyration, denoted by k…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The radius of gyration, denoted by k, is a geometric property that characterises the distribution of mass of a rigid body about a given axis of rotation. For a body of total mass M and moment of inertia I about that axis, the radius of gyration is defined by the relation I = M k^2, or equivalently k = √(I/M). Its SI unit is the metre (m). Unlike the centre of mass, which locates the average position of mass, the radius of gyration quantifies how far the mass is spread from the axis; a larger k indicates mass concentrated farther away, leading to a larger moment of inertia for the same mass. For a system of point masses, k = √(Σ m_i r_i^2 / Σ m_i), where r_i are perpendicular distances from the axis. For continuous bodies, the summation becomes an integral. The concept is directly linked to the moment of inertia (covered in node) and provides a single length scale that simplifies comparisons between different shapes. For example, a thin ring of radius R has k = R, while a solid disc of the same radius has k = R/√(2). The radius of gyration is independent of the body's orientation as long as the axis is fixed, and it is used in the rotational analogues of Newton's second law (node). It does not depend on the angular velocity or torque, only on mass geometry.
steps: The radius of gyration condenses the entire mass distribution of a rotating body into a single distance from the axis, such that a point mass placed at that distance would have the same moment of inertia as the actual…

First, it follows directly from the definition of moment of inertia I = Σ m_i r_i^2; by factoring out the total mass M = Σ m_i, we obtain I = M (Σ m_i r_i^2 / M) = M k^2, where k is the root-mean-square distance.
Second, k is independent of the angular speed or applied torque; it is a purely geometric property of the body and the chosen axis.

Third, for standard shapes the values are tabulated: a thin ring of radius R has k = R, a solid disc k = R/√(2), a solid sphere about a diameter k = √(2/5)\,R, and a thin rod about its centre k = L/√(12).

Fourth, knowing k allows quick comparison of rotational inertia without recalculating integrals; for instance, a flywheel designed with a large k stores more kinetic energy at a given angular velocity.
Fifth, in engineering practice, the radius of gyration of a structural column predicts its buckling resistance, linking rotational dynamics to civil design.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "k is the distance of the centre of mass from the axis") reveals the misconception that radius of gyration coincides with the centre-of-mass distance, confusing the first moment of mass with the second moment.
remember: State the definition of radius of gyration and its SI unit.
A solid cylinder and a thin cylindrical shell have the same mass and radius. Which has the larger radius of gyration about their common symmetry axis? Explain.
A student claims that the radius of gyration of a body about an axis through its centre of mass is always less than the body's largest physical….

cards.title: Rotational motion equations describe the kinematics and dynamics of a rigid…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Rotational motion equations describe the kinematics and dynamics of a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis under constant angular acceleration α. The primary kinematic relations are: ω = ω_0 + α t, θ = ω_0 t + 12 α t^2, ω^2 = ω_0^2 + 2αθ, where ω_0 and ω are initial and final angular velocities (rad s^-1), θ is angular displacement (rad), and t is time (s). The dynamic equation links torque τ (N m), moment of inertia I (kg m^2), and angular acceleration: τ = Iα. Angular momentum L = Iω (kg m^2 s^-1) is conserved when net external torque is zero. These equations connect directly to the centre‑of‑mass motion (node), torque and angular momentum (node), and moment of inertia (node) concepts already covered.
steps: The rotational kinematic equations are exact analogues of the linear equations v = u + at, s = ut + 12 at^2, v^2 = u^2 + 2as; replace linear quantities with their angular counterparts.
Here is why: angular velocity ω is the rate of change of angular displacement θ, just as velocity is the rate of change of linear displacement.
Angular acceleration α is the rate of change of ω.
Integrating α = dω/dt with constant α gives ω = ω_0 + α t. Integrating ω = dθ/dt yields θ = ω_0 t + 12 α t^2.
Eliminating t between the two gives ω^2 = ω_0^2 + 2αθ.
Consider a flywheel of moment of inertia I = 0.5\ kg m^2 initially at rest.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., writing v = u + at with linear symbols) reveals the misconception that rotational equations are merely a rename without checking units — students must recognise that θ is dimensionless (rad) but still carries the unit rad for clarity.
remember: State the three rotational kinematic equations for constant angular acceleration, identifying each symbol and its SI unit.
A wheel starts from rest and reaches an angular speed of 20\ rad s^-1 in 5\ s under constant angular….
Evaluate the statement: “If the net torque on a rotating body is zero, its angular velocity must be constant.” Provide a justification.

cards.title: Newton’s law of universal gravitation states that every point mass attracts…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Newton’s law of universal gravitation states that every point mass attracts every other point mass with a force acting along the line joining their centres. The magnitude of this force is directly proportional to the product of the two masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centres. Mathematically, F = G (m_1 m_2)/(r^2), where F is the gravitational force, m_1 and m_2 are the masses, r is the centre‑to‑centre separation, and G is the universal gravitational constant (6.67430 × 10^-11\,N·m^2/kg^2). The force is always attractive, obeys Newton’s third law (equal and opposite), and is a central force. For extended bodies, the law applies to each mass element; the net force can be found by integration, leading to the shell theorem (treated in later nodes). This law underpins the relation between g and G, the variation of g with altitude and latitude, gravitational field intensity, potential, escape velocity, satellite motion, and Kepler’s laws — each developed in subsequent concept nodes of this chapter.
steps: Newton’s law of universal gravitation asserts that every particle in the universe attracts every other particle with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the…
Here is why: first, the law is universal — it applies to a falling mango, the Earth‑Moon system, and distant galaxies alike.
Second, the inverse‑square dependence means that doubling the separation reduces the force to one‑quarter; this geometric dilution is the same reason light intensity falls off as 1/r^2.

Third, the force is a vector directed along the line joining the centres, so each mass pulls the other toward itself, satisfying Newton’s third law. Fourth, the constant G quantifies the strength of gravity; its small…
Consider two cricket balls of mass 0.16\,kg placed 0.1\,m apart: the force is only 1.7×10^-9\,N, far too small to feel.
Now imagine the Earth (mass 5.97×10^24\,kg) and a 1\,kg textbook at the surface (r=6.37×10^6\,m); the force computes to 9.8\,N, which we recognise as weight.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “F = G (m_1+m_2)/(r)”) reveals the misconception that force depends on the sum of masses and varies linearly with distance, confusing gravitational force with a simple additive model.
remember: State Newton’s law of universal gravitation in words and write its mathematical expression with all symbols defined.
Explain why the gravitational force between two 1 kg masses placed 1 m apart is extremely small, using the value of G.
A student claims that if the distance between two masses is halved, the gravitational force becomes half. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: The acceleration due to gravity g at a point near a massive body is the…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The acceleration due to gravity g at a point near a massive body is the gravitational force per unit mass experienced by a test mass placed at that point. From Newton’s law of universal gravitation, the force between two masses M (the planet) and m (test mass) separated by distance r is F = G M m/r², where G = 6.67430 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻² is the universal gravitational constant. Dividing the force by the test mass m gives the gravitational field intensity, which equals the acceleration g = G M/r². At Earth’s surface r = R (mean radius ≈ 6.371 × 10⁶ m), so g = G M/R². This relation links the local measurable quantity g (SI unit m s⁻²) to the universal constant G and the planetary parameters M (kg) and R (m). It also shows that g varies with altitude (r > R) and with latitude due to Earth’s rotation and oblateness, while G remains invariant. The derivation assumes a spherically symmetric mass distribution and neglects rotational effects; those refinements are treated in later nodes.
steps: The acceleration due to gravity g at a planet’s surface is directly proportional to the planet’s mass M and inversely proportional to the square of its radius R, with the universal constant G as the proportionality…
Here is why: Newton’s law gives the gravitational force F = G M m/r² on a test mass m at distance r from the planet’s centre.
By Newton’s second law, F = m g, so g = F/m = G M/r².
At the surface r = R, yielding g = G M/R².
This formula shows that if Earth’s mass doubled while its radius stayed the same, g would double; if Earth’s radius doubled with the same mass, g would fall to one‑quarter.
Consider an Indian satellite launch: the rocket must overcome g ≈ 9.8 m s⁻² at the launch pad, but at 400 km altitude g drops to about 8.7 m s⁻², reducing the required thrust.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., g = G M/R) reveals the misconception that gravitational acceleration follows an inverse‑first‑power law instead of the correct inverse‑square law.
remember: State the mathematical relation between acceleration due to gravity g and the universal gravitational constant G for a spherical planet of mass M and radius R.
Explain why the value of g decreases as you go higher above Earth’s surface, while G remains unchanged.
If Earth’s mass were doubled and its radius halved, by what factor would g at the surface change.

cards.title: The acceleration due to gravity g at a point near Earth’s surface is the…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The acceleration due to gravity g at a point near Earth’s surface is the gravitational force per unit mass experienced by a test mass placed at that point. Its standard value at sea level is g₀ = 9.80665 m s⁻². Variation of g arises from four main factors: 1. Altitude (height h above surface) – For h ≪ R (Earth’s radius), the inverse‑square law gives gₕ = g₀ (1 – 2h/R). The exact expression is gₕ = GM/(R+h)². 2. Depth (distance d below surface) – Assuming uniform density, only the mass inside radius (R–d) contributes, yielding g_d = g₀ (1 – d/R). Real Earth’s density increases inward, so the actual decrease is slower. 3. Latitude (φ) – Earth’s rotation produces a centrifugal acceleration ω²R cos²φ directed outward, reducing the effective g. Additionally, Earth’s equatorial bulge makes R larger at the equator, further lowering g there. The combined effect: g_eff(φ) = g₀ – ω²R cos²φ + (g_pole – g_equator) sin²φ (the last term accounts for shape). 4. Local geology – Density anomalies (mountains, ore bodies) cause small residuals (≈ 10⁻⁴ g₀) measured in gravimetry. These variations are measured with gravimeters and are essential for satellite orbit determination, geodesy and mineral exploration.
steps: The acceleration due to gravity g is not a universal constant; it varies with altitude, depth, latitude and local geology, and each variation follows directly from Newton’s inverse‑square law combined with Earth’s…
Here is why: 1.
Altitude – Newton’s law gives F = GMm/(R+h)².
Dividing by m yields gₕ = GM/(R+h)².
For h ≪ R, expand (1 + h/R)⁻² ≈ 1 – 2h/R (binomial theorem), giving the linear approximation gₕ ≈ g₀ (1 – 2h/R).
This shows g falls roughly 0.3 % per 100 km. 2.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., gₕ = g₀ (1 – h/R)) reveals the misconception that the inverse‑square dependence reduces to a single power of (1 + h/R) instead of the square.
remember: State the approximate formula for the variation of g with altitude h (h ≪ R) and name the mathematical approximation used.
Explain why g decreases with increasing altitude, referencing Newton’s law of universal gravitation.
A student claims that the value of g at the poles is exactly the same as at the equator. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Gravitational field intensity (often denoted E or g) at a point in space is…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Gravitational field intensity (often denoted E or g) at a point in space is defined as the gravitational force F experienced by a unit test mass m₀ placed at that point, provided the test mass does not disturb the original field. Mathematically, E = F / m₀. Its SI unit is newton per kilogram (N kg⁻¹), which is equivalent to metre per second squared (m s⁻²). For a point mass M, the field intensity at a distance r from its centre is E = GM / r², directed radially inward toward M. The field is a vector quantity; its direction is the direction of the force that would act on a positive test mass. The principle of superposition applies: the net field due to multiple masses is the vector sum of the individual fields. This concept links directly to the variation of g with altitude and depth (covered in the previous node) and provides the foundation for gravitational potential (next node), where the potential at a point is the work done per unit mass in bringing a test mass from infinity to that point against the field.
steps: The gravitational field intensity at any point is the force per unit mass that a small test mass would feel there — it quantifies the “pull” of gravity without needing a second massive object.
Here is why: the field concept lets us describe gravity as a property of space itself, not just a force between two bodies.
First, we place a test mass m₀ at the point of interest; the force F on it is measured (or calculated via Newton’s law).
Dividing by m₀ removes the test mass’s own influence, leaving a property of the source mass M and the geometry.

Second, for a point mass M, Newton’s law gives F = GMm₀ / r², so E = GM / r² directed toward M. Third, because the field obeys superposition, the net field from several masses is the vector sum of each GMᵢ / rᵢ²…
Fourth, the field lines for a point mass are radial straight lines pointing inward; their density represents magnitude — closer lines mean stronger field.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “field intensity is the force between two masses”) reveals the misconception that field intensity is a force rather than force per unit mass, confusing the field concept with Newton’s law of force.
remember: Define gravitational field intensity and state its SI unit.
A point mass M creates a gravitational field at a distance r. What is the direction of the field vector at that point? Justify.
Two identical point masses M are placed on the x‑axis at x = -a and x = +a. Evaluate the gravitational field intensity at the origin.

cards.title: Gravitational potential V at a point in a gravitational field is defined as the…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Gravitational potential V at a point in a gravitational field is defined as the work done per unit mass in bringing a test mass from infinity to that point without acceleration. It is a scalar quantity, negative because the field does positive work as the mass approaches the source. For a point mass M the potential at distance r is V = - GMr, where G is the universal gravitational constant. The potential difference between two points A and B is Δ V = V_B - V_A = -GM ( 1r_B - 1r_A ). The gravitational field intensity g is the negative gradient of the potential: g = - V. For a spherically symmetric body, g = GMr^2 and V = - GMr. Potential energy of a mass m placed at the point is U = mV. The zero of potential is conventionally taken at infinity. This node links the field concept (node) to energy concepts used in escape velocity (node) and satellite motion (node).
steps: The one thing to remember: Gravitational potential at a point is the negative of the work done by the field per unit mass in bringing a test mass from infinity to that point.
Here is why: 1.
Work‑energy foundation – From node we know the gravitational force on a test mass m at distance r from a source mass M is F = GMm/r^2 directed inward.
To move the mass quasi‑statically from infinity to r, an external agent must apply an equal and opposite force.
The work done by the agent is W_ext = _∞^r (GMm)/(r'^2)\,dr' = -(GMm)/(r).
Dividing by m gives the potential V = -GM/r. 2.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “newton per kilogram”) reveals the misconception that potential is a force per unit mass — confusing field intensity (g) with potential.
remember: State the SI unit of gravitational potential and write its dimensional formula.
Explain why gravitational potential is negative for a point mass, using the definition of work done by the field.
A student claims that the gravitational potential at the surface of a uniform solid sphere of mass M and radius R is -GM/R, but inside the sphere at r = R/2 it becomes….

cards.title: Escape velocity (vₑ) is the minimum initial speed required for an object at a…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Escape velocity (vₑ) is the minimum initial speed required for an object at a given distance from a massive body to overcome the gravitational attraction and reach an infinite distance with zero residual kinetic energy, assuming no other forces act. For a spherically symmetric body of mass M and radius R, the escape velocity from its surface is derived by equating the initial kinetic energy (½ mvₑ²) to the magnitude of the gravitational potential energy (GMm/R). This yields vₑ = √(2GM/R) = √(2gR), where g = GM/R² is the acceleration due to gravity at the surface. The concept links directly to gravitational potential (node) because the potential at the surface is –GM/R; the kinetic energy needed to bring the total mechanical energy to zero is exactly the magnitude of that potential energy per unit mass. Escape velocity is independent of the projectile’s mass and direction (provided the path does not intersect the body). It is a scalar speed, not a vector velocity. For Earth, vₑ ≈ 11.2 km/s; for the Moon, vₑ ≈ 2.38 km/s. The same formula applies at any distance r from the centre: vₑ(r) = √(2GM/r).
steps: The one thing to remember: Escape velocity is the speed that makes total mechanical energy exactly zero, so the object just barely escapes to infinity with zero kinetic energy left.
Here is why: 1.
Gravitational potential energy at distance r is U = –GMm/r.
At the surface (r = R) it is –GMm/R. 2.
Kinetic energy at launch is K = ½ mv².
For the object to reach infinity (where U = 0) with zero speed, the initial total energy E = K + U must be ≥ 0.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “heavier objects need more speed because they have more inertia”) reveals the misconception that inertia alone determines escape, neglecting that gravitational force also scales with mass.
remember: Define escape velocity and state its SI unit.
Explain why escape velocity is independent of the mass of the projectile.
If a planet’s mass is doubled and its radius is halved, by what factor does its surface escape velocity change.

cards.title: A satellite is any body that revolves around a larger body under the influence…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: A satellite is any body that revolves around a larger body under the influence of gravitational force. For an artificial satellite of mass m orbiting Earth (mass M, radius R) at a distance r from Earth’s centre ( r = R + h where h is altitude), the gravitational force provides the necessary centripetal force: GMmr^2 = mv^2r From this, the orbital speed v = √(GM/r), the orbital period T = 2π√(r³/GM), and the total mechanical energy E = –GMm/(2r). A geostationary satellite has T = 24 h and orbits in the equatorial plane at h ≈ 35 786 km. Natural satellites (e.g., the Moon) obey the same relations. The concepts of gravitational field intensity, potential, and escape velocity (covered in earlier nodes) are prerequisites for deriving these results.
steps: The single most important takeaway: For a satellite in a stable circular orbit, gravitational force exactly equals the required centripetal force, fixing its speed, period, and energy uniquely by the orbital radius.
Here is why: Newton showed that the same force pulling an apple down also keeps the Moon circling Earth.
Consider a satellite of mass m at distance r from Earth’s centre.
The gravitational pull is F_g = GMm/r².
To move in a circle of radius r with speed v, the satellite needs a centripetal force F_c = mv²/r.
Equating F_g = F_c gives v = √(GM/r) — the orbital speed depends only on r, not on m. From v = 2πr/T we obtain the period T = 2π√(r³/GM), which is Kepler’s third law for circular orbits.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., v = √(gR)) reveals the misconception that surface gravity g can be used directly without adjusting for orbital radius.
remember: State the expression for the orbital speed of a satellite in a circular orbit of radius r around Earth.
Explain why the orbital period of a satellite depends only on the orbital radius and not on the satellite’s mass.
A satellite orbits at an altitude of 800 km. Evaluate whether its total mechanical energy is positive, zero, or negative, and justify.

cards.title: Kepler’s laws describe the motion of planets (or any body) around a massive…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Kepler’s laws describe the motion of planets (or any body) around a massive central object under an inverse‑square gravitational force. First Law (Law of Ellipses): The orbit of a planet is an ellipse with the Sun at one focus. The semi‑major axis a defines the size of the orbit; the eccentricity e (0 ≤ e < 1) defines its shape. Second Law (Law of Equal Areas): A line joining the planet to the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal intervals of time. Consequently, the planet moves faster at perihelion (closest approach) and slower at aphelion (farthest point). Third Law (Law of Periods): The square of the orbital period T is proportional to the cube of the semi‑major axis a: T^2 = 4π^2GM\,a^3 where G is the universal gravitational constant and M is the mass of the central body. This law holds for any two bodies orbiting the same central mass, allowing the determination of M from observed T and a. The three laws together link geometry (ellipse), dynamics (area speed), and scaling (period–distance relation). They are empirical generalisations that Newton later derived from his law of universal gravitation and the laws of motion.
steps: Kepler’s three laws compress the entire architecture of planetary motion into three testable statements that any student can verify with a telescope and a clock.

Here is why: the first law replaces the ancient perfect circles with ellipses, placing the Sun at a focus rather than the centre; this geometric shift alone explains why planets appear to speed up and slow down.
The second law quantifies that speed change: the radius vector sweeps equal areas in equal times, a direct consequence of angular momentum conservation under a central force.
The third law provides a scaling rule — the period squared grows as the cube of the mean distance — which lets us weigh the Sun without ever leaving Earth.
Consider a planet of mass m moving in a circle of radius r around the Sun of mass M. The gravitational force F = GMmr^2 supplies the required centripetal force mv^2r.
Equating gives v^2 = (GM)/(r).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the Sun is at the centre of a circular orbit”) reveals the misconception that planetary orbits are perfect circles — confusing the historical Ptolemaic model with Kepler’s elliptical description.
remember: State Kepler’s first law and define the terms “focus” and “semi‑major axis” in the context of a planetary orbit.
Explain why a planet moves faster at perihelion than at aphelion using Kepler’s second law.
A student claims that Kepler’s third law can be written as T ∝ r^3/2 for any instantaneous distance r. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Stress is the internal restoring force per unit cross‑sectional area developed…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Stress is the internal restoring force per unit cross‑sectional area developed when a deforming force acts on a body. Its symbol is σ (sigma) and SI unit is pascal (Pa) = N m⁻². Strain is the ratio of change in dimension to the original dimension; it is dimensionless. For longitudinal deformation, tensile stress = F/A and longitudinal strain = ΔL/L. Within the elastic limit, stress is directly proportional to strain (Hooke’s law); the constant of proportionality is the modulus of elasticity (Young’s modulus for longitudinal stress, covered in the next node). The stress‑strain curve shows a linear elastic region, a yield point, plastic region, and fracture point. Types of stress: tensile, compressive, shear. Types of strain: longitudinal, volumetric, shear. The elastic limit is the maximum stress up to which the body regains its original shape on removal of load. Beyond this limit, permanent deformation occurs.
steps: Takeaway: Stress and strain are the two fundamental quantities that describe how a solid deforms under load; their ratio (within the elastic limit) defines the material’s stiffness.
Here is why: 1.
Stress quantifies the internal resistance – when you hang a weight on a wire, the wire’s atoms pull back with a force distributed over its cross‑section.
That distributed force is stress (σ = F/A). 2.
Strain quantifies the relative deformation – the same wire elongates by ΔL; the fractional change ΔL/L is strain (ε).
It has no unit because it is a ratio. 3.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “stress is force per unit length, unit N/m”) reveals the misconception that stress is a linear force density rather than an areal force density, confusing it with pressure gradient or line load.
remember: Define stress and state its SI unit.
A student says, “Strain has the same unit as stress because both are ratios.” Evaluate this statement.
A wire of length 1.5 m and cross‑sectional area 2 mm² is stretched by a force of 200 N. Calculate the stress and the strain if the elongation is 0.3 mm. Comment on whether the….

cards.title: Young’s modulus (Y) is the ratio of longitudinal stress to longitudinal strain…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Young’s modulus (Y) is the ratio of longitudinal stress to longitudinal strain within the elastic limit of a homogeneous, isotropic solid. Stress (σ) is the restoring force per unit cross‑sectional area (σ = F/A, SI unit pascal, Pa). Strain (ε) is the fractional change in length (ε = ΔL/L, dimensionless). Therefore Y = σ/ε = (F/A)/(ΔL/L) = FL/(AΔL). Its SI unit is also pascal (N m⁻²). A larger Y means the material is stiffer — it deforms less for a given stress. The concept links directly to the stress–strain curve: the initial linear region obeys Hooke’s law, and the slope of that line is Y. Young’s modulus is a material constant (for a given temperature) and is independent of the specimen’s dimensions. It is used to predict elongation in wires, rods, and structural members under tensile or compressive loads.
steps: The one thing to remember: Young’s modulus is the slope of the linear part of the stress–strain curve and quantifies a material’s stiffness.
Here is why: when a wire of original length L and cross‑section A is pulled by a force F, it extends by ΔL.
The stress σ = F/A measures how hard the material is pushed; the strain ε = ΔL/L measures how much it yields.
In the elastic region σ ∝ ε, so σ = Yε, giving Y = σ/ε = FL/(AΔL).
Consider a steel wire (Y ≈ 2×10¹¹ Pa) and a copper wire of same dimensions.
Hanging a 10 kg mass (≈98 N) produces a stress of 98 N/A.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “N m⁻¹” or “kg m⁻¹ s⁻²”) reveals the misconception that strain carries units or that modulus is a force per length rather than force per area.
remember: State the SI unit of Young’s modulus and write its dimensional formula.
A student claims that a thicker wire of the same material and length will have a larger Young’s modulus. Evaluate this claim.
Given a stress–strain graph for a metal wire, the linear portion passes through (0,0) and (2×10⁸ Pa….

cards.title: Pressure (symbol P) is the normal force F exerted per unit area A of a surface…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Pressure (symbol P) is the normal force F exerted per unit area A of a surface: P = F/A. Its SI unit is the pascal (Pa), where 1 Pa = 1 N m⁻². In a fluid at rest, pressure acts equally in all directions (Pascal’s law) and increases with depth due to the weight of the fluid column above. The hydrostatic pressure at depth h in a fluid of density ρ under gravity g is P = P₀ + ρgh, where P₀ is the pressure at the free surface (often atmospheric pressure). Pressure is a scalar; it has magnitude but no direction, unlike force. The concept links to stress in solids (covered in the elastic behaviour nodes) and underpins viscosity, surface tension, and Bernoulli’s theorem later in this chapter.
steps: Pressure in a fluid at rest is the same in every direction at a given depth and grows linearly with depth because of the weight of the fluid above.
Here is why: a fluid cannot sustain shear stress, so any element experiences only normal forces.
Consider a small cubic element of fluid at depth h. The forces on its top and bottom faces differ by the weight of the fluid column of height Δh and cross‑section A, giving ΔP = ρgΔh.
Integrating from the free surface (where pressure equals atmospheric pressure P₀) yields P = P₀ + ρgh.
This linear relationship explains why dams are thicker at the base and why divers feel more pressure deeper down.
Pascal’s law follows: an external pressure applied to a confined fluid is transmitted undiminished to every part of the fluid and the container walls.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “pressure is measured in newtons”) reveals the misconception that pressure and force are the same quantity, confusing a scalar (pressure) with a vector (force).
remember: State the SI unit of pressure and write its expression in base units.
A rectangular tank 2 m wide, 3 m long, and 1.5 m deep is filled with water (ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³). Calculate the gauge pressure at the bottom of the tank. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻².
Explain why a hydraulic lift can raise a heavy car with a small input force. Use Pascal’s law in your answer.

cards.title: Viscosity (η) is the internal friction of a fluid that opposes the relative…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Viscosity (η) is the internal friction of a fluid that opposes the relative motion of its layers. When a fluid flows, adjacent layers move with different velocities; the faster layer tries to drag the slower one forward, while the slower layer exerts a backward drag. The tangential force per unit area required to maintain a unit velocity gradient between the layers is defined as shear stress (τ). Newton’s law of viscous flow states that τ is directly proportional to the velocity gradient (dv/dy): τ = η (dv/dy). Thus, η = τ / (dv/dy). The SI unit of viscosity is the pascal‑second (Pa·s), equivalent to N·s·m⁻². Viscosity depends on temperature: for liquids it decreases with rising temperature (reduced intermolecular cohesion), whereas for gases it increases (greater momentum transfer). It also depends on the nature of the fluid (e.g., honey > water > air). Viscosity is a scalar quantity; it has no direction but characterizes the fluid’s resistance to shear deformation. Understanding viscosity bridges the concepts of pressure (force normal to a surface) and surface tension (force along a surface), completing the picture of mechanical properties of fluids.
steps: Viscosity quantifies a fluid’s internal resistance to flow, arising from momentum transfer between adjacent layers.

Here is why: when a fluid is sheared, each layer exerts a drag on its neighbour; the magnitude of this drag per unit area is the shear stress, and the proportionality constant linking stress to the rate of deformation…

First, consider two large parallel plates of area A separated by a thin liquid layer of thickness L. If the top plate moves with speed v while the bottom plate stays fixed, the fluid velocity varies linearly from 0 at…
The force F needed to keep the top plate moving at constant speed equals the shear stress times the area: F = τA.
Substituting τ = η(dv/dy) yields F = ηA(v/L), which rearranges to η = FL/(Av).
This shows that viscosity is the ratio of the applied force times plate separation to the product of area and relative speed.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “viscosity is measured in kilograms per cubic metre”) reveals the misconception that viscosity is a density‑type property, confusing mass per volume with resistance to shear.
remember: State the definition of viscosity and give its SI unit with symbol.
Explain why the viscosity of a liquid generally decreases with increasing temperature, using molecular reasoning.
A student claims that “the viscosity of gases increases with temperature because gas molecules become heavier.” Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Surface tension (γ) is the force per unit length acting tangentially to the…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Surface tension (γ) is the force per unit length acting tangentially to the liquid surface, or equivalently the surface energy per unit area. SI unit: newton per metre (N m⁻¹) or joule per square metre (J m⁻²). For a liquid film with two surfaces, the total force F = 2γL where L is the length of the movable side. The excess pressure inside a spherical liquid drop is ΔP = 2γ/R; inside a soap bubble (two surfaces) ΔP = 4γ/R. Capillary rise in a tube of radius r is h = 2γ cosθ/(ρ g r), where θ is the contact angle, ρ the liquid density and g the acceleration due to gravity. Surface tension decreases with temperature because increased molecular kinetic energy weakens cohesive forces. It is a scalar quantity, independent of the shape of the surface, and is measured by methods such as the capillary‑rise, drop‑weight, or ring‑detachment techniques.
steps: Surface tension arises because molecules at a liquid’s surface experience a net inward pull from neighbours below and beside them, creating a contractile “skin” that minimises surface area.
Here is why: the cohesive forces are unbalanced at the interface, so the surface behaves as if it were under tension.
First, consider a rectangular wire frame with a movable side of length L dipped in soap solution; the film pulls the side with force F = 2γL (two surfaces).
This directly yields γ = F/(2L).
Second, for a spherical liquid drop of radius R, the inward surface‑tension force 2πRγ balances the outward pressure force ΔP·πR², giving ΔP = 2γ/R.
A soap bubble has two surfaces, so the balance becomes 4πRγ = ΔP·πR² → ΔP = 4γ/R.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “surface tension is pressure inside a bubble”) reveals the misconception that surface tension is a bulk pressure rather than a surface‑specific force.
remember: State the definition of surface tension and its SI unit.
Explain why a steel needle can float on water despite being denser than water.
Compare the surface tension of water (≈0.072 N m⁻¹ at 20 °C) and mercury (≈0.465 N m⁻¹ at 20 °C) and explain the difference in terms of intermolecular forces.

cards.title: Bernoulli's theorem states that for an incompressible…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Bernoulli's theorem states that for an incompressible, non‑viscous fluid in steady flow along a streamline, the total mechanical energy per unit volume — pressure energy (P), kinetic energy per unit volume (½ρv²), and gravitational potential energy per unit volume (ρgh) — remains constant. Mathematically, P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant. The theorem follows from the work‑energy principle applied to a fluid element moving between two points. It connects pressure (node), density, velocity, and height, and assumes no energy loss due to viscosity (node) or turbulence. Applications include the Venturi meter (pressure drop measures flow rate), atomizers (high‑speed air lowers pressure to draw liquid), and aerofoil lift (faster flow over the upper surface creates lower pressure). The theorem is limited to ideal fluids; real fluids require correction terms for viscous dissipation and compressibility, which are treated in higher‑level fluid dynamics.
steps: Bernoulli's theorem is the statement that the total mechanical energy per unit volume of an ideal fluid remains constant along a streamline.
Here is why: the work done by pressure forces on a fluid element equals the change in its kinetic and potential energy, provided no energy is lost to viscosity or turbulence.
First, consider a fluid element moving from point 1 to point 2 in a horizontal pipe of varying cross‑section.
The pressure forces at the two ends do net work P₁V – P₂V, where V is the element’s volume.
This work changes the element’s kinetic energy from ½ρVv₁² to ½ρVv₂².
Equating work to kinetic‑energy change gives P₁ + ½ρv₁² = P₂ + ½ρv₂².
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., writing P + ρv² + ρgh = constant) reveals the misconception that kinetic energy per unit volume is ρv² instead of ½ρv², confusing energy with momentum flux.
remember: State Bernoulli's equation for an incompressible, non‑viscous fluid in steady flow along a streamline, defining each symbol and its SI unit.
A horizontal pipe narrows from cross‑sectional area A₁ to A₂ =….
Evaluate the claim: “In a Venturi meter, the pressure at the throat is higher than at the inlet because the fluid is compressed.” Use Bernoulli’s theorem to justify your answer.

cards.title: Heat (symbol Q) is the transfer of thermal energy between two systems or…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Heat (symbol Q) is the transfer of thermal energy between two systems or between a system and its surroundings due solely to a temperature difference. It is measured in joules (J) in the SI system; the older calorie (cal) is still used in some contexts where 1 cal = 4.184 J. Heat is not a property possessed by a body; it is a process quantity that appears only when energy crosses a boundary. When heat flows into a body, its internal energy increases, which may raise its temperature or change its phase, depending on the body’s specific heat capacity (c) and latent heat (L). The relationship for a temperature change without phase change is given by Q = mcΔθ, where m is mass (kg), c is specific heat capacity (J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹), and Δθ is the temperature change (K or °C). Heat flows spontaneously from the hotter body to the colder one until thermal equilibrium is reached, at which point the net heat exchange is zero.
steps: Heat is energy in transit that appears only when there is a temperature difference.
Consider a steel spoon left in a pot of boiling water.
The spoon’s end that is in the water becomes hot, while the handle remains cooler.
After a minute, the whole spoon feels warm.
This observation shows that energy has moved from the hot water to the cooler spoon until their temperatures equalised.
Here is why: 1.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “calorie, symbol cal”) reveals the misconception that heat has a unique unit separate from energy, ignoring that the calorie is a non‑SI unit and that heat, like all energy, is measured in joules.
remember: State the SI unit of heat and its symbol.
Two identical metal blocks are at 300 K each and are placed in contact. Will there be a net flow of heat between them? Explain.
A student claims that “heat is a substance that flows into a body and makes it hotter.” Evaluate this statement.

cards.title: Temperature is a scalar thermodynamic quantity that quantifies the average…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Temperature is a scalar thermodynamic quantity that quantifies the average kinetic energy of the microscopic particles (atoms, molecules) in a system. It determines the direction of spontaneous heat flow: heat moves from a body at higher temperature to one at lower temperature until thermal equilibrium is reached. The SI unit of thermodynamic temperature is the kelvin (K), defined by fixing the numerical value of the Boltzmann constant k = 1.380649 × 10⁻²³ J·K⁻¹. The Celsius scale (°C) is related to kelvin by T(°C) = T(K) − 273.15, with 0 °C defined as the ice point of water at standard atmospheric pressure. The Fahrenheit scale (°F) uses T(°F) = T(°C) × 9/5 + 32. Absolute zero (0 K = −273.15 °C) is the theoretical lower limit where all classical motion ceases. Temperature is an intensive property; it does not depend on the amount of substance. It is measured using thermometers based on thermal expansion (mercury, alcohol), electrical resistance (platinum resistance thermometer), thermoelectric effect (thermocouple), or radiation (pyrometer). The concept of temperature underpins the zeroth law of thermodynamics, which establishes thermal equilibrium as an equivalence relation and allows the definition of temperature scales.
steps: Temperature is the quantitative measure of how hot or cold a body is, rooted in the average kinetic energy of its constituent particles.
Here is why: temperature determines the direction of heat flow, it is an intensive property independent of mass, and it can be expressed on absolute (kelvin) or relative (Celsius, Fahrenheit) scales.
First, recall from the previous node that heat is energy transferred due to a temperature difference; temperature itself is not energy but a parameter that tells us which way that energy will move.
Second, the kelvin scale is absolute because its zero corresponds to the complete cessation of classical particle motion, making it the natural scale for thermodynamic equations.
Third, the Celsius scale is a shifted kelvin scale where 0 °C is the ice point of water at 1 atm, and 100 °C is the steam point; the conversion T(K) = T(°C) + 273.15 is exact.
Fourth, the Fahrenheit scale, still used in some contexts, relates by T(°F) = T(°C) × 9/5 + 32.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "the SI unit is degree Celsius") reveals the misconception that Celsius is an SI base unit — it is a derived unit for temperature difference, not the base unit for thermodynamic temperature.
remember: What is the SI unit of thermodynamic temperature and how is it defined in the current SI system.
Explain why temperature is considered an intensive property while heat is extensive.
A student claims that a temperature of −10 °C is twice as cold as −5 °C. Evaluate this statement using the Kelvin scale.

cards.title: Specific heat capacity
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Specific heat capacity (symbol c, SI unit J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) of a substance is defined as the heat energy Q required to raise the temperature of a unit mass m of that substance by a unit temperature change ΔT, provided no phase change occurs: c = (Q)/(m\,Δ T) It is an intensive property — independent of the amount of substance — and varies with temperature and pressure, though for most solids and liquids over modest ranges it is treated as constant. The molar specific heat Cₘ (J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹) relates to c by Cₘ = c M, where M is the molar mass (kg mol⁻¹). Two common specific heats are defined for gases: cᵥ (constant volume) and cₚ (constant pressure), linked by Mayer’s relation cₚ – cᵥ = R/M. Specific heat connects the macroscopic heat transfer Q to the microscopic kinetic energy of particles; a larger c means more energy is stored per degree of temperature rise. It is distinct from latent heat (node), which governs phase changes at constant temperature.
steps: Specific heat capacity quantifies how much heat a material stores per kilogram per kelvin, making it the key link between heat transfer and temperature change.
Here is why: the same amount of heat raises the temperature of a low‑c substance (e.g., copper) far more than a high‑c substance (e.g., water).
Consider a 0.5 kg copper block (c ≈ 385 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) and 0.5 kg water (c ≈ 4186 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) each receiving 10 kJ of heat.

The copper’s temperature rises by ΔT = Q/(mc) ≈ 10 000/(0.5×385) ≈ 52 K, while water rises only ≈ 4.8 K. This huge difference explains why a copper kadhai heats oil quickly, yet a water‑filled earthen pot keeps milk…
Next, connect to molar specific heat: for water (M = 0.018 kg mol⁻¹), Cₘ = c M ≈ 75.3 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, a value that appears in thermodynamic tables.
For gases, the distinction between cᵥ and cₚ matters because at constant pressure the gas does work expanding, so more heat is needed for the same ΔT.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “J kg⁻¹ °C⁻¹” or “cal g⁻¹ K⁻¹”) reveals the misconception that the temperature unit in the denominator must be Celsius — while numerically ΔT in °C equals ΔT in K, the SI base unit for thermodynamic temperature is kelvin, so the correct…
remember: State the SI unit of specific heat capacity and write its dimensional formula.
A 200 g aluminium block (c = 900 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) is heated from 25 °C to 75 °C. Calculate the heat supplied.
Two identical calorimeters contain 100 g water at 20 °C and 100 g oil (c = 2000 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) at 80….

cards.title: Latent heat (symbol L) is the amount of heat energy Q required to change the…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Latent heat (symbol L) is the amount of heat energy Q required to change the phase of a unit mass m of a substance at constant temperature and pressure. It is defined by L = Q/m (SI unit: joule per kilogram, J kg⁻¹). Two principal values are used: specific latent heat of fusion (L_f) for solid ↔ liquid transition, and specific latent heat of vaporisation (L_v) for liquid ↔ gas transition. During a phase change the temperature remains constant because the supplied energy increases the potential energy of intermolecular bonds rather than the kinetic energy of molecules. The total heat for a phase change of mass m is Q = m L. Latent heat is a material property; for water at 1 atm, L_f ≈ 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹ and L_v ≈ 2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹. It is distinct from specific heat capacity (c), which relates heat to temperature change (Q = mcΔT). Latent heat values are tabulated for pure substances and are essential in calorimetry, meteorology, and engineering design of refrigeration and power cycles.
steps: Latent heat is the energy a substance absorbs or releases during a phase change at constant temperature, and it is calculated by Q = mL. Here is why: when you heat ice at 0 °C, the temperature does not rise until all…
The heat you supply goes into overcoming the hydrogen‑bond network that holds water molecules in a rigid lattice, increasing their potential energy.
Only after the last crystal disappears does the temperature climb again.
The same principle applies when water boils at 100 °C: energy breaks intermolecular forces to create vapour, not to speed molecules up. Consider a practical Indian kitchen example: a pressure cooker.
Water inside reaches 100 °C (or higher under pressure) and turns to steam.
The steam carries a huge amount of latent heat (L_v ≈ 2.26 MJ kg⁻¹).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “the thermometer is faulty”) reveals the misconception that temperature must always rise when heat is added — ignoring the distinction between kinetic and potential energy at the molecular level.
remember: Define latent heat and give its SI unit.
Why does the temperature of a substance remain constant during a phase change even though heat is continuously supplied.
Distinguish between specific latent heat of fusion and specific latent heat of vaporisation.

cards.title: Heat conduction is the transfer of thermal energy through a material due to a…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Heat conduction is the transfer of thermal energy through a material due to a temperature gradient, without bulk motion of the material. In steady state, the rate of heat flow Q (power) through a uniform slab is given by Fourier’s law: Q = -k A (dT)/(dx), where k is the thermal conductivity (SI unit W m⁻¹ K⁻¹), A the cross‑sectional area (m²), and (dT)/(dx) the temperature gradient (K m⁻¹). For a slab of thickness L with constant k, this simplifies to Q = k A (Δ T)/(L). Thermal resistance R = (L)/(kA) (K W⁻¹) quantifies opposition to heat flow; resistances add in series and reciprocals add in parallel. Conduction in cylinders and spheres follows analogous logarithmic or inverse‑radius formulas. This node focuses on steady‑state conduction in simple geometries; transient effects, convection, and radiation are treated in sibling nodes.
steps: The central idea is that heat flows from hot to cold through a material at a rate proportional to the temperature difference, the cross‑sectional area, and the material’s thermal conductivity, and inversely proportional…

Here is why: (1) At the microscopic level, conduction in solids occurs via lattice vibrations (phonons) and free electrons; metals have many free electrons, giving high k. (2) Fourier’s law quantifies this macroscopic…
(3) Thermal resistance R = L/(kA) lets us treat conduction like an electrical circuit, making composite walls easy to analyse.
(4) For a hollow cylinder, the area changes with radius, leading to a logarithmic dependence: Q = (2π k L Δ T)/( (r_2/r_1)).
(5) In a sphere, Q = (4π k r_1 r_2 Δ T)/(r_2 - r_1).
Consider a copper rod (k = 385 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹) of length 0.5 m and cross‑section 2 cm² joining a 100 °C reservoir to a 30 °C sink.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “unit is J m⁻¹ K⁻¹”) reveals the misconception that thermal conductivity is an energy quantity rather than a power‑per‑gradient quantity, confusing heat with heat flow rate.
remember: State Fourier’s law of heat conduction and give the SI unit of thermal conductivity.
Why does a metal spoon feel colder than a wooden spoon when both are at room temperature.
A student claims that increasing the cross‑sectional area of a rod always increases the heat current for a given temperature difference. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Convection is the mode of heat transfer that occurs through the bulk motion of…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Convection is the mode of heat transfer that occurs through the bulk motion of a fluid (liquid or gas) driven by temperature‑induced density differences (natural convection) or by an external agency such as a fan or pump (forced convection). In natural convection, a temperature gradient creates a buoyancy force: warmer fluid expands, becomes less dense, and rises; cooler, denser fluid descends, establishing a continuous circulation loop. The rate of convective heat transfer is quantified by Newton’s law of cooling for convection: Q = h A (T_s - T_f), where Q is the heat transfer rate, h the convective heat‑transfer coefficient, A the surface area, T_s the surface temperature, and T_f the bulk fluid temperature. The coefficient h depends on fluid properties (density, viscosity, thermal conductivity, specific heat), flow geometry, and flow regime (laminar or turbulent). Dimensionless groups — Grashof number (Gr), Reynolds number (Re), Prandtl number (Pr), and Nusselt number (Nu) — correlate these variables; for example, Nu = f(Gr, Pr) for natural convection and Nu = f(Re, Pr) for forced convection. Convection links the thermal properties of the fluid (covered in earlier nodes on specific heat and thermal conductivity) with fluid mechanics concepts (pressure, viscosity) and precedes radiation, the third heat‑transfer mode.
steps: Convection transfers heat by moving the fluid itself, unlike conduction where energy passes through stationary matter.
Here is why: the fluid’s density changes with temperature, creating buoyancy forces that set up circulation (natural convection), or an external device forces the flow (forced convection).
Consider a vertical hot plate in air: air adjacent to the plate warms, expands, and rises along the surface, drawing cooler air from the sides — this is a natural convection boundary layer.
The heat‑transfer rate is Q = h A (T_s - T_f).
The coefficient h is not a material constant; it emerges from the flow and thermal fields.
To estimate h, we use dimensionless groups.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., “convection is heat transfer through a solid”) reveals the misconception that convection and conduction are the same mechanism — confusing stationary‑medium diffusion with fluid advection.
remember: Define convection and state the two main types.
Explain why natural convection occurs in a fluid heated from below.
A student claims that convection cannot occur in a microgravity environment. Evaluate this claim.

cards.title: Thermal radiation is the emission of electromagnetic waves due to the…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Thermal radiation is the emission of electromagnetic waves due to the temperature of a body. Every object at a temperature above 0 K emits a continuous spectrum of radiation whose spectral distribution depends only on its temperature and surface properties. A perfect blackbody absorbs all incident radiation (absorptivity α = 1) and emits the maximum possible radiation for a given temperature.
